aaron: Moses’ brother and Israel’s first high priest. In the books of Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers, Aaron was Moses’ spokesman and assistant during the Israelites’ exodus from Egypt.
aaronites: Collective name for the priests who descended from Aaron through his sons Eleazar and Ithamar. The term is used twice in the KJV to refer to the 3,700 men who supported David against Saul and of whom Zadok later became leader.
aaron's rod: Staff belonging to Moses’ brother, Aaron, symbolizing the two brothers’ authority in Israel. When the Israelites were wandering in the wilderness, a threat against Moses and Aaron’s leadership was led by Korah, Dathan, and Abiram.
ab: Month in the Hebrew calendar, about mid-July to mid-August.
abaddon: Hebrew word that means “place of destruction.” The word occurs six times in the OT, generally referring to the place of the dead.
abagtha: One of the seven eunuchs commanded by King Ahasuerus to bring Queen Vashti to his drunken party.
abana: Syrian river (modern Barada) running through the city of Damascus.
abarim: Mountainous area located east of the Jordan River and the Dead Sea, and extending northward from the plains of Moab.
abba: Aramaic word for “father,” which is applied to God in Mark 14:36; Romans 8:15; and Galatians 4:6. The name expresses a very intimate and inseparable relationship between Christ and the Father and between believers (children) and God (Father).
abdeel: Shelemiah’s father. Shelemiah was an officer sent by King Jehoiakim of Judah to arrest Jeremiah and Baruch after the king had read and burned their prophetic scroll.
abdi: 1. Member of the Merari clan of Levites.
abdiel: Guni’s son and father of Ahi. Ahi was a clan leader in Gad’s tribe during the reigns of King Jotham of Judah and King Jeroboam II of Israel.
abdon (person): 1. Hillel’s son who judged Israel for eight years.
abdon (place): One of four cities in Asher’s territory given to the Levites after the conquest of Canaan, the Promised Land. Abdon is probably the same as Ebron.
abednego: One of Daniel’s three friends who was sentenced to death by Nebuchadnezzar but was protected in the fiery furnace by an angel.
abel (person): Second male child of Adam and Eve. The name is probably related to Sumerian and Akkadian words meaning “son” and was thus used as a generic term for the human race.
abel (place): Fortified border city in upper Galilee to which King David’s general Joab pursued the rebel Sheba. After a wise woman of the city negotiated with Joab, the citizens executed Sheba and threw his head over the wall.
abel-beth-maacah (maachah): Alternate name for Abel, a fortified city in upper Galilee in 1 Kings 15:20 and 2 Kings 15:29. It was also called Abel of Beth-Maacah (Maachah) in 2 Sm 20:14-15.
abel-keramim: City taken by Jephthah the Israelite judge when he conquered the Ammonites. It was located south of the Jabbok River.
abel-maim: Alternate name for Abel, a fortified city in upper Galilee, in 2 Chronicles 16:4.
abel-meholah: Birthplace of the prophet Elisha. Here Elijah found Elisha plowing and threw his coat over Elisha’s shoulders, symbolizing God’s call to Elisha to become a prophet.
abel-mizraim: Alternate name for Atad, a place in Canaan, in Genesis 50:11.
abel-shittim: Alternate name for Shittim, a place on the plains of Moab, in Numbers 33:49.
abez: KJV form of Ebez, a place in Issachar’s territory, in Joshua 19:20.
abi: Shortened form of Abijah, the name of the mother of Judah’s King Hezekiah.
abia: 1. KJV rendering of Abijam, Rehoboam’s son and king of Judah, in 1 Chronicles 3:10 and Matthew 1:7.
abiah: 1. KJV translation for Abijah, Samuel’s son, in 1 Samuel 8:2 and 1 Chronicles 6:28.
abi-albon: Alternate name of Abiel in 2 Samuel 23:31.
abiasaph: Alternate form of Ebiasaph, a descendant of Korah, in Exodus 6:24.
abiathar: One of two high priests during the reign of King David. The other high priest was Zadok, who evidently was appointed by David after his conquest of Jerusalem.
abib: Canaanite name of the Hebrew month Nisan, about mid-March to mid-April.
abida: One of Midian’s sons. Midian was Abraham’s son by his concubine Keturah.
abidan: Gideoni’s son and leader of Benjamin’s tribe when the Israelites were wandering in the Sinai wilderness after their escape from Egypt. As leader, he presented his tribe’s offering at the consecration of the tabernacle.
abiel: 1. Father of Kish and Ner and grandfather of King Saul, according to 1 Samuel 9:1 and 14:51.
abigail: 1. Nabal’s wife, who later became the wife of David.
abigal: RSV rendering of Abigail, David’s sister, in 2 Samuel 17:25.
abihail: Name used for both men and women in the OT.
abihu: Second son of Aaron and Elisheba. Abihu and his brother Nadab joined Moses, Aaron, and the 70 elders of Israel in worshiping the glory of God on Mt Sinai.
abihud: One of Bela’s nine sons. Abihud should not be confused with the Abiud of Matthew’s genealogy of Christ in the NT.
abijah: 1. Samuel’s second son who, with his older brother, Joel, was a corrupt judge in Beersheba.
abijam: Rehoboam’s son and successor as king of Judah, 913–910 BC (1 Chr 3:10; alternately called “Abijah” in 2 Chr 11:18-22; 12:16; 13:1-22; 14:1). A major focus of Abijam’s reign was his war with King Jeroboam I of Israel.
abilene: Region on the east side of the Anti-Lebanon Mountains in Syria. The district took its name from the capital city of Abila, located about 18 miles (29 kilometers) from Damascus.
abimael: One of the many sons or descendants of Joktan, and thus a descendant of Shem.
abimelech: Royal title for Philistine rulers, similar to the designation “pharaoh” among the Egyptians and “agag” among the Amalekites.
abinadab: 1. Resident of Kiriath-jearim to whose home the ark of God was brought on its return by the Philistines.
abinoam: Barak’s father. Barak was the companion of Deborah, an Israelite judge, in the war against the Canaanites.
abishag: Beautiful young woman from Shunem who was appointed to care for David during his last days. After David’s death, Adonijah asked permission from his half brother King Solomon to marry Abishag.
abishai: David’s nephew, son of Zeruiah (by an unnamed father) and brother of Joab and Asahel. Abishai volunteered to accompany David to Saul’s camp one night and would have killed the sleeping Saul if David had not restrained him.
abishalom: Alternate name for Absalom, King David’s son, in 1 Kings 15:2, 10.
abishua: 1. Aaron’s great-grandson, son of Phinehas and ancestor of Ezra.
abishur: Shammai’s son and the father of Ahban and Molid from Judah’s tribe. Abishur’s wife was Abihail.
abital: Mother of King David’s fifth son, Shephatiah.
abitub: Son of Shaharaim and Hushim from Benjamin’s tribe.
abiud: Individual listed in Matthew’s genealogy of Christ in the NT as Eliakim’s father.
abner: Ner’s son and Saul’s cousin. Abner was commander of Saul’s army.
abomination: Repugnant or detestable act, person, or thing. The idea of abomination derives from the specific demands God’s holiness makes upon his people.
abraham: One of the Bible’s most significant personalities, whom God called from the city of Ur to become patriarch of God’s own people.
abron: Brook or wadi mentioned in the book of Judith, located on the route of attack of Nebuchadnezzar’s general, Holofernes (2:24). Some early commentators identified it with the biblical Jabbok.
abronah: Place near Elath where the Israelites camped on their journey from Egypt to Canaan.
absalom: Son of King David and his wife Maacah. The name is also spelled Abishalom.
abubus: Ptolemy’s father. Ptolemy was a military governor of Jericho who treacherously killed his father-in-law Simon Maccabeus and two of Simon’s sons in 134 BC.
acacia: Palestinian wood used in the construction of the ark of the covenant.
acbor: 1. Father of the Edomite king Baal-hanan before the establishment of Israel’s monarchy.
accad: One of the three cities (Babel, Erech, and Accad, RSV) in the plains between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers said to have been founded by Nimrod.
accho, acco: Major Palestinian port city from the earliest Canaanite period. The only clear OT reference to Acco is the statement that at the time of Israel’s conquest of Canaan, Asher’s tribe failed to drive out its inhabitants.
aceldama: KJV form of Akeldama, meaning “Field of Blood,” in Acts 1:19.
achaia: Name generally used in NT times to refer to the entire Greek peninsula south of Thessalonica.
achaicus: Early Christian convert in Corinth. Achaicus, Stephanas, and Fortunatus were visiting Paul in Ephesus when he wrote 1 Corinthians.
achan, achar: Member of Judah’s tribe who kept some of the spoils from the Israelite victory at Jericho in violation of Joshua’s order and God’s command. A subsequent Israelite defeat at Ai, a weaker city than Jericho, revealed God’s anger to Joshua.
achaz: KJV form of Ahaz, Judah’s king, in Matthew 1:9.
achim: Descendant of Zerubbabel, listed in the NT as an ancestor of Jesus.
achior: The book of Judith introduces Achior as “leader of all the Ammonites” (5:5). The main part of Judith 5 is devoted to Achior’s version of the history of Israel and culminates in his warning Holofernes that God would protect Israel.
achish: King of the Philistine city of Gath. Although David had killed Goliath, Gath’s champion, David later fled from Saul to Achish’s court.
achmetha: KJV form of Ecbatana, a Persian city, in Ezra 6:2.
achor: Valley that received its name when Achan, the troubler of Israel, was stoned and burned there (Jos 7:24-26; cf. 1 Chr 2:7). Achor was on the northern boundary of Judah’s tribal allotment.
achsa, achsah: Caleb’s daughter. Othniel, Caleb’s nephew, accepted his uncle’s challenge to capture Kiriath-sepher in order to marry Achsah.
achshaph: Canaanite royal city in Joshua’s time. Its king joined an alliance led by Jabin, king of Hazor, against Israel in a battle at the springs of Merom.
acra: Citadel of Jerusalem during the Seleucid and Hasmonean periods. The citadel was located on a high point near the temple.
acraba: Site where a contingent of the Edomite-Ammonite division of Holofernes’ army was stationed during the siege of Bethulia. Acraba was probably located about 10 miles (16 kilometers) southeast of Shechem, modern Nablus.
acre: Measure of an area of land. Literally, the Hebrew word means “yoke” and probably refers to the amount of land a yoke of oxen could plow in a day.
acrocorinth: Massive, precipitous hilltop 1,886 feet (575 meters) above sea level to the south of the ancient city of Corinth.
acropolis: This term is a combination of the Greek akros (“highest”) polis (“city”), which originally applied to any fortified natural stronghold or citadel in ancient Greece. The typical acropolis was built on a hill as a place of refuge.
acrostic: Poetic composition in which the first letters of successive lines or stanzas spell out the alphabet, a word, or a motto.
acsah: Caleb’s daughter. Othniel, Caleb’s nephew, accepted his uncle’s challenge to capture Kiriath-sepher in order to marry Achsah.
acshaph: Canaanite royal city in Joshua’s time. Its king joined an alliance led by Jabin, king of Hazor, against Israel in a battle at the springs of Merom.
acts of the apostles, book of the: Acts of the Apostles, Book of the
NT book presenting the history of the early church and written as a sequel to the Gospel of Luke. In the arrangement of the NT books, Acts comes after the four Gospels and before the Epistles.
adadah: One of 30 cities assigned to Judah’s tribe in the Negev, or southern desert region. A Greek textual variant in the Septuagint is Ararah, which appears as “Aroer” in 1 Samuel 30:28.
adah: 1. One of Lamech’s two wives, and mother of two sons, Jabal and Jubal.
adalia: Fifth of Haman’s ten sons, all of whom were killed with their father when his plot to destroy the Jews was foiled.
adam (person): First man and father of the human race. Adam’s role in biblical history is important not only in OT considerations but also in understanding the meaning of salvation and the person and work of Jesus Christ.
adam (place): City on the Jordan River. When Joshua led the Israelites across the river, the stretch of riverbed from this city to the Dead Sea dried up miraculously so the people could cross on dry land.
adam, the second: Analogy that compares and contrasts the first man with the one he is seen to typify, the Lord Jesus Christ.
adamah: One of the 19 fortified cities belonging to Naphtali’s tribe. It is possibly identified with Qarn Hattin.
adami, adami-nekeb: Names of a city located near the southern border of Naphtali’s territory, although the KJV lists it as two cities. Adami-nekeb is usually identified as modern Khirbet ed-Damiyeh.
adar (month): Babylonian name for a Hebrew month.
adar (place): KJV form of Addar in Joshua 15:3.
adasa: 1. Town mentioned only in the period of the Maccabean revolt.
addan: Persian city from which Israelite exiles returned with Ezra to Jerusalem, probably named after a Babylonian god called Addu. The exiles returning from this city were unable to give evidence of their Jewish descent, having lost their genealogical credentials.
addar (person): Alternate name for Ard, one of Benjamin’s descendants, in 1 Chronicles 8:3.
addar (place): Town on Judah’s southwest border, northwest of Kadesh-barnea. The towns Hezron and Addar were called Hazar-addar.
adder: Any of several kinds of poisonous and nonpoisonous snakes, especially the common viper of Europe and Asia.
addi: 1. One whose descendants obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce their pagan wives after the exile.
addon: Alternate form of Addan, a place in Babylonia, in Nehemiah 7:61.
addus: One of Solomon’s servants. His descendants were among those who returned with Zerubbabel from the exile.
ader: KJV form of Eder, Beriah’s son, in 1 Chronicles 8:15.
adida: Town fortified by Simon Maccabeus. Adida was in the foothills of southern Judea four miles (6.4 kilometers) east of Lydda between the Mediterranean coastal plain and the central highlands.
adiel: 1. Prince of Simeon’s tribe who led some Simeonites to the entrance of Gedor to find pasture for their flocks.
adin: 1. Ancestor of a group of people who returned to Judah with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile.
adina: Shiza’s son and a warrior among David’s mighty men who were known as “the thirty”.
adino: Possibly another name for Josheb-basshebeth, one of the top three of David’s military heroes; he was also called Jashobeam.
adithaim: Town in the lowlands of Judah’s territory.
adlai: Father of Shaphat, the chief herdsman of the king’s cattle in the valleys during David’s reign.
admah: City associated with Sodom, Gomorrah, and Zeboiim and thus probably destroyed in God’s judgment of Sodom and Gomorrah (Dt 29:23; not specifically mentioned in Gn 19:28-29).
admatha: One of seven counselors of King Ahasuerus. The king’s counselors advised him to banish Queen Vashti for refusing his summons to appear at a drunken party.
admin: Ancestor of Jesus mentioned in Luke’s genealogy (3:33).
adna: 1. Descendant of Pahath-moab who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile.
adnah: 1. Captain from Manasseh’s tribe who left Saul to join David’s army at Ziklag.
adonai: Divine name translated as “Lord” signifying honor, majesty, and sovereignty.
adoni-bezek: Title of the Canaanite king of Bezek, a city in northern Palestine. Soon after Joshua’s death, the tribes of Judah and Simeon defeated Adoni-bezek and amputated his thumbs and big toes.
adonijah: 1. David’s fourth son, born to Haggith at Hebron.
adonikam: Head of a family whose descendants returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile. Ezra states the number of Adonikam’s family returning as 666; Nehemiah gives the number as 667 (as does 1 Esd 5:14), probably a scribal variation.
adoniram: Important official in Israel during the reigns of David, Solomon, and Rehoboam. Adoniram is also referred to as Adoram, possibly a contraction of his name, and as Hadoram.
adoni-zedek: Amorite king of Jerusalem at the time of the Israelite conquest of the Promised Land. A battle between the Amorites and Israelites for control of Gibeon was the occasion on which Joshua prayed for the sun to stand still.
adoption: Theologically, the act of God by which believers become members of “God’s family” with all the privileges and obligations of family membership. “Sons of God,” a common KJV expression, includes individuals of both sexes numbered among God’s children.
adoraim: City in the southern kingdom of Judah fortified by King Rehoboam. Adoraim and Mareshah later became the two principal cities of Idumea.
adoram: Alternate spelling of Adoniram in 2 Samuel 20:24 and 1 Kings 12:18.
adrammelech: 1. Son of the Assyrian monarch Sennacherib.
adramyttium: Ancient port city in Asia Minor. En route to Rome as a prisoner, Paul embarked on a ship having Adramyttium as its home port.
adria: The Adriatic Sea, an arm of the Mediterranean Sea bordered by Italy on the west and by Greece, Albania, and Yugoslavia on the east. The apostle Paul was tossed about in a ship for 14 days in a violent storm on this body of water.
adriel: Barzillai’s son, to whom Saul gave his daughter Merab in marriage, although she had been promised to David. King David later handed over Adriel’s five sons to the Gibeonites to execute in vengeance against Saul’s family.
adullam, adullamite: Old Canaanite city between Lachish and Hebron, as well as a cave region nearby. The first biblical mention of the city is in the word “Adullamite” (someone from Adullam), used of Hirah, a friend of Judah.
adultery: A breach of the unity of marriage. It describes any act of sexual intercourse between a married woman and a man other than her husband, and all sexual intercourse involving a married man and a woman other than his wife.
adummim: Pass extending from the hill country into the Jordan Valley, which formed part of Judah’s northern border. It is a reference point establishing the location of Geliloth on Benjamin’s southern border.
advent of christ: Literally, “in flesh”; theologically, the doctrine that in Jesus of Nazareth God took on human flesh and became the God-man.
adversary: Any foe, opponent, or enemy of God and his people. The apostle Peter’s description of the devil as “your adversary” (1 Pt 5:8, KJV) has led to use of “the adversary” as a reference to Satan in literature and popular speech.
advocate: Translation for the Greek term parakletos, a term used for the Holy Spirit in John’s Gospel and for Jesus in 1 John 2:1.
aegean sea: Extension of the Mediterranean Sea between Greece on the west and north and Turkey on the east. The large island of Crete is its traditional southern limit.
aeneas: Bedridden paralytic in Lydda who was miraculously healed by the apostle Peter.
aenon: Small town near the Jordan River. Scholars think Aenon may have been about 30 miles (48 kilometers) north of the Dead Sea.
aeon: Greek word for a long period of time or age, from which comes the English word “eon.” See Age.
aesora: Town alerted to prepare for the invasion of Holofernes, Nebuchadnezzar’s chief general. Most ancient translators omitted this city and mentioned only Samaria, Jericho, and sometimes Beth-horon.
affliction: Anything causing pain or distress; calamity. From the biblical viewpoint, affliction began with the entrance of sin into the world.
agabus: Prophet of NT times who made two predictions referred to in the book of Acts. His prophecy of a severe famine was fulfilled in the time of Claudius.
agag: 1. Name of an Amalekite king, or perhaps a general title for their kings (like the Egyptian “pharaoh”).
agagite: Term used to describe Haman, “the enemy of all the Jews,” in the Persian court of King Ahasuerus. Agag, an Amalekite king, had been Saul’s mortal enemy.
agape: English transliteration of the NT Greek word for “love” or “love feast.” See Love.
agate: Hard, semiprecious stone, a variety of chalcedony (a kind of quartz), with striped or clouded coloring.
age: Long, but indefinite, period of time, past or future. The ages, past and future, make up the whole of time.
agee: Father of Shammah, one of the warriors among David’s mighty men who were known as “the thirty”.
agia: Jaddus’s wife, mentioned in the Apocrypha as a descendant of Barzillai the Gileadite. Her sons, who had assumed the priesthood, were excluded from serving as priests when the Jews returned from Babylon and demanded verification of priestly ancestry.
agora: Place for the buying and selling of goods in antiquity. Generally, the marketplaces of the ancient Near East would be much like the open air bazaars one can still see in any city throughout Israel, Greece, and Turkey.
agriculture: During Bible times agriculture took the same three main forms found in Palestine today. Emphasis on each of these has depended upon the social and technological status of the people.
agrippa: Name of two Roman rulers of Judea from the Herodian family line.
ague: Intense fever marked by recurring chills, common in malaria. Our English word comes from the same stem as “acute.” The “fever” can cause “your eyes to fail and your life to ebb away” (Lv 26:16, NLT).
agur: Jakeh’s son. Although not an Israelite, he wrote or collected the sayings in Proverbs 30.
ahab: 1. Eighth king of the northern kingdom of Israel, who reigned about 874–853 BC.
aharah: Alternate name for Ahiram, Benjamin’s third son, in 1 Chronicles 8:1.
ahasai: KJV form of Ahzai, the priest, in Nehemiah 11:13.
ahasbai: Eliphelet’s father. Eliphelet, from the city of Maacah, was a warrior among David’s mighty men who were known as “the thirty”.
ahasuerus: 1. Persian king better known to Western readers as Xerxes I (486–465 BC); the son and successor of Darius I (Hystaspis).
ahava: The name of the river (and possibly town) in Babylonia where Ezra added some Levites to the remnant of exiles. There he also declared a fast for the Jews to humble themselves before God and seek his protection before returning to Palestine.
ahaz: 1. King of Judah (735–715 BC) who was especially remembered for his apostasy.
ahaziah: 1. Ahab’s son, who ruled the northern kingdom of Israel for two years as its ninth king (853–852 BC).
ahban: Son of Abishur and Abihail from Judah’s tribe.
aher: Alternate name for Ahiram, Benjamin’s third son, in 1 Chronicles 7:12.
ahi: 1. Abdiel’s son, a clan leader in Gad’s tribe.
ahiam: Sharar’s son and a warrior among David’s mighty men who were known as “the thirty”.
ahian: One of Shemida’s four sons from Naphtali’s tribe.
ahiezer: 1. Ammishaddai’s son, a leader of Dan’s tribe when the Israelites were roaming in the Sinai wilderness after their escape from Egypt.
ahihud: 1. Shelomi’s son, a leader of Asher’s tribe.
ahijah: 1. Ahitub’s son who served as priest at Shiloh and had charge of the ark of the covenant at Gibeah during Saul’s last campaign.
ahikam: Shaphan’s son, an officer of the court of King Josiah of Judah. Ahikam was among the group sent to the prophetess Huldah to ask about the Book of the Law.
ahilud: Father of the court historian Jehoshaphat. Jehoshaphat served under both David and Solomon.
ahimaaz: 1. Father of Ahinoam, who was King Saul’s wife.
ahimelech: 1. A priest at Nob who aided David in his flight from Saul.
ahimoth: Elkanah’s son, a Levite in the family of Kohath.
ahinadab: Iddo’s son and one of 12 officers appointed to requisition food for King Solomon’s household. Ahinadab’s headquarters were in Mahanaim.
ahinoam: 1. Daughter of Ahimaaz and wife of King Saul.
ahira: Enan’s son and the leader of Naphtali’s tribe when the Israelites were roaming in the Sinai wilderness after their escape from Egypt. As leader he presented his tribe’s offering at the consecration of the tabernacle.
ahiram, ahiramite: Benjamin’s third son and the ancestral head of the Ahiramite clan (Nm 26:38; 1 Chr 8:1, “Aharah”). Two abbreviated forms of the name Ahiram in genealogies may be Ehi and Aher.
ahisamach: Father of the craftsman Oholiab, of Dan’s tribe. Oholiab helped construct the tabernacle and its furnishings.
ahishahar: Bilhan’s son and chief of the subclan of Jediael, of Benjamin’s tribe, in the time of King David.
ahishar: Overseer in charge of Solomon’s palace affairs.
ahithophel: King David’s trusted counselor who turned traitor and joined Absalom’s conspiracy. Ahithophel’s counsel was highly regarded, almost as though it were an oracle of God.
ahitub: 1. Member of the priestly line of Aaron’s youngest son, Ithamar.
ahlab: Canaanite city in Asher’s territory. The Israelites failed to drive out its inhabitants in their conquest of Canaan.
ahlai: 1. Sheshan’s daughter, a member of Judah’s tribe.
ahoah, ahohi, ahohite: One of Bela’s nine sons, a member of Benjamin’s tribe.
aholah: KJV form of Oholah, the symbolic name for Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, in Ezekiel 23.
aholiab: KJV form of Oholiab, a craftsman from Dan’s tribe.
aholibah: KJV form of Oholibah, the symbolic name for Jerusalem in Ezekiel 23.
aholibamah: KJV form of Oholibamah, a name associated with two members of Esau’s family.
ahuzam, ahuzzam: Son of Ashur and Naarah and a member of Judah’s tribe.
ahuzzath: Royal advisor to Abimelech of Gerar. Ahuzzath accompanied Abimelech to Beersheba to make a treaty with Isaac.
ahzai: Priest of the order of Immer. Ahzai’s descendant, Amashsai, was a leading priest in Jerusalem in Ezra’s day.
ai: Canaanite city that was settled before the time of Abraham. The name suggests a “ruin” of special significance or striking appearance.
aiah: 1. Zibeon’s son, a Horite descended from Seir.
aiath: Alternate name for Ai, the Canaanite city, in Isaiah 10:28.
aija: Alternate name for Ai, the Canaanite city, in Nehemiah 11:31.
aijalon: 1. City located in a valley 15 miles (24 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem (at modern Yalo) and originally allotted to Dan’s tribe.
aijeleth shahar: Hebrew phrase in the title of Psalm 22 (KJV), translated “according to The Hind of the Dawn” (RSV); perhaps a familiar ancient melody to which the psalm was sung.
ain: 1. City on the eastern border of Canaan, the Promised Land, northeast of the Sea of Galilee.
ajah: KJV rendering of Aiah, Zibeon’s son, in Genesis 36:24.
ajalon: KJV rendering of Aijalon in Joshua 10:12; 19:42; and 2 Chronicles 28:18.
akan: Alternate name for Jaakan, Ezer’s son, in Genesis 36:27.
akeldama: Name given to the field where Judas committed suicide after betraying Jesus; translated as “Field of Blood”.
akiba, rabbi: Jewish leader, prominent about AD 110–135. Akiba came from a humble background and began his scholarly training at the age of 40.
akim: Descendant of Zerubbabel, listed in the NT as an ancestor of Jesus.
akkad: One of the three cities (Babel, Erech, and Accad, RSV) in the plains between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers said to have been founded by Nimrod.
akkadians: Sumer was a region settled before 3500 BC in the lower part of Mesopotamia, now called Iraq. The Sumerians had a highly civilized society, developing cuneiform (a type of writing), medicine, mathematics, and astronomy.
akkub: 1. One of Elioenai’s seven sons and a distant descendant of David.
akrabattene: Place where Judas Maccabeus destroyed the strongholds of the “sons of Esau,” from which they were harassing the Jews.
akrabbim: A mountain pass or slope in southern Palestine between the southwestern tip of the Dead Sea and the wilderness of Zin.
alabaster: White or translucent stone, sometimes veined, frequently used to make vases and flasks.
alameth: KJV form of Alemeth, Becher’s son, in 1 Chronicles 7:8.
alammelech: KJV form of Allammelech in Joshua 19:26.
alamoth: Hebrew term in the title of Psalm 46 and also in 1 Chronicles 15:20.
alcimus: Treacherous high priest of the intertestamental period of Jewish history. A descendant of Aaron but not of the legitimate high-priestly family, Alcimus was declared high priest by the Syrian king Demetrius I, about 163 BC.
alema: City in Gilead from which Judas Maccabeus liberated Jews who had been surrounded by hostile Gentiles. Most authorities place it some 25 to 35 miles (40 to 55 kilometers) east of the Sea of Galilee, perhaps at modern Alma in Gilead.
alemeth (place): Levitical city in the territory of Benjamin’s tribe (1 Chr 6:60; NASB “Allemeth”); alternately called Almon in Joshua 21:18. Its site was at Khirbet ‘Almit, about five miles (8 kilometers) northeast of Jerusalem.
alexander: 1. The Macedonian conqueror, Alexander the Great (356–323 BC), whose life has influenced history and culture for more than two millennia, down to the present time.
alexander (balas) epiphanes: Pretender who claimed to be the son of Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Alexander landed at Ptolemais in 152 BC and from 150 BC onward claimed to be the king.
alexander jannaeus (janneus): Jewish ruler of the Hasmonean dynasty.
alexandra: Wife of the first Hasmonean to call himself king, Aristobulus (reigned 104–103 BC), and then of his brother Alexander Janneus (103–76 BC), probably through a “levirate” marriage.
alexandria: Egyptian city established by Alexander the Great in 331 BC. Alexandria was the capital city of Egypt through the Hellenistic and Roman periods and, next to Rome, was the most important city in the ancient world.
alexandrinus, codex: One of the three most important “codexes,” or bound books, containing early copies of the whole Bible in Greek (the other two being the Vaticanus and Sinaiticus codexes).
algum: Wood imported from Lebanon and possibly Ophir for the construction of the temple and the palace and for musical instruments. The term may be a copyist’s error of transposition for “almug” tree.
aliah: Alternate name for Alvah, Esau’s descendant, in 1 Chronicles 1:51.
alian: Alternate name for Alvan, Shobal’s son, in 1 Chronicles 1:40.
alien: Noncitizen or alien, temporary guest, sojourner, or stranger.
allegory: A method of interpretation (“allegorizing”), especially biblical interpretation, that seeks to find a deeper moral, theological, spiritual meaning behind the words and literal imagery of the text.
allemeth: NASB rendering of Alemeth in 1 Chronicles 6:60.
alliance: Close association of powerful individuals or nations for a common objective. Such alliances were ratified by various means, including gifts, oaths, dowries and marriages, and covenants.
allon (place): Landmark oak tree in Naphtali’s territory, considered in some translations to be the name of a town (Jos 19:33, KJV). The NLT better reads “the oak at Zaanannim.” See Zaanannim.
allon-bachuth, allon-bacuth: Oak tree near Bethel under which Deborah, Rebekah’s aged nurse, was buried. The tree was named the “Oak of Weeping.”
allotment of the land: Assignment of large territories of the Promised Land of Canaan to the 12 tribes of Israel following the Conquest. The specific territory in Canaan to be occupied by each of the 12 tribes of Israel was not left to their own initiative.
almighty: Divine name found in several books of the Bible but particularly in the books of Job and Revelation.
almodad: Son or descendant of Joktan in the family of Noah’s son Shem.
almon: Alternate name for Alemeth in Joshua 21:18.
almond: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
almon-diblathaim: Area in Moab where the Israelites camped during their 40 years of wandering. Some identify it with Beth-diblathaim.
alms: Charitable gifts. The practice of giving alms to the poor.
almug: Wood imported from Ophir for the construction of the temple, the palaces, and for lyres and harps of the temple musicians.
aloe: Tree known for its fragrant wood; also a plant from which is pressed a juice used in embalming.
aloth: A place in one of Solomon’s administrative districts.
alpha and omega: Phrase used as a title in the NT for both God and Jesus Christ. The English equivalent is “the A and the Z.” Similar epithets are “the beginning and the end” and “the first and the last”.
alphaeus: 1. Father of James, one of the 12 apostles, thought by some to be the same as Clopas of John 19:25.
altar: The platform upon which offerings are made to the deity. This may include a ritual sacrifice of animals or a burning of incense before God.
al-taschith: Hebrew phrase in the titles of Psalms 57, 58, 59, and 75 (KJV), translated “Do Not Destroy!”; perhaps a familiar ancient melody to which the psalms were performed.
alush: Place where Israel encamped during the wilderness wanderings, mentioned as being between Dophkah and Rephidim on the way to Mt Sinai.
alvah: Esau’s descendant and a chief of Edom; alternately called Aliah in 1 Chronicles 1:51.
alvan: Shobal’s son and a descendant of Esau; alternately spelled Alian in 1 Chronicles 1:40.
amad: Town in northern Palestine near Mt Carmel, within the boundaries of Asher’s territory.
amal: Helem’s son and a descendant of Asher.
amalek, amalekites: Amalek was the son of Eliphaz (Esau’s son) by his concubine, Timna. Descendants of this tribal chief of Edom were known as Amalekites.
amalekites, hill country (mount) of the: An area near Pirathon in Ephraim, probably about six miles (9.6 kilometers) west of Shechem. It is mentioned in the Hebrew Bible but not in the Greek manuscripts of the OT.
amam: Town in the southern part of the kingdom of Judah, along the border of Edom.
amana: Mountain ridge, probably in the Anti-Lebanon range, mentioned along with Mt Senir and Mt Hermon. It is perhaps the source of the Abana (Amana) River.
amariah: Common OT name, meaning “the Lord has spoken” or “the Lord has promised.”
amarna tablets: Clay tablets, mostly letters from royal archives, the only cuneiform records ever found in Egypt. The 379 Amarna tablets were recovered from ruins located on a plain on the east bank of the Nile about 190 miles (305.7 kilometers) south of Cairo.
amasa: 1. Son of Ithra (Jether) and David’s sister Abigail, and therefore David’s nephew.
amasai: 1. Elkanah’s son and Mahath’s father, listed in the genealogy of Heman the singer.
amashai, amashsai: Azarel’s son and one of the leading priests who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. Amashsai may possibly be identical with Maasai.
amasiah: Military leader in the time of Jehoshaphat, in charge of 200,000 men. Amasiah was Zichri’s son and a man of unusual piety.
amaw: Region near the Euphrates River that included the city of Pethor, to which King Balak of Moab sent messengers in search of the soothsayer Balaam.
amaziah: 1. Ninth king of Judah (796–767 BC), who at age 25 succeeded his father, King Joash, when Joash was assassinated after a 40-year reign.
ambassador: Messenger or envoy officially representing a higher authority. In the OT, an ambassador was a messenger, envoy, or negotiator sent on a special, temporary mission as an official representative of the king, government, or authority who sent him.
amber: Fossilized resin of certain cone-bearing plants. The resinous product of these conifers loses its volatile components and turns into a translucent yellow or orange solid.
ambush: The means by which one nation seeks to impose its will upon another by force. An index to the importance of warfare in antiquity is provided by the amount of technical skill directed to perfecting devices for destruction and defense.
amen: Hebrew word meaning “so it is” or “let it be,” derived from a verb meaning “to be firm or sure.” Some translations of the Bible always retain the Hebrew word amen in the text.
amethyst: Purple variety of quartz used in jewelry.
ami: Official in Solomon’s court whose descendants returned to Jerusalem after the exile. Also spelled Amon in Nehemiah 7:59.
amillennialism: Biblical term (taken from the Latin word meaning “a thousand”) referring to the thousand-year reign of Christ. The primary biblical context for the doctrine of the millennium is found in Revelation 20:1-6 (where the Greek word for thousand is used five times).
aminadab: KJV form of Amminadab in Matthew 1:4 and Luke 3:33.
amittai: Father of the prophet Jonah from Zebulun’s tribe. Amittai came from the small village of Gath-hepher northeast of Nazareth.
ammah: Hill north of Jerusalem in the area of Gibeon. A battle fought there between David’s troops under Joab and Ishbosheth’s troops under Abner was the beginning of a long war between followers of Saul and followers of David.
ammi: Hebrew word meaning “my people.” The expression “people of God” is the most common designation for the nation of Israel in the OT.
ammidians: Name used in a list of towns identifying groups of exiles that returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel around 538 BC. Corresponding lists in Ezra 2:25-26 and Nehemiah 7:29-30 make no mention of a group from such a place.
ammiel: 1. Gemalli’s son, one of 12 men sent by Moses to spy out the land of Canaan.
ammihud: 1. Father of a leader of Ephraim’s tribe, Elishama.
amminadab: 1. Father of Elisheba, who was Aaron’s wife.
amminadib: Word occurring in some English versions of the Song of Songs 6:12, “or ever I was aware, my soul made me like the chariots of Amminadib” (ASV mg, NASB mg). More recent translators have not regarded the term as a proper name.
ammishaddai: Ahiezer’s father. Ahiezer was leader of Dan’s tribe when the Israelites were wandering in the Sinai wilderness after their escape from Egypt.
ammizabad: Benaiah’s son. Both Benaiah and Ammizabad were high-ranking officers in King David’s army.
ammon, ammonites: A Semitic people who occupied a fertile area northeast of Moab in Transjordan between the Arnon and Jabbok Rivers and extending eastward to the Syrian Desert. The chief city was Rabbah (Rabbath-ammon), modern Amman, capital of Jordan.
amnon: 1. David’s oldest son by his wife Ahinoam, born in Hebron.
amok: Priest who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile. Amok was the ancestor of Eber, a priest under Joiakim.
amon (person): 1. Governor of the city of Samaria during the reign of Ahab in Israel.
amon (place): Part of the Hebrew name for Thebes, the capital of upper Egypt.
amorites: Semitic people found throughout the Fertile Crescent of the Near East at the beginning of the second millennium BC. Amorites are first mentioned in the Bible as descendants of Canaan in a list of ancient peoples (Gn 10:16; cf. 1 Chr 1:13-16).
amorites, hill country (mount) of the: Central mountainous region between the plains of Philistia, Sharon, and Phoenicia on the west and the valley of the Jordan on the east.
amos (person): Hebrew prophet of the eighth century BC. Nothing is known about Amos apart from the book that bears his name.
amos, book of: Writings of the prophet Amos, one of the 12 minor prophets of the Hebrew OT. The book of Amos is called minor only because it is relatively short.
amoz: Isaiah’s father, not to be confused with the prophet Amos.
amphipolis: City in ancient Greece, once the home of the Thracian Edoni tribe. Amphipolis occupied a strategic location in a fertile area on the eastern bank of the Strymon River.
amplias, ampliatus: Name of a Christian to whom the apostle Paul sent greetings at the end of his Letter to the Romans (16:8). Called “my beloved in the Lord” (RSV) by Paul, nothing further is known of this Christian who bore a common Roman name.
amram: 1. Kohath’s son, a member of Levi’s tribe.
amraphel: King of Shinar (Babylonia), who helped King Chedorlaomer of Elam quell a revolt of five vassal cities in Palestine.
amulet: Small object worn by an individual, usually around the neck, as a charm or means of protection against evil, witchcraft, disease, or other physical and spiritual threats.
amzi: 1. Merarite Levite and an ancestor of Ethan the musician.
anab: Town in the hill country of Hebron inhabited by giant warriors. After Joshua eliminated the giants, Anab was allotted to Judah’s tribe.
anael: Brother of Tobit. After the death of King Sennacherib (681 BC), Anael’s son Ahikar was appointed by the Assyrian king Esarhaddon to a high court position in Nineveh.
anah: 1. Son of Zibeon the Hivite and father of Oholibamah.
anaharath: Town in the valley of Jezreel allotted to Issachar’s tribe when the land was divided by Joshua.
anaiah: 1. Priest and assistant of Ezra who explained to the people passages from the law read by Ezra.
anak, anakim, anakites: Ancestor of a race of giants in old Canaan. When Israel first reached Canaan, the Anakim were well established in Hebron.
anamim, anamites: Unidentified group of people, possibly related to the Egyptians, mentioned in the biblical records of earliest nations.
anammelech: Deity associated with Adrammelech, who was worshiped by the people of Sepharvaim, whom the Assyrians relocated in Samaria after 722 BC.
anan: One of the chiefs of the people who set his seal on Ezra’s covenant to keep God’s law during the postexilic era.
anani: One of seven sons of Elioenai, a descendant of David.
ananiah (person): Azariah’s grandfather. Azariah was one of three men who repaired the Jerusalem wall near their homes after the exile.
ananiah (place): Town in Benjamin’s territory after the exile that may have become the Bethany of the NT (“Bethany” is a contraction of Beth-ananiah).
ananias: 1. Member of the early church in Jerusalem.
anath: 1. Parent of Shamgar, one of the judges of Israel.
anathema: Greek word meaning “cursed” or “banned,” and associated with destruction.
anathoth (place), anathothite: Town in Benjamin’s territory set aside for the Levites. Anathoth may have been named by the Canaanites for their goddess Anath, or later by the Israelites for one of Benjamin’s descendants.
anchor: Object used to keep a ship or boat stationary in the water. An anchor is attached to a ship by a cable or chain, and when thrown overboard, its weight and/or ability to dig into the sea bottom keeps the vessel from drifting.
ancient of days, ancient one: Name of God used by Daniel to describe God as judge.
andreas: Chief of the bodyguard of Egyptian king Ptolemy Philadelphus, sent by the king to Palestine to procure scribes to translate the OT into Greek (about 275 BC). The result was the translation known as the Septuagint.
andrew, the apostle: One of Christ’s 12 apostles. Andrew first appears in the NT as a disciple of John the Baptist.
andronicus: 1. Deputy of Seleucid king Antiochus Epiphanes.
anem: Town in Issachar’s territory given to the priestly family of Gershom. It was also called En-gannim and was probably located southeast of Mt Tabor.
anemone: Plant of the buttercup family, with cup-shaped flowers that are usually white, pink, red, or purple.
aner (person): Amorite ally of Abram and brother of Mamre and Eshcol. With his brothers, Aner helped Abram defeat a confederation of four kings who had plundered Sodom and Gomorrah and had captured Abram’s nephew Lot.
anethothite, anetothite: KJV forms of Anathothite, a resident of Anathoth, in 2 Samuel 23:27 and 1 Chronicles 27:12, respectively.
angel: Messenger of God or supernatural being, either good or evil, with powers greater than humans possess.
anger: The word normally used in the Bible to refer to rage, fury, and indignation. In most instances, anger is considered to be wrong.
anim: One of 44 cities of the hill country given to Judah’s tribe in the allotment of the land. Anim is probably modern Khirbet Ghowein et-Tahta.
animals: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
anise: KJV translation of dill in Matthew 23:23.
anna: Phanuel’s daughter from Asher’s tribe and a prophetess in Jerusalem when Jesus was a young child. Advanced in years, she worshiped with prayer and fasting day and night in the temple.
annan: Father of five sons who divorced their foreign wives under the direction of Ezra, also called Harim.
annas: Jewish high priest from AD 7 to 15. Appointed by Quirinius, Roman governor of Syria, Annas was put out of office by Valerius Gratus, procurator of Judea.
annias: Ancestor of a family of 101 sons that undertook the rigorous migration from Babylon with Zerubbabel, according to the Apocrypha. Parallel canonical texts omit this family.
anniuth: Apocryphal name of Bani in 1 Esdras 9:48.
annunciation: The angel Gabriel’s announcement to Mary that she would bear a son by the Holy Spirit.
annunus: One of the men supplied by the Lord in response to Ezra’s request for priests to serve in Jerusalem. Annunus was probably one of Jeshaiah’s brothers.
anoint: To pour oil or ointment onto a person or object in a ritualistic fashion.
anointed one, anointed ones: In the NT, Jesus Christ is portrayed as fulfilling the three offices of prophet, priest, and king. He is, supremely, God’s Anointed One.
ant: Insect used as an example of industriousness for storing up food in the summer.
antediluvian: Name given to the whole period before the Flood of Noah’s time. The adjective, which literally means “before the flood [deluge],” designates a major epoch in biblical history.
antelope: Swift, deerlike animal mentioned in Deuteronomy 14:5 and Isaiah 51:20.
anthropology: In a theological sense, the study of what the Bible says about man and the relation in which he stands and should stand to God.
antichrist: According to 1 John, anyone who denies that Jesus is the Christ, that he is the unique Son of God, or that he has come in the flesh.
antigonus: Name of three Greek kings and two Hasmonean (Jewish) kings in the intertestamental period.
anti-lebanon: Mountain range stretching from Mt Hermon, its southern extremity, toward the north-northeast, running parallel to the Lebanon range west of it. Drainage from the two ranges provides most of the water for the Jordan River.
antilegomena: Those books in the Jewish and Christian Bible considered to be Scripture and therefore authoritative in matters of faith and doctrine.
antiochians: “Turncoat” Jews of the intertestamental period who had largely abandoned their Judaism for Greek ideas and practices. During the reign of the Syrian king Antiochus Epiphanes (second century BC), Palestine was subjected to an intensive “Hellenizing” program.
antiochis: Concubine of the Syrian king Antiochus Epiphanes. When the cities of Tarsus and Mallus were given to Antiochis as a gift, their inhabitants revolted in protest.
antioch of pisidia: City in Asia Minor between the districts of Phrygia and Pisidia to which the apostle Paul traveled to introduce the gospel. Paul was invited by the elders of the synagogue in Antioch to deliver any message of exhortation he might have at their Sabbath meeting.
antioch of syria: Principal city among 16 others of the same name built about 300 BC by the Syrian emperor Seleucus I in honor of his father Antiochus.
antiochus iv: Hellenistic king called Epiphanes meaning the “illustrious” or “god manifest”; he was the eighth in the Seleucid dynasty (c. 215–164 BC). The year 189 BC found this younger son of Antiochus III the Great hostage in Rome after the Battle of Magnesia.
antiochus v: Called Antiochus Eupator, meaning “of a noble father” (173–162 BC), the son of Antiochus IV, and king of Syria from 163 to 162 BC. The boy king traveled with his regent Lysias to relieve the besieged Jerusalem in 163 BC.
antiochus vii: Called Antiochus Sidetes (c. 159–129 BC), was king of Syria from 139/138 to 129 BC, son of Demetrius I and brother of Demetrius II.
antipas: 1. Early martyr in the church at Pergamum.
antipater: 1. Goodwill ambassador sent out with Numenius to the Spartans and Romans by Jonathan, the high priest.
antipatris: City some 26 miles (41.8 kilometers) south of Caesarea rebuilt by Herod the Great in 9 BC in honor of his father, Antipater. Before its rebuilding, it was known as Aphek.
antitype: Fulfillment or resolution of a corresponding earlier type.
antothijah: KJV spelling of Anthothijah, Shashak’s descendant, in 1 Chronicles 8:24.
antothite: KJV form of Anathothite, a resident of Anathoth, in 1 Chronicles 11:28 and 12:3.
apame: Concubine of Darius I of Persia.
ape: Large, tailless primate. Apes, or perhaps other monkeys and baboons, were imported to Israel by King Solomon.
apelles: Roman Christian who received special greetings from the apostle Paul and the complimentary assessment of being one who is “approved in Christ” (Rom 16:10, RSV).
aphairema: One of the cities taken from Samaria and added to Judea by Demetrius Nicator (the Conqueror), king of Syria. The name is thought by some scholars to be a corruption of Ephraim.
apharsachites, apharsathchites, apharsit: Words used in the book of Ezra to designate certain groups of people in Samaria who joined in writing King Artaxerxes of Babylon to stop the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem.
aphek: 1. Canaanite city west of the Jordan River conquered by Israel and later included in Ephraim’s territory.
aphekah: City in the hill country of Canaan given to Judah’s tribe after the conquest of the Promised Land by Joshua.
aphiah: Ancestor of King Saul in Benjamin’s tribe.
aphik: Alternate form of Aphek in Judges 1:31.
aphrah: KJV for Beth-leaphrah, possibly the name of a Philistine city, in Micah 1:10.
aphses: KJV form of Happizzez, a priest in David’s time, in 1 Chronicles 24:15.
apocalypse: Term meaning a “revelation” or a “disclosure.” The books of Daniel and Revelation are the two apocalypses in the Bible.
apocalypses: Group of extra-canonical writings, apocalyptic in nature, and purported to be written by biblical characters.
apocalyptic: Term derived from a Greek word meaning “revelation” and used to refer to a pattern of thought and to a form of literature, both dealing with future judgment (eschatology).
apocrypha: Books excluded from the canon of Scripture.
apollonia: Town located on the Egnatian Way in eastern Macedonia. Paul passed through Apollonia on his second missionary journey west from Philippi to Thessalonica, a trip of about 90 miles (145 kilometers).
apollonius: Name of probably four different men in the Maccabean literature.
apollophanes: Syrian warrior during the intertestamental period. Apollophanes was killed at a fortress named Gazara by the forces of Judas Maccabeus.
apollos: Native of Alexandria (Egypt), a Christian Jew who was an eloquent preacher at the time of the apostle Paul’s missionary journeys. The chief biblical passage about Apollos is Acts 18:24–19:1.
apollyon: Angel of the “bottomless pit,” also called Abaddon.
apostasy: Turning against God, as evidenced by abandonment and repudiation of former beliefs. The term generally refers to a deliberate renouncing of the faith by a once sincere believer rather than a state of ignorance or mistaken knowledge.
apostle, apostleship: Official designation given to certain leading individuals in the NT churches. Apostleship is the more comprehensive term, denoting the functions of the one who serves in such a capacity.
apothecary: KJV rendering of “perfumer” in Exodus 30:25, 35; 37:29; 2 Chronicles 16:14; Nehemiah 3:8; and Ecclesiastes 10:1.
apothegm: Short, pithy saying. As used by some biblical scholars, the term “apothegm” denotes brief stories in the Gospels that culminate in a saying of Jesus (e.g., Mt 8:18-22; 9:10-13; 16:1-4; Mk 2:18-22; 10:13-15; Lk 6:1-5; 11:37-44).
appaim: Nadab’s son, and the father of Ishi in Judah’s tribe.
appeal: Legal term meaning to request a higher court review of a decision by a lower one. OT law made no provision for appeals.
appearances of christ: Occasions on which Jesus Christ was seen by human witnesses after his resurrection.
apphia: Christian woman in Colosse, possibly the wife or sister of Philemon. The apostle Paul greeted her in his letter to Philemon (v 2).
apphus: Nickname of Jonathan, one of Judas Maccabeus’s four brothers. As with the other Maccabean nicknames, the meaning of the word apphus is uncertain.
appian way: Main highway from Rome southward to the heel of the Italian peninsula. Originally the Appian Way terminated at Capua, but later it was extended to Brundisium, about 350 miles (560 kilometers) from Rome.
appius, forum of: Marketplace mentioned in Acts 28:15 as the place where Christians met the apostle Paul when he came to appear before the caesar. It was apparently named for Appius Claudius, builder of the Appian Way (major artery of western Italy).
apple, apple tree: Fruit and tree not native to the Near East but used by some versions to translate certain references to fruit in the OT.
apricot: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
aqaba, gulf of: Eastern branch (of two northern arms) of the Red Sea that penetrates northeast between Saudi Arabia and the Sinai Peninsula. The gulf varies in width from 12 to 17 miles (19 to 27 kilometers) and is 100 miles (161 kilometers) long.
aqueduct: Conduit or artificial channel for conducting water from a distance, usually by means of gravity; also a structure carrying a conduit or canal across a valley or over a river.
ar: Capital city of Moab located on the northern border near the Arnon River. Ar was sometimes used figuratively to refer to all of Moab.
ara: Son of Jether, a chief among Asher’s tribe.
arab: City in the hill country southwest of Hebron, given to Judah’s tribe after the conquest of Canaan, the Promised Land.
arabah: Great valley dividing eastern and western Palestine. The Arabah extends south from the Sea of Galilee through the Jordan River valley to the Dead Sea and the Gulf of Aqaba.
arabah, brook of the: Dry stream bed in southern Palestine.
arabah, sea of the: Alternate name for the Dead Sea, since that body of water lies within the area of the land of Israel called Arabah.
arabia, arabs: Peninsula in southwestern Asia, surrounded by sea on three sides and by the Fertile Crescent on the fourth. Politically, the Arabian peninsula is bounded on the north by the modern Hashemite kingdom of Jordan and by Iraq and on the south by the Indian Ocean.
arad (place): Name of a Canaanite settlement or region in the Negev Desert at the time of the Israelite conquest of Canaan. The king of Arad attacked the Israelites and was defeated.
aradus: Greek name for the Phoenician city of Arvad. Aradus was one of the cities receiving a “letter of recommendation” for the Jews written by the Roman consul Lucius.
aram (place): Designation for the territory now called Syria.
aramaic: One of the three original languages of the Bible, found in sections of the book of Daniel (2:4b–7:28) and Ezra (4:8–6:18; 7:12-26). Aramaic phrases and expressions also appear in Genesis (31:47), Jeremiah (10:11), and the NT.
arameans: People of Aram and predecessors of the Syrians.
aram-geshur: Small kingdom between Mt Hermon and Bashan bordering Argob.
aram-maacah (maachah): Alternate name for Maacah in 1 Chronicles 19:6.
aram-naharaim: Hebrew word meaning “Aram of the two rivers”; it refers to the area bounded by the upper Euphrates and the Habur Rivers. It is sometimes translated “Mesopotamia” (Dt 23:4, RSV).
aram of damascus: One of the several city-kingdoms in the land of Aram (Syria). This kingdom, whose principal city was Damascus, was conquered by King David.
aram-zobah: Syrian territory ruled in David’s time by King Hadadezer, whom David defeated. This form of the name occurs in the title to Psalm 60.
aran: Dishan’s son, grandson of Seir the Horite, and a descendant of Esau.
ararat: Name of a craggy, rugged range of mountains in Armenia. Ararat lies just south of the Black Sea and between it and the Caspian Sea.
araunah: Jebusite whose threshing floor was the scene of some significant events in biblical history.
arba: Ancestor of the giant Anakim and a great hero among them. Arba was the founder of Kiriath-arba (city of Arba), later known as Hebron.
arbathite: Resident of the city of Beth-arabah, and the hometown of Abi-albon (Abiel), one of David’s 30 “mighty men”.
arbatta: Region south of the Esdraelon Valley in the southwest corner of Galilee. When its inhabitants were threatened by non-Jewish forces of Ptolemais, Tyre, and Sidon, they sent an urgent letter requesting help from Judas Maccabeus.
arbela: Site of a great slaughter when General Bacchides invaded Judea from Syria.
arbite: Title given to Paarai, warrior among David’s 30 “mighty men”. The expression may indicate that he was a native of Arab, a village in southern Judah.
arch: Curved structure, usually of masonry, supporting the weight over a doorway or other open space. The capstone or keystone is the most important part of an arch and the last stone put in place.
archaeology and the bible: Simply defined, archaeology is the science that recovers and studies the relics of human antiquity. Biblical archaeology is concerned with the remains scattered across the Near East.
archangel: Chief angel; a title given to the angel Michael.
archelaus: Son of Herod the Great who followed his father in governing Idumea, Samaria, and Judea.
archer, archery: The archer used bow and arrows in peace and war. Nomads, hunters, raiders, and warriors used this weapon throughout the biblical period.
archevites: KJV translation for the inhabitants of Erech (Uruk) in southern Babylonia who were transported to Samaria by Asnappar, the Assyrian King Ashurbanipal.
archippus: Contemporary of Paul whom the apostle encouraged to fulfill his ministry and referred to as a “fellow soldier”.
archi, archite: A tribe descended from Canaan or a member of this tribe; also spelled “Arkite.” Hushai, David’s loyal adviser, was an Archite.
architecture: Science, art, or profession of designing and constructing buildings, bridges, etc.
archives: Building used for storage of records, annals, and decrees; a common structure in Near Eastern nations in the second millennium BC.
arcturus: Constellation Ursa Major (the Great Bear), referred to in Job 9:9 and 38:32 (KJV) in connection with the constellation Orion and the Pleiades.
ard, ardite: One of the nine sons of Bela, Benjamin’s firstborn son. Ard is called Benjamin’s son in the Hebrew sense, meaning descendant.
ardon: Caleb’s third son by Azubah; a descendant of Judah.
areli, arelite: One of Gad’s seven sons. After the plague of Baal-peor, Areli’s descendants, the Arelites, were numbered in Moses’ census in preparation for war with the Midianites.
areopagite: Member of the council or court of the Areopagus in Athens.
areopagus: Hill northwest of the Acropolis in Athens overlooking the marketplace. “Areopagus” also refers to the Athenian council or court that met there.
aretas: 1. Name of several kings of an Arabian people called the Nabateans, considered to be descendants of Nebaioth, Ishmael’s oldest son.
argob (person): Individual supposedly killed with King Pekahiah of Israel in Pekah’s revolt. The early church father Jerome thought the name Argob (along with Arieh) referred to a place.
argob (place): Region in Bashan won by the Israelites when they defeated King Og at Edrei. Argob was located east of the Sea of Chinnereth (later called Sea of Galilee), beyond the regions of Geshur and Maacah.
ariarathes: King of Cappadocia in Asia Minor (163–130 BC). Educated in Rome, Ariarathes absorbed Roman ideas and became a close ally of the Romans.
aridai: One of Haman’s ten sons, who was killed with his father when Haman’s plot to destroy the Jews was foiled.
aridatha: One of Haman’s ten sons, who was killed along with his father when Haman’s plot to destroy the Jews was foiled.
arieh: Person mentioned along with Argob in 2 Kings 15:25 (KJV, NIV, NLT).
ariel (person): 1. Person or thing overcome in a heroic deed by Benaiah, chief of David’s bodyguard.
ariel (place): Poetic designation for Jerusalem, used by the prophet Isaiah in a “woe” oracle warning people to turn from their wrongdoing.
arimathea: Hometown of the Joseph who obtained Jesus’ crucified body and buried it in his own tomb.
arioch: 1. King of Ellasar, who with three other kings captured five cities and took a number of prisoners, including Abraham’s nephew Lot.
arisai: One of Haman’s ten sons, who was killed with his father when Haman’s plot to destroy the Jews was foiled.
aristarchus: Companion of the apostle Paul; Macedonian from Thessalonica, possibly of Jewish ancestry. He is first mentioned as one of those seized by an angry mob in Ephesus.
aristobulus: Name (of Greek origin, meaning “best advising”) used in intertestamental times by ruling families in Palestine.
ark, noah's: 1. Son of Lamech and the grandson of Methuselah, a descendant of Seth, third son of Adam.
arkite: Name of a clan descended from Ham’s son Canaan. The Arkites were probably residents of Arqa, a Phoenician town north of Tripolis in Syria.
ark of the covenant: Most important piece of furniture in the wilderness tabernacle (tent-sanctuary) that God instructed Moses to build. The Hebrew word for ark can also mean “chest” or “coffin”, but it is not the same word used for Noah’s ark.
ark's cover: Gold slab placed on top of the ark of the covenant with cherubim attached to it on either end, termed the “mercy seat” in many English versions of the Bible (cf. Ex 25:17-22).
armageddon: Hebrew word in Revelation 16:16 meaning “Mount Megiddo.” It is generally thought that the term refers to the town of Megiddo, strategically located between the western coastal area and the broad plain of Jezreel in northern Palestine.
armenia: KJV translation of Ararat in 2 Kings 19:37 and Isaiah 37:38, mentioned as the place where Sennacherib’s two sons fled after murdering their father.
armoni: One of Saul’s two sons by his concubine Rizpah. Seven of Saul’s sons, including Armoni, were handed over to the Gibeonites by David to be killed to avenge Saul’s slaughter of the Gibeonites.
armor and weapons: The location of Palestine at the crossroads of three continents gave it a strategic importance in the ancient world quite out of proportion to its size.
armor bearer: One who carried the protective gear (armor) and weapons of a warrior.
army: Large organized body of soldiers for waging war, especially on land.
arnan: Rephaiah’s son and Obadiah’s father, a descendant of David through Zerubbabel.
arni: Ancestor of Jesus according to Luke’s genealogy (3:33); also called Ram in Ruth 4:19 and 1 Chronicles 2:9-10.
arnon: River of Transjordan, the present Wadi el-Mojib, running from east to west through a canyon with walls 1,500 feet (457 meters) high into the Dead Sea.
arod, arodi, arodite: Gad’s sixth son, founder of the Arodite family. He is called Arodi in the list of those who went to Egypt with Jacob.
aroer: 1. Transjordanian city existing from Moses’ time until the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC).
aroerite: Resident of Aroer. The Aroerite Hotham, father of two of David’s “mighty men,” was a native of Aroer.
aromatic cane: Species of fragrant reed used by the Israelites as a perfume and as an ingredient of the anointing oil.
arpad: City in northern Syria. Arpad was overrun twice by the Assyrians: in 740 BC by Tiglath-pileser III and in 720 BC by Sargon II.
arphaxad: Shem’s son and Noah’s grandson, born two years after the Flood. Arphaxad’s descendants were probably the Chaldeans.
arrow: The location of Palestine at the crossroads of three continents gave it a strategic importance in the ancient world quite out of proportion to its size.
arsaces: Title shared by Parthian rulers beginning with Arsaces I, founder of the kingdom (250? BC).
artaxerxes: Name of three kings of the Persian Empire.
artemas: Christian coworker with Paul, whom the apostle considered as a replacement for Titus on the island of Crete. Later tradition describes Artemas as bishop of Lystra.
artemis: Greek goddess of the moon, wild animals, and hunting. The cult of Artemis at Ephesus, where she is called Diana by the Romans, regarded her especially as a fertility goddess.
artificer: KJV rendering of “craftsman” in Genesis 4:22; 1 Chronicles 29:5; 2 Chronicles 34:11; and Isaiah 3:3.
artisan: Skilled craftsman working in the major mediums of wood, stone, metals, gems, and clay; important guild in the middle class of Hebrew society during the period of the monarchy.
arubboth: Town that served as headquarters for one of King Solomon’s 12 administrative districts. Arubboth was probably in Manasseh’s tribal territory, about nine miles (14.5 kilometers) north of Samaria, at the site of modern ’Aarabeh.
arumah: City where Gideon’s son Abimelech lived after he was driven out of Shechem by its inhabitants; perhaps alternately called Rumah in 2 Kings 23:36.
arvad, arvadite: Small fortified island about 2 miles (3.2 kilometers) off the coast of Syria (ancient Phoenicia) and 30 miles (48 kilometers) north of Tripolis.
arza: Superintendent of the palace at Tirzah belonging to King Elah of the northern kingdom of Israel. The drunken king was murdered in Arza’s home by Zimri, who then declared himself king.
asa: 1. Third king of the southern kingdom of Judah (910–869 BC) after the split of Solomon’s Empire into independent kingdoms.
asahel: 1. Warrior among David’s mighty men known as “the thirty”.
asahiah: KJV form of Asaiah, Josiah’s servant, in 2 Kings 22:12, 14.
asaiah: 1. Royal servant sent by King Josiah of Judah to ask the prophetess Huldah about the meaning of the Book of the Law found in the renovation of the temple.
asaph: 1. Berechiah’s son, an important tabernacle musician during King David’s reign.
asaramel: Enigmatic Hebrew word found in the dedicatory inscription honoring Simon, ruling high priest of Israel and brother of Judas Maccabeus.
asarelah: Alternate form of Asharelah, Asaph’s son, in 1 Chronicles 25:2.
ascalon: Alternate form of Ashkelon in Judith 2:28.
ascension of christ: Transference of the resurrected body of Jesus from this world to heaven. Among the NT writers, only Luke described Jesus’ ascension.
asenath: Joseph’s Egyptian wife who became the mother of Manasseh and Ephraim. Asenath was the daughter of the priest Potiphera.
aser: KJV form of Asher in Luke 2:36 and Revelation 7:6.
ash: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
ashan: Town in the southwestern Judean foothills slightly northwest of Beersheba. Ashan first belonged to Judah’s tribe, then to Simeon’s, and finally to the Levites as a city of refuge.
asharelah: One of Asaph’s four sons appointed by David to assist with prophecy and music in the sanctuary; alternately called Jesharelah in verse 14.
ashbea: Name of a family in 1 Chronicles 4:21 (KJV). The NLT is probably correct in translating the name as the family’s place of residence.
ashbel, ashbelite: Benjamin’s son who emigrated to Egypt with his grandfather Jacob. The Ashbelites, his descendants, were included in Moses’ census in the wilderness.
ashchenaz: KJV form of Ashkenaz, Gomer’s son, in 1 Chronicles 1:6 and Jeremiah 51:27.
ashdod, ashdodite, ashdothite: One of the Philistines’ five main cities (the “pentapolis”) along with Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. Ashdod was located midway between Joppa and Gaza, about three miles (4.8 kilometers) from the coast.
ashdoth-pisgah: KJV form of “slopes of Pisgah”, referring to the slopes of Mt Pisgah.
asher (person): Jacob’s son born to Leah’s maid Zilpah. The name Asher, probably meaning “happy,” was given to the child by Leah in her delight at his birth.
asher (place): Place mentioned in Tobit 1:2, identified as Hazor.
asher (tribe): Israelite tribe that inhabited the fertile coastal territory when the Promised Land was divided for settlement. Asher’s allotment stretched north of Mt Carmel to a point slightly above the city of Sidon.
asherah, asherim, asheroth: Singular and plural form of the name of a Canaanite goddess associated with Baal. The words also refer to the wooden poles erected to worship this goddess.
ashes: Fine powder left after something has been thoroughly burned. The burning of sacrificial offerings on the tabernacle or temple altar produced ashes that were disposed of ceremonially (Lv 1:16; 4:12; 6:10-11; cf.
ashhur: Caleb’s son and Tekoa’s father, or perhaps the founder of a village named Tekoa.
ashima: Deity of uncertain origin, worshiped by the inhabitants of Hamath and relocated in Samaria after the fall of Israel in 722 BC.
ashkelon: City dating back to ancient times, also spelled Askelon (KJV). In the Bible, Ashkelon was one of the Philistines’ five main cities (the “pentapolis”), along with Gaza, Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron.
ashkenaz: Gomer’s son and Noah’s great-grandson in Japheth’s line. Mention of the kingdom of Ashkenaz along with Ararat and Minni suggests that he was the ancestor of the Scythians, a people who resided in the Ararat region in Jeremiah’s time.
ashnah: Name of the two towns that Judah’s tribe received after the conquest of Canaan. No certain location for either is known, but both were in the lowlands separating Judah and Philistia.
ashpenaz: Official under Nebuchadnezzar in charge of palace personnel. Ashpenaz was reluctant to grant the captives from Judah, Daniel and his friends, a reprieve from eating the king’s food, but eventually he did so.
ashriel: KJV form of Asriel, Manasseh’s son, in 1 Chronicles 7:14.
ashtaroth, ashterathite: Town of Bashan, named along with Edrei as the home of King Og. Ashtaroth is the plural form of Ashtoreth, the name of the Canaanite fertility goddess who was worshiped there.
ashteroth-karnaim: City where a coalition of four kings led by Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, defeated the tribe of Rephaim giants (Gn 14:5; cf. Dt 3:11).
ashtoreth: Pagan mother-goddess widely worshiped throughout the ancient Near East; also known as Astarte.
ashur: KJV form of Ashhur, Caleb’s son, in 1 Chronicles 2:24 and 4:5.
ashurbanipal: Esarhaddon’s son and the Assyrian ruler (669–633 BC) who reigned in the years during which kings Manasseh, Amon, and Josiah governed the southern kingdom of Judah.
ashurite: Probably a variant spelling for Asherite, a member of Asher’s tribe. The Ashurites were among those who supported Ishbosheth, Saul’s son, instead of David as king over Israel after Saul’s death.
ashurnasirpal: 1. Ashurnasirpal I (1049?–1031 BC), Assyrian king listed in the synchronistic Assyrian chronicle as the legitimate successor ofShamshi-adad IV (1053?–1050 BC).
ashvath: Japhlet’s son, a great warrior and head of a clan in Asher’s tribe.
asia: In NT times, the Roman province immediately east of the Aegean Sea. The province was established in 133 BC out of the kingdom left to the Romans in the will of Attalus III, king of Pergamum.
asia minor: Peninsula synonymous with the Asia of the NT and Anatolia, identifiable with part of modern Turkey.
asiarch: Title of an official of unknown function in the Roman province of Asia. Several such officials were concerned for the safety of Paul during a silversmiths’ riot in Ephesus.
asibias: Israelite who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile. He may be the same person as Hashabiah (Ezr 10:25, KJV “Malchijah”).
asiel: Jehu’s great-grandfather. Jehu was a prince of Simeon’s tribe.
askelon: KJV alternate form of Ashkelon, a Philistine city, in Judges 1:18; 1 Samuel 6:17; and 2 Samuel 1:20.
asmodeus: An evil demon and jealous lover in the story of Tobit. In the story, Sarah, only daughter of Raguel of Ecbatana, lost seven husbands to Asmodeus on seven different wedding nights.
asnapper: KJV form of Osnappar, an alternate name for the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal in Ezra 4:10.
asp: Poisonous snake mentioned in the Bible, probably the Egyptian cobra.
aspatha: One of Haman’s ten sons, who was killed with his father when Haman’s plot to destroy the Jews was foiled.
aspen: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
asphalt: Brown or black tarlike substance, a variety of bitumen, obtained in ancient times from natural oil seeps and used for mortar and caulking. Mortar, pitch, slime, and tar are other translations of the related terms in Hebrew.
asphar: Watering hole in the Tekoa wilderness, perhaps the modern Bir Selhub south of Engedi. Jonathan and Simon Maccabeus camped at Asphar when fleeing from the Syrians under General Bacchides.
asriel, asrielite: Manasseh’s son. His descendants, the Asrielites, were included in Moses’ census in the wilderness and were later given a portion of the land allotted to Manasseh’s tribe.
ass: Beast of burden used widely in the Near East.
assarion: Coin of small value; a farthing.
asshur: Uncertain translation of a Hebrew word, appearing in English translations of the Bible as Assyria, Assyrian, Assyrians, or merely “Asshur.” These variants come from the Assyrian word asshur.
asshur (place): Ancient name of a city on the Tigris River whose habitation can be traced back to about 2500 BC. Asshur was not a large city (less than one-tenth the size of Babylon or Nineveh), but it formed the homeland and first capital of the later Assyrian kingdom.
asshurim, asshurites: Descendants of Abraham and his second wife, Keturah, through Dedan. The Asshurim probably settled in Arabia.
assir: 1. Korah’s son and a descendant of Levi through Kohath.
assos: Seaport of Mysia in the Roman province of Asia (Minor). The apostle Paul and Luke were reunited in Assos after Paul’s journey by land from Troas.
assur: KJV transliteration of a Hebrew word usually rendered Assyria by most English versions.
assurance: Certainty or confidence about one’s beliefs or actions. The “assurance of hope” and the “assurance of faith” are mentioned as qualities of wholeness that lead believers to responsible living.
assurbanipal: Variant spelling of Ashurbanipal, the Assyrian king.
assyria, assyrians: Ancient empire considered the symbol of terror and tyranny in the Near East for more than three centuries. Assyria received its name from the tiny city-state Asshur, on the western bank of the Tigris River in northern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq).
astaroth: KJV form of Ashtaroth, a town known for its pagan worship of the goddess Ashtoreth, in Deuteronomy 1:4.
astarte: Pagan mother-goddess widely worshiped throughout the ancient Near East; also known as Ashtoreth.
astrology: Pseudoscience dealing with the supposed influence of the heavenly bodies on human character and destiny.
astronomy: Science dealing with the phenomena outside the earth’s atmosphere but especially concerned with the observable arrangements, motions, and characteristics of the heavenly bodies. The word “astronomy” is based on two Greek words meaning “the law of the stars.”
astyages: Fourth and final king of the Medes (according to an early Greek historian, Herodotus), reigning 35 years until 550 BC. At that time his Persian grandson, Cyrus II, revolted and overthrew Astyages’ kingdom.
asuppim: KJV transliteration of a Hebrew word meaning “storehouses,” a part of the temple complex, in 1 Chronicles 26:15, 17.
asur: One of the temple servants whose descendants were among those who returned with Zerubbabel from the exile. The name Harhur appears in the parallel lists of Ezra 2:51 and Nehemiah 7:53.
aswan: Southern Egyptian village (modern Aswan) demarcating Egypt’s border with Ethiopia. The Hebrew form possibly derives from a word for “market” or “trading center,” reflecting the importance of the outpost as a place of commerce.
asylum: Place of refuge where a fugitive from justice is immune to arrest or retribution; also, the protection afforded by such a place.
asyncritus: One of the Christians in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings.
atad: Site, probably in Canaan, where Jacob’s funeral cortege stopped on the way to Hebron. There, at the threshing floor, the household of Joseph and many Egyptians from the pharaoh’s house spent seven days mourning the death of the patriarch.
atarah: Onam’s mother and second wife of Jerahmeel.
ataroth: 1. Town in the mountainous region east of the Jordan River.
ataroth-addar: Town on the boundary between Ephraim’s territory and that of Benjamin, about seven miles (11 kilometers) north of Jerusalem.
ater: 1. Ancestor of a group of people who returned to Judah with Zerubbabel after the exile.
athach: City, probably near Ziklag in southern Judah, to which David sent part of his booty after a victory over the Amalekites.
athaiah: Uzziah’s son from Judah’s tribe, a resident of Jerusalem after the exile.
athaliah: 1. Wife of King Jehoram of Judah, and daughter of King Ahab of Israel and his wife, Jezebel.
atharim: Place, according to the NLT, where the Israelites sought to enter Canaan when attacked by the king of Arad. The name means “tracks” and is generally thought to be located near Tamar or Hazazon-tamar several miles south of the Dead Sea.
athbash: Hebrew cryptograph in which the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet is substituted for the last, the second for the next-to-last, etc., to produce a code.
athenobius: Friend of King Antiochus VII of Syria. When Antiochus besieged the city of Dor the high priest Simon Maccabeus sent him 2,000 soldiers along with gold, silver, and military equipment.
athens: Capital of modern Greece and for centuries chief city of the province of Attica.
athlai: Bebai’s descendant, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile.
atonement: In Christian thought, the act by which God and man are brought together in personal relationship.
atonement, day of: Yom Kippur, the most important day in the religious calendar of Israel, falling on the 10th day of Tishri (the Hebrew month corresponding to mid-September through mid-October).
atroth-beth-joab: Town in Judah near Bethlehem. Since the Hebrew word ‘ataroth means “crowns,” some scholars think that the phrase may not be a town name at all but a reference to Salma’s descendants as chiefs of Joab’s clan.
atroth-shophan: City in Transjordan in Gad’s allotment. The KJV mistakenly lists this compound name as two cities.
attai: 1. Son of Sheshan’s daughter and of Jarha, Sheshan’s Egyptian slave.
attalia: Mediterranean seaport in Asia Minor from which the apostle Paul and Barnabas sailed back to Antioch at the end of Paul’s first missionary journey.
attalus: Name or title of several kings of Pergamum. The one who received a “letter of recommendation” for the Jews from the Roman consul Lucius was probably Attalus II Philadelphus (reigned 159–138 BC).
attendant: High-ranking officer in the service of the king.
attharates: Persian word meaning “governor”. “Attharates” is a corrupt form of the title Tirshatha, rendered as a proper name in a parallel verse in the Apocrypha.
attharias: Greek transliteration of the Persian title, Tirshatha, meaning “governor” (1 Esd 5:40; cf. Ezr 2:63).
attributes of god: Virtues, excellencies, and perfections of God.
augustus caesar: Roman emperor from 31 BC to AD 14.
augustus's band: Roman military unit mentioned in Acts 27:1 (KJV). Julius, the centurion who had custody of the apostle Paul on the way to Rome, was a member of Augustus’s Band.
aul: KJV spelling of awl in Exodus 21:6 and Deuteronomy 15:17.
auranus: Leader chosen by the sacrilegious Lysimachus, brother of the high priest, to put down the angry Jews. He was demented, and, according to the Syriac version of the Apocrypha, head of a gang of cutthroats.
autograph: One of the original handwritten documents of a book that eventually became part of the Bible. None of the original manuscripts remain but copies called apographs, made by scribes whose occupation was the careful copying of manuscripts, are available.
ava: KJV spelling of Avva, a Syrian district, in 2 Kings 17:24.
