avaran: Nickname of Eleazar, brother of Judas Maccabeus. “Awake,” “Paleface,” and “Piercer” have all been suggested as possible meanings.
aven: 1. Term used by Ezekiel to describe On (Heliopolis), center of worship of the Egyptian sun god Ra.
avenger of blood: Person who performed the duty of pursuing and ultimately executing the murderer of a close relative. Such a “redeemer” was expected to act in instances of deliberate murder but not of accidental manslaughter.
avim: KJV spelling of Avvim, a Benjamite city, in Joshua 18:23.
avims, avites: KJV forms of Avvim and Avvites in Deuteronomy 2:23 and Joshua 13:3, respectively.
avith: Capital city for Hadad, Edom’s fourth king.
avva: District in Syria (the same as Ivvah in 2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13) conquered by Sargon of Assyria in the eighth century BC.
avvim (persons): 1. Ancient people who lived in villages near Gaza before they were largely destroyed by a Philistine invasion.
avvim (place): City in Benjamin’s allotment, located south of Bethel.
avvites: 1. Ancient people who lived in villages near Gaza before they were largely destroyed by a Philistine invasion.
ayyah: Town belonging to Ephraim’s tribe, Gaza, but different from the Philistine Gaza. Some scholars think that Aija refers to Ayyah or to Ai, possibly a neighboring town.
azael: Ezora’s son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile. Azael is omitted in the list of Ezra 10:40-42.
azal: Unknown place supposedly on the eastern outskirts of Jerusalem.
azaliah: Meshullam’s son and the father of Josiah’s scribe, Shaphan.
azaniah: Jeshua’s father. Jeshua was a Levite who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God with Nehemiah and others after the exile.
azarael: KJV form of Azarel in Nehemiah 12:36.
azarel: 1. Warrior from Benjamin’s tribe who joined David at Ziklag in his struggle against King Saul.
azariah: Very common Jewish name. Its numerous occurrences in the priestly genealogies has caused much confusion.
azariah, prayer of: Part of the Deuterocanonical works, consists of three supplementary sections to the book of Daniel. This additional material is in the Greek translation of the OT book of Daniel, but not in the ancient Hebrew-Aramaic texts.
azarias: Name or pseudonym taken by the angel Raphael as he accompanied Tobit’s son Tobias, in the apocryphal story of Tobias’s journey to Media.
azaz: Shema’s son and Bela’s father from Reuben’s tribe.
azazel: Hebrew term of uncertain origin and meaning, occurring in Leviticus 16:8, 10, 26. Since biblical or extrabiblical information is lacking, the meaning of Azazel has been interpreted in at least four ways:
azaziah: 1. Levitical musician who played the lyre when King David brought the ark of the covenant into Jerusalem.
azbuk: Father of the Nehemiah who was ruler of half the Beth-zur district. Azbuk’s son assisted the more famous Nehemiah, the governor, in rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem.
azekah: Town in the agricultural plain known as the Shephelah. It existed at least as early as the conquest of Canaan (the Promised Land), since Joshua drove the confederation of Amorite kings to Azekah.
azel: Descendant of Benjamin, Saul, and Jonathan. Azel was the son of Eleasah and the father of six sons.
azem: KJV form of Ezem, a town in the Negev Desert area, in Joshua 15:29 and 19:3.
azgad: 1. Ancestor of a group that returned to Judah with Zerubbabel after the exile.
aziel: Alternative name for Jaaziel, a Levitical musician, in 1 Chronicles 15:20.
aziza: Zattu’s descendant who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife.
azmaveth (person): 1. Warrior among David’s mighty men who were known as “the thirty.” Bahurim was his hometown.
azmaveth (place): Town near Anathoth. Forty-two men from the town returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezr 2:24; “Beth-azmaveth,” Neh 7:28).
azmon: City on the southern border of Judah between Kadesh-barnea and the “brook of Egypt”.
aznoth-tabor: Literally the “peaks (or slopes) of Tabor,” a location on the southwest border of Naphtali’s tribal allotment.
azor: Descendant of Zerubbabel and an ancestor of Jesus.
azotus: NT form of Ashdod in Acts 8:40.
azriel: 1. Family chief in the half-tribe of Manasseh that settled east of the Jordan River.
azrikam: 1. One of three sons of Neariah, a descendant of David through Zerubbabel.
azubah: 1. Shilhi’s daughter and mother of King Jehoshaphat of Judah.
azur: KJV form of Azzur in Jeremiah 28:1 and Ezekiel 11:1.
azzah: KJV rendering of the Philistine city of Gaza in Deuteronomy 2:23; 1 Kings 4:24; and Jeremiah 25:20.
azzan: Paltiel’s father and a member of Issachar’s tribe. Paltiel was appointed to help Eleazar and Joshua in apportioning the Promised Land.
azzur: 1. Political leader who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God with Nehemiah and others after the exile.
baal (idol): Name of the most prominent Canaanite deity. As the god of fertility in the Canaanite pantheon (roster of gods), Baal’s sphere of influence included agriculture, animal husbandry, and human sexuality.
baal (person): 1. Reubenite, the son of Reaiah and the father of Beerah.
baal (place): Alternate name for Baalath-beer, a city defining a portion of the boundary of Simeon’s territory, in 1 Chronicles 4:33.
baalah: City in southern Canaan, probably identical with Baalah and Bilhah.
baalath: 1. Town of Dan that may be the same city as #2 below, although some scholars separate the two.
baalath-beer: Place-name meaning “mistress” or “lady of the well.” Like the masculine counterpart Baal, Baalath often appears in a compound place-name. It seems to suggest that the Canaanite goddess Baalath, patron of Byblos, was associated with the particular place or well.
baal-berith: Pagan god worshiped in central Canaan around the city of Shechem. Baal-berith (“lord of the covenant”) was probably a local form of Baal, the leading Canaanite fertility god.
baale-judah, baale of judah: Alternate name for Kiriath-jearim, a village on the road from Jerusalem to Tel Aviv.
baal-gad: Site in the valley of Lebanon at the foot of Mt Hermon marking the northern border of Joshua’s conquest of Canaan.
baal-hamon: Site of a vineyard owned by Solomon and rented by local farmers. The poetic context indicates that the vineyard produced superb grapes.
baal-hanan: 1. Acbor’s son, a king of Edom.
baal-hazor: Mountain home of King David’s son Absalom. Two years after Amnon raped Absalom’s sister Tamar (Amnon’s half sister), Absalom invited Amnon and his other brothers to a feast at Baal-hazor at sheepshearing time.
baal-hermon: Hivite territory in Transjordan near Mt Hermon, not captured in the Israelite conquest. It was one of the regions God wanted to use to test the younger generation of Israel.
baali: Hebrew title meaning “my lord” or “my master”. The title was rejected by God because of its association with the Canaanite Baal.
baalis: Ammonite king who arranged for the murder of Gedaliah, governor of the “remnant” left behind after Nebuchadnezzar’s capture of Jerusalem and deportation of its inhabitants.
baal-meon: City in northern Moab assigned to Reuben’s tribe. It is called Beth-baal-meon in Joshua 13:17, Beth-meon in Jeremiah 48:23, and Beon in Numbers 32:3.
baal-peor: Moabite god worshiped on Mt Peor. It is probable that this god was Chemosh, the national deity of Moab.
baal-perazim: Location near Jerusalem of a battle in which Israel’s newly anointed King David defeated the Philistines.
baalsamus: Levite assistant who explained to the people passages from the law read by Ezra. In the parallel passage in Nehemiah, the name Maaseiah appears.
baal-shalishah: Home of a man who brought a sack of fresh grain and 20 barley loaves to Elisha at Gilgal. Elisha had his servant feed 100 young prophets with it and had some left over.
baal-tamar: Place between Gibeah and Bethel in Benjamin’s territory, north of Jerusalem. There the 11 other Israelite tribes rallied their forces in a final victorious battle against the tribe of Benjamin over crimes committed in the city of Gibeah.
baal-zebub: Pagan god of the Philistine city of Ekron. After King Ahaziah of Israel fell from his upstairs porch (852 BC), he sent messengers to Baal-zebub to ask about his recovery.
baal-zephon: Area opposite the Israelites’ encampment just before they crossed the Red Sea. The exact location of Baal-zephon is unknown but probably was in northeast Egypt.
baana: 1. Ahilud’s son, one of 12 officers appointed to requisition food for King Solomon’s household.
baanah: 1. Rimmon’s son, a member of Benjamin’s tribe.
baara: Divorced wife of Shaharaim from Benjamin’s tribe.
baaseiah: Malchijah’s son and ancestor of the temple musician Asaph. Baaseiah may be a copyist’s error for the common name Maaseiah.
baasha: Third ruler of the northern kingdom of Israel from 908 to 886 BC and violent founder of the second of its nine dynasties. Baasha was the son of Ahijah of Issachar’s tribe, an unknown whom the Lord lifted “out of the dust” to leadership in the army.
baba bathra: Tractate, or treatise, in the Talmudic Mishnah (a body of Jewish traditional lore relating to Hebrew law). The Mishnah is divided into six main sections called orders, with each order containing from 7 to 12 tractates.
babel: Translation of a Hebrew word in Genesis 10:10 and 11:9. Elsewhere it is translated “Babylonia” or “Babylon” (see 2 Kgs 17:24).
babylon, babylonia: Land of southern Mesopotamia. Politically, Babylonia refers to the ancient kingdoms that flourished in southern Mesopotamia, especially in the seventh and sixth centuries BC, whose capital city was Babylon (or Bab-ilu, meaning “gate of god”).
babylonian captivity: Period when many inhabitants of Judah, the southern kingdom, were exiled in Babylonia after Nebuchadnezzar’s conquest of Jerusalem (sixth century BC).
baca, valley of: Phrase in Psalm 84:6 often translated “valley of weeping.” The Hebrew word baca refers to some kind of tree in 2 Samuel 5:23-24 and 1 Chronicles 14:14-15, where it is translated mulberry (KJV), aspen, or balsam.
bacchides: Syrian general, governor of the Seleucid territories west of the Euphrates River.
bacenor: One of Judas Maccabeus’s officers, according to 2 Maccabees 12:35. The name, however, can be shown to be a corrupt form of “Toubiani,” so that the verse should read, “Dositheus, a Toubian, who was on horseback” (see 2 Macc 12:17).
bachrite: KJV form of Becherite, a descendant of Becher in Numbers 26:35.
backsliding: To wane in religious commitment, to become less arduous in piety or less upright in morals.
badger: Small burrowing mammal with a broad back, thick, short legs, and long claws on the forefeet.
baean: Tribe annihilated by Judas Maccabeus because of its practice of ambushing Jewish travelers. This otherwise unknown tribe was probably located east of the Jordan River.
bagoas: Steward in charge of the personal affairs of Nebuchadnezzar’s general Holofernes. Bagoas discovered the general’s body after Judith beheaded Holofernes in his tent (14:14-18).
bagpipe: An uncertain term sometimes rendered “bagpipe.” The instrument used in King Nebuchadnezzar’s court may actually have been a stringed instument.
baharum, baharumite, bahurim: Village in Benjamin’s territory on the old road connecting Jericho and Jerusalem, east of the Mt of Olives. Bahurim was located at the site of the present Ras et-Temim.
bajith: Town in Moab, according to the KJV. But other translations render it as “daughter” or “temple.”
bakbakkar: Levite who returned to Jerusalem from the Babylonian exile. His name is missing in a parallel list, unless it is the same as Bakbukiah.
bakbuk: Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile.
bakbukiah: 1. Shammua’s son, a Levite who assisted Mattaniah at the thanksgiving services in the temple.
baker: One who prepares food. In biblical times, the baker operated in the home, in the public bakery, and in the palaces of kings and nobles, preparing bread and cakes from the basic staples of oil and flour.
balaam: Beor’s son, a prophet or soothsayer from northern Mesopotamia who was hired by a Moabite king, Balak, to curse the Israelites who had arrived at the Jordan Valley opposite Jericho after 40 years of wandering in the wilderness.
balac: KJV form of Balak, king of Moab in Moses’ time, in Revelation 2:14.
baladan: King of Babylon and father of Merodach-baladan. Baladan’s son sent letters and a gift to King Hezekiah of Judah after Hezekiah’s recovery from a serious illness.
balah: City in southern Canaan, probably identical with Baalah and Bilhah.
balak: Zippor’s son, king of Moab. Balak became fearful after the Israelites defeated the Amorites, so he attempted to hire a soothsayer named Balaam to pronounce a curse against Israel.
balamon: City near where Judith’s husband, Manasseh, was said to be buried.
balance, balances: Devices used to weigh an object by opposing it with a known weight. Balances or scales have been used to measure weight since at least the middle of the second millennium BC.
balbaim: Town lying to the south of Dothan, mentioned in the book of Judith; perhaps the same as Belmain, mentioned in the same book (4:4).
bald locust: Variety of locust considered clean and therefore edible.
baldness: Condition of having little or no hair on the scalp. Natural baldness due to age is referred to only indirectly in the Bible, where it is contrasted with baldness due to leprosy.
balm, balsam: Resinous plant gum used in medicine, or the plant from which it is derived.
balthasar: Traditional given name for one of the wise men who brought a gift to Jesus in Matthew 2:1-2.
bamah: Hebrew word meaning height, ridge, or elevation in the topography of the land; transliterated into English once (Ez 20:29; see NLT). It is a term designating hills or mountains overlooking the Arnon River.
bamoth, bamoth-baal: Town in Moab allotted to Reuben’s tribe by Joshua (Jos 13:17, called Bamoth-baal). It had been one of Israel’s last encampments on the route into Canaan, the Promised Land.
ban: Religious practice whereby those hostile to God are devoted to destruction. It is especially associated with Israel’s wartime tactics involving the total destruction of the Canaanites because of their wickedness and abominable practices.
bani: 1. Member of Gad’s tribe and warrior among David’s mighty men who were known as “the thirty”.
banish, banishment: Exclusion of a person from a country or group as a form of punishment.
banker, banking: A person who engages in loaning, exchanging, and issuing money. The development of interstate and international trade made it imperative to devise a method of banking to facilitate the transfer of funds.
banquet: Lavish ceremonial meal, usually held in honor of some notable event or person; also a symbol of the feast to be given by Christ in the kingdom of God. Banqueting and feasting were major parts of the social and religious life of biblical times.
baptism: Term generally meaning “to dip” or “immerse,” but representing a group of words employed to signify a religious rite for ritual cleansing.
baptism for the dead: Custom of uncertain meaning, referred to once in the NT. Many interpretations have been offered for that much-disputed verse.
baptism of fire: Metaphor coined by John the Baptist. John was looking for the coming of One who would “baptize in Spirit and fire”.
baptism of jesus: Major event in Jesus’ life, which marked the beginning of his ministry. The fact that John the Baptist baptized Jesus is disputed by very few scholars today, but the purpose and significance of Jesus’ baptism remain controversial.
baptism of the spirit: A popularly used phrase, which never occurs as such in the Bible. The NT always uses the verbal phrase “baptize [or baptized] in the Spirit.” That gives it a dynamic character that the noun phrase cannot fully convey.
bar: Term used in the Aramaic language to denote a close familial relationship; for example, Simon Bar-Jona means “Simon, son of John.”
barabbas: Criminal who was released instead of Jesus. All four Gospel writers took note of that event, as did the apostle Peter in his temple sermon.
barachel: Elihu’s father, described as a Buzite (Jb 32:2, 6; cf. Gn 22:21; Jer 25:23).
barachiah, barachias: Name attributed in the NT to Zechariah’s father. Zechariah, executed in the temple by order of King Joash, was said to be the son of Jehoiada.
barak: Son of Abinoam of Kedesh in Naphtali and an associate of the prophetess Deborah. Barak led an army of Israel that defeated the forces of Jabin, king of the Canaanites.
barbarian: Foreigner, especially a person from a culture regarded as primitive or uncivilized. The Greek word barbaros, translated “barbarian” (KJV), originated as a repeated nonsense syllable, “bar-bar,” in imitation of the strange sound of a foreign language.
barhumite: KJV form for a person from the village of Bahurim in 2 Samuel 23:31.
bariah: Shemaiah’s son, a descendant of King David.
bar-jesus: Jewish sorcerer, a “false prophet” who worked with the governor of Paphos on the island of Cyprus. When the governor, Sergius Paulus, took an interest in the message of Paul and Barnabas, Bar-Jesus tried to influence him against their teachings.
bar-jona: Aramaic form of Simon Peter’s surname, meaning “son of Jonah”. Another variant of the name appears in John 1:42 and 21:15-17, where the best Greek texts have “son of John” rather than “son of Jona[s]” (KJV).
bar-kochba, bar-kokba: Hero of the second Jewish revolt against Rome (AD 132-135) during the latter days of the emperor Hadrian’s rule.
barkos: Ancestor of a group of temple servants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile.
bar-koziba: Original name of Simeon Bar-Kochba, leader of the Jewish revolt against the Romans in Palestine during the reign of Emperor Hadrian.
barley: Important grain and dietary staple in Bible lands.
barnabas: Name given by the apostles to an early convert to Christianity in Jerusalem. Formerly called Joseph, Barnabas probably earned his new name through effective preaching and teaching.
barodis: Ancestor of a group of people who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile. The name Barodis does not appear in parallel lists of returnees.
barrenness: Condition of being barren or childless. A closed womb was a personal tragedy in OT times.
barsabas, barsabbas: Biblical surname. Barsabas (KJV) means “son of Saba” in Aramaic.
bartholomew, the apostle: Disciple of Jesus included in all four lists of the 12 apostles, though not otherwise mentioned in the NT. Nothing is told about him in any of the lists.
bartimaeus: Timaeus’s son, a blind beggar who called out to Jesus as he left Jericho on his final journey to Jerusalem. Seeing Bartimaeus’s faith, Jesus healed his blindness.
baruch: 1. Neriah’s son, secretary of the prophet Jeremiah.
baruch, book of: Deuterocanonical work named after Baruch, who was secretary to the prophet Jeremiah. In antiquity several books were ascribed to Baruch, whose well-known connection with Jeremiah undoubtedly increased their circulation and acceptance.
barzillai: 1. One of three men who offered hospitality to David and his supporters at Mahanaim during the dangerous time of Absalom’s rebellion.
bashan: Region east and northeast of the Sea of Galilee.
bashan-havoth-jair: KJV translation in Deuteronomy 3:14 for Havvoth-jair, 60 villages in the region of Bashan.
bashemath: 1. KJV form of Basemath, one of Esau’s wives, in Genesis 26:34.
basilisk: Word used to translate a particular Hebrew word in two passages of some editions of the KJV. “Basilisk” refers to a kind of lizard and is a mistranslation.
baskama: Site where Trypho, commander of the Seleucid army, killed his captive, Jonathan Maccabeus. Trypho was holding Jonathan hostage, and when Jonathan was no longer useful, Trypho put him to the sword.
basmath: KJV form of Basemath, King Solomon’s daughter, in 1 Kings 4:15.
bat: Mouselike flying mammal with a furry body and membranous wings, included in the two lists of unclean birds.
bath: Unit of liquid measure in the OT, equal to about six gallons (23 liters).
bathe, bathing: To cleanse as with water; to wash oneself. In the Bible the terms “bathing” and “washing” translate, often interchangeably, a number of different words.
bath-rabbim, gate of: Gate in the city of Heshbon near which were several pools of clear water. A poetic biblical passage described a young woman’s eyes as being like those pools.
bathsheba: Uriah’s wife, with whom David committed adultery and whom he later married. Bathsheba, also spelled Bathshua, was the daughter of Ammiel or Eliam and possibly the granddaughter of Ahithophel, the king’s adviser.
bathshua: 1. Canaanite wife of Judah who bore him three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah.
battering ram: Ancient military machine with a heavy wooden beam used to batter down gates or walls. Some battering rams had an iron ram’s head at the end of the beam.
battle-ax: Heavy ax with a wide blade used as a weapon of war.
battlement: Defensive wall, with openings for shooting, on top of a fortress; by extension, a parapet or railing around any flat roof. Houses in the Near East were built with flat roofs, which were used for many different purposes.
bavvai: Individual who directed the repair of a section of the Jerusalem wall under Nehemiah’s supervision. Bavvai was Henadad’s son and the official of half the district of Keilah, a town 17 miles (27.4 kilometers) southwest of Jerusalem.
bay tree: Tree 40 to 60 feet (12 to 18 meters) high with fragrant, evergreen leaves and native to the Holy Land.
bazlith, bazluth: Ancestor of a group of temple assistants returning to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile (Ezr 2:52, “Bazluth”; Neh 7:54).
bdellium: Substance mentioned twice in the OT, evidently the resinous gum of an Arabian shrub (known scientifically as Commiphora africana).
bealiah: Warrior from Benjamin’s tribe who joined David at Ziklag in his struggle against King Saul. Bealiah was one of David’s ambidextrous archers and slingers.
bealoth: 1. Town along the border of Edom in the Negev Desert area.
beam: 1. Weaver’s beam—round wooden roller on which the cloth or carpet was wound during the weaving process in Bible times.
bean: Any of various plants of the legume family, and part of the diet of the peoples of Bible lands.
bear (animal): Large, short-tailed, shaggy animal that feeds on plants as well as small animals. The bear mentioned several times in the Bible is the Syrian brown bear still found in Syria and Turkey but no longer in Israel.
bear (astronomy): Constellation of stars (Ursa Major, also known as the Big Dipper) mentioned in Job 9:9 and 38:32.
beard: Hair growing on the lower part of a man’s face, worn as a sign of maturity among all ancient Semitic peoples, including the Israelites. Among the Israelites, care of the beard took on religious significance.
beast: Animal in both the OT and NT, having in some cases a figurative significance. The word has a variety of meanings in the OT.
beatitudes, the: Term derived from Latin beatitudo; it is not used in the English Bible. Technically it means “blessedness” as described in the OT and NT.
beautiful gate: Gate of Herod’s temple in Jerusalem where a man born lame was miraculously healed through the ministry of Peter and John.
beauty: Harmonious combination of qualities pleasant to see. Archaeological materials indicate that the ancient Hebrews were concerned more with usefulness than with beauty.
bebai (person): 1. Ancestor of a family that returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile.
bebai (place): Unidentified Israelite city mentioned in Judith 15:4.
becher, becherite: 1. Benjamin’s second son, who migrated to Egypt with his grandfather Jacob.
becorath: Zeror’s father, a member of Benjamin’s tribe and an ancestor of King Saul.
bectileth: Plain mentioned only in the Apocrypha. Nebuchadnezzar’s general, Holofernes, camped there on his western conquest.
bed: Items of material culture used in homes, palaces, and temples. Because of its close geographical proximity to other nations, Israel had extensive contact with neighboring cultures.
bedad: Father of Hadad, one of the kings of Edom before the Israelite monarchy.
bedan: 1. One of Israel’s deliverers, along with Gideon, Jephthah, and Samuel, during the time of the judges (1 Sm 12:11, KJV; RSV mg).
bedeiah: Bani’s son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile.
bee: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
beeliada: Former name of Eliada, one of King David’s sons, in 1 Chronicles 14:7.
beelzebul: Epithet meaning “lord of the flies” or “lord of the manure pile,” referring to Satan. It was used against Jesus by his enemies (Mt 10:25, KJV “Beelzebub”; 12:24; Lk 11:15).
beer: 1. Israelite campsite on their wilderness journey, probably just north of the Arnon River on the Moabite-Amorite border.
beera: Zophah’s son, a warrior in Asher’s tribe.
beerah: Chief of Reuben’s tribe taken captive by the Assyrian king Tilgath-pilneser (a later spelling of Tiglath-pileser).
beer-elim: One of the cities of Moab that Isaiah predicted would hear wailing at the fall of the Moabite kingdom; perhaps the same as Beer.
beer-lahairoi: Well between Kadesh and Bered where Hagar, pregnant with Ishmael, was confronted by the angel of the Lord. The name given to the site means “the well of the Living One who sees me,” referring to God’s appearance to Sarai’s servant girl.
beeroth: One of four Hivite cities that secured Joshua’s promise not to destroy them when the Israelites marched into Canaan. Beeroth was later identified as a city in Benjamin’s territory.
beeroth bene-jaakan: Site where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey from Egypt, near Moserah or Moseroth (Dt 10:6; see NLT mg); also called Bene-jaakan in Numbers 33:31-32. Beeroth Bene-jaakan means “well of Jaakan’s sons.” See Wilderness Wanderings.
beerothite: Inhabitant of Beeroth (2 Sm 4:2-9, KJV, RSV).
beersheba: Scriptural designation for the southern extremity of the Promised Land, located 28 miles (45.1 kilometers) southwest of Hebron. It was an important Negev site at an early time.
be-eshterah: City of the half-tribe of Manasseh given to the Levitical family of Gershonites in the partitioning of the Promised Land. The spelling is a shortened form for Beth-ashtaroth (“house or place of Ashtaroth”).
beggar: One who asks for charity, especially one who lives by begging, a mendicant.
beheading: Form of execution practiced in Bible times.
behemoth: Hebrew word in plural form usually translated “beasts” or “wild animals” (as in Dt 28:26; 32:24; Ps 50:10; Is 18:6; 2 Esd 6:49, 51; Hb 2:17).
behistun inscription: Term used to refer to writing in the ancient world that was done on a material of a permanent nature, such as stone or clay, rather than on ordinary and impermanent substances, such as papyri or parchment.
beka, bekah: Six-gram weight called “half a shekel, by the shekel of the sanctuary”.
beker, bekerite: Alternate spelling for Ephraim’s second son and his descendants.
bel: Title of the state god of Babylon, Marduk, mentioned disdainfully by Isaiah. Jeremiah speaks of Bel, and Bel is the idol in the apocryphal Bel and the Dragon.
bela (person): 1. Beor’s son, a king of Edom who ruled before Israel had a king.
bela (place): Alternate name for Zoar, a city of the plain, in Genesis 14:2.
belah, belaite: KJV rendering of Bela, Benjamin’s oldest son, in 1 Chronicles 8:1. His descendants were called Belaites (Nm 26:38-40; see NLT).
bel and the dragon: Part of the Deuterocanonical works, consists of three supplementary sections to the book of Daniel. This additional material is in the Greek translation of the OT book of Daniel, but not in the ancient Hebrew-Aramaic texts.
belial, beliar: Common Hebrew noun meaning “baseness,” “worthlessness,” “wickedness,” or “lawlessness.” Belial, however, is often rendered as a proper noun.
belief, believe: Conviction based on testimony that something is true or that someone is reliable. As used in the Bible, to believe in God involves the element of trust, not mere acknowledgment of his existence.
believers: Those who believe; in the NT, specifically, those who believe in Jesus as Lord and follow him. One would expect the term “believers” (sometimes translated “faithful”) to be a title for Christians, since the NT stresses belief in Jesus.
bell: Small noisemaker. Bells were intermittently attached between ornamental pomegranates around the lower hem of the high priestly robe.
belmain: Samaritan city that served as a camp for Nebuchadnezzar’s invading general, Holofernes, against the Jews. Probably the same as Balbaim (7:3), Balamon (8:3), and perhaps Bebai (15:4).
beloved disciple: Designation of one disciple, evidently the author of the Gospel of John.
belshazzar: Babylonian king who was co-regent with Nabonidus in the final days of the Babylonian Empire. His name means “Bel protect the king.” Daniel identifies him as the son of Nebuchadnezzar, though in fact he was the natural son of Nabunaid (Nabonidus).
belteshazzar: Daniel’s Babylonian name. Daniel was one of the young men taken captive to Babylon to be trained as counselors for King Nebuchadnezzar (ch 1).
bema: Greek term for a judgment seat or tribunal of a Roman official.
ben (noun): Hebrew word often used as a prefix to describe a relationship. Literally meaning “son,” it is found some 4,850 times in the OT.
ben (person): Levite musician appointed by King David (1 Chr 15:18, KJV).
ben-abinadab: One of 12 officers appointed to requisition food for King Solomon’s household. His administrative district comprised the area around Naphath-dor, the coastal city south of Mt Carmel.
benaiah: Popular name meaning “the Lord has built,” used primarily by Levites.
ben-ammi: Son born to Lot and his younger daughter. A similar incestuous liaison between Lot and his older daughter produced a son named Moab.
ben-deker: One of 12 officers appointed to requisition food for King Solomon’s household (1 Kgs 4:9, KJV “son of Dekar”). Ben-deker’s administrative district comprised an area along the southern border of Dan’s tribe near Beth-shemesh.
bene-berak: One of the cities of Dan. The modern name is Ibn Ibrak, a suburb northwest of Tel Aviv.
benediction: Pronouncement of God’s favor upon an assembled congregation.
bene-jaakan: Place where Israel camped near Edom’s border.
ben-geber: Literally, “Geber’s son,” an official in King Solomon’s court who administered the sixth of 12 districts. Ben-geber’s area of responsibility began at Ramoth-gilead in northern Transjordan and extended north as far as Argob in Bashan.
ben-hadad: Title of two or possibly three kings of Syria, meaning “son of Hadad.” Hadad was the Syrian storm god probably identical with Rimmon.
ben-hail: One of five officials sent out by King Jehoshaphat of the southern kingdom of Judah to teach the people the law of the Lord.
ben-hesed: One of the 12 officers appointed to requisition food for King Solomon’s household (1 Kgs 4:10, KJV “son of Hesed”). His administrative district comprised an area south and west of Arubboth in the western part of Manasseh’s tribe.
ben-hur: One of 12 officers appointed to requisition food for King Solomon’s household (1 Kgs 4:8, KJV “son of Hur”). His district was the hill country of Ephraim.
beninu: Levite who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God with Nehemiah and others after the exile.
benjamin (person): 1. Youngest of Jacob’s 12 sons and full brother to Joseph.
benjamin, gate of: One of the gates in Jerusalem’s old wall. The Gate of Benjamin was probably at the northeast corner, since the prophet Jeremiah passed through it on his way to Benjamin’s territory northeast of Jerusalem.
benjamin, tribe of: One of the smallest of the 12 tribes of Israel, made up of descendants of Jacob’s youngest son.
beno: Jaaziah’s son in a list of Levites assigned to temple duty. It is possible that the Hebrew word is not a proper name; it has sometimes been translated “his son.”
ben-oni: Name Rachel gave to her last son as she died in childbirth. His father, Jacob, changed his name from Ben-oni (“son of my sorrow”) to Benjamin (“son of my right hand”).
ben sirach, jesus: Son of Sirach and author of Wisdom of Jesus ben Sirach (also known as Ecclesiasticus).
beon: Alternate name for Baal-meon, a city east of the Jordan, in Numbers 32:3.
bera: Ruler of Sodom in the days of Abraham and Lot. Bera was one of five Canaanite city kings who unsuccessfully rebelled against King Chedorlaomer of Elam and his three allies.
beracah: Warrior from Benjamin’s tribe who joined David at Ziklag in his struggle against King Saul. Beracah was one of David’s ambidextrous archers and slingers.
beracah, valley of: Place where King Jehoshaphat gathered the people of Judah to praise the Lord. The people were grateful for God’s help in defeating the attacking armies of Moab, Ammon, and Mt Seir.
berachiah: KJV spelling of Berechiah, Asaph’s father, in 1 Chronicles 6:39.
beraiah: One of Shimei’s sons from Benjamin’s tribe.
berea: 1. Place north of Jerusalem where the Syrian army camped before launching an attack that killed Judas Maccabeus in 161 BC.
berechiah: 1. Son of Zerubbabel and descendant of King David.
bered (person): Alternate name for Beker, one of Ephraim’s sons, in 1 Chronicles 7:20.
bered (place): Unknown site in Israel’s southern Negev Desert region. God spoke to Sarai’s maid, Hagar, at a well between Kadesh and Bered.
beri: Zophah’s son, head of a subclan. Beri was a skilled warrior listed with Asher’s descendants.
beriah: 1. Asher’s son, who migrated to Egypt with his family, relatives, and grandfather Jacob.
beriite: Member of a family descended from Beriah, one of Asher’s sons.
berite: KJV rendering of Bichrite, a descendant of Bichri, in 2 Samuel 20:14.
bernice: Eldest daughter of Herod Agrippa I. Bernice was present during the apostle Paul’s speech before her brother King Agrippa II.
berodach-baladan: KJV spelling of Merodach-baladan, the king of Babylon during the reign of Judah’s King Hezekiah, in 2 Kings 20:12.
beroea: 1. Place north of Jerusalem where the Syrian army camped before launching an attack that killed Judas Maccabeus in 161 BC.
berothah, berothai: City between Damascus and Hamath mentioned by the prophet Ezekiel as lying on the northern border of the restored Israel. Berothah is probably the same as Berothai, a city captured by David (2 Sm 8:8; called Cun in 1 Chr 18:8).
berothite: KJV form of Beerothite, an inhabitant of Beeroth, in 1 Chronicles 11:39.
berry: Fleshy fruit, usually with many seeds and having no stony seed covering.
beryl: Hard, lustrous mineral of various colors, mentioned in the Bible as a gemstone.
besai: Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile.
besodeiah: Meshullam’s father. Along with Joiada, Meshullam helped rebuild a portion of the Jerusalem wall after the exile in Babylonia.
besom: Old English word meaning “broom” (Is 14:23, KJV). The besom, or broom, of destruction is a Near Eastern metaphor signifying total destruction.
besor, brook of: Brook that David crossed to pursue the Amalekites southward after they had raided Ziklag, his home base. Exhausted, 200 of David’s men remained at the brook while the other 400 overtook and defeated the enemy.
betah: Alternate name for Tibhath, a town in the city-kingdom of Aram-zobah, subjugated by King David, in 2 Samuel 8:8.
beten: City allotted to Asher’s tribe for an inheritance, mentioned between Hali and Achshaph.
bethabara: Village where messengers from the Pharisees questioned John the Baptist (Jn 1:28, KJV). Modern translations have “Bethany” instead of Bethabara in accordance with superior manuscript evidence.
beth-anath: Town assigned to Naphtali’s tribe from which the tribe failed to drive out the original inhabitants. The Israelites, who often made slaves of the remaining Canaanite people, were in many cases eventually corrupted by their pagan religious practices.
beth-anoth: Village in the hill country assigned to Judah’s tribe after the Israelite conquest of Canaan.
bethany: 1. Village on the eastern slope of the Mt of Olives about a mile and a half (2.4 kilometers) east of Jerusalem.
beth-arabah: One of six cities in the wilderness southeast of Jericho on the boundary between the territories of Judah and Benjamin. The modern Ain Gharbeh in the Wadi el-Quelt may be the site of Beth-arabah.
beth-aram: KJV rendering of Beth-haram, a Gadite town, in Joshua 13:27.
beth-arbel: Town whose violent destruction at the hands of the Assyrians was compared by the prophet Hosea to Ephraim’s forthcoming destruction.
beth-ashbea: Place where certain families descended from Judah were known for their production of linen. The KJV renders “Ashbea” as a family name rather than a place of residence.
beth-aven: 1. Town in Benjamin’s territory, located west of Michmash on the border of the wilderness, near Ai, to the east of Bethel.
beth-azmaveth: Alternate name for Azmaveth, a town near Jerusalem, in Nehemiah 7:28.
beth-baal-meon: Alternate name for Baal-meon, a city in Reuben’s territory, in Joshua 13:17.
beth-barah: Place where warriors of Ephraim’s tribe under Gideon tried to block the retreat of the Midianites over the Jordan River.
bethbasi: Town in the Judean wilderness where Jonathan and Simon Maccabeus took refuge from General Bacchides and, having fortified it successfully, withstood the onslaught of the Syrian forces.
beth-biri: Alternate name for Lebaoth, a city in Judah’s southern territory.
beth-car: Place in Benjamin’s territory to which a Philistine army was pursued by the Israelites after the second battle of Ebenezer.
beth-dagon: Shrine of the Philistine and Canaanite god Dagon mentioned in several sources other than the Bible. A fortress called Dagon near Jericho was mentioned by the Jewish historian Josephus, for example.
beth-diblathaim: Town in Moab, and probably identical with Almon-diblathaim.
beth-eden: Small Aramean (Syrian) state north of Damascus. Assyria conquered Beth-eden and deported its people to Kir, fulfilling the prediction in Amos 1:5 (KJV “house of Eden”).
beth-eked: Place between Jezreel and Samaria where Jehu killed Ahaziah’s kinsmen at a pit or cistern (2 Kgs 10:12, 14, KJV “shearing house”).
bethel (god): Pagan deity mentioned in ancient texts and thought by some to have biblical reference.
bethel (place), bethelite: 1. Important OT city located about 11 miles (17.7 kilometers) north of Jerusalem on the north-south ridge road at the tribal borders of Benjamin and Ephraim.
beth-emek: Town on the territorial boundary between the tribes of Asher and Zebulun.
bether: Hebrew word occurring in the phrase “upon rugged mountains” and regarded as a proper name in the KJV (“mountains of Bether,” Sg 2:17).
bethesda: Name of a pool in Jerusalem to which many sick and infirm people came.
beth-ezel: One of several small towns, probably in southwest Judah, whose destruction was lamented by the prophet Micah (1:11).
beth-gader: Town mentioned in connection with its founder, Hareph, a Calebite.
beth-gamul: City of Moab against which Jeremiah prophesied God’s judgment for their ill treatment of Israel. It has been identified as Khirbet Jumeil, located eight miles (12.9 kilometers) east of Dibon.
beth-gilgal: Town from which Levitical singers came to Jerusalem to celebrate the rebuilding of the wall under Nehemiah.
beth-haggan: Town to which King Ahaziah of Judah fled for his life from Jehu of Israel. Beth-haggan was probably the same as En-gannim.
beth-hakkerem: Town in the hilly area between Jerusalem and Bethlehem. The prophet Jeremiah referred to signal fires set at Beth-hakkerem to warn of invasion from the north.
beth-haram, beth-haran: Town given to Gad’s tribe at the partitioning of Canaan. Fortified and used to accommodate sheep herds, it is probably the same as Beth-aramphtha, a city mentioned by the Jewish historian Josephus.
beth-hoglah: City allotted to Benjamin’s tribe. It was southeast of Jericho near the mouth of the Jordan River on the boundary line between the territories of Judah and Benjamin.
beth-horon: Canaanite place-name perhaps meaning “the house of Hauron,” the god of the underworld. Beth-horon was a dual settlement 10 and 12 miles (16.1 and 19.3 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem.
beth-jeshimoth: City assigned to Reuben’s tribe, later described as a Moabite town. Prior to Israel’s conquest of the Promised Land, they made camp along the Jordan from Beth-jeshimoth to Abel-shittim.
beth-leaphrah: Town mentioned by the prophet Micah. Since Beth-leaphrah (KJV “house of Aphrah”) means “house of dust,” Micah made a sarcastic pun by telling its idolatrous inhabitants to “roll in the dust” (Mi 1:10, NLT).
beth-lebaoth: Alternate name for Lebaoth, a city of Simeon in the southern extremity of Judah’s tribe, in Joshua 19:6.
bethlehem: 1. “City of David” and the birthplace of Jesus Christ, five miles (8 kilometers) south of Jerusalem.
beth-maacah, beth-maachah: Alternate name for Abel-beth-maacah in 2 Samuel 20:14-15.
beth-marcaboth: City in Judah’s territory given to the tribe of Simeon, possibly the same as Madmannah. The name Beth-marcaboth means “house of chariots,” and consequently some have seen a link to the chariot cities of Solomon.
beth-meon: Alternate name for Baal-meon, a town formerly belonging to Reuben’s tribe, in Jeremiah 48:23.
beth-millo: House or fortress associated with the city of Shechem mentioned in connection with the crowning of Abimelech (son of Gideon) as king there.
beth-nimrah: Moabite city given to and rebuilt by Gad’s tribe at the partitioning of Canaan, the Promised Land. Beth-nimrah has been identified with modern Tell el-Bleibil, eight miles (12.9 kilometers) east of the Jordan River.
beth-palet: KJV spelling of Beth-pelet, a city of Judah, in Joshua 15:27.
beth-pazzez: City given to Issachar’s tribe at the partitioning of the Promised Land, apparently near Mt Tabor.
beth-pelet: City assigned to Judah at the partitioning of the Promised Land. Later resettled by the people of Judah after the return from exile in Babylon, Beth-pelet was possibly the hometown of David’s warrior Helez the Paltite (2 Sm 23:26; 1 Chr 11:27, “Pelonite”).
beth-peor: Moabite city given to Reuben’s tribe in the partitioning of the Promised Land. Prior to the Israelites’ entrance into the land of Canaan, they made camp in a valley opposite Beth-peor.
bethphage: Village on the Mt of Olives adjacent to Jerusalem. At Bethphage two disciples obtained the donkey colt on which Jesus rode into Jerusalem.
beth-phelet: KJV spelling of Beth-pelet, a city of Judah, in Nehemiah 11:26.
beth-rapha: Place or clan name listed among the descendants of Eshton in Judah’s tribe.
beth-rehob: City or district mentioned in Judges 18:28 and 2 Samuel 10:6; probably the northernmost point reached by the 12 Israelite spies when they searched out the land of Canaan. It is probably identifiable with Rehob.
bethsaida: 1. Town northeast of the Sea of Galilee.
beth-shan, beth-shean: Strategic Palestinian town located in the subtropical Jordan Valley 15 miles (24.1 kilometers) south of the Sea of Galilee and 4 miles (6.4 kilometers) west of the Jordan River.
beth-shemesh: 1. Canaanite city on the northern border of Judah’s territory and the southern border of Dan’s (before that tribe migrated north).
beth-shittah: Town between the Jordan River and the valley of Jezreel to which the Midianites fled when defeated by Gideon.
beth-tappuah: Town in the hill country of Judah’s territory named “place of fruit trees” because of its high ridge location and many fruitful orchards. Beth-tappuah is identified with modern Taffuh about four miles (6.4 kilometers) northwest of Hebron.
beth-togarmah: Hebrew phrase meaning “house of Togarmah,” referring to the nation descended from Gomer’s son of this name, and which traded with Tyre.
bethuel (person): Youngest son of Abraham’s brother Nahor and his wife, Milcah. Bethuel was thus Abraham’s nephew.
bethuel, bethul (place): One of the cities allotted to Simeon’s tribe within Judah’s inheritance.
bethulia: Town described in the book of Judith as being near Dothan on a hill overlooking the plain of Esdraelon. Nebuchadnezzar’s general, Holofernes, tried to bring Bethulia into submission by controlling its water sources.
beth-zaith: City where Bacchides, a Syrian general of the Maccabean period, camped after his massacre of 60 Hasidian Jews in Jerusalem. At Beth-zaith more Jews were slaughtered and thrown into a pit.
beth-zatha: Variant name for the pool in Jerusalem. The name is generally believed to mean “house of olives,” occurring only in John 5:2.
beth-zechariah: Place 10 miles (16.1 kilometers) southwest of Jerusalem where Judas Maccabeus was defeated by a Seleucid ruler, Antiochus V Eupator, son of Antiochus Epiphanes.
beth-zur: Hill town of Judah in the mountains north of Hebron. Beth-zur was settled by Maon, one of Caleb’s descendants, and was one of the natural strongholds of Judah.
betomasthaim, betomesthaim: Unidentified place located near Dothan, mentioned in the book of Judith. The inhabitants of Betomasthaim and Bethulia were ordered by the high priest to block the advancing Assyrian army that was led by Holofernes.
betonim: City in the territory assigned to Gad’s tribe for an inheritance. It has been identified with modern Khirbet Bat-neh, 16 miles (25.7 kilometers) northeast of Jericho.
betrothal: First stage of marriage transaction; engagement.
beulah: Hebrew word used once in the KJV as a proper name for Jerusalem, denoting a promised blessing for the people of God.
bezai: 1. Ancestor of a group of people who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile.
bezaleel, bezalel: 1. Uri’s son and the master craftsman from Judah’s tribe who was specially equipped by God to be in charge of the construction and furnishing of the tabernacle In the KJV the name is Bezaleel.
bezek: 1. Site of a major victory for the tribes of Simeon and Judah over the Perizzites and Canaanites.
bezer (place): City of refuge in Reuben’s desert territory east of the Jordan River, later allotted to the Merari family of Levites. It is probably a variant spelling of Bozrah in Jeremiah 48:24.
bible: Derived from the Greek biblia (“books”), which, though plural, came to be used as a singular noun and to stand for the collection of books known as the Scriptures. The idea of a collection of holy writings developed early in Hebrew-Christian thought.
bible, canon of the: Those books in the Jewish and Christian Bible considered to be Scripture and therefore authoritative in matters of faith and doctrine.
bible, inspiration of the: Theological term for the influence God exerted on the writers of Scripture, enabling them to transmit his revelations in writing.
bible, manuscripts and text of the (old: Bible, Manuscripts and Text of the (Old Testament)

Copies of the OT books produced by scribes and editions made from these copies. The ancient manuscripts of the OT are the basic working material used to seek out the original text of the Bible with as great a degree of accuracy as possible.
bible, manuscripts and text of the (new: Bible, Manuscripts and Text of the (New Testament)
Copies of the NT books produced by scribes and editions made from these copies.
bible, quotations of the old testament i: Bible, Quotations of the Old Testament in the New Testament
OT passages cited or alluded to in the NT writings.
bible, versions of the (ancient): To get a picture of how the Bible has come to different peoples in the world, spread out a map of the eastern hemisphere and imagine Palestine as the center of a pool.
bible, versions of the (english): Translations of the Bible in the English language.
bichri, bichrite, bicri: Sheba’s father in Benjamin’s tribe. Sheba led a revolt against King David.
bidkar: Aide of King Jehu of the northern kingdom of Israel. Bidkar fulfilled a prophecy about the fate of Ahab’s family by throwing the body of Joram, Ahab’s son, into Naboth’s field after Jehu had killed Joram.
bigamy: Marriage to a second wife while still legally married to another.
bigtha: Eunuch who served King Ahasuerus of Persia. He and six others were in charge of the royal household.
bigthan, bigthana: Eunuch who served King Ahasuerus of Persia as a palace guard. He and a fellow guard named Teresh planned an assassination attempt on the king’s life.
bigvai: 1. Ancestor of a group of people who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile.
bildad: One of three friends who came to comfort Job in his anguish, identified as a Shuhite. That term suggests that he was a descendant of Shuah, son of Abraham and his second wife Keturah.
bileam: Alternate name for Ibleam, a Levitical city in Manasseh’s territory, in 1 Chronicles 6:70.
bilgah: 1. Head of the 15th of 24 divisions of priests whom King David assigned to official duties in the temple.
bilgai: Priest who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God with Nehemiah and others after the exile; possibly the same person as Bilgah in Nehemiah 12:18.
bilhah (person): Servant given by Laban to his daughter Rachel when she married Jacob. Realizing her own childlessness, Rachel gave Bilhah to her husband as a concubine and accepted their two sons as her own, naming them Dan and Naphtali (30:3-8; 35:25; 46:25).
bilhah (place): Town in the territory allotted to Simeon’s tribe, probably identical with Baalah and Balah (19:3).
bilhan: 1. Ezer’s firstborn son and a descendant of Seir.
bilshan: One, who with Nehemiah and Zerubbabel, led a group of Jews to Jerusalem following the exile.
bimhal: Japhlet’s son, a great warrior and head of a clan in Asher’s tribe.
binding and loosing: Biblical concept much discussed and debated throughout Christian history. Jesus referred to binding and loosing on two different occasions.
binea: Moza’s son from Benjamin’s tribe and a descendant of King Saul through Jonathan’s line.
birds: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
birsha: Ruler of Gomorrah in the days of Abraham and Lot. Birsha was one of five Canaanite city-kings who unsuccessfully rebelled against King Chedorlaomer of Elam and his three allies.
birth, new: Means of receiving “spiritual life” and entering the kingdom of God.
birthright: Right or privilege belonging to the firstborn son in a Hebrew family. The eldest son ranked highest after the father and in the father’s absence had the father’s authority and responsibility, as illustrated by Reuben’s relationship to his younger brothers.
birzaith, birzavith: Malchiel’s son of Asher’s tribe. Since parallel lists fail to mention him, it is possible that Birzaith (KJV “Birzavith”) was the name of a city Malchiel founded.
bishlam: Resident of the vicinity of Jerusalem who opposed the rebuilding of the city after the exile. He and his associates wrote a letter complaining about the rebuilding to the Persian king Artaxerxes.
bishop: Official in the church whose qualifications are listed in 1 Timothy 3:2-7 and Titus 1:6-9.
bithiah: Mered’s wife. Bithiah may have been a princess, or the phrase “daughter of Pharaoh” (KJV) may merely indicate that she was Egyptian.
bithron: Term in 2 Samuel 2:29 (KJV; NLT mg) whose meaning is uncertain. Abner, commander of Ishbosheth’s army, fled through Bithron after losing a battle to David’s army.
bithynia: Roman province located in the northwest corner of Asia Minor. The apostle Paul and Silas wanted to preach the gospel in Bithynia on Paul’s second missionary journey but were prevented by the Holy Spirit from doing so.
bitter herbs: Some kind of bitter vegetable(s), perhaps a certain variety of lettuce. The people of Israel were commanded to eat bitter herbs, roast lamb, and unleavened bread on the night when the Lord inflicted the plague of death on all the Egyptian firstborn.
bittern: KJV translation for the Hebrew word that may designate some kind of bird. Most modern translations substitute the word “porcupine” in Isaiah 34:11.
bitterness or jealousy, water of: OT “trial” procedure employed when a husband suspected his wife of adultery but had no evidence to support his suspicion.
bitumen: Asphalt as found in its natural state; pitch, tar. “Bitumen” (KJV “slime”) was used for mortar in the Tower of Babel’s construction and to seal the reed basket in which baby Moses was concealed.
biziothiah, bizjothjah: Listed in Joshua 15:28 (KJV “Bizjothjah”) as a city in the Negev Desert area of Judah.
biztha: One of the seven eunuchs King Ahasuerus commanded to bring Queen Vashti to his drunken party.
black: The OT and NT have no exact word for “color,” although the word appears several times in our English Bibles. The words translated “color” have quite different meanings in the original languages.
black obelisk: Shaft of black limestone describing the military successes of Shalmaneser III of Assyria (858–824 BC) during the first 31 years of his reign.
blasphemy: Profane or contemptuous speech or writing about (or action toward) God. In a general sense, “blasphemy” can refer to any slander, including any word or action that insults or devalues another being.
blastus: Royal secretary to Herod Agrippa I. The cities of Tyre and Sidon were looked down upon by Herod, so when their delegates wanted an appointment with the king when he was in nearby Caesarea, they approached him through Blastus.
bless, blessing: Pronouncement of the favor of God upon an assembled congregation. Worship services, especially observances of Holy Communion in Eastern Orthodox, Roman Catholic, and most Protestant churches, usually end with a blessing spoken by the senior clergyman present.
blindness: Condition of lacking the ability to see. Physical blindness was common in the ancient Near East and is still prevalent among the poor and tribal peoples lacking the benefits of modern medicine.
blood: Fluid that circulates through the body of a person or a vertebrate animal. Aside from reference to the common physical substance, the term “blood” has a number of metaphorical uses in the Bible.
blood, avenger of: Person who sought justice by killing a murderer. The avenger of blood was usually the nearest relative of the one who had been murdered.
blood, field of: Name given to the field purchased with the “blood money” Judas accepted to betray Jesus. The field was purchased by the chief priests as a burial ground for strangers (formerly, the potter’s field).
blood, flow of: 1. Vaginal discharge such as that during menstruation.
bloodguilt: Term used in some English Bibles to translate a Hebrew word meaning “blood” or “bloods”. The translation “bloodguiltiness” occurs only in Psalm 51:14.
bloody sweat: Rare medical condition called hemohydrosis, thought to result from hemorrhage of small blood vessels into the sweat glands.
blue: The OT and NT have no exact word for “color,” although the word appears several times in our English Bibles. The words translated “color” have quite different meanings in the original languages.
boanerges: Name meaning “sons of thunder” given by Jesus to James and John, Zebedee’s sons. Its derivation is uncertain.
boar: Wild or domesticated animal of the swine family.
boast: To speak of deeds, abilities, or characteristics in a manner showing pride or self-satisfaction. In the Bible the word also has a more positive connotation (“to glory in”).
boat: Small watercraft. Boats mentioned in the Bible were propelled by oars or sails and used for fishing or travel, or as lifeboats on larger vessels.
boaz (person): Salmon’s son of Judah’s tribe. Boaz lived in Bethlehem in the days of the judges and married Ruth, a Moabite woman.
boaz (pillar): Name (meaning “strength”) given to one of the two pillars erected in front of King Solomon’s temple.
bocheru: Azel’s son, a descendant of King Saul.
bochim: Place near Gilgal mentioned in Judges 2:1-5 where the angel of the Lord confronted the nation of Israel with their failure to drive out the Canaanite inhabitants of the land. For their disobedience, judgment was pronounced.
bodily presence: Phrase used to describe the relation of Christ’s body to the elements of the Lord’s Supper.
bodily resurrection of christ: Act of being raised from the dead, used in the Bible in three different contexts: (1) It refers to miraculous raising of the dead back to earthly life, such as when Elijah raised a boy, Elisha raised the Shunammite’s son, Jesus raised both Jairus’s daughter…
body: Term used biblically in several different ways, including certain metaphorical or theological expressions. Many of the biblical references illustrate special features of Hebrew thought about human life.
body of christ: Scriptural phrase referring to (1) the physical body of Jesus Christ, (2) his broken body and shed blood viewed symbolically and memorially in the bread and wine of the Lord’s Supper, and (3) both the local and universal church viewed metaphorically.
bohan, stone of: Stone marking the northeast boundary between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. Bohan, a descendant of Reuben, is not mentioned elsewhere in the OT.
boil: Inflamed localized swelling on the skin. In modern medicine the term “boil” is restricted to a pus-filled swelling caused by infectious germs, usually staphylococci.
bond, bondage: Anything that fastens or restrains; subjection or slavery. The basic concept in Hebrew and Greek words translated “bond” or “bondage” is “loss of freedom.” The concept connotes servitude to another.
bondage, house of: Expression used in the OT for Egypt, where Israel was enslaved before the exodus.
bondmaid, bondman, bondservant: A person under obligation to serve a master, who in turn would provide a measure of protection. Some servants were slaves under legal bondage; others were servants voluntarily.
bone: One of the separate parts of the human or animal skeleton. After death, bones retain their form long after the soft tissues have decomposed, so bones are often associated with dead bodies or with death itself.
book: A set of written sheets or a scroll—whether composed of wood, parchment, papyrus, or paper—containing records or a literary composition.
book of life: Term used to refer to a heavenly record. The phrase appears seven times in the NT: Philippians 4:3; Revelation 3:5; 13:8; 17:8; 20:12, 15; 21:27.
book of remembrance: Divine record of the names of those who fear God, referred to once in the OT (Mal 3:16, NLT “scroll”). The prophet Malachi was struggling against moral decline in his day.
book of the covenant: Term occurring in two OT contexts. It describes, first, a document read by Moses to the people of Israel at Mt Sinai, and second, a document discovered in the temple by Hilkiah the priest at the time of King Josiah’s program of repairing the temple.
book of the dead: Modern name (nonbiblical) given to ancient Egyptian funerary (burial) texts. In the broadest sense, it designates all such texts, whether found on pyramid walls, coffins, or papyri.
book of the law: Term occurring in two OT contexts. It describes, first, a document read by Moses to the people of Israel at Mt Sinai, and second, a document discovered in the temple by Hilkiah the priest at the time of King Josiah’s program of repairing the temple.
booth: Small, temporary hut or shelter constructed of branches and sticks when permanent buildings were unavailable. Booths provided shade during the day and protection from the dew and winds during the night.
booths, feast of: One of the three great festivals of Israel, celebrating the completion of the agricultural year. The Jews built booths (temporary shelters) to commemorate their deliverance from Egypt by the hand of God.
booz: KJV form of Boaz in Matthew 1:5 and Luke 3:32.
bor-ashan: Alternate name for Ashan, a town originally assigned to Judah’s tribe, in 1 Samuel 30:30.
born again: Expression used by Jesus in explaining to Nicodemus how one enters the kingdom of God.
borrow, borrowing: Receiving money or goods that one pledges to return. The Mosaic law regulated borrowing and lending.
boscath: KJV form of Bozkath, a city in Judah, in 2 Kings 22:1.
bosor (person): KJV form of Beor, Balaam’s father, in 2 Peter 2:15.
bosor (place): City in Gilead captured by Judas Maccabeus in order to rescue the Jews living there. Today this city is known as Busr El-Hariri.
bottomless pit: Phrase used in the Bible to denote the abode of the dead and of demonic forces. The Hebrew word (literally “the deep”) is translated “abyss” in many versions of the Bible.
bow: The archer used bow and arrows in peace and war. Nomads, hunters, raiders, and warriors used this weapon throughout the biblical period.
bowels: A portion of the intestines. The word was also used metaphorically in the KJV to connote the place where pity, mercy, and tenderness are felt (see Phil 1:8; 2:1-2).
bowels, disease of: Term used 37 times in Scripture (KJV) but only once in connection with a disease. The evil King Jehoram was punished with an incurable chronic disease of the bowels, which resulted in his painful death two years later.
bowl: The manufacture of clayware and earthenware.
bowman: The archer used bow and arrows in peace and war. Nomads, hunters, raiders, and warriors used this weapon throughout the biblical period.
box tree: KJV translation of a tree of uncertain identity in Isaiah 41:19 and 60:13, called “pine” in the RSV.
bozez: One of a pair of distinctive rocks (Seneh was the other) flanking the road between Michmash and Gaba. Jonathan and his armor bearer scaled one of these crags to take on a Philistine outpost.
bozkath: Town near Lachish and Eglon in Judah’s territory, home of King Josiah’s mother.
bozrah: 1. Well-fortified city in northern Edom, regarded as impossible to conquer because it was protected by cliffs on three sides.
bracelet: Ornamental band or chain worn on the wrist or arm in the ancient world.
bramble: Translation of several words designating a shrub with prickly stems and runners, often forming tangled masses of vegetation.
branch: Literally, a shoot or sprout from a tree or bush; figuratively, a messianic or other spiritual metaphor.
brass: A “mineral” is a naturally occurring substance, normally an ore that must be mined and treated before the metal can be extracted. A “metal” is a chemical element such as iron or copper, which is free from contamination by other materials.
brazen serpent: Piece of sculpture that God commanded Moses to make when the Israelites were being bitten by “fiery serpents”. The serpents had been sent as a judgment because the people were grumbling against God and against Moses.
bread: Food made from the dough of flour or meal from grain.
bread of the presence: Loaves of bread placed on a special table in the sanctuary or Holy Place of the tabernacle and later in the temple. Two other terms in the OT are used to describe the “bread of the Presence,” which means bread that has been set before the Lord’s face.
breakfast: First meal of the day, “breaking the fast.” See Family Life and Relations; Food and Food Preparation.
breaking of bread: Phrase used in the NT in reference to the Lord’s Supper.
breastpiece, breastplate: 1. Part of the ceremonial garment of the high priest.
briar: Prickly or thorny bush, frequently mentioned in the Bible.
bribe, bribery: To give a person in authority something valuable in order to influence that person’s decision or action. Bribery was prohibited under OT law and condemned by the prophets.
brick, brick kiln: Oblong block of shaped mud or clay that has been dried either by the sun or by burning in a kiln for use in building or paving, and the furnace in which bricks are burned and hardened.
bride and bridegroom: Terms used for a woman and man about to be married or just married; also used to describe the relation of Christ to his church.
bridechamber: Room in which the marriage ceremonies were held.
bride of christ: One of the NT metaphors for the church. In it Christ is pictured as a husband, and the church as his bride.
brier: Prickly or thorny bush, frequently mentioned in the Bible.
brimstone: Old name for the nonmetallic element sulfur, literally “the stone that burns.” Sulfur ignites at a relatively low temperature and burns to produce acrid fumes of sulfur dioxide. Sulfur occurs naturally in volcanic regions such as the valley of the Dead Sea.
broad wall, the: Section of the outer wall of Jerusalem that Nehemiah rebuilt in the fifth century BC. The Broad Wall was possibly located on the city’s northwest side.
bronze: Durable alloy of copper and tin widely used for ornaments, weapons, coins, and other purposes in ancient times.
bronze sea: Large tank of water in Solomon’s temple yard for the priests’ washing.
bronze serpent, bronze snake: Piece of sculpture that God commanded Moses to make when the Israelites were being bitten by “fiery serpents”. The serpents had been sent as a judgment because the people were grumbling against God and against Moses.
brood: Term often used in the Bible for young birds, especially of the domestic fowl. Also used of snakes or vipers, as a metaphor for “sinners”.
brook: Intermittent stream or torrent in the arid and semiarid regions of the Middle East. Although the streambeds were usually dry, they could attain flood stage during spring runoff or after heavy rainfalls.
brook of egypt: Natural border between the Negev Desert area of Israel and the Sinai Peninsula, about 50 miles (80.5 kilometers) southwest of Gaza. The brook of Egypt, modern Wadi el-Arish, flows only during the rainy season.
brook of the arabah: Unidentifiable brook presumably draining into the Arabah. The Arabah is part of the desert rift extending from the Sea of Galilee to East Africa.
broom: Palestinian shrub or bush that often grows quite large, providing shade. KJV translates the Hebrew word as “juniper.” See Plants.
brother: Man or boy in his relationship to the other children of his parents; also a close male friend or fellow member of the same race, creed, profession, organization, and the like; a kinsman.
brothers (and sisters): Designation of those in the household of God. Good evidence exists that Jews at the time of Jesus frequently referred to themselves as brothers.
brothers of jesus: James, Joses (or Joseph), Simon, and Judas, identified in the NT as members of Jesus’ own family. They are described as visiting Jesus with Mary, his mother, and hearing Jesus’ statement that all who did the will of God were brother, sister, and mother to him.
buckler: Small, usually round shield carried in the hand or worn on the arm in battle.
build, building: Construction, usually with wood, masonry, and similar materials. The Bible has many references to the building or rebuilding of altars, temples, houses, and whole cities.
bukki: 1. Leader of Dan’s tribe who assisted Joshua in dividing up the land of Canaan.
bukkiah: Heman’s eldest son, who served with his father and 13 brothers as a temple musician.
bul: Eighth month of the preexilic Canaanite calendar. In this month King Solomon’s temple was completed.
bull, bullock: Male, adult and young, of any bovine animal, such as oxen, cattle.
bulrush: Any of a number of reed plants that grow in marshes and beside streams and rivers.
bunni: 1. Levite who sang praise to God after Ezra’s public reading of the law.
burial, burial customs: The Bible makes frequent reference to burial practices. A society’s burial customs are a reflection of its views about death and the afterlife.
burning bush: Flaming bush on Mt Horeb, where Moses experienced God’s presence and received the commission to lead the people of Israel out of Egypt.
burnt offering: Form of Israelite sacrifice in which a choice animal offered to make atonement for sin was completely consumed by fire.
bush: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
bushel: 1. Small vessel (“basket,” NLT) that could cover a light.
butler: Translation of a Hebrew word meaning “cupbearer” or “wine taster” in Genesis 40 and 41.
buz (person): 1. Abraham’s nephew, and one of Nahor’s eight sons.
buz (place): Place of uncertain location mentioned along with two Arabian villages or oases, Dedan and Tema.
buzite: Resident of Buz. Elihu, one of Job’s protagonists, is described as being the son of Barachel the Buzite.
buzzard: Any of a number of birds of prey declared ritually unclean.
cabbon: Town in the foothills of Judah east of Lachish, identified with Hebra and sometimes equated with Macbenah.
cabul: 1. Asherite town near Mt Carmel on the border between Israel and Tyre.
caesarea: City named in honor of Augustus Caesar, built by Herod the Great from 22 to 10 BC. The 8,000-acre (3,240-hectare) site lies 25 miles (40 kilometers) south of modern Haifa, in the beautiful plain of Sharon on Israel’s Mediterranean coast.
caesarea philippi: City at the northern extremity of Palestine, on the southern slopes of Mt Hermon near the ancient city of Dan. Caesarea Philippi lies in a beautiful area on one of the three sources of the Jordan River, the Wadi Banias.
caesars, the: Succession of Roman emperors. The name Caesar, which has derivatives in the German Kaiser, Dutch Keizer, and Russian Czar, goes back to the family name of Julius Caesar (100–44 BC), which his successors took to themselves.
caesar's household: Term referring to imperial servants, both slave and free, in Rome and in the provinces of the Roman Empire. The apostle Paul closed his letter to the Philippian Christians with greetings from those “of Caesar’s household” (4:22, RSV).
caiaphas: High priest during the life and ministry of Jesus. As official head of the Jewish state, Caiaphas presided over the council, or Sanhedrin—its highest court.
cain (person): First son of Adam and Eve, who became a tiller of the soil while his brother, Abel, was a keeper of sheep. Cain’s murder of Abel became proverbial of similarly violent and destructive sins.
cain (place): KJV spelling of Kain, the name of a city in the southern hill country of Judah’s territory, in Joshua 15:57.
cainan: 1. A son of Arphaxad (Lk 3:36; Gn 10:24, LXX; 11:12-13).
calah: One of the ancient capital cities of Assyria built by Nimrod. Calah is the ancient name for modern Nimrud, which is located 24 miles (38.6 kilometers) south of Nineveh on the east bank of the Tigris River.
calcol: One of Mahol’s three sons and a member of Judah’s tribe (1 Kgs 4:31, KJV “Chalcol”; 1 Chr 2:6). He and his brothers were noted for their wisdom and musical abilities.
caleb: 1. Son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite and older brother of Kenaz.
caleb-ephrathah: Possibly a Hebrew place-name (1 Chr 2:24, KJV, NLT). A number of modern translations follow the Septuagint (early Greek translation of the OT) in treating Ephrathah as the name of one of Caleb’s wives instead of a place.
calendars, ancient and modern: Systematic arrangements showing the beginning and length of each year and its division into days, weeks, and months. The modern calendar is usually taken for granted.
calf: Domestic animals of the bovine species (Bos primigenius). The OT often emphasized the beauty of cattle.
calf, golden: Calf-shaped idol fashioned at the Israelites’ request from their own gold jewelry. Under Aaron’s supervision, the idol was created while Moses was receiving the Ten Commandments on Mt Sinai.
call, calling: In modern English, terms referring to the selection of a leader or representative by a group of people. An element of choice is involved, since usually there are several candidates out of whom one must be chosen.
callisthenes: A Syrian in General Nicanor’s army who set fire to the temple gates during the persecution of the Jews by Antiochus Epiphanes. After Nicanor’s defeat in 165 BC, Callisthenes and others responsible for burning the sacred gates were burned to death by the Jews.
calno: Alternate name for Calneh, a city in northern Syria, in Isaiah 10:9.
calvary: In Luke 23:33, KJV translation of Golgotha (“the skull”), the place of Jesus’ crucifixion.
camel: Domestic animal used as a means of travel and for carrying goods in the Near East.
camel's thorn: Low, thorny shrub whose root is used in making a fragrant ointment.
camon: KJV form of Kamon, the burial place of the Israelite judge Jair, in Judges 10:5.
camphire: KJV name for henna, a shrub with pale-green leaves and clusters of white, pink, or yellow blossoms that emit a delightful fragrance.
cana: Galilean town that was the scene of Jesus’ first miracle: changing water into wine at a wedding feast. Jesus was again in Cana when he told a nobleman that his son, who was seriously ill at Capernaum, would live.
canaan, canaanite: Palestinian territory (the Promised Land) west of the Jordan River, settled by the Israelites at the time of Joshua’s leadership.
canaanite deities and religion: Study of the polytheistic religion of the Canaanites has contributed much to our understanding of the religion of ancient Israel. The Hebrew theological and religious structures were given by God to a people who were influenced and affected by other religions.
candace: Title given to ancient Ethiopian queens. Philip, a leader in the early church, met and baptized an Ethiopian eunuch, who was a minister under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians.
candle, candlestick: KJV words more correctly translated as “lamp” and “lampstand.” Candles in the modern sense, typically made of wax and containing a wick, were unknown in ancient times.
cane: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
canker: KJV rendering of “gangrene” or “cancer” in 2 Timothy 2:17.
cankerworm: KJV translation of the Hebrew word meaning “locust.” See Animals (Locust).
canneh: Alternate name for Calneh, a city in northern Syria, in Ezekiel 27:23.
canon of the bible: Those books in the Jewish and Christian Bible considered to be Scripture and therefore authoritative in matters of faith and doctrine.
canticles: Alternate title for the biblical book Song of Songs, derived from the Latin name of the book, Canticum Canticorum.
capernaum: City of Galilee, mentioned only in the Gospels, which was the headquarters of much of Jesus’ ministry. It lay on the northwest side of the Sea of Galilee (or Lake of Gennesaret).
caper plant: Low, spreading plant whose fruit was used as an appetite stimulant.
caphar-salama: Village where a battle was fought between Judas Maccabeus and the Syrian commander Nicanor. After about 500 of Nicanor’s men had been killed, the fugitives took refuge in the “city of David,” so Caphar-salama must have been near Jerusalem.
caphtor, caphtorim, caphtorites: Place-name and the name of the people associated with the place. The Caphtorim among the Hamitic peoples in the “table of nations” are listed as the “sons” of Egypt (Gn 10:13-14; 1 Chr 1:12, KJV “Caphthorim”).
capital: In architecture, the uppermost part of a pillar, often ornately fashioned.
capital punishment: The science or philosophy of law is called jurisprudence. Although modern jurisprudence bears little resemblance to biblical concepts of law, the Scriptures have played a definite role in its development.
cappadocia: Plateau region of eastern Asia Minor intersected by mountain ranges. The name Cappadocia does not occur in the Hebrew OT.
captivity, the: Period when many inhabitants of the southern kingdom of Judah were exiled in Babylonia after Nebuchadnezzar’s conquest of Jerusalem (sixth century BC).
caravan: Traveling group of merchants, pilgrims, or others in Bible times who joined together for mutual protection. Usually travelers used pack animals to carry their wares or personal belongings.
carbon dating: In archaeology, a method of dating objects of organic material by using the radioactive isotope carbon-14.
carbuncle: Red or fiery colored stone such as a garnet or ruby; mentioned as one of the gems in the high priest’s breastplate.
carcas: One of King Ahasuerus’s seven counselors, in Esther 1:10.
carchemish: Ancient city commanding an important ford on the west bank of the upper Euphrates River, about 65 miles (104.6 kilometers) northeast of Aleppo. Today part of the ruin is located in Turkey and part in Syria.
careah: KJV spelling of Kareah, Johanan’s father, in 2 Kings 25:23.
caria: Region in southwest Asia Minor. When Simon was high priest at Jerusalem, Lucius, the Roman consul, sent a letter to King Ptolemy (reigned 145–116 BC) concerning friendly relations between Rome and Simon.
carmel: 1. Mountainous ridge extending about 20 miles (32.2 kilometers) along the Mediterranean Sea and jutting southeastward into the Jezreel Valley.
carmi: 1. One of Reuben’s sons; he accompanied his grandfather Jacob into Egypt and founded the family of Carmites.
carnaim: Important fortress city in Gilead after the Babylonian exile. Judas Maccabeus destroyed Carnaim, including its temple of Atargatis, the Syrian fish goddess.
carnelian: Variety of chalcedony that may vary in color from deep red to almost white; mentioned as one of the foundation jewels in the wall of the new Jerusalem.
carob tree: Evergreen leguminous tree commonly found throughout the Middle East, yielding edible pealike seeds contained in a pod.
carpenter: One who worked with timber, setting up the framework of houses, the roofing, windows, and doors. Often small structures were erected by the householder, but temples and palaces required specialized artisans where carpenters worked alongside stonemasons.
carpus: Man with whom the apostle Paul left his cloak at Troas. Paul instructed Timothy to bring it when he came to see him in prison.
carrion vulture: Bird of prey, also called the gier eagle in the KJV.
carshena: One of seven princes who were wise men of Persia and Media, and whom King Ahasuerus (Xerxes) consulted for legal advice.
casiphia: Place to which Ezra sent for Levites when he realized that his company of returnees from the exile lacked persons qualified for temple service. Casiphia was perhaps Ctesiphon on the Tigris River near modern Baghdad.
casluhim, casluhites: Descendants of Noah through his son Ham and grandson Mizraim (“Egypt” in some versions), and ancestors of the Philistines.
caspin: A town east of the Jordan River, probably the same place as Chaspho, although ancient and modern authorities differ on the precise location. The historian Josephus identifies Caspin with Maked.
cassia: Type of tree that produces a spice resembling cinnamon.
castor and pollux: Twin sons of Zeus according to Greek and Roman mythology. The apostle Paul sailed from Malta to Puteoli on a ship whose sign or figurehead was the “Twin Brothers”.
caterpillar: Wormlike larva of a butterfly, moth, and some other insects.
catholic letters: Traditional name for seven NT books (letters): James; 1 and 2 Peter; 1, 2, and 3 John; and Jude. The term “catholic” has been given various interpretations: (1) These letters express the views of all the apostles.
cattle: Domesticated bovine animals such as cows and oxen, but in the Bible sometimes also sheep and goats.
cauda: Small island south of Crete. The ship carrying the apostle Paul to Rome sought temporary refuge at Cauda during a storm.
caulk, caulker: A waterproofing substance, such as bitumen, and the one who puts it into the seams of a ship’s planking to make them watertight (Ez 27:9, KJV “calker”).
