cavalry: The means by which one nation seeks to impose its will upon another by force. An index to the importance of warfare in antiquity is provided by the amount of technical skill directed to perfecting devices for destruction and defense.
cedar: Tree indigenous to Palestine whose wood was used in construction.
cedron: KJV name for Kidron, the river valley between Jerusalem and the Mt of Olives, in John 18:1.
cenchrea, cenchreae: Seaport city that served the maritime needs of the larger city of Corinth, about eight miles (12.9 kilometers) to the west. Cenchrea is known as early as the fifth century BC in connection with an Athenian attack on Corinth.
cendebeus: Commander-in-chief of the seacoast of Syria-Palestine about 138 BC under Antiochus VII.
censer: Vessel used to burn incense. On the Day of Atonement, the high priest was to burn two handfuls of incense in the censer within the Holy of Holies before the Lord.
census: Registration and enumeration of a people, usually for purposes of war or taxation. A few censuses are mentioned in the Bible.
centurion: Commander of 100 men in the Roman army. There were generally six centurions in each cohort and ten cohorts in a legion.
cephas: Aramaic name of Simon Peter the apostle in John 1:42; 1 Corinthians 1:12; and Galatians 1:18.
cereal offering: RSV for “grain offering,“one of the several types of offerings to God that reflected consecration and commitment.
cerinthus: Gnostic heretic (died c. 100) whose heresy was condemned by the apostle John. Probably born in Egypt and reared a Jew, Cerinthus was leader of a group of Christians who had Gnostic tendencies.
certificate of divorce: Document a man was obligated to give to his wife if he divorced her.
chabris: Gothoniel’s son, and one of three magistrates of Bethulia. Chabris and his colleagues were rebuked by Judith for putting a time limit on how long they would wait for the Lord to deliver their city from the Assyrians.
chaereas: Brother of Timothy and governor of Gazara. Both Chaereas and Timothy were killed along with many others in the assault by the Maccabees on the city (vv 36-37).
chaff: Loose hulls separated from the edible grains by threshing and winnowing.
chalcedony: Kind of quartz, variously colored, usually grayish or milky.
chalcol: KJV spelling of Calcol, a man of wisdom, in 1 Kings 4:31.
chaldea, chaldeans: Ancient region in Mesopotamia and its inhabitants. The name comes from the Chaldean (or Kaldu) tribes that shared Babylonia in southeastern Mesopotamia with several other peoples, especially the Sumerians and Akkadians.
chalkstone: Literally “stones of chalk,” mentioned as illustrative of the destruction of the pagan altars in Judah. Chalk beds cap many of the Judean hills, and since the substance easily erodes, Isaiah’s prophecy is apt.
chalphi: Father of Judas, one of the two captains of Jonathan Maccabeus’s army who stood firm at the battle of Gennesarat when others fled after being ambushed. Jonathan, Judas, and the other captain, Mattathias, rallied the troops and repulsed the enemy.
chamberlain: Originally, a royal official in charge of the private quarters of the king. They sometimes had other significant tasks and had great influence with those in authority.
chambers of the south: Possibly a constellation of stars, or the vast stretches of southern sky without stars (Jb 9:9, KJV).
chameleon: Any of a number of lizards having the ability to change color rapidly, declared ritually unclean.
chamois: Small, goatlike antelope that lives primarily in the high mountains of Europe. In Deuteronomy 14:5 “chamois” is an inaccurate translation of the Hebrew word that is better rendered “mountain sheep.” See Animals (Sheep).
chanaan: KJV spelling of Canaan in Acts 7:11 and 13:19.
channels of the sea: Valleys or stream beds in the ocean floor. When the Lord delivered David from all his enemies and from King Saul, David praised God’s great power, which could expose the ocean floor with a blast of his breath.
chant: Recitation in song or monotonous voice.
chaos, waters of: In ancient thought, the primeval seas that were divided. The world was then situated between the “waters above” and “waters below,” or “the Deep”.
chaphenatha: A section of Jerusalem that Jonathan Maccabeus repaired to protect the city from enemy attack. Pinpointing the exact location has given rise to much unsettled debate.
chapiter: KJV rendering of capital, architecturally the uppermost part of a pillar.
charashim: KJV rendering of Ge-harashim, a valley on the plain of Sharon’s southern border, in 1 Chronicles 4:14.
charax: Place, possibly in the land of Tob, through which Judas Maccabeus and his army passed in the pursuit of their Syrian enemies.
charchemish: KJV spelling of the city Carchemish in 2 Chronicles 35:20.
chariot: Ancient two-wheeled vehicle pulled by animals, usually horses, and normally thought of as an instrument of war. Chariots were also used as a means of transportation for persons of rank or wealth, and for hunting.
charismata: Abilities the Holy Spirit gives to the church.
charm: Small object worn around the neck to ward off evil.
charmis: Melchiel’s son and one of three magistrates of Bethulia. Charmis and his colleagues were rebuked by Judith for putting a time limit on how long they would wait for the Lord to deliver their city from the Assyrians (8:9-27).
charran: KJV spelling of Haran, a Mesopotamian city, in Acts 7:2-4.
chaspho: Town east of the Sea of Galilee mentioned in 1 and 2 Maccabees. Judas and Jonathan Maccabeus led their army into Transjordan and “took Chaspho, Maked, and Bosor, and the other cities of Gilead”.
chebar: Canal in Babylonia. The prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles from the southern kingdom of Judah, received visions from God while living in the area of the Kebar Canal.
chedorlaomer: King of Elam who participated with three other kings in a campaign against five cities near the southern end of the Dead Sea plain. Although Kedorlaomer is initially third in the list (v 1), he was evidently the leader of the four kings.
cheese: Milk product produced by curdling milk, draining the whey, pressing the curds into cakes, and drying them. One of the earliest biblical references to cheese is in Job 10:10: “Didst thou not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese?” (RSV).
chelal: Pahath-moab’s son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile. Also spelled Kelal.
chelleans: People mentioned in the book of Judith. There is little agreement about the identity of the Chelleans, who are listed in connection with a campaign of Holofernes, chief general of Nebuchadnezzar’s army.
chelluh: KJV rendering of Keluhi, Bani’s son, in Ezra 10:35.
chelous: According to Judith 1:9, Chelous was one of the cities to which messengers were sent by King Nebuchadnezzar to procure aid for his campaign against Arphaxad.
chelub: 1. Shuhah’s brother and the father of Mehir from Judah’s tribe.
chelubai: Hezron’s son and the brother of Jerahmeel; alternately called Caleb in 1 Chronicles 2:18, 42.
chemarim, chemarims: Hebrew term often translated “idolatrous priests”. In the KJV this word appears in Zephaniah 1:4 as a proper name, spelled either Chemarim or Chemarims.
chemosh: Name of the national god of Moab; also associated with the Ammonites.
chenaanah: 1. Father of Zedekiah, the false prophet who incorrectly prophesied victory for kings Ahab and Jehoshaphat over the Syrians.
chenani: Levite who participated in Ezra’s public reading of the law after the exile.
chenaniah: 1. Levite chief who led processional singing when King David brought the ark of the covenant to the new tabernacle in Jerusalem.
chephar-ammoni, chephar-haammonai: City allotted to Benjamin’s tribe for an inheritance after the initial conquest of Canaan by Joshua.
chephirah: Hivite city included in a treaty with Joshua that the Gibeonites secured by deception. When the Israelites conquered the land of Canaan, Kephirah became the property of Benjamin’s tribe (18:26).
cheran: Dishon’s son, a member of the Horite tribe during Esau’s time.
cherethims, cherethites: Members of a tribal group that lived in southern Judah near Hebron, mentioned along with the Pelethites. The Kerethites were associated with the Philistines, according to Ezekiel 25:15-17 (cf.
cherith, the brook: Also rendered the “Kerith Ravine” (NIV), it was the place where the Lord told the prophet Elijah to hide from King Ahab during a famine Elijah had predicted. There he had sufficient water to drink and was fed by ravens each morning and evening.
cherub (place): One of five Babylonian cities from which Israelites who could not trace their ancestry returned after the exile.
cherub, cherubim: Winged creatures mentioned occasionally in Scripture (“cherubim” is the plural form of the Hebrew “cherub”). They belong to a supernatural created order along with the seraphim and angels.
chesalon: City in northern Judah near the border of Dan, situated on the northern slope of Mt Jearim; usually identified with modern Kesla, about nine miles (14.5 kilometers) west of Jerusalem.
chesed: Son of Milcah and Nahor, Abraham’s brother.
chesil: City situated along the borders of Edom in the Negev, allotted to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance. In parallel lists of towns Kesil is replaced by Bethul, Bethuel, and perhaps Bethel—not to be confused with the Bethel north of Jerusalem.
chestnut: KJV mistranslation for plane tree, a tree indigenous to Palestine.
chesulloth: Town in Issachar; also called Kisloth-tabor in Joshua 19:12. It is probably to be identified with the modern Iksal, about three miles (4.8 kilometers) southeast of Nazareth.
chezib: Alternate name for Aczib, a city in Judah’s territory, in Genesis 38:5.
chicken: Common domestic fowl raised for its edible eggs and flesh.
chidon: Threshing floor where Uzzah was struck down by God as he attempted to steady the ark of the covenant (1 Chr 13:9, NLT mg).
chief priest: Highest office in the hierarchy of priests and Levites. It was the chief priest who alone went into the Most Holy Place of the temple once a year to make atonement for the sins of the whole nation of Israel.
child: In Bible times, the family comprised members of a household, including not only parents and children, along with other relatives and concubines, but also servants, travelers, aliens, and anyone else who happened to be within the house and was therefore under the protection of the head of the family.
childless: Condition of being barren or childless. A closed womb was a personal tragedy in OT times.
children, song of the three: Addition to Daniel that begins with the “Prayer of Azariah”; the song is also called “Song of the Three Young Men.” See Daniel, Additions to.
children of eden: KJV name for the inhabitants of Beth-eden, an Aramaic city-state conquered by Assyria, in 2 Kings 19:12.
children of god: Expression designating human beings who have been born of God and have become part of his family. When the Bible speaks of God’s sons, it does not intend to exclude females.
chileab: David’s second son, and the first born to him by Abigail; alternately called Daniel in 1 Chronicles 3:1.
chilion: One of the two sons of Elimelech and Naomi. He married a Moabite girl named Orpah (v 4) and eventually died in Moab (v 5).
chilmad: Mesopotamian city listed with Haran, Canneh, Eden, and Asshur as traders with Tyre.
chimham: Son of Barzillai (according to Josephus), a very wealthy man who supplied David and his men with food while they were in Mahanaim during their flight from Absalom.
chinnereth, chinneroth: 1. Fortified town in the territory allotted to Naphtali’s tribe.
chios: Rocky, mountainous island in the east-central area of the Aegean Sea. On his third missionary journey, Paul’s ship anchored opposite Kios between stops at Mitylene and Samos en route to Jerusalem.
chisleu, chislev: Month in the Hebrew calendar, about mid-November to mid-December; also spelled Chislev or Chisleu.
chislon: Father of Elidad, leader of Benjamin’s tribe during the Israelites’ wilderness wanderings and one of those appointed by Moses to divide the land of Canaan among the tribes.
chitlish: City assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance.
chittim: Ancient Hebrew name for the island of Cyprus.
chiun: KJV form of Kaiwan, an Assyrian astral deity, in Amos 5:26.
chloe: Woman whose household members (possibly slaves) informed Paul in Ephesus of arguments in the Corinthian church. It is not known whether Chloe lived in Corinth or Ephesus, or even whether she herself was a believer.
choba: Village mentioned in the book of Judith as being fortified by the Jews when Assyrian commander Holofernes invaded Palestine.
choinix: Dry commodity measure equivalent to a little more than a quart (one liter) (Rv 6:6; see NLT mg). The RSV and NIV read “quart.” See Weights and Measures.
choir director, choirmaster: Director of music; referred to in the superscriptions of 55 psalms.
choose: In modern English, terms referring to the selection of a leader or representative by a group of people. An element of choice is involved, since usually there are several candidates out of whom one must be chosen.
chor-ashan: KJV rendering of Bor-ashan in 1 Samuel 30:30. Bor-ashan was an alternate name for Ashan, a town originally in Judah’s territory.
chorazin: Palestinian city on which Jesus pronounced woe. It was in Korazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum that “most of his miracles” had been done, but the people were generally unresponsive and had not repented.
chosen: In modern English, terms referring to the selection of a leader or representative by a group of people. An element of choice is involved, since usually there are several candidates out of whom one must be chosen.
chozeba: KJV form of Cozeba in 1 Chronicles 4:22. Cozeba was an alternate name for Achzib, a city in Judah’s territory.
christ: Official title given to Jesus in the NT. It signifies his office as anointed Savior and alludes to his spiritual qualifications for the task of saving his people.
christian: Name first given to the followers of Jesus Christ. When the Christian movement reached Antioch in Syria, the gospel was preached to Gentiles as well as Jews.
christology: The study of the person and work of Jesus Christ. The confession that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, first ventured by Peter at Caesarea Philippi, is the heart of the Christian faith.
chronicles, books of first and second: Chronicles, Books of First and Second

Two OT books, historical records of King David and his successors in the land of Judah. The books of Chronicles are among the most neglected books in the Bible, partly because most of the material can be found in Samuel, Kings, or elsewhere in the OT.
chronology of the bible (old testament): Branch of biblical studies that attempts to assign dates and sequences to OT events. Chronology is a science.
chronology of the bible (new testament): Branch of biblical studies that attempts to discover the sequence of NT events and the amount of time that elapsed between them. Chronology is essential to historians, whose task it is to determine the causes and effects of past events.
chrysolite: Magnesium, iron silicate, usually olive green; mentioned in Ezekiel’s vision of the four wheels and as one of the gems in the foundation wall of the new Jerusalem.
chrysoprase, chrysoprasus: Light-green variety of chalcedony; mentioned as one of the gems in the foundation wall of the new Jerusalem (Rv 21:20; KJV “chrysoprasus”).
chub: KJV spelling of Kub, a place in Ezekiel 30:5 identified as Libya.
chun: KJV spelling of Cun, a city from which David took much bronze, in 1 Chronicles 18:8.
church: A group or assembly of persons called together for a particular purpose.
church meetings: The assembling together of the believers.
church officers: Official in the church whose qualifications are listed in 1 Timothy 3:2-7 and Titus 1:6-9.
chushan-rishathaim: KJV spelling of Cushan-rishathaim, a Mesopotamian king and oppressor of Israel, in Judges 3:8-10.
chusi: Place mentioned near Acraba and beside the brook Mochmur. Chusi is probably south of modern Nablus in Israel.
chuza: Steward of Herod Antipas, either a manager of Herod’s property or a political appointee; a man of influence and prestige. He was married to Joanna, who was healed by Jesus and subsequently accompanied Jesus and his disciples on their travels.
cilicia: Province of the Roman Empire, located in southeastern Asia Minor. Its capital was Tarsus, Paul’s hometown, hence permitting Paul Roman citizenship (16:37) even though he was a Jew.
cinnamon: Spice made from the dried inner bark of several oriental trees.
cinneroth: KJV spelling of the place-name Kinnereth in 1 Kings 15:20.
circumcision: Surgical removal of the foreskin of the male reproductive organ. In Bible times circumcision was the seal of God’s covenant with Abraham.
cis: KJV form of Kish, King Saul’s father, in Acts 13:21.
cistern: Place to store water; a man-made catch basin or reservoir. Stone cisterns plastered with lime came into common use in Palestine in the 13th century BC.
citadel: A city’s stronghold, tower, or fortification of last resort where people sought safety during an attack. The citadel of Penuel was destroyed by Gideon after he captured two Midianite kings.
cities of refuge: Six cities, three in Canaan and three in Transjordan (area east of the Jordan River), designated as places of safety for persons suspected of manslaughter. The six cities were among the 48 assigned to the Levites.
cities of the plain: Group of five cities in the plain or basin of the Jordan River which were also referred to as “cities of the valley.” Since the region in which these cities were located was particularly fruitful, it attracted Abraham’s nephew Lot when the growing size of the…
citizenship: In NT usage (1) designation of belonging to the city or city-state where one was born and reared, and (2) status of sharing in the privileges and responsibilities of the Roman Empire.
city: The Bible does not generally distinguish between city, town, and village.
city of david: 1. Southeastern hill (Ophel) in the present-day city of Jerusalem, the site occupied by King David as his royal city; also called Zion (e.g., 1 Kgs 8:1).
city of destruction: KJV translation in Isaiah 19:18 (NLT “City of the Sun”), generally understood as a reference to the Egyptian city Heliopolis.
city of palms: Phrase referring to Jericho, so named for its many palms.
city of salt: City located near the Dead Sea, assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance.
city of the sun: Phrase in Isaiah 19:18, generally taken as a reference to the Egyptian city Heliopolis.
civil law and justice: Civil law deals with private disputes between individuals occasioned by debt, divorce, inheritance, or other relationships. In contrast, criminal law deals with crimes such as murder, treason, or theft.
clauda: Ancient name (and variant spelling) of a small island south of Crete, in Acts 27:16.
claudia: Christian woman known to the apostle Paul and to Timothy.
claudius: Roman emperor from AD 41 to 54, mentioned twice in the NT.
claudius, edict of: Marble slab inscription from Nazareth prohibiting grave robbing, dated to Claudius’s reign (AD 41–54).
claudius lysias: Commander of the Roman garrison in Jerusalem who wrote a letter to the Roman procurator Felix concerning the apostle Paul. His title in Greek (chiliarch) identifies him as a commander of 1,000 troops.
clay: A “mineral” is a naturally occurring substance, normally an ore that must be mined and treated before the metal can be extracted. A “metal” is a chemical element such as iron or copper, which is free from contamination by other materials.
clay tablet: The process that goes into producing books.
cleanness and uncleanness, regulations c: Aspect of Hebrew religion having physical, ceremonial, moral, and spiritual significance.
cleanthes: Leader of the Athenian Stoic school of philosophy from 269 to 232 BC.
clement: Coworker with Paul at Philippi who worked side by side with him in the furtherance of the gospel there. Paul includes him in the group of those whose names are written in the Book of Life.
clement, epistle of: Letter written by Clement of Rome to the church at Corinth around AD 96. This letter is probably the earliest extant Christian epistle outside the NT.
clement of rome: A presbyter and bishop in Rome who wrote a letter to the church at Corinth (AD 96), probably the earliest Christian writing outside the NT. Dionysius of Corinth (AD 170) was the first to name Clement as the author of that letter.
cleopas: Follower of Jesus who conversed with him on the way to Emmaus. Some identify this Cleopas with the Clopas of John 19:25, but this is unlikely.
cleopatra: Name of a queen of Egypt and her daughter mentioned in the Apocrypha and in the writings of the Jewish historian Flavius Josephus.
cleophas: KJV form of Clopas, Mary’s husband, in John 19:25.
cloak: Translation of several words referring to outer garments.
clopas: Husband of Mary, one of the women who was present at Jesus’ crucifixion. From the Greek it cannot be determined if Mary the wife of Clopas was also the sister of Jesus’ mother or a different person.
closed womb: Condition of being barren or childless. A closed womb was a personal tragedy in OT times.
cloth and cloth manufacturing: Since antiquity, cloth has been made from such natural fibers as flax, wool, cotton, silk, and hair. Linen (spun from flax), wool, and sackcloth (woven from goat’s or camel’s hair) are the fabrics most frequently mentioned in Scripture.
clothing: Clothing mentioned in the Bible is usually referred to in such general terms as “inner garment,” “outer garment,” or “tunic.” Few descriptions give specific details of costumes or clothing, and it is therefore necessary to rely on paintings, pottery,…
cloud, pillar of: Supernatural phenomenon of God’s presence that guided the Israelites through the wilderness.
cnidus: Port city situated off the southwest corner of Asia Minor, mentioned as a harbor passed by the apostle Paul en route to Italy. During the second century BC, it had a Jewish colony.
coal: Translation of several Hebrew or Greek words in the Bible referring primarily to charcoal (mineral coal is not found in Palestine). The glowing embers from a wood fire were used for heating, cooking, and by blacksmiths.
coat: Translation of several words referring to various garments.
coat of mail: Piece of armor, covering the body from the neck to the girdle, probably made of leather with small interlaced metal places sewn onto it.
cock: Adult male of the domestic fowl.
cockatrice: KJV rendering of serpent, adder, and viper in Isaiah 11:8; 14:29; and 59:5, respectively.
cockle: KJV term for “foul weeds” in Job 31:40.
codex: Earliest form of the book, consisting of sheets of papyrus or vellum folded and bound together and enclosed between two wooden leaves or tablets.
coelesyria: Literally, the term means “hollow Syria.” It was used somewhat loosely in referring to parts of the Jordan Valley.
coffin: The Bible makes frequent reference to burial practices. A society’s burial customs are a reflection of its views about death and the afterlife.
coins: Pieces of metal used and accepted as a medium of exchange. A coin has a specific weight and bears some type of authentication to make it easily recognizable.
col-hozeh: The father of Shallum, who was ruler of the district of Mizpah. Col-hozeh, the son of Hazaiah in Nehemiah 11:5, may be another person.
color: The OT and NT have no exact word for “color,” although the word appears several times in our English Bibles. The words translated “color” have quite different meanings in the original languages.
colossae, colosse: Ancient city in Asia Minor, located in the southwestern part of present-day Turkey, and remembered primarily for the apostle Paul’s letter to the church there. Colosse was near the Lycus River, a tributary of the Meander.
colossians, letter to the: NT epistle, one of four “prison letters” attributed to the apostle Paul. As with Ephesians, Philippians, and Philemon, Paul said he was in prison when he wrote Colossians (Col 4:3, 10; cf.
comforter: KJV translation of the Greek word parakletos in John 14:16, 26; 15:26; and 16:7.
command, commandment: Christ’s commandment for Christians to love each other. The phrase “new commandment” occurs four times in the NT, all in the writings of John.
commandment, the new: Christ’s commandment for Christians to love each other. The phrase “new commandment” occurs four times in the NT, all in the writings of John.
commandments, the ten: List of commands given by God to Moses.
communication: The act of transmitting a message. Fire, light, and smoke signals were probably the earliest methods of communicating over any distance.
communion, holy: The supper Jesus shared with his disciples a few hours before he was arrested and taken to his trial and death (thus often called “The Last Supper”); the ceremony of partaking of the bread and wine that Christians have come to call the Lord’s Supper, the…
compassion: Quality of showing kindness or favor, of being gracious, or of having pity or mercy. In the Bible, God is described as being like a compassionate father to those who revere him.
conaniah: 1. Levite and chief officer who supervised tithes, contributions, and the dedicated things given to the temple during the reign of Hezekiah.
concision: KJV translation in the text of Philippians 3:2, meaning “mutilation of the flesh.”
concubinage, concubines: Practice of a man cohabiting with a woman (concubine) who is regarded only as his sexual partner or as a secondary wife in his household, of lower station than his primary wife.
coney: Small, rabbitlike animal declared unclean in Leviticus 11:5 and Deuteronomy 14:7 (KJV).
confection, confectionaries: KJV rendering of perfumer in Exodus 30:35 and 1 Samuel 8:13.
confession: Admission, especially of guilt or sin; also, a statement of religious belief. “To confess” can mean to agree, to promise, or to admit something.
conform, conformation: Spiritual process of molding the believer into the image of Jesus. Paul speaks of this in Romans 8:28-30:
congregation: Assembly of people, particularly for religious purposes. The Bible describes Israel as the congregation of the Lord because it was a covenant nation.
congregation, mount of the: KJV translation for “mount of assembly,” the name of a mountain that figured in Babylonian and Canaanite mythology, in Isaiah 14:13.
coniah: Alternate name for Jehoiachin, king of Judah, in Jeremiah 22:24, 28; 37:1.
cononiah: KJV spelling of Conaniah the Levite, in 2 Chronicles 31:12-13.
conquest and allotment of the land: Conquest and Allotment of the Land
Terms referring to Israel’s winning of the Promised Land and the distinctive way in which it was divided among the Israelite tribes.
conscience: Self-awareness that judges whether or not an act one has carried out or plans to carry out is in harmony with one’s moral standards. The conscience also functions to make a person aware of actions taken that were wrong.
consecration: Separation of persons, utensils, buildings, or places from everyday secular uses for exclusive dedication to holy or sacred use. In the Bible consecration was demonstrated by an appropriate rite or vow.
constellation: Certain number of stars in the sky, arbitrarily chosen as a group and named for an object, animal, or person that the outline of the group is said to resemble. A number of constellations are mentioned in the Bible.
consul: Title of the two highest civil and military magistrates of Rome in the time of the Republic. The consuls functioned as the heads of state, commanding the army and governing with the Senate.
consumption: Medical term historically referring to pulmonary tuberculosis. The word “consumption” appears twice in the Bible (Lv 26:16; Dt 28:22, RSV).
conversion: Total change in one’s direction in life or moral orientation. For Christians this means a change from an orientation that does not take God into account to one in which the person is submitted to Christ.
convocation, holy: Solemn assemblies celebrated in Israel at appointed feasts in order that the people and the temple might be sanctified; the days were specially devoted to rest and sacrifice to God.
coos: KJV spelling of Cos, an Aegean island and city, in Acts 21:1.
copper: Reddish-brown, malleable metal found in the ground and fashioned into ornaments, tools, and coins.
coppersmith: One who worked in copper and fashioned bronze and copper tools, implements, and ornaments. Only in the NT is the term “coppersmith” used; however, the occupation was important throughout Bible history.
coral: Calcareous skeletal deposits of marine organisms of a low order. The red coral of the Mediterranean was used for jewelry.
corban: Greek transliteration of a Hebrew term (korban) that occurs only in Mark 7:11, where Mark provides an editorial explanation: corban is “given,” that is, “dedicated or given to God.” Hence, corban is an offering.
core: KJV spelling of Korah, Izhar’s son, in Jude 1:11.
coriander: Annual herb native to Palestine. The fragrant seeds of this plant are mentioned twice in the description of manna.
corinth: Prominent city of Greece, formerly the capital of the ancient province of Achaia, in which the apostle Paul preached. The site of ancient Corinth lies to the west of the isthmus separating the Peloponnesian Peninsula from mainland Greece.
corinthians, first letter to the: There is no doubt about who wrote 1 Corinthians, for all scholars agree that the apostle Paul wrote it on his third missionary journey while he was living in Ephesus.
corinthians, second letter to the: The apostle Paul is the acknowledged author of 2 Corinthians. While some scholars argue that 2 Corinthians 2:14–7:4 and 10–13 are separate letters, only in the case of 6:14–7:1 is Paul’s authorship disputed.
cormorant: Large, black web-footed waterfowl, considered ceremonially unclean for the Israelites.
corn: Word often used to denote grain, especially wheat. Maize, the plant known in America as corn, was unknown in the Middle East in biblical times.
cornelius: Roman centurion and the first gentile Christian mentioned in the book of Acts.
corner gate: Gate presumably located in the northwest corner of the Jerusalem wall.
corners of the earth: Figurative term denoting the borders and extremities of the earth.
cornerstone: Term used in the NT to describe the exalted position of Jesus.
cornet: Stringed, wind, and percussion instruments used to make music.
correction: Learning that molds character and enforces correct behavior—from a Latin word meaning “instruction” or “training.” To discipline a person or a group means to put them in a state of good order so that they function in the way intended.
corruption, mount of: Southern end of the Mt of Olives, called “corruption” because King Solomon built idols there for his foreign wives.
cos: Island of the Sporades group in the Aegean, containing a city of the same name, located off the coast of Caria in Asia Minor.
cosam: Ancestor of Jesus, Addi’s father and Elmadam’s son, listed only in Luke’s genealogy (3:28).
cosmetics: That which is applied to the body to enhance one’s appearance.
cotton: Soft, white, fibrous hairs surrounding the seeds in the boll of various plants of the mallow family (genus Gossypium), woven into thread and cloth.
couch: Article of furniture for reclining in sleep or rest.
counsel, counselor: Advice; adviser, especially on legal matters (such as a lawyer). In Bible times a counselor in a king’s court was like a U.S. cabinet member today.
court: Area enclosed by buildings or walls and without a roof. The temple had courts for priests, women, and Gentiles.
courts and trials: Legal disputes were as much a part of life in Bible times as they are today. The ways that courts operated and trials were conducted, however, were quite different.
covenant: Arrangement between two parties involving mutual obligations; especially the arrangement that established the relationship between God and his people, expressed in grace first with Israel and then with the church.
covenant, book of the: Phrase used by Moses in reference to the Ten Commandments and the laws and stipulations recorded in Exodus 20:22–23:33.
covenant, the new: A gracious provision of God given through Jesus Christ for the redemption of fallen humanity—replacing and fulfilling the old covenant, which was expressed primarily through the Mosaic law. The expression “new covenant” is found principally in the NT.
covenant of salt: Biblical phrase for a two-way agreement, the inviolability of which was symbolized by salt. A Middle Eastern saying, “There is bread and salt between us,” meant that a relationship had been confirmed by sharing a meal.
covering of the head: Issue pertaining to female decor discussed by the apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 11:2-16. In Paul’s day Jewish women always wore veils in public and Greek women generally went veiled—a practice that showed deference to authority and dignified the wearer.
covet, covetousness: The desire to have something for oneself that belongs to another—a craving or passionate desire. Three Hebrew words are translated “covet” in the OT (see RSV).
cow: Domestic animals of the bovine species (Bos primigenius). The OT often emphasized the beauty of cattle.
coz: KJV spelling of Koz in 1 Chronicles 4:8.
cozbi: Midianite woman with whom a Hebrew named Zimri entered into an illicit relationship. Phinehas, the grandson of Aaron, stopped a plague on Israel by executing Zimri and Cozbi.
cozeba: Alternate name of Aczib, a city in Judah’s territory, in 1 Chronicles 4:22.
craftsmen, valley of: Place named for a community of craftsmen who lived in a valley on the southern border of the plain of Sharon.
crane: Translation of a Hebrew word in Isaiah 38:14 and Jeremiah 8:7, the meaning of which is uncertain.
crawling things: Translation of various Hebrew words primarily referring to reptiles.
creation: The divine act of making something out of nothing; the divine act of bringing the world into ordered existence.
creation, new: Concept of redemption developed throughout the OT and NT to its final consummation in the second coming of Jesus Christ.
creation myths: Religious stories explaining the origin and order of the universe. Parts of some Mesopotamian creation myths bear a close resemblance to the biblical accounts of Creation and earliest times.
creature, new: Concept of redemption developed throughout the OT and NT to its final consummation in the second coming of Jesus Christ.
credit, creditor: Acknowledgment of payment on a debt incurred through goods or services sold on trust, and the one who operates the business of selling on credit. The Mosaic law regulated credit and creditors.
creeping things: Reference to insects, reptiles, and some other animals that crawl on the belly or creep on four or more feet.
crescens: Coworker of the apostle Paul. Crescens went on to Galatia when Paul was imprisoned in Rome.
crete: Fourth largest island in the Mediterranean, lying approximately 60 miles (97 kilometers) southeast of Greece and 110 miles (177 kilometers) southwest of Turkey.
cricket: A four-footed winged insect, considered edible by the Israelites.
criminal law and punishment: The science or philosophy of law is called jurisprudence. Although modern jurisprudence bears little resemblance to biblical concepts of law, the Scriptures have played a definite role in its development.
crimson: The OT and NT have no exact word for “color,” although the word appears several times in our English Bibles. The words translated “color” have quite different meanings in the original languages.
crispus: Synagogue leader at Corinth who (along with all his household) was converted during the apostle Paul’s 18-month missionary visit to the city. Paul referred to Crispus as one of the few persons he personally baptized in Corinth.
crocodile: Large aquatic, flesh-eating reptile with a lizardlike body; long, pointed head; long, powerful tail; and short legs. Although specifically mentioned once in some versions, it is often identified with the Leviathan of Job 41.
crookbackt: KJV reading for hunchback in Leviticus 21:20.
cross: Form of execution employed in the death of Jesus Christ. Two concepts related to crucifixion occur in Scripture: the “cross,” a pagan mode of capital punishment, and the “tree,” which was a Jewish form.
crown: Headpiece symbolizing honor or high office. In addition to using the word metaphorically, the OT refers to three kinds of crowns.
crucifixion: Form of execution employed in the death of Jesus Christ. Two concepts related to crucifixion occur in Scripture: the “cross,” a pagan mode of capital punishment, and the “tree,” which was a Jewish form.
cruse: Small earthen vessel or flask, about four to six inches (10 to15 centimeters) tall, used for holding liquids.
crystal: Variety of quartz, usually clear or nearly so. Two Hebrew words and two Greek words are translated “crystal.” See Minerals and Metals; Stones, Precious.
cub: Name of a place, identified as Libya (RSV mg), in Ezekiel 30:5.
cubit: Linear measure, about 18 inches (46 centimeters), the length of a man’s forearm from the elbow to the tip of his middle finger.
cuckow: KJV translation of a Hebrew word better rendered “seagull” in Leviticus 11:16 and Deuteronomy 14:15 (RSV).
cucumber: Garden vegetable of the gourd family, mentioned as one of the foods desired by the wandering Israelites.
cummin: Herb of the carrot family cultivated for its aromatic seeds, which are used for seasoning food.
cun: Syrian city belonging to Hadadezer, king of Zobah. David raided Cun, taking away large quantities of bronze.
cuneiform: Ancient writing script in which nail or wedge-shaped marks are impressed into a writing material, usually clay, in specific patterns. Each pattern, or “sign,” represents a sound or word.
cup: The word may refer either to the vessel itself or to its contents and may be intended literally or figuratively.
cup-bearer: Official whose primary duty was to taste the wine served to the king as a precaution against poisoning. Cup-bearers frequented the courts of kings and high officials in antiquity.
cup of blessing: Theological phrase used in two contexts: (1) in Jewish usage, a cup of wine drunk at the end of a meal and having special Passover significance; (2) in Christian usage, the Communion goblet.
curse, cursed: Invocation of evil or injury against one’s enemies. As practiced in Bible times, cursing was the opposite of blessing and should not be confused with profanity in the modern sense.
curtains: Items of material culture used in homes, palaces, and temples. Because of its close geographical proximity to other nations, Israel had extensive contact with neighboring cultures.
cush (place): Egyptian, Akkadian, and Hebrew term broadly referring to the countries of the Upper Nile south of Egypt.
cushan: Name of a tribe or place mentioned only once in the Bible. Some have identified Cushan with the people and land referred to in the OT as Cush, or Ethiopia in most English versions.
cushan-rishathaim: King of Mesopotamia whom Israel served for eight years. The Lord raised up Othniel, Kenaz’s son, to deliver Israel out of his hand; later, Cushan-rishathaim was defeated by Othniel in war.
cushi: 1. Joab’s messenger sent to David to announce Absalom’s defeat.
cushite: Person from the African region of Nubia.
custodian: Servant whose responsibility was to accompany, protect, and sometimes discipline his master’s son until the boy reached maturity. These custodians supervised their charges’ moral conduct and general behavior.
cuth, cuthah: Town in southern Babylonia from which some people were taken and relocated in Samaria after the Assyrian conquest (722 BC). The name appears also in Assyrian and Babylonian sources.
cyamon: Site mentioned in the book of Judith as demarcating the camp of Holofernes’ army.
cylinder seals: Inscribed stone cylinders used for identification of ownership, developed by the ancient Sumerians but used primarily by other Mesopotamian peoples between about 3200 BC and the fourth century BC.
cymbal: Percussion instrument consisting of two round, thin, slightly concave, metal plates that are struck together. Cymbals were used in the worship of God.
cypress: Evergreen tree with dark foliage and distinctive symmetrical form. Cypress is mentioned as one of the materials in Solomon’s temple.
cyprus: Island country located in the northeastern Mediterranean Sea, 50 miles (80.5 kilometers) south of Turkey (Asia Minor), 70 miles (112.6 kilometers) west of Syria, and 245 miles (394.2 kilometers) north of Egypt.
cyrene, cyrenians: City and its people on the coast of North Africa that was the capital of Cyrenaica. It was founded in the seventh century BC by Greeks who engaged primarily in agricultural pursuits.
cyrenius: KJV rendering of Quirinius, the governor of Syria when Christ was born, in Luke 2:2.
cyrus cylinder: Baked clay barrel nine inches (22.9 centimeters) long inscribed in cuneiform, found by archaeologist Hormuzd Rassam during his excavations at Babylon (1879–82).
cyrus the great: Persian king (559–530 BC) who founded the Achaemenid dynasty and the Persian Empire. Cyrus (II) was the son of Cambyses I (600–599 BC), who ruled the unified territories of Parshumash-anshan and Parsa.
dabareh: KJV spelling of the town Daberath in Joshua 21:28.
dabbesheth: Designation for a camel’s hump. The name also refers to a town (“camel’s hump hill”) situated on the western border of the land allotted to Zebulun’s tribe for an inheritance.
daberath: Town in Issachar’s territory given to the Levite family of Gershon. It was located west of Mt Tabor on the Issachar-Zebulun border, and has been identified with the modern Deburiyeh.
dagon: Deity worshiped throughout the Mesopotamian world. In the OT, Dagon is the principal god of the Philistines.
dalaiah: KJV spelling of Delaiah, Elioenai’s son, in 1 Chronicles 3:24.
dalmanutha: Area on the west side of the Sea of Galilee near the southern end of the plain of Gennesaret. Its exact location is uncertain.
dalmatia: Mountainous region on the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, across from Italy. The Dalmatians were an Illyrian (Greek) tribe, or group of tribes banded together, coming from the area around the town of Delmion (or Delminium).
dalphon: Haman’s son killed by the Jews in the aftermath of the plot against Mordecai.
damaris: Woman mentioned as one of the first converts in the city of Athens, following Paul’s preaching there. Since Luke singles her out by name, she may have been a person of importance (see Acts 13:50; 17:12).
damascus: Syrian oasis city protected on three sides by mountains and situated on trade routes about 160 miles (257 kilometers) northeast of Jerusalem. The name Damascus can also refer to the surrounding area and to the southern Syrian state.
damnation: Place of future punishment for the lost, unrepentant, wicked dead.
dan (person): Fifth son of the Jewish patriarch Jacob. Dan’s mother was Bilhah, maid of Jacob’s wife Rachel.
dan (place): 1. Phoenician city, originally named Leshem or Laish, which was conquered by Dan’s tribe when it migrated northward.
dan, tribe of: Israelite tribe named for the patriarch Jacob’s fifth son. The tribe of Dan, descended from Dan’s only known son, Hushim (cf.
dance: Form of artistic expression incorporated into Israel’s worship, used especially during times of celebration.
daniel (person): 1. David’s second son, the first by his wife Abigail; also called Kileab.
daniel, additions to: Part of the Deuterocanonical works, consists of three supplementary sections to the book of Daniel. This additional material is in the Greek translation of the OT book of Daniel, but not in the ancient Hebrew-Aramaic texts.
daniel, book of: Fourth book of the Major Prophets in the OT, characterized by vivid symbolism and reflecting heroic historical events during the Babylonian exile of the Jewish people.
dan-jaan: Geographical landmark denoting the northern limit of David’s kingdom. Joab’s census taking stopped here.
dannah: Town located in the hill country of Judah between Socoh and Kiriath-sannah (Debir).
daphne: A beautiful grove and sanctuary to Apollo located near Antioch in Syria. The Greek ruler Seleucus I lived here and built a huge statue of Apollo in addition to a temple.
dara, darda: Mahol’s son, a Judahite of the family of Zerah. With Ethan the Ezrahite and Heman and Calcol, also sons of Mahol, Darda is mentioned as the proverbial example of wisdom, though he is surpassed by Solomon.
darius: Name of three emperors in the Persian dynasty of the legendary King Achaemenes. A Darius appears in the biblical books of Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai, and Zechariah as a Persian king, and in the book of Daniel as a Mede who became king over the Chaldeans.
darkness: Absence of light or brightness. Although the Bible seldom refers to literal darkness, a number of words translated “darkness” are used in a figurative or metaphorical sense.
darkon: Ancestor of a group of people who returned to Judah with Zerubbabel after the exile.
dart: Sharp, pointed weapon used as an arrow or light spear for thrusting.
date, date palm: Fruit and tree mentioned only a few times in the Bible.
dathan: Reubenite, son of Eliab and brother of Abiram; one of the leaders of Israel who, with Korah, rebelled against Moses during the wilderness wanderings.
dathema: A fortress in Bashan where Jews took refuge during the Maccabean revolt. Here they hid from Timothy until Judas the Maccabee rescued them by defeating the enemy (v 29).
daughter: In Bible times, the family comprised members of a household, including not only parents and children, along with other relatives and concubines, but also servants, travelers, aliens, and anyone else who happened to be within the house and was therefore under the protection of the head of the family.
daughter-in-law: In Bible times, the family comprised members of a household, including not only parents and children, along with other relatives and concubines, but also servants, travelers, aliens, and anyone else who happened to be within the house and was therefore under the protection of the head of the family.
david: Israel’s most important king. David’s kingdom represented the epitome of Israel’s power and influence during the nation’s OT history.
david, city of: 1. In the OT, the city of Jerusalem.
david, root of: Phrase applied to Jesus Christ in the book of Revelation. Though “root” usually means “source,” the metaphor depicts Jesus as David’s royal descendant, as indicated by the parallel word “offspring” in Revelation 22:16.
david, tower of: 1. Fortress built by David, with a thousand shields hung on it, commemorated in Song of Songs 4:4 but otherwise unknown.
day: Most literally, a period of time delimited by the earth’s rotation around its axis, such as the period between two consecutive sunrises; also, the portion of that period in which the sun is visible, the other portion being called “night.” The word “day” occurs over 2,000 times in the OT, over 350 times in the NT.
day of atonement: Yom Kippur, the most important day in the religious calendar of Israel, falling on the 10th day of Tishri (the Hebrew month corresponding to mid-September through mid-October).
day of christ: Phrase used by the apostle Paul in reference to the second advent of Christ.
day of the lord: Expression used by OT prophets (as early as the eighth-century BC prophet Amos) to signify a time in which God actively intervenes in history, primarily for judgment. Thus “the day of the Lord” is also called “the day of the LORD’s anger”.
day's journey: Way of estimating distances in Bible times. A day’s journey approximated 20 miles (32.2 kilometers) but depended on such things as mode of travel, the terrain, and the weather.
dayspring, day star: KJV translations in Job 38:12 (“dawn,” RSV), Luke 1:78 (“day,” RSV), and 2 Peter 1:19 (“morning star,” RSV) referring to Venus, the star that heralds the dawn, or to the first light of dawn itself.
deacon, deaconess: Terms designating an officer in a local church, derived from a Greek word meaning “servant” or “minister.” The term “diaconate” is used for the office itself or for the collective body of deacons and deaconesses.
dead, place of the: Term covering a number of descriptive biblical images of the whereabouts of those who have died. Those images include Sheol and “the pit” in the OT, plus hades, Gehenna, paradise, and “Abraham’s bosom” in the NT.
dead sea: A large saltwater lake into which the river Jordan empties.
dead sea scrolls: Copies of the OT books produced by scribes and editions made from these copies. The ancient manuscripts of the OT are the basic working material used to seek out the original text of the Bible with as great a degree of accuracy as possible.
deaf, deafness: Inability to hear; term used in Scripture to describe both a literal, physical inability and a figurative, spiritual defect.
death: Cessation of life (physical death) or separation from God (spiritual death).
death, the second: Term used in the NT only in the book of Revelation, to describe God’s eternal judgment on sin. Originally a rabbinic expression, the second death will be experienced by those whose names are not written in the “Book of Life”.
death of christ: Form of execution employed in the death of Jesus Christ. Two concepts related to crucifixion occur in Scripture: the “cross,” a pagan mode of capital punishment, and the “tree,” which was a Jewish form.
debir (person): One of the kings of Eglon who became an ally of Adoni-zedek, the king of Jerusalem. Debir was executed by Joshua.
debir (place): 1. Canaanite city originally held by the Anakim before being conquered by the Israelites.
deborah: Name of two OT women. The word in Hebrew means “honeybee”.
deborah, song of: Ancient poem found in Judges 5, celebrating an Israelite victory over the Canaanites.
debt: Something owed to another person, such as goods, property, or money. In the Bible, righteous conduct is something one “owes” to God; hence, in theology, sin is described figuratively as being “in debt.”
decalogue: Greek term meaning “ten words,” referring to the Ten Commandments.
decapolis: Group of city-states where Greeks settled following Alexander the Great’s conquest of the area in the fourth century BC. They were located to the southeast of the Sea of Galilee, with the exception of Scythopolis, which was west of the Jordan River.
decision, valley of: Place mentioned in Joel 3:14, where the Lord will judge the heathen nations gathered against Judah. It is the same as the valley of Jehoshaphat (see Jl 3:2).
decrees of god: Activity of God by which he establishes events and outcomes before they occur. In common usage, “foreordination” and the term “predestination” are synonymous.
dedan (person): 1. Grandson of Cush in the list of Noah’s descendants.
dedan (place): Region located in the Arabian Peninsula. The Dedanites were listed among those who rejoiced at the downfall of Israel during the time of the Babylonian captivity.
dedication, feast of: Designation by the apostle John for the Feast of Lights, or Hanukkah. The feast lasts eight days and begins on the 25th day of Kislev (November to December).
deer: Hoofed, cud-chewing mammal, considered clean by the law.
defile: To make ethically or ritually unclean.
deformity: Any obvious physical abnormality. In the OT sacrificial system both the animal to be sacrificed and the priest who performed the sacrifice (ch 21) had to be perfect physical specimens, without defect or blemish.
dehavites: Group of people among those colonized in Samaria by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal.
dekar: KJV spelling of Deker, one of King Solomon’s officials, in 1 Kings 4:9.
delaiah: 1. Son of Elioenai who traced his line of descent through Zerubbabel to David (1 Chr 3:24, KJV “Dalaiah”).
delilah: Samson’s mistress, who betrayed him to his Philistine enemies. Because Philistia held southern Israel in vassalage at the time (c. 1070 BC), Samson was chosen by God to begin the delivery of Israel.
deliverance, deliverer: Rescue or redemption and the agent of such a rescue. Scripture teaches that God’s ultimate goal in history is to rescue people from the curse of sin, death, Satan, and hell.
deluge, the: Rising and overflowing of water to cover the land, specifically the flood of Noah.
demas: One of Paul’s associates who was with him during one of his imprisonments. Little is known about Demas beyond the brief information given in the NT.
demetrius: Name (“Son of Demeter”) of five persons in biblical times: three Syrian kings and two NT figures.
demon: Fallen angel who, under the leadership of Satan, rebelled against God.
demon-possession: Demonic occupation of a human being. The term “possession” is misleading and is not the best translation for the Greek word daimonizomai, which literally means to be “demonized” and can often best be translated as “to have a demon.” The noun form is “demoniac.”
demophon: Syrian officer and district governor in Palestine, under the command of Antiochus V (about 164 BC).
denarius: Roman silver coin, equivalent to one day’s wage.
deputy: 1. Official of superior rank whose authority is normally granted by a king.
derbe: A city of the Roman province of Asia located in the district of Lycaonia in the province of Galatia.
descent into hell: Reference to a controversial statement about Christ in the Apostles’ Creed.
desert: Empty waste place, often arid, sandy, and incapable of sustaining vegetable life, as for example the Negev of southern Palestine. A desert frequently includes local areas where marginal life is possible.
desert of sin: Arid, sandy region in the southwestern part of the Sinai peninsula, described in the Bible as being “between Elim and Sinai”. It is mentioned only four times in the Bible in itineraries of the exodus from Egypt.
desire: To long for, want, or covet; also the object so desired. The word “desire” occurs many times in the KJV.
dessau: A village in Judea where the Jews led by Judas Maccabeus attacked forces of Nicanor. Nicanor was a Syrian officer under the command of Lysias.
destiny: 1. Pagan god (Meni) mentioned in connection with another pagan god (Gad); presumably a deity of good luck or fortune.
destroyer, the: 1. Divine agent sent to carry out a sentence of destruction.
destruction, city of: Phrase in Isaiah 19:18 (KJV), generally taken as a reference to Heliopolis.
deuel: Eliasaph’s father. Eliasaph led the tribe of Gad during the Israelites’ wilderness wanderings.
deutero-isaiah: The prophet Isaiah, whose name means “the Lord saves,” lived and ministered in Jerusalem. Because of his repeated contact with the kings of Judah, some scholars believed that Isaiah was related to the royal family, but this is not certain.
deuteronomy, book of: Fifth book of the OT, and last of the Pentateuch (the five books of the Law). In it Moses restated to the people of Israel various laws and precepts of the covenant that God had revealed to them at Mt Sinai.
devil, the: Spirit being who opposes God and seeks to frustrate his plans and lead his people into rebellion.
devoted things: Persons, animals, or objects that God forbade the children of Israel to possess.
dew: Moisture condensed from warm air during a cool night, usually found as small droplets on surfaces the next morning.
diadem: Headpiece symbolizing honor or high office. In addition to using the word metaphorically, the OT refers to three kinds of crowns.
diamond: Precious gem, usually colorless, consisting of crystalized carbon. In the Bible “diamond” seems to indicate the hardness, rather than the actual identification, of the stone.
diana: Roman name for the mythological Greek goddess Artemis, daughter of Jupiter and Latona and the twin sister of Apollo.
diaspora of the jews: Dispersion of Jewish people from Israel to foreign lands. Diaspora, a Greek noun meaning a “sowing” or “scattering,” is regularly used in the Septuagint to mean “exile” (Jer 25:34; cf.
diblah: ASV form of Riblah, the name of the place from which King Nebuchadnezzar directed operations against Jerusalem in 588–586 BC (Ez 6:14; cf. Jer 52:9-27).
diblaim: Father of Gomer, Hosea’s wife. The name Diblaim is thought by some to be an allusion to Gomer’s harlotry, since the name means “raisin cakes” and raisin cakes were used in ancient fertility-cult rites.
diblath: KJV rendering of Riblah in Ezekiel 6:14. Compare Jeremiah 52:9-27.
dibon: 1. City in Moab, east of the Dead Sea and north of the Arnon River.
dibon-gad: Alternate name for Dibon, a Moabite city, in Numbers 33:45-46.
dibri: Father of Shelomith from Dan’s tribe. Shelomith married an Egyptian man, and her son by this marriage was stoned in the wilderness for blaspheming the name of God.
didache (teaching): A manual of church discipline, otherwise known as “The Teaching of the Lord to the Gentiles through the Twelve Apostles.” Its origin and date are difficult to determine precisely, but scholars generally agree that it was written in Syria or Palestine during the late first century or early second century.
didrachma: Greek silver coin worth two drachmas and equivalent to the Jewish half-shekel. Every Jew was required to pay this amount as the annual temple tax.
didymus: Greek for “twin” and another name for the apostle Thomas in John 11:16, 20:24, and 21:2, NLT mg.
dietary laws: Regulations of food preparation and consumption provided by God for his people in OT times. The dietary laws formed part of broader regulations on “cleanness” that were designed to maintain Israel’s status as a holy people.
diklah: Son of Joktan in the list of nations descended from Noah’s sons; perhaps the name refers to an Arabian tribe or territory, living in or near a palm-bearing area, as the name suggests (Diklah is a variant of the Hebrew word dikla, which means date tree or palm tree).
dilean: Obscure Judean village near Lachish. It is mentioned only once in the OT.
dill: Herb from an annual plant known in Bible times. Dill has been widely used as a seasoning, especially for pickles, and for certain medicinal purposes.
dimnah: Alternate name for Rimmon, a Levitical city in Zebulun’s territory, in Joshua 21:35.
dimon: KJV translation of a Moabite city in Isaiah 15:9, alternately named Dibon in the large Dead Sea Isaiah Scroll. The site of Dimon is identified with Khirbet Dimneh, nearly three miles (5 kilometers) northwest of Rabbah.
dimonah: Town mentioned in Joshua 15:22 as being located in the Judean Negev, close to Edomite territory. It was one of 29 towns in the general area of Beersheba; some scholars have identified it with the Dibon mentioned in Nehemiah 11:25.
dinah: Daughter born to Jacob and Leah, whose name means “judgment.” Living with her family at Shechem, a Canaanite city (33:18), Dinah went in to visit some neighboring pagan women (34:1).
dinaites: Postexilic group involved in a protest to Artaxerxes about the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple (Ezr 4:9, KJV). The name is evidently an Aramaic title for “judge” (RSV); such judges are mentioned in fifth-century BC Aramaic administrative papyri.
dinhabah: Capital city of Edom before the time of Israel’s monarchy, whose king Bela is mentioned in the Bible. Its site is unknown.
dion: One of the cities of the Decapolis, built after the death of Alexander the Great by some of his soldiers. The city (not mentioned in the Bible) was culturally Greek, attracting many Greek immigrants; it was also a mercantile center of exchange.
dionysius: Prominent citizen of Athens; a member of the Areopagus, the Athenian supreme court, and one of Paul’s few converts during his brief ministry at Athens.
dioscorinthius: Problematic word occurring once in 2 Maccabees 11:21. “Dioscorinthius” formed part of the date in a letter written by Lysias, a Syrian official, to the Jewish people during the Maccabean revolts around 164 BC.
dioscuri: Twin sons of Zeus known as Castor and Pollux. In Greek mythology they were the patron deities of navigation and represented in the constellation Gemini.
diotrephes: A church member whom John reprimanded for his contentious behavior. He spoke against John; had resisted John’s authority by refusing to receive an earlier letter; and refused to show Christian hospitality, urging others to do likewise.
diphath: Alternate spelling of Riphath, Gomer’s son, in 1 Chronicles 1:6.
discerning of spirits: Phrase regularly used to translate two Greek words, charismata and pneumatika (the plural forms of charisma and pneumatikon). Both words are almost exclusively Pauline within the biblical writings; elsewhere in the NT, they appear only in 1 Peter 2:5 and 4:10.
disciple: Someone who follows another person or another way of life and who submits himself to the discipline (teaching) of that leader or way.
discipline: Learning that molds character and enforces correct behavior—from a Latin word meaning “instruction” or “training.” To discipline a person or a group means to put them in a state of good order so that they function in the way intended.
disease: Term used in Scripture synonymously with sickness, infirmity, illness, plague, and pestilence. However, plague and pestilence are generally used when there are large numbers of victims, as in epidemics.
dish: A vessel, usually made of baked clay or metal, used in everyday life and in religious ceremony. Dishes were used to serve or preserve food.
dishan: Chieftain in the land of Seir, a mountainous area southwest of the Dead Sea. Dishan’s father was Seir the Horite.
dishon: 1. Seir’s fifth son and a Horite leader in Edom, whose people were eventually displaced by the Edomites.
dispersion of the jews: Dispersion of Jewish people from Israel to foreign lands. Diaspora, a Greek noun meaning a “sowing” or “scattering,” is regularly used in the Septuagint to mean “exile” (Jer 25:34; cf.
dives: Traditional name of the rich man in Christ’s parable about the beggar Lazarus.
divination: Attempt to influence or control people or events through supernatural forces. These forces are called upon by means of ceremonies, the recitation of spells, charms, incantations, and other forms of ritual.
divine presence: Inherent characteristics of God revealed in Scripture and displayed in God’s actions in biblical history. They are characteristics equally of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
diviners' oak: Place apparently near Shechem; mistakenly called “the plain of Meonenim” in the KJV. The Diviners’ Oak may have been associated with those who practiced divination, hence the name.
division of the land: Assignment of portions of the Promised Land to the 12 tribes of Israel following the Conquest.
divorce: Biblical provisions regulating divorce are closely bound up with the various definitions given to marriage within the successive phases of God’s progressive revelation in history.
divorce, certificate of: A document declaring the separation of a husband and wife, mandated by Mosaic law (Dt 24:1-4; see Mt 5:31; 19:7; Mk 10:4).
di-zahab: Name, listed along with Paran, Tophel, Laban, and Hazeroth, meant to designate the locale of Moses’ final address to Israel.
doctor of the law: Translation in the KJV for “teacher of the law” in Luke 5:17, and Acts 5:34.
dodai: Ahohi’s descendant and a commander of one of Israel’s 12 contingents of soldiers (24,000 men each) during David’s reign. Dodai is perhaps alternately called Dodo, Eleazar’s father, in 2 Samuel 23:9 and 1 Chronicles 11:12.
dodanim: Descendants of Noah’s son Japheth. The name is emended to Rodanim in 1 Chronicles 1:7.
dodavah, dodavahu: Inhabitant of Mareshah and father of Eliezer the prophet. Eliezer spoke against King Jehoshaphat of Judah because of his alliance with King Ahaziah of Israel (2 Chr 20:37, KJV “Dodavah”).
dodo: 1. Grandfather of Tola, a minor judge who judged Israel from his native city, Shamir.
doeg: Official of Saul who was commanded to kill the innocent priests at Nob. An Edomite, he was either a proselyte or a prominent Edomite chieftain captured by Saul (14:47).
dog: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
doleful creature: Designation for animal of uncertain identity in Isaiah 13:21 (KJV), better rendered “howling creature” (NLT). The context implies such beasts are unclean; hence, suggested creatures include the horned owl, hyena, jackal, and leopard.
domitian: Roman emperor (AD 81–96) who persecuted both Jews and Christians. Tradition says that under Domitian the apostle John was banished to Patmos, where he wrote the book of Revelation.
doorkeeper: Those who guarded gates of the cities and doors of palaces, temples, and other large buildings. Their task was to admit or reject visitors.
dophkah: Name of an area near the wilderness of Sin where the Israelites camped on their way to Mt Sinai. Its site is perhaps identical with Serabit el-Khadem, an Egyptian turquoise mining center.
dor: Fortified Palestinian city (modern el-Burj) situated along the Mediterranean coast, south of Mt Carmel and eight miles (12.9 kilometers) north of Caesarea.
dorcas: Christian woman in Joppa of Judea, noted for her acts of charity. Dorcas is called a disciple in Acts 9:36, which is the only instance where the feminine form of the word is used in the Greek NT.
dositheus: 1. A Jew representing himself as a priest and Levite.
dothan: Ancient city located about 60 miles (97 kilometers) north of Jerusalem, 13 miles (21 kilometers) north of the city of Samaria, and about 5 miles (8 kilometers) southeast of Megiddo.
dove's dung: Source of food eaten when Samaria was besieged by Ben-hadad, king of Syria. Taken literally as pigeon excrement, the reference would indicate how desperate conditions were in the famished city.
dowry: Gift of property or goods from the bride’s family to the bride or groom prior to marriage.
drachma: Greek coin made of silver, roughly equivalent to the Roman denarius.
dragon: Term indicating a number of monstrous land or sea creatures.
dragon's well: Unknown location along the Jerusalem wall between the Valley Gate and the Dung Gate visited by Nehemiah during his night inspection of the wall. It is also called Dragon’s Well or Serpent’s Well.
dram: KJV for daric, a Persian gold coin, in 1 Chronicles 29:7, Ezra 2:69, 8:27, and Nehemiah 7:70-72.
dreams: Thoughts, images, or emotions occurring during sleep. Dreams have always fascinated people; the events experienced in dreams are too vivid and real to be ignored.
drink offering: Major ritual expressions of religious life with accompanying rites, such as libations, effusions, and sacred meals. The ideology expressed in Israel’s ritual complex made its religion unique in the ancient Near East.
dromedary: Swift-footed camel of the Arabian species.
dropsy: Old medical term for excessive accumulation of watery fluid in any tissue or space of the body.
drusilla: Third and youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa, king of Judea. A Jewess, Drusilla was born about AD 38 and had two sisters, Bernice and Mariamne.
dumah (person): Ishmael’s son, who founded an Arab tribe.
dumah (place): 1. Region of the 12 tribes of Ishmael where there were a number of oases; identified with el-Jof, modern Dumat el-Jendel.
dumbness: The inability to speak. Muteness, or aphasia, can be a momentary phenomenon or a permanent handicap.
dung gate: One of the 11 gates in the Jerusalem wall in Nehemiah’s time. It was located near the southwest corner of the city and led to the valley of Hinnom, where rubbish and refuse were dumped.
dura, plain of: Location in the province of Babylon where Nebuchadnezzar set up the great image of gold, which all his subjects were ordered to worship. Its exact location is uncertain.
dye, dyeing, dyer: Method of coloring textiles practiced in the Near East with natural materials even before the time of the patriarch Abraham. The Bible mentions four colors of dyes: purple, blue (actually a shade of violet), crimson, and scarlet.
dysentery: Diarrhea caused by parasitic bacteria, protozoa (amoeba), or worms in contaminated food or drink. Dysentery is accompanied by intestinal spasms and ulceration, with the appearance of blood and pus in the excrement.
dysmas: Name given to the repentant thief on the cross in apocryphal narratives based on Luke 23:39-43. Sources such as the Arabic Gospel of the Infancy and the Acts of Pilate contain fanciful accounts of earlier dealings between Christ and Dysmas.
eagle: Large, carnivorous bird of the falcon family noted for its strength, keen eyesight, and graceful flight.
earring: Decorated adornments. In the Bible, jewelry was used by both men and women.
earth: Term used for our inhabited planet; the world, as distinguished from heaven and hell; land; soil; and in several other ways. Biblical usage is as broad as modern usage.
earth, new: Concept of a new or renewed universe first found in the book of Isaiah. God declares, “For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind. . . .
earthenware: The manufacture of clayware and earthenware.
earthquake: Shaking or trembling of the earth originated by volcanic or tectonic activity. Earthquakes occur frequently in Palestine due mostly to the volcanic nature of the regions around the Dead Sea and the Sea of Galilee.
east, children of the: Phrase used in reference to those nations that were east of Israel (e.g., Jgs 6:3, NLT “people of the east”).
eastern sea: Alternate name for the Salt Sea, or Dead Sea, derived from the sea’s location on the eastern boundary of the land of Israel.
east gate: Gate in the walled city of Jerusalem. “East gate” also refers to the gate of the temple mentioned in Ezekiel 10:19; 11:1; and 43:1.
east sea: KJV name for the “eastern sea,” an alternate name for the Dead Sea, in Ezekiel 47:18.
east wind: Wind coming mostly in May, September, and October. This scorching wind, also called a sirocco, destroyed vegetation, withered flowers, and dried up fountains and springs.
ebal: 1. Shobal’s son and descendant of Seir the Horite.
ebal, mount: Mountain just over 3,000 feet (914.4 meters) high in the central hill country of Israel. Mt Gerizim is usually mentioned with it.
ebed-melech: Ethiopian eunuch in King Zedekiah’s court. He secured the king’s permission to rescue the prophet Jeremiah out of a cistern where he had been thrown to die.
ebenezer: 1. Site where the Israelite army encamped before a battle with the Philistines.
eber: 1. Abraham’s ancestor from whom the word “Hebrew” may be derived.
ebez: City in the plain of Esdraelon, allotted to Issachar’s tribe for an inheritance.
ebiasaph: Kohathite Levite, Elkanah’s son and the father of Assir; alternately called Abiasaph in Exodus 6:24.
ebla tablets: Tablets, dating c. 2220–2240 BC, discovered in the ancient Syrian city-state of Ebla, now identified with the site of Tell Mardikh.
ebony: Black wood, highly prized in antiquity for use in home furnishings.
ebron: Town belonging to Asher’s tribe, in Joshua 19:28, according to some Hebrew manuscripts. Other manuscripts read Abdon.
ebronah: KJV form of Abronah, an Israelite stopping place in the wilderness, in Numbers 33:34-35.
ecbatana: Greek name for the capital of the ancient Median Empire, later one of the capital cities of the Persian and Parthian empires. It is often spelled Achmetha (Ezr 6:2, KJV), approximating its Aramaic name.
ecclesiastes, book of: OT book of Wisdom Literature. Ecclesiastes is philosophical in character, posing deep questions about the meaning and nature of human existence.
ecclesiasticus: Deuterocanonical book that is also known as Ecclesiasticus (to be distinguished from the canonical book Ecclesiastes).
eclipse: Total or partial obscuration of the sun as a result of the passing of the moon between the sun and the earth; thus, a possible explanation for certain unusual astronomical events in the Bible.
edar: KJV spelling of Eder in Genesis 35:21.
eden: 1. Place where Adam and Eve lived until they sinned against God and were banished.
eder (person): 1. Member of Benjamin’s tribe and the son of Beriah, a leader in the town of Aijalon.
eder (place): 1. First camping place of Jacob between Ephrath (Bethlehem) and Hebron, following Rachel’s death.
edh: Hebrew name of an altar built in God’s honor by the Reubenites, Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh (Jos 22:10, 34, NLT mg) when these tribes took possession of Gilead.
edna: Raguel’s wife and mother of Sarah. Sarah married Tobias, son of Tobit (7:13).
edom, edomites: Land and its inhabitants found on the high plateau to the south and southeast of the Dead Sea.
edrei: 1. City of residence for Og, king of Bashan.
education: The act or process of educating or being educated. The original purpose of Jewish education was to teach children to know and understand their special relationship with God, to teach them to serve him, and to educate them in holiness.
eduth: Hebrew word usually translated “testimony,” “witness,” or “commandment.” It is used with reference to the tabernacle, the ark, the Ten Commandments, and the law of God in general.
eglah: One of King David’s wives and mother of Ithream. Born while David was still in Hebron, Ithream was the sixth son.
eglaim: Town mentioned in Isaiah 15:8. It cannot be located with certainty, but it was probably in southern Moab.
eglath-shelishiyah: Place in Moab mentioned in Isaiah 15:5 and Jeremiah 48:34 in pronouncements of judgment. The name means literally “the third Eglath.” It was probably near Zoar at the southern end of the Dead Sea, but its exact location is uncertain.
eglon (person): Moabite king who captured Jericho and held it for 18 years, exacting a tribute from Israel. Ehud, an Israelite judge pretending to bring tribute, killed Eglon.
eglon (place): Town situated seven miles (11.3 kilometers) southwest of Lachish, assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance. It is generally identified with the modern Tell el-Hesi.
egypt, brook of: Natural border between the Negev Desert area of Israel and the Sinai Peninsula, about 50 miles (80.5 kilometers) southwest of Gaza. The brook of Egypt, modern Wadi el-Arish, flows only during the rainy season.
egypt, egyptian: Egypt figured significantly as a stage on which the biblical narrative was enacted. Here Abraham lived in time of famine.
egyptian, the: Unidentified antagonist of Rome who led a revolt into the wilderness with a host of barbarous assassins (the Sicarii).
ehi: Benjamin’s son; perhaps a scribal error for Ahiram.
ehud: 1. Judge of Israel from Benjamin’s tribe who delivered Israel from Eglon, king of the Moabites.
eker: Jerahmeelite and the son of Ram from Judah’s tribe.
ekrebel: Mentioned in Judith 7:18 as a place “located near Chusi in the vicinity of the brook Mochmur.” It is possibly modern Akrabeh, which is about 25 miles (40.2 kilometers) north of Jerusalem near the city of Shechem.
ekron, ekronites: Most northerly city among the major Philistine settlements. During the Hebrew conquest of Palestine, Ekron was not taken by Joshua.
el: Ancient Semitic name for deity, perhaps meaning “power” (cf. Gn 17:1); used by the Hebrews generally in a poetic sense to denote the true God of Israel.
ela: Father of Shimei, one of the 12 officers appointed to requisition food for King Solomon’s household.
eladah: KJV form of Eleadah, Ephraim’s descendant, in 1 Chronicles 7:20.
elah: 1. Esau’s descendant and a chief of Edom.
elah, valley of: Southernmost valley in the Shephelah, starting at Hebron and descending in a northerly direction before turning west.
elam (person): 1. Firstborn son of Shem and a grandson of Noah.
elam (place), elamites: Occupying an area roughly the size of Denmark, Elam was located in southwest Asia, east of Babylonia and north of the Persian Gulf, on a plain known to the Iranians since the Middle Ages as Khuzistan. The region today corresponds to southwest Iran.
elasah: 1. Priest of Pashhur’s clan who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile.
elath: Edomite city (also spelled Eloth) at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, on the eastern border of the wilderness of Paran (Gn 14:6, where it is alternately called El-paran).
el-berith: Local god worshiped at Shechem. He is usually identified with the god Baal-berith (8:33; 9:4).
el-bethel: Name Jacob gave to the place at Luz (Bethel) where he built an altar after he returned from Haran with his family.
elchasai, the book of: Lost Jewish work composed in Aramaic by Elchasai during the reign of Emperor Trajan (AD 98–117). It was intended for his followers, the Elchasaites (or Sabai), but was read by both Jews and Jewish Christian groups.
eldaah: Midian’s fifth son and a descendant of Abraham and his wife Keturah.
eldad: One of the 70 elders of Israel who were commissioned to assist Moses in governing the people.
elder: Person who, by virtue of position in the family, clan, or tribe; or by reason of personality, prowess, stature, or influence; or through a process of appointment and ordination, exercised leadership and judicial functions in both religious and secular spheres…
elead: Ephraim’s descendant who was killed in a raid against the Philistine city of Gath.
elealeh: Town in the Transjordan northeast of Heshbon conquered by Reuben and Gad. It was taken back by the Moabites and is associated with Heshbon in the prophetic denunciations of Moab.
eleasah: 1. Helez’s son and member of Judah’s tribe.
elect, election: In modern English, terms referring to the selection of a leader or representative by a group of people. An element of choice is involved, since usually there are several candidates out of whom one must be chosen.
elect lady: Greeting found in 2 John 1:1. The phrase has been interpreted two ways.
el-elohe-israel: Name of an altar built by Jacob on land he purchased from the sons of Hamor, near Shechem. Jacob used the Canaanite deity’s name, El, as a designation for Israel’s God.
elemental spirits, elements: Alternative translations of a Greek word used in the NT, “elemental spirits” being spiritual forces at work in the world, and “elements” being either the basic constituents of the physical world or of human life or the basic principles of a system of thought.
eleph: KJV translation for the town Haeleph in Joshua 18:28.
elephantine papyri: Aramaic documents from the fifth century BC discovered at Elephantine, an island in the Nile River. At the time of the documents’ writing, Elephantine was a Persian military outpost, manned in part by a group of Jewish mercenaries with their families.
eleutherus: A small river mentioned in 1 Maccabees 11:7 and 12:30 and almost certainly to be identified with the Nahr-el-Kebir, which begins in the northeast base of Lebanon and flows into the Mediterranean about 18 miles (29 kilometers) north of Tripoli.
eleven, the: Designation for the disciples after the resurrection of Jesus, and at Pentecost, Judas Iscariot having committed suicide.
elhanan: 1. Hebrew soldier who distinguished himself by killing a Philistine giant.
eli: Priest in the sanctuary of the Lord at Shiloh in the period of the judges. Shiloh, about 10 miles (16 kilometers) north of Jerusalem, was the central shrine of the Israelite tribal confederation.
eli, eli, lama sabachthani?: One of Jesus’ cries from the cross, properly translated “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (The NLT uses an alternate spelling, “lema,” for the third word in the expression.) This form of the “cry of dereliction” is slightly different from its other recorded form, “Eloi, eloi, lama sabachthani?”.
eliab: 1. Helon’s son and leader of Zebulun’s tribe when the Israelites were roaming in the Sinai wilderness after their escape from Egypt.
