eliada: 1. One of King David’s sons, born in Jerusalem.
eliadah: KJV spelling of Eliada, Rezon’s father, in 1 Kings 11:23.
eliah: KJV form of the name Elijah in 1 Chronicles 8:27 and Ezra 10:26.
eliahba: Warrior among David’s mighty men who were known as “the thirty”.
eliakim: 1. Hilkiah’s son and a royal officer in the household and court of King Hezekiah.
eliam: 1. Alternate name for Ammiel, Bathsheba’s father, in 2 Samuel 11:3.
elias: KJV rendering of the prophet Elijah’s name in the NT.
eliasaph: 1. Leader of Gad’s tribe appointed by Moses.
eliashib: 1. Elioenai’s son and a descendant of Zerubbabel in the royal lineage of David.
eliathah: Son of Heman appointed to assist in the temple service during David’s reign.
elidad: Benjamite, of the sons of Kislon, appointed to work under Eleazar and Joshua in allotting Canaanite territory west of the Jordan to the 10 tribes.
eliehoenai: 1. Korahite Levite who, with his six brothers and his father, Meshelemiah, served as a temple doorkeeper during David’s reign.
eliel: 1. Warrior and head of a family of the half-tribe of Manasseh that lived east of the Jordan River.
elienai: Benjamite and the son of Shimei. His name may be a contraction of Eliehoenai (see 1 Chr 26:3).
eliezer: 1. Native of Damascus and Abraham’s servant, who according to custom was the adopted heir before Ishmael and Isaac were born.
elihoenai: KJV spelling of Eliehoenai, Zerahiah’s son, in Ezra 8:4.
elihoreph: Prominent official in the time of Solomon who, with his brother Ahijah, was a royal secretary. Attempts to regard Elihoreph as the title of an official and not a personal name find no support in the Hebrew text.
elihu: 1. Ephraimite, Tohu’s son and an ancestor of Samuel the prophet; perhaps also called Eliab and Eliel in 1 Chronicles 6:27, 34, respectively.
elika: Harodite, listed as one of David’s mighty men. His name is not included in a similar list in 1 Chronicles 11:27.
elim: Early encampment of the Israelites after their passage through the Red Sea. Elim was situated between Marah and the desert of Sin.
elimelech: Man from Bethlehem who took his wife, Naomi, and his sons, Mahlon and Chilion, to sojourn in Moab because of famine in Judah. While in Moab, he died; then his sons also died; and Naomi decided to return to Judah.
elioenai: 1. Postexilic descendant of Solomon and the father of Hodaviah and Eliashib.
eliphal: Ur’s son and one of David’s mighty men; alternately called Eliphelet, son of Ahasbai, in 2 Samuel 23:34.
eliphalet: KJV spelling of Eliphelet, David’s son, in 2 Samuel 5:16 and 1 Chronicles 14:7.
eliphaz: 1. Oldest son of Esau and his wife Adah.
eliphelehu: Levitical musician who played the lyre (harp) when the ark was brought to Jerusalem in David’s time.
eliphelet: 1. One of David’s 13 sons born in Jerusalem.
elisabeth: KJV spelling of Elizabeth, John the Baptist’s mother.
elisha: Prophet in Israel during the ninth century BC.
elishah: Javan’s son. The Hebrew term for Greece is Javan; hence, Elishah could be the term for the western Aegean islands or coastlands (cf.
elishama: 1. Ammihud’s son and leader of the Ephraimites at the beginning of the journey in the wilderness.
elishaphat: Military commander in Judah who supported Jehoiada the priest in overthrowing Queen Athaliah and making the young Joash king.
elisheba: Wife of Aaron, who bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. Her father was Amminadab and her brother was Nahshon, the leader of Judah, the tribe to which Elisheba also belonged.
elishua: One of the 13 children fathered by David during his reign in Jerusalem. In the parallel passage of 1 Chronicles 3:6, the name Elishama appears in Elishua’s place in most Hebrew manuscripts.
eliud: Achim’s son, Eleazar’s father, and an ancestor of Jesus Christ according to Matthew’s genealogy.
elizabeth: Woman of priestly descent and mother of John the Baptist, she was a relative of Mary, mother of Jesus (v 36).
elizaphan: 1. Kohathite Levite and Uzziel’s son, who assisted in removing the bodies of Nadab and Abihu from the camp.
elizur: Shedeur’s son and leader of Reuben’s tribe at the start of Israel’s wilderness journey.
elkanah: 1. Levite of Korah’s family from the house of Izhar (v 21).
elkiah: Ananias’s son and father of Oziel, an ancestor of Judith.
elkosh: Home or birthplace of the prophet Nahum.
ellasar: Place in Babylonia; a few scholars have suggested that Arioch was its king. He joined a coalition that included Kedorlaomer, king of Elam, and together they raided the Jordan Valley during the time of Abraham.
elm: KJV mistranslation for terebinth, a large Palestinian tree, in Hosea 4:13.
elmadam, elmodam: Ancestor of Jesus Christ, according to Luke’s genealogy (Lk 3:28, KJV “Elmodam”).
elnaam: Father of two mighty warriors in David’s army, Jeribai and Joshaviah.
eloah: Hebrew name for God stressing that he alone is deserving of worship.
elohim: General name for God in the OT.
eloi, eloi, lama sabachthani?: One of Jesus’ cries from the cross.
elon (person): 1. Hittite who was the father of Basemath (perhaps also called Adah, Gn 36:2), one of Esau’s wives (26:34).
elon (place): Village near Timnah, the home of Samson’s first wife. Elon was included in the inheritance allotted to Dan’s tribe in Joshua’s distribution of the Promised Land (Jos 19:43; cf. 14:1-2).
elon-bethhanan: Administrative district in Dan during the reign of Solomon. It is perhaps identifiable with the Danite town of Elon.
eloth: Alternate spelling of the Edomite town Elath, in 1 Kings 9:26; 2 Chronicles 8:17; and 26:2.
elpaal: Benjamite and one of Shaharaim’s sons.
elpalet: KJV spelling of Elpelet, an alternate name for David’s son Eliphelet in 1 Chronicles 14:5.
el-paran: Place located on the edge of the wilderness of Paran, probably at the southern tip of the mountains of Seir in the Sinai Peninsula, present-day Arabia.
elpelet: Alternative name of David’s son Eliphelet in 1 Chronicles 14:5.
elasa: Mentioned in 1 Maccabees 9:5 as the place where Judas Maccabeus pitched his tents when Bacchides engaged him in battle and Judas was killed (9:18). It is usually identified with Il’asa near Beth-horon.
eltekeh: City allotted to Dan’s tribe for an inheritance; it was later assigned to the Kohathite Levites (21:23). An important battle was fought near Eltekeh between King Sennacherib of Assyria and the Egyptians.
eltekon: Town located in the hill country of Judah. It was assigned by Joshua to Judah’s tribe, and may be the modern Khirbet ed-Deir, west of Bethlehem.
eltolad: Town assigned to Simeon’s tribe in the southern portion of Judah’s inheritance. It is alternately called Tolad in 1 Chronicles 4:29.
elul: Hebrew month generally corresponding to mid-August to mid-September (Neh 6:15, NLT mg).
eluzai: One of the men of Benjamin who came to join David in Ziklag. Eluzai was an ambidextrous slinger and bowman.
elymais: Formerly thought to be a city in Persia, greatly renowned for riches, silver, and gold, but now generally regarded as a district of Persia. Josephus (Antiquities 12.9.1), following 1 Maccabees, alludes to it as a city, but it is otherwise unknown.
elymas: Another name for Bar-Jesus, a Jewish magician and false prophet, in Acts 13:8.
elyon: Hebrew name for God meaning “Most High.” See God, Names of.
elzabad: 1. Military leader from Gad’s tribe who joined David at Ziklag.
elzaphan: Alternate spelling of Elizaphan, a Levite chief, in Exodus 6:22 and Leviticus 10:4.
embalm: The Bible makes frequent reference to burial practices. A society’s burial customs are a reflection of its views about death and the afterlife.
embroiderer, embroidery: The art of making decorative designs on clothing. This was an art practiced both in the home and as a profession; it was done on a loom or with a needle.
emek-keziz: City allotted to Benjamin’s tribe for an inheritance; it was mentioned between Beth-hoglah and Beth-arabah.
emerald: Rich green variety of beryl, regarded as a precious stone.
emerod: 1. KJV rendering of ulcer in Deuteronomy 28:27.
emim, emites: Name given to the original inhabitants of Moab by the Moabites who ousted them from their land. They were a tall people, known also as Rephaim, and were compared with the Zuzites, Anakim, and Horites for their size.
emmanuel: Alternate spelling of Immanuel in Matthew 1:23.
emmaus: Town in Judea that appears in Luke (see 24:13) and also in 1 Maccabees (3:40, 57). It was the destination of two disciples to whom Jesus appeared after the Crucifixion.
emmor: KJV rendering of Hamor, Shechem’s father, in Acts 7:16.
emperor: Official designation of the Roman sovereign beginning in 27 BC with the reign of Caesar Augustus; a derivation of imperator, an honorary title of supreme command conferred by the Roman Senate upon one of its victorious generals.
enan: Ahira’s father. Ahira was appointed by Moses as the commander of the tribe of Naphtali during the first census of Israel in the desert of Sinai.
enchantment: Act of casting charms or incantations to influence others or to obtain knowledge. Balaam could place no enchantment against Israel but could only bless them.
end of the world: Expression used by OT prophets (as early as the eighth-century BC prophet Amos) to signify a time in which God actively intervenes in history, primarily for judgment. Thus “the day of the Lord” is also called “the day of the LORD’s anger”.
endor: Ancient Canaanite city, four miles (6.5 kilometers) south of Mt Tabor, assigned to the tribe of Manasseh, though never fully taken by them. The city witnessed the defeat of Jabin and Sisera by Barak.
en-eglaim: Place mentioned in Ezekiel 47:10 where, in a description of the millennial age, it is said that “fishermen will stand beside the sea; from En-gedi to En-eglaim it will be a place for the spreading of nets; its fish will be of very many kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea” (RSV).
engagement: Act of commiting oneself to another by a pledge to marry.
en-gannim: 1. Village in the lowland of Judah near Beth-shemesh.
en-gedi: A vital oasis on the west side of the Dead Sea about 35 miles (56.3 kilometers) southeast of Jerusalem.
engraver, engraving: A stonemason who removed stone from the quarry and squared it up for use in large buildings like palaces, the temple, administrative buildings, and large houses.
en-haddah: City allotted to Issachar’s tribe for an inheritance, mentioned between En-gannim and Beth-pazzez.
en-hakkore: Spring of water that burst forth when Samson cried to the Lord after he had slaughtered the Philistines (Jgs 15:19, NLT mg).
en-hazor: Fortified city of the OT. One of several Hazors in the OT, En-hazor was probably located in Galilee.
en-mishpat: Early name for Kadesh, mentioned in the account of Kedorlaomer’s battles.
enoch (person): 1. Cain’s son and grandson of Adam.
enoch (place): City that Cain named for his first son, Enoch.
enosh: Seth’s son and the grandson of Adam. He became the father of Kenan at 90 years of age, after which he fathered other sons and daughters, dying at the age of 905.
en-rimmon: Town assigned first to Judah and then to Simeon. These verses refer to two places, Ain and Rimmon, but this was probably a scribal error for the one town, En-rimmon (see Jos 19:7).
en-rogel: Spring that was an important landmark identifying the boundary line between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin.
enrollment: Registration of people according to tribe, family, and position.
en-shemesh: Place mentioned only in Joshua 15:7 and 18:17 as a boundary marker between Judah’s northern border and Benjamin’s southern border. The usual identification is with ’Ain el-Hod, about three miles (4.8 kilometers) east of Jerusalem on the road to Jericho.
en-tappuah: Canaanite town located on the border between Ephraim’s and Manasseh’s territory. It is usually identified with the modern Sheikh Abu-Zarad, about eight miles (12.9 kilometers) south of Shechem.
enuma elish: Title of the Babylonian creation epic found during excavations at Nineveh (1848–76).
epaphras: Coworker with the apostle Paul. Epaphras, a native of Colosse, was responsible for the city’s evangelization, as well as that of Laodicea and Hierapolis.
epaphroditus: Leader in the Philippian church. Epaphroditus was sent to the apostle Paul during Paul’s first Roman imprisonment; his mission was to deliver gifts and to assist the apostle in his work (2:25).
epenetus: Believer greeted by Paul in Romans 16:5 as “my dear friend” and “the very first person to become a Christian in the province of Asia” (NLT). It is not known if Epenetus was a personal convert of Paul.
ephah (measurement): Measure of grain, about half a bushel (18 liters).
ephah (person): 1. Son of Midian, an offspring of Abraham through his concubine Keturah.
ephai: Netophathite (resident of the town Netophah, near Bethlehem) whose sons fought against the Babylonian army. They, with others, approached Gedaliah, the governor of Judah appointed by Babylon, and requested his protection.
epher: 1. Son of Midian and grandson of Abraham through his concubine Keturah, whose tribe was sent to the east.
ephes-dammim: Location between Socoh and Azekah in Judah where the Philistines encamped. It was called Pas-dammim in 1 Chronicles 11:13.
ephesians, letter to the: Letter to the Christians in Ephesus and the surrouding churches written with a magnificence that both instructs and inspires the reader.
ephesus: Most important city of the Roman province of Asia, located on the western shore of Asia Minor (modern Turkey).
ephlal: Jerahmeel’s descendant, who could trace his ancestry through Perez to Judah.
ephod (garment): Upper garment worn during religious services associated with the tabernacle or temple. “Ephod” generally referred to the ornamented vest that the high priest wore over a blue robe.
ephod (person): Father of Hanniel, the prince of the children of Joseph. Hanniel was responsible for distributing Canaanite territory among the Israelite tribes.
ephphatha: Transliteration in the imperative voice of the Aramaic expression “be opened,” used by Jesus in the healing of a deaf mute (Mk 7:34, NLT mg). No attempt at establishing a magical word formula was intended; Mark simply preserved Jesus’ actual wording.
ephraemi syri, codex: Copies of the NT books produced by scribes and editions made from these copies.
ephraim (person): Joseph’s younger son, born of Joseph and Asenath before the seven years of famine in Egypt. He was the ancestor of an Israelite tribe, and his name came to designate the northern kingdom of Israel.
ephraim (place): 1. Area allotted to Ephraim’s tribe for an inheritance.
ephraim, forest of: Rocky, wooded stretch of country east of the Jordan in the area of Mahanaim. It was here that David’s army defeated Absalom.
ephraim, gate of: Gate in the Jerusalem wall positioned about 600 feet (182.9 meters) east of the Corner Gate. It was rebuilt in Nehemiah’s day and was situated close to the Water Gate and courts of the temple.
ephraim, mount: KJV expression referring to the hill country in central Palestine where Ephraim’s tribe was located. The area was one of the most productive in Palestine.
ephraim, tribe of: Tribe descended from the patriarch Joseph’s second son. Both Ephraim and his brother Manasseh were regarded as sons also by their grandfather Jacob and became his heirs.
ephraimite: Name given to a person from the tribal area of Ephraim.
ephrain: KJV form of Ephron, a town near Bethel, in 2 Chronicles 13:19.
ephrath (person): Mother of Hur and Caleb’s second wife.
ephrath (place): 1. Town in the Judean hill country later named Bethlehem.
ephrathite: Inhabitant of the town of Ephrath (Bethlehem) in Judah.
ephron (person): Hittite from whom Abraham purchased the cave of Machpelah with its adjoining field for 400 shekels of silver. Sarah was buried there, as was Abraham (25:9) and Jacob (50:13).
ephron (place): 1. Mountainous district on the northern edge of Judah.
epicureans: Those who followed the teachings of the Greek philosopher Epicurus (342–270 BC). Paul encountered some of them while in Athens.
epilepsy, epileptic: Disease of the central nervous system, and one afflicted with the disease, characterized by unconsciousness and convulsions.
epiphanes: Name taken by Antiochus IV, meaning the “Manifest God.” Alexander Balas also used the name Epiphanes in his claim to the kingship.
epistle: A communication, especially from a king or high official, usually containing commands, promulgations, or reports.
epistle of the apostles: Letter purporting to come from the 11 apostles to the churches “of the east and the west, of the north and the south, declaring and imparting to you that which concerns our Lord Jesus Christ.” Some believe that the epistle was written in Asia Minor about AD 160; others think that it originated in Egypt.
epistles, apocryphal: Writings in epistolary form and apocryphal in nature.
er: 1. Eldest son of Judah and Bathshua, a Canaanite woman.
eran: Grandson of Ephraim and the oldest son of Shuthelah, from whom came the Eranite family. In 1 Chronicles 7:20, Eran was replaced by Eleadah, which may be a copyist’s error.
erastus: Name mentioned three times in the NT. Whether only one individual is being referred to cannot be ascertained, although in each case Erastus is an associate of Paul’s.
erech: Important Sumerian city, located at what is now called Warka near the Euphrates River, 40 miles (64.4 kilometers) northwest of Ur and 160 miles (257.4 kilometers) south of Baghdad. Genesis 10:10 refers to Erech as the second of four cities founded by Nimrod.
eri: Gad’s fifth son and founder of the Erite family.
esaias: KJV form of Isaiah the prophet, in the NT.
esarhaddon: King of Assyria (681–669 BC). Though probably not the eldest son of Sennacherib, he was the eldest surviving son following several interfamily murders.
esau: Isaac’s son, and the older twin brother of Jacob, who was given this name because of the hair on his body at birth.
eschatology: Branch of theology concerned with the study of the last things, or end times, whether in relation to the individual or the world.
esdras, first book of: Book that is largely a compilation of material from 2 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah.
esdras, second book of: Composite Jewish and Christian writing included in some canons of the Bible (see discussion above under 1 Esdras).
esdris: Mentioned in 2 Maccabees 12:36 as an army officer under Judas Maccabeus. Some Greek texts and the KJV read Gorgias, which may be either a place or a person.
esek: Name Isaac gave to a well dug by his servants in the valley of Gerar (Gn 26:20; see NLT mg).
eshan: Town in the hill country of the territory allotted to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance.
eshbaal: King Saul’s fourth son, who became Israel’s king after his father’s death. Eshbaal literally means “man of Baal,” or “Baal exists”.
eshban: Dishon’s second son and grandson of Seir the Horite.
eshcol (person): Amorite who, with his brothers Mamre and Aner, helped the patriarch Abraham defeat the forces of Kedorlaomer and rescue Lot and his family.
eshcol (place): Valley near Hebron from which the spies sent by Moses brought back pomegranates, figs, and a large cluster of grapes. This site may be identifiable with ’Ain Eshkali, just north of Hebron.
eshean: KJV spelling of the town Eshan in Joshua 15:52.
eshek: Descendant of Jonathan, Saul’s son. Eshek’s grandsons were mighty men of valor in the tribe of Benjamin.
eshkalonite: Inhabitant of the Philistine city Ashkelon (Jos 13:3, KJV).
eshtaol: Lowland town on the border between Judah and Dan, always mentioned along with nearby Zorah. In this area the young Samson began to be moved by the Spirit of the Lord, and here he was later buried (16:31).
eshtemoa, eshtemoh (place): City south of Jerusalem allotted to Judah when Palestine was divided among the 12 tribes. Eshtemoa was assigned to the Levites.
eshton: Mehir’s son and the grandson of Chelub from Judah’s tribe.
esli: Nahum’s father and ancestor of Jesus, according to Luke’s genealogy (3:25).
espousal: The joining together of male and female in matrimony, as practiced by various cultures.
esrom: KJV rendering of Hezron, Perez’s son, in Matthew 1:3 and Luke 3:33.
essenes: Jewish sect or community in Palestine in the last century BC and the first century AD.
esther (person): One of two names borne by the Jewish queen of Persia. Hadassah (Hebrew “Myrtle”) apparently was her Jewish name, and Esther (Persian “Star”) her name as queen of Persia.
esther, additions to: Six passages of about 105 verses added to the Hebrew text of Esther. The Additions to Esther was apparently the work of a Jewish writer eager to supply a spiritual and universal note that was thought to be lacking in the book.
esther, book of: Old Testament book telling the story of a Jewish woman’s protection of her people after her marriage to a gentile king.
etam: 1. Rocky area in western Judah where Samson hid from his pursuers.
eternal life: Mode of existence referred to in Scripture characterized by either timelessness or immortality; kind of life attributed to God and distributed to believers.
eternal punishment: Place of future punishment for the lost, unrepentant, wicked dead.
eternity: Duration of time that cannot be measured.
etham: First encampment of the Hebrews after leaving Succoth, perhaps located on the border of the wilderness of Shur. The suggestion that it was an Egyptian fortress is improbable.
ethan: 1. Wise man comparable to Solomon and probably the author of Psalm 89.
ethanim: Early name for the seventh month in the Jewish calendar (1 Kgs 8:2, NLT mg).
ethbaal: King of Sidon whose daughter Jezebel entered into a political marriage with Ahab of Israel. Ethbaal was credited with building Botrys in Phoenicia and founding the colony of Auza in Libya.
ether: 1. A town in Judah in the Shephelah region.
ethiopia: In the OT, Ethiopia was generally referred to as Cush (Gn 10:6; 1 Chr 1:8; Is 11:11, KJV), which is a transliteration of the only Hebrew word used to describe the land lying to the south of Egypt.
eth-kazin: One of the towns marking the eastern boundary of Zebulun’s tribe.
ethnan: Member of Helah’s family from Judah’s tribe.
ethnarch: Title given to one who rules by the authority of another country. Ethnarch was a position below a king but above a tetrarch or governor.
ethni: Alternate name for Jeatherai, Zerah’s son, in 1 Chronicles 6:41.
eubulus: Roman believer who sent greetings to Timothy during Paul’s second Roman imprisonment. His Greek name indicates his probable gentile origin.
eucharist: The supper Jesus shared with his disciples a few hours before he was arrested and taken to his trial and death (thus often called “The Last Supper”); the ceremony of partaking of the bread and wine that Christians have come to call the Lord’s Supper, the…
euergetes: Title of honor belonging to two Ptolemaic rulers. From the Greek word meaning “Benefactor,” the title was ascribed to rulers known for their benevolent actions.
eumenes: The designation of a king of Pergamum, Eumenes II (197–158 BC) mentioned in 1 Maccabees 8:8 in connection with an alliance that Judas Maccabeus made with the Romans during their war with Antiochus the Great.
eunice: Timothy’s mother, daughter of Lois, and the wife of a pagan Greek. She was a Jewish Christian.
eunuch: Officer or chamberlain in the court or household of a ruler, often assigned to the women’s quarters. Many of these men were emasculated, though not always (cf.
euodia, euodias: Prominent woman in the Philippian church whom Paul asked to resolve her differences with Syntyche. The nature of their disagreement is not known, but it was of enough severity to reach Paul in Rome.
eupator: Surname of Antiochus V, the Seleucid king. The name means “son of a noble father.” See Antiochus V.
euphrates river: Largest river in western Asia, formed by the union of two rivers in Asia Minor, the Kara-Su and the Murat-Suyu. Its source is in central Armenia.
eupolemus: A Jewish ambassador sent by Judas Maccabeus to Rome along with Jason, the son of Eleazar, to establish an alliance. He is identified in 1 Maccabees 8:17 as the son of John, the son of Accos.
euroclydon: KJV transliteration of the Greek word for the northeasterly wind mentioned in Paul’s journey to Rome in Acts 27:14.
eutychus: Common slave name, mentioned only in Acts 20:9. It was Eutychus’s misfortune to become sleepy while sitting on a windowsill listening to the apostle Paul preach at Troas.
evangelist: NT term referring to one who proclaims the gospel of Jesus Christ. There are only three occurrences of the word in the NT.
eve: First woman, “the mother of all living”. The book of Genesis recounts that after God had finished his creation of Adam, he saw that it was not good for Adam to be alone.
evening: Most literally, a period of time delimited by the earth’s rotation around its axis, such as the period between two consecutive sunrises; also, the portion of that period in which the sun is visible, the other portion being called “night.” The word “day” occurs over 2,000 times in the OT, over 350 times in the NT.
evening sacrifice: Major ritual expressions of religious life with accompanying rites, such as libations, effusions, and sacred meals. The ideology expressed in Israel’s ritual complex made its religion unique in the ancient Near East.
everlasting life: Mode of existence referred to in Scripture characterized by either timelessness or immortality; kind of life attributed to God and distributed to believers.
evi: One of five Midianite kings killed in a battle against Israel under the leadership of Moses. Apparently, God directed Moses to go to battle against Midian because the Midianites had led the Israelites into pagan religious practices.
evil: Evildoing that is not only against humanity, society, others, or oneself, but against God. The concept of God, therefore, gives to the idea of sin its many-sided meaning.
evil-merodach: Son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar as king of Babylon, who reigned for two years (561–560 BC). During his reign, he released Jehoiachin, former king of Judah, from imprisonment.
exaltation of christ: The glory and dominion which Jesus attained subsequent to the completion of his earthly work of suffering and death. It is at one and the same time the consummation of his redemptive sacrifice and the reward of his full obedience to the will of the Father.
execration texts: Certain Egyptian Middle Kingdom texts containing curses (execrations) directed against the pharaoh’s enemies. Such texts have been found on 20th- to 19th-century BC bowls from Thebes, and on 19th- to 18th-century figurines from Saqqara.
execution: The science or philosophy of law is called jurisprudence. Although modern jurisprudence bears little resemblance to biblical concepts of law, the Scriptures have played a definite role in its development.
exhortation: Translation of a Greek word literally meaning “a calling of someone alongside to help.” Its primary meaning in the NT is the urging of someone to do something—particularly some ethical course of action.
exile: Dispersion of Jewish people from Israel to foreign lands. Diaspora, a Greek noun meaning a “sowing” or “scattering,” is regularly used in the Septuagint to mean “exile” (Jer 25:34; cf.
exodus, book of: Second book of the Bible, containing the story of God’s liberation of the people of Israel from slavery in Egypt. Few books of the OT are as important historically and theologically as the book of Exodus.
exodus, the: Departure of Israel from Egypt led by Moses. The exodus was one of the most significant events in the history of the Hebrews.
exorcism, exorcist: Art of expelling demons and evil spirits, and the practitioner of this art.
expiation: Atonement, purification, or removal of sin or its guilt. The term occurs in some English translations (such as ASV, ERV) for “reconciliation” or “propitiation”.
eye paint: That which is applied to the body to enhance one’s appearance.
ezar: KJV spelling of Ezer, Seir’s son, in 1 Chronicles 1:38.
ezbai: Father of Naarai, one of David’s elite force known as “the thirty”. In 2 Samuel 23:35 he is called Paarai the Arbite.
ezbon: 1. Gad’s son, called Ozni in Numbers 26:16; perhaps an eponym of a Gadite family.
ezekias: KJV spelling of Hezekiah, Judah’s king, in Matthew 1:9-10.
ezekiel (person): Priest and prophet during Israel’s Babylonian exile. Ezekiel was a descendant of the influential priestly family of Zadok.
ezekiel, book of: Prophetic book of the OT, originating in the time of the Babylonian exile.
ezel: Hebrew word designating a stone where Jonathan and David met prior to David’s departure from the court of Saul (1 Sm 20:19, NLT mg).
ezem: City allotted to Judah’s tribe, then later to Simeon’s tribe, for an inheritance. Joshua 15 locates the city in the extreme southern part of Canaan.
ezion-geber: Important port near some significant ruins at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba. Ezion-geber was one of the stations where the Israelites encamped while on their way to the plains of Moab.
eznite: KJV designation for the preeminent leader of David’s mighty men in 2 Samuel 23:8. Most consider Adino the Eznite a later scribal alteration of the Hebrew text and prefer the reading “Jashobeam the Hacmonite.”
ezra (person): 1. Religious reformer following Israel’s return from exile.
ezra, book of: One of the historical books of the OT, associated with 2 Chronicles and Nehemiah.
ezrah: Father of four sons from Judah’s tribe.
ezrahite: Word occurring only three times in the OT. Twice it is used as a title for Ethan (1 Kgs 4:31; Ps 89 title) and once as a name given to Heman (Ps 88 title).
ezri: Son of Kelub and one of the men who supervised the tilling of David’s lands.
fair havens: Small harbor, identifiable with modern Limenes Kali, positioned along Crete’s southern coast about five miles (8.1 kilometers) east of Cape Matala near the city of Lasea. Here Paul’s ship sought shelter from contrary winds on his voyage to Rome.
faith: Belief in that which has no tangible proof; trust in God.
faithfulness: Maintaining faith or allegiance; showing a strong sense of duty or conscientiousness. In biblical Hebrew, “faith” and “faithfulness” are grammatically related.
falcon: Bird of prey noted for keen eyesight, and declared unclean in the OT.
fall of man: Transition from a condition of moral innocence and favor with God to a condition of being condemned to death, which occurred in the history of humankind with Adam’s eating of the forbidden fruit.
fallow deer: KJV translation of roebuck, a ruminant and member of the deer family, in Deuteronomy 14:5.
false christs, false messiahs: Those who falsely claim to be the Christ or Messiah. False christs are mentioned only in the eschatological discourse of Jesus recorded by Matthew (24:24) and Mark (13:22).
false prophets: Spokesmen, heralds, or messengers falsely speaking for, or on behalf of, someone else. The false prophet was often motivated not by loyalty to God but by a desire for popularity.
family life and relations: In Bible times, the family comprised members of a household, including not only parents and children, along with other relatives and concubines, but also servants, travelers, aliens, and anyone else who happened to be within the house and was therefore under the protection of the head of the family.
famine: Prolonged and extreme lack of food. Famine, along with other disasters (such as war and disease), has always been part of the human experience.
farmer, farming: During Bible times agriculture took the same three main forms found in Palestine today. Emphasis on each of these has depended upon the social and technological status of the people.
farthing: 1. KJV translation for penny, a copper coin equivalent to one-sixteenth of the silver denarius.
fast, fasting: Eating sparingly or abstaining from food altogether, either from necessity or desire. In medical terms, fasting is the detoxification of the body through the restriction of food.
father, god as: God’s self-identifications expressing various aspects of his being.
father, human: In Bible times, the family comprised members of a household, including not only parents and children, along with other relatives and concubines, but also servants, travelers, aliens, and anyone else who happened to be within the house and was therefore under the protection of the head of the family.
father-in-law: In Bible times, the family comprised members of a household, including not only parents and children, along with other relatives and concubines, but also servants, travelers, aliens, and anyone else who happened to be within the house and was therefore under the protection of the head of the family.
fathom: Unit of measure equivalent to about six feet (1.8 meters) (Acts 27:28, NLT mg).
fawn: Designation for a young animal, usually a deer.
fayum: Egypt’s largest oasis, about 70 miles (112.6 kilometers) southwest of Cairo.
fear: Emotional foreboding or dread of impending distress or misfortune. Often spoken of as the cause of people wanting religion.
feast of lights: Alternate name for Hanukkah, one of Israel’s festivals celebrating the rededication of the temple in 164 BC.
feasts and festivals of israel: Occasions of public or private rejoicing to commemorate some significant event or personage. The element of celebration has a special meaning in the cycle of religious occasions and the rites and ceremonies associated with these particular days.
felix, antonius: Roman procurator (governor) of Judea (AD 52–60) succeeding Cumanus, appointed by Claudius and succeeded by Festus Porcius.
fellowship: Communion with God, which results in common participation with other believers in the Spirit of God and God’s blessings.
ferret: KJV translation for gecko, a kind of reptile, in Leviticus 11:30.
fertility cults: Study of the polytheistic religion of the Canaanites has contributed much to our understanding of the religion of ancient Israel. The Hebrew theological and religious structures were given by God to a people who were influenced and affected by other religions.
festival: Occasions of public or private rejoicing to commemorate some significant event or personage. The element of celebration has a special meaning in the cycle of religious occasions and the rites and ceremonies associated with these particular days.
festus, porcius: Roman procurator (governor) of Judea, who succeeded Felix Antonius and who was succeeded by Albinus. The precise date of Porcius Festus’s accession to power is debatable but has been narrowed to sometime between AD 55 and 60.
field of blood: Name given to the field purchased with the “blood money” Judas accepted to betray Jesus. The field was purchased by the chief priests as a burial ground for strangers (formerly, the potter’s field).
fiery serpent: Bronze symbol of a snake made by Moses on God’s instruction to save the Israelites.
fig, fig tree: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
finance: Medium of exchange, measurement of value, means of payment.
finger (measure): Linear measure equivalent to the width of a finger.
fire, lake of: Final abode of Satan, his servants, and unrepentant human beings.
fire, pillar of: Supernatural phenomenon of God’s presence that guided the Israelites in the wilderness.
firkin: Measure of about 10 gallons (37.9 liters). In John 2:6, firkin is the KJV translation for the name of a Greek liquid measure.
firmament: Bible word for the atmosphere about the earth. The original meaning of this word refers to space that is stretched out or expanded.
firstborn: Term used in the Bible to describe a family’s oldest son or daughter. Israel was called God’s firstborn because of that nation’s miraculous beginning and special deliverance out of Egypt.
firstfruits: Firstborn child or animal or first parts of any crop that, in Hebrew thought, were considered as holy and therefore belonged to the Lord. The firstfruits, as a foretaste of more to come, were offered to God in thanksgiving for his goodness in providing them.
first jewish revolt: Uprising in AD 66–70, which occurred as the result of a series of ineffective Roman governors in Judea.
fir tree: Translation of several Hebrew words in the OT that possibly designate a conifer. Positive identification is not possible.
fish: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
fishermen: Those who caught fish for a living. Fishing was carried on by fishermen in the Holy Land from early times and is referred to in both the OT and the NT.
fish gate: Gate probably located in the north wall of the city of Jerusalem. The Fish Gate was built in David’s time and later formed part of Manasseh’s fortifications.
fitch: KJV translation of two Hebrew words. “Fitch” is actually an older form of the word “vetch,” the name of many species of leguminous plants.
flag: KJV rendering of an uncertain marshland plant in Job 8:11.
flax: Cultivated plant providing one of the oldest textile fibers. The term may also refer to the fiber itself, thread spun from it, or the woven linen cloth.
flea: Small, wingless insect with strong legs for jumping. The flea is mentioned only in 1 Samuel 24:14 and 26:20, where David refers to himself as a flea.
flesh: The body; the physical being of humans; the human person and human existence; the carnal nature of humans.
flint: Dark, fine-grained, hard silica (rock) used for blades of tools. Flint when struck against other hard surfaces produces sparks and so was used for lighting fires.
flogging: Beating a person with a whip or other instrument, sometimes used as a legislated punishment.
flood, the: Rising and overflowing of water to cover the land, specifically the flood of Noah.
flood myths: Popular legendary composition about a Sumerian hero’s life of adventure and acquisition of wisdom. Gilgamesh was king of Uruk, or Erech (Tell Obeid; modern Warka), at the end of the fourth millennium BC.
flour: Fine, powdery substance produced by grinding the inner kernels of wheat. Flour was used in baking and also for cereal offerings.
flower: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
flute: Translation of several Hebrew words designating various kinds of wind instruments played by blowing across or through a hole.
fly: Two-winged insect. In Scripture, several species are in view, including the common housefly and the horsefly.
followers of the way: Designation for Christians in the book of Acts. In its early years, Christianity was called “the Way.” See Way, The.
food and food preparation: Substances required by the body to sustain life, and the methods of making them edible. Food consumed in Bible times included bread, milk products, fruit, meat, and fish.
footstool: Low stool used to support one’s feet. Part of King Solomon’s great revenue of gold was used to fashion a footstool for his ivory throne.
fords of the jordan: Shallow places where people and animals could wade through the Jordan River. Many OT personalities crossed over the Jordan at its two main fords: these people include Jacob, Gideon, David, Absalom (17:24), Abner and his men (2:29).
foreigner: Noncitizen or alien, temporary guest, sojourner, or stranger.
foreknowledge: Knowledge of things or events before they exist or happen.
foreordination: Activity of God by which he establishes events and outcomes before they occur. In common usage, “foreordination” and the term “predestination” are synonymous.
forerunner: Scout sent in advance of troops, or a herald who precedes a high official to announce his coming.
forgetfulness, land of: Euphemism for the abode of the dead. Once in the land of forgetfulness, the dead are thought to be forgotten by God and people alike.
forgiveness: Pardon, involving restoration of broken relationships; ceasing to feel resentment for wrongs and offenses. Primarily, forgiveness is an act of God, releasing sinners from judgment and freeing them from the divine penalty of their sin.
former rain: KJV term for important rainfall that begins the agricultural year in Palestine, usually in October.
fornication: Unchastity, sexual immorality. The word “fornication” is used in the Scriptures to mean several different things.
fort, fortification: Walls, citadels, and sometimes moats protecting most cities in the ancient world. Fortifications followed the natural contour of the area encircling a city.
fortunatus: Member of the church at Corinth. Fortunatus is a Roman proper name written in Greek and found only once in the NT.
forum: Open area in Roman cities used for commerce, political affairs, and judicial matters. The forum was usually on level ground, rectangular in shape, and surrounded by temples, law courts, colonnades, and other public buildings.
foundation gate: Structure mentioned in 2 Chronicles 23:5, in the narrative about Queen Athaliah’s execution. The parallel passage in 2 Kings 11:6 reads “Sur Gate,” while the Septuagint has “gate of the ways,” indicating some difficulties within the Hebrew text.
fowl: KJV common translation for bird. In modern usage and the RSV, the term is reserved for domestic birds or wild fowl that are eaten.
fowler: One who traps or shoots wild birds. The catching of birds for pets, food, and sacrifices was the business of the fowler.
fox: Small, wild, carnivorous, doglike mammal, several species of which existed in Palestine in the biblical period.
frankincense: Fragrant gum resin that can be ground into powder and burned to produce a balsamlike odor. It was often associated with myrrh.
freedmen: Members of a Jewish synagogue in Jerusalem, descended from Jews who had been captured and taken to Rome by the general Pompey (106–48 BC), then later released.
freedom: Quality or state of being free. In the ancient world slavery was universal.
freed slaves: NLT rendering of Freedmen in Acts 6:9.
friends: Term used to indicate close acquaintances.
fringe: The border of a garment, or a “tassel,” four of which were worn on the upper garments of Jewish men according to the Lord’s commandment. Those tassels were to be reminders of God’s laws.
frog: Aquatic, tailless, smooth-skinned amphibian, mentioned in connection with the second plague in Egypt.
frontlet: Translation of a Hebrew word referring to anything bound on the forehead. The phylacteries of Jesus’ day were worn daily at morning prayer by every male Israelite over the age of 13.
fruit: Substances required by the body to sustain life, and the methods of making them edible. Food consumed in Bible times included bread, milk products, fruit, meat, and fish.
fruit of the spirit: Expression taken from Galatians 5:22-23. As listed there, this fruit is the evidence one may expect from a life in which the Spirit of God is living and reigning.
fuller: One who cleans, shrinks, thickens, or dyes cloth or newly shorn wool. It was the fuller’s job to prepare fibers used for weaving by cleansing them of oil and other impurities.
fuller's field: Place outside Jerusalem that was linked to a spring or pool by a causeway or aqueduct. It has been generally identified with an area near En-rogel (“spring of the fuller”).
fullness: Common translation of the Greek term pleroma. The word carries various shades of meaning that must be determined by observing its use in context.
fullness of time: Expression meaning “when the time was ripe,” occurring in English translations of Galatians 4:4 and Ephesians 1:10.
funeral customs: Practices and rites that encompass the dying and death of human beings. Funerary rites have been practiced by all social groups from their very beginnings.
furlong: Linear measure of about 202 yards (184.6 meters).
furnace: Brick or stone structure varying in size and shape, depending on whether it was to be used domestically or commercially.
furnaces, tower of the: KJV rendering of Tower of the Ovens in Nehemiah 3:11 and 12:38.
furniture: Items of material culture used in homes, palaces, and temples. Because of its close geographical proximity to other nations, Israel had extensive contact with neighboring cultures.
gaal: Ebed’s son, who persuaded the men of Shechem to revolt against Abimelech, the judge of Israel. The revolt, however, was quickly crushed and Shechem was destroyed.
gaash: 1. Mountain about 20 miles (32.2 kilometers) southwest of Shechem.
gaba: KJV spelling of the Benjamite city, Geba, in Joshua 18:24, Ezra 2:26, and Nehemiah 7:30.
gabael: 1. Ancestor of Tobit and a member of the tribe of Naphtali.
gabatha: Alternate name for Bigthan, one of Ahasuerus’s eunuchs (Add Est 12:1).
gabbai: Head of a family that returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile.
gabbatha: Transliteration of an uncertain Aramaic expression, which is rendered in Greek as “paved with stones” and refers to the raised area before the palace in Jerusalem where formal sentencing by the governor occurred.
gabri, gabrias: Brother or father of Gabael. The genitive case of the original does not make the exact relationship certain; it simply specifies that there is a relationship.
gabriel: One of the two angels mentioned by name in the Bible (the other is Michael). Gabriel appeared in human form to Daniel to reveal to him the meaning of a vision, to show what would transpire on the Day of Judgment, and to give Daniel wisdom and understanding.
gad (person): 1. One of the 12 sons of Jacob.
gad (idol): Canaanite god of fortune or fate whom the Israelites worshiped.
gad, tribe of: Descendants of Jacob’s seventh son Gad, and eighth largest of the 12 tribes that came out of Egypt with Moses (according to the number of warriors in Nm 1:1-3, 24-25). They raised livestock and had a reputation for being fierce in battle.
gad, valley of: Translation of a Hebrew phrase in 2 Samuel 24:5, meaning literally “the river or streambed of Gad.” It is rendered “in the midst of the river of Gad” (KJV), “in the middle of the valley, toward Gad” (RSV), “the valley of Gad” (ASV) and “in the direction of Gad” (NLT).
gadara, gadarenes: City of the Decapolis and its inhabitants, mentioned only once in the better manuscripts of the NT. Jesus had crossed to the eastern side of the Sea of Galilee and healed the demoniac named Legion, whom he encountered in “the country of the Gadarenes”.
gaddi: Man from Manasseh’s tribe sent by Moses to search out the land of Canaan.
gaddiel: Sodi’s son from Zebulun’s tribe, sent by Moses to search out the land of Canaan.
gadfly: Any of a number of large flies, including the horsefly and botfly, that irritate livestock. King Nebuchadnezzar is called a gadfly in the only biblical reference to this insect.
gadi: Father of Menahem. Menahem revolted and killed Shallum, king of Israel, placing himself on the throne as king.
gaham: Son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, and his concubine Reumah.
gahar: Ancestor of a group of temple assistants that returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile.
gaius: 1. Native of Macedonia and traveling companion of Paul during the apostle’s third missionary journey.
galal: 1. Levite and Mica’s son, who returned from exile in Babylon.
galatia: Ancient kingdom resulting from migrations of Gallic people from the west and settlement on the central plain of Asia Minor.
galatians, letter to the: This letter has an important place in the NT. It reveals much of Paul’s character and sheds light on his teaching.
galbanum: One of the ingredients used to make a special perfume for the tabernacle. Galbanum comes from a waxy, brownish gum excreted from the lower part of a plant that is a member of the carrot or parsley family and is native to Syria and Persia.
galeed: Name meaning literally “a heap of witness.” Jacob gave this name to a pile of stones erected as a witness to the pact of friendship made between himself and his father-in-law, Laban, who named the cairn Jegar-sahadutha. Its location is unknown.
galilee: Area in northern Palestine that, in Israel’s earlier history, had boundaries that were not clearly defined but that became more precisely defined in the period of Roman rule. The English name Galilee comes from two Hebrew words meaning “circuit” or “district.”
galilee, sea of: A large body of water in Palestine. It has had many names in its history.
gall: 1. Yellowish-brown bitter secretion of the liver or the organ containing the gall (20:25).
gallim: Village near Gibeah of Saul and Anathoth in Benjamin, north of Jerusalem and close to Bahurim; probably present-day Khirbet Kakul.
gallio: Marcus Annaeus Seneca’s son, and brother of the philosopher Seneca, who lived from 3 BC to AD 65. Born in Cordoba, Spain, Gallio came to Rome during Tiberius’s reign.
gallio inscription: Dated Greek inscription found in Delphi, Greece, mentioning Gallio as proconsul, and establishing the time of Paul’s initial visit to Corinth (cf. Acts 18:12-17).
gallows: Upright frame with a crossbeam and a rope for hanging criminals. In the book of Esther, a gibbet is mentioned, upon which men were impaled and left to hang in scorn.
gamaliel: 1. Pedahzur’s son and captain or prince of Manasseh’s tribe.
gammad: Home of mercenaries who served in the army of Tyre, according to Ezekiel’s prophecy. Gammad may have been located in Syria and is identified as Kumidi in the Tell el-Amarna letters.
gammadims: KJV form of “men of Gamad” (RSV) in Ezekiel 27:11.
gamul: Priest assigned to temple duty in David’s time.
gangrene: Death of tissue due to loss of the vital blood supply to that part of the body.
garden house: KJV translation of Beth-haggan in 2 Kings 9:27.
garden of eden: Location in the east of Eden in the Tigris-Euphrates area of Mesopotamia, referred to 14 times in the OT.
gareb (place): Hill near Jerusalem mentioned in Jeremiah 31:39 as a future boundary of the city, perhaps on the south or west side.
garlic: Bulbous herb cultivated for use in cooking See Food and Food Preparation; Plants (Onion).
garmite: Designation for Keilah in 1 Chronicles 4:19. The word, which means “bony,” seems to denote strength (the same Hebrew word is used in Jb 40:18 and Prv 25:15).
gashmu: KJV spelling of Geshem the Arab in Nehemiah 6:6.
gaspar: Traditional name for one of the wise men who brought a gift to Jesus in Matthew 2:1-2.
gatam: Esau’s grandson, the fourth son of Eliphaz and an Edomite chief.
gate: Science, art, or profession of designing and constructing buildings, bridges, etc.
gate between the two walls: Entrance in the southeast part of the city of Jerusalem, possibly the same as the Fountain Gate.
gatekeepers: Those who guarded gates of the cities and doors of palaces, temples, and other large buildings. Their task was to admit or reject visitors.
gath: Walled city and one of the five chief cities of the Philistines, which also included Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, and Ekron, all situated on or near the southern coast of Palestine.
gath-hepher: Town in Galilee, in Zebulun’s territory, which was the birthplace of Jonah. Modern el-Meshad occupies the site of Gath-hepher.
gath-rimmon: 1. City located in the land allotted to Dan’s tribe for an inheritance.
gaulanitis: Small province east of the Sea of Galilee, situated between Mt Hermon and the Yarmuk River and extending perhaps to the Jordan River. It took its name from the ancient town of Golan.
gaza: City near the Palestinian coast, about 50 miles (80.5 kilometers) west-southwest of Jerusalem. It has been occupied almost continuously since ancient times; modern Gaza has played an important part in the conflict between Arabs and Israelis.
gazara: Alternate name for the city of Gezer in 1 and 2 Maccabees.
gazathites: KJV alternate spelling for residents of Gaza.
gazer: KJV alternate spelling of the town Gezer in 2 Samuel 5:25 and 1 Chronicles 14:16.
gazez: 1. Caleb’s son by his concubine Ephah, and the brother of Haran.
gazzam: Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile.
geba: Levitical city in the territory of Benjamin, about seven miles (11.3 kilometers) northeast of Jerusalem and south of Michmash. It is easily confused with Gibeah, the hometown of Saul, which is also in Benjamin, to the southwest of Geba.
gebal: 1. One of the earliest villages in Phoenicia and Syria (along with Ras Shamra and Tell Judeideh); also called Byblos (“books”) by the Greeks.
geber: 1. Alternate name for Ben-geber, one of Solomon’s commissariat officers, in 1 Kings 4:13.
gebim: Small town just north of Jerusalem. Isaiah 10:31 prophesied that its inhabitants would flee when the Assyrian army came to invade.
gecko: Small lizard, incorrectly identified with the ferret by the KJV translators in Leviticus 11:30.
gedaliah: 1. Ahikam’s son, and grandson of Shaphan (King Josiah’s royal scribe).
geddalti: Heman’s son and a temple singer appointed by David to serve under the direction of his father. The 22d of the 24 divisions of service was appointed to Giddalti (1 Chr 25:29, NLT mg).
gedeon: KJV spelling of Gideon, Joash’s son and judge of Israel, in Hebrews 11:32.
geder: One of the 31 royal cities in Canaan, whose kings were defeated by Joshua. Geder is perhaps identifiable with Gedor in the mountains of Judah (15:58) or with Beth-gader.
gederah, gederathites: Town and its inhabitants situated in the Shephelah (lowland hills) of the territory allotted to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance. It was a place where potters lived.
gederoth: Town (modern Qatra) in the Shephelah (lowland hills) assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance and later captured by the Philistines from King Ahaz.
gederothaim: Village in the Judean Shephelah of unknown location. The Hebrew list contains 14 cities without Gederothaim (vv 33-36), while the Greek version reads, “Gederah and her sheepfolds” (v 36).
gedor (person): Jeiel’s son, who was an ancestor of King Saul. Gedor’s family lived in Gibeon.
gedor (place): 1. City in the Shephelah (hill country) allotted to Judah’s tribe named with Halhul, Beth-zur, Maarath, Beth-anoth, and Eltekon.
ge-harashim: Name for a richly wooded valley near Lod and Ono, settled by Joab from Judah’s tribe, whose posterity called the valley Ge-harashim, meaning “valley of craftsmen,” after their own trade (1 Chr 4:14, NLT mg).
gehazi: Servant of Elisha who instructed the prophet how best to recompense the generous Shunammite woman for her kindness to him (4:11-17).
gehenna: English transliteration of the Greek form of an Aramaic word, which is derived from the Hebrew phrase “the Valley of [the son(s) of] Hinnom.” The name properly designates a deep valley delimiting the territories of the tribes of Benjamin and Judah.
geliloth: Place mentioned in the boundary line of Benjamin, usually identified with Gilgal.
gemalli: Father of Ammiel, one of the 12 spies sent by Moses to explore the land of Canaan.
gemara: Summary of the important points of rabbinic discussion on the Mishnah (the oral tradition). The Gemara and Mishnah together form the Talmud (which many Jews consider authoritative for their faith).
gemariah: 1. Hilkiah’s son and emissary to Nebuchadnezzar from King Zedekiah.
gematria: One of the rabbinic hermeneutic rules for interpreting the OT. It consisted of explaining a word or group of words according to the numerical value of the letters or by substituting and rearranging certain letters according to a set system.
genealogy: Record or study of descent involving a tracing backward or forward of the ancestry of a nation, tribe, family, or individual. The Hebrews were not the only people in the ancient world to take an interest in maintaining genealogical records.
genealogy of jesus christ: Account of Jesus’ human descent. The NT records Jesus’ genealogy twice in great detail: in Matthew 1:1-17 and in Luke 3:23-38.
genesis, book of: The name Genesis comes into English as a transliteration of the Greek word meaning “origin” or “beginning.” This name was given to the book in the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, known as the Septuagint.
geneva bible: Translation of the Bible into English in 1560 in the city of Geneva, Switzerland.
gennaeus, genneus: Apollonius’s father. Since Gennaeus means “noble” or “highborn,” it may be an epithet rather than a name.
gennesaret: Area on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee between Capernaum and Magdala, where many of Jesus’ healing miracles took place.
gennesaret, lake of: Alternate name for the Sea of Galilee in Luke 5:1.
gentiles: The non-Jewish nations, known as goyim in Hebrew and ethnoi in Greek. According to the OT perspective, there are but two categories of people, the Jews (God’s elect) and the nations.
gentiles, court of the: Large outer portion of King Herod’s temple complex. The court was of irregular oblong shape, somewhat broader at the north than the south.
gentleness: In the OT an attitude of humility or bending low (2 Sm 22:36, KJV; cf. Ps 18:35, KJV).
genubath: Son of Hadad, the Edomite prince who, as a young lad, was taken to Egypt to escape Joab’s slaughter. There Hadad married a sister of Queen Tahpenes.
gerah: Measure of weight defined as one-twentieth of a shekel, the latter being the basic weight among Semitic peoples.
gerar: City located in the western Negev. It was used as a geographical landmark defining the western boundary of the Canaanite territory from Sidon to Gaza.
gerasa, gerasenes: City and district in the Decapolis. Gerasa was a well-known Roman city situated in the hills of the Transjordan about 35 miles (56 kilometers) southeast of the Sea of Galilee and 19 miles (31 kilometers) east of the Jordan River.
gergesa, gergesenes: City on the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee. Gergesa is near Gadara, probable site of Jesus’ miracle of healing a demon-possessed man and casting the demons into a nearby herd of swine.
gerizim, mount: Mountain (modern Jebel et-Tor) from which the blessings were to be pronounced, just as the cursings were to come from Mt Ebal.
geron: Athenian senator who compelled the Jews to forsake the laws of their fathers and their God during the time of Antiochus IV Epiphanes (2 Macc 6:1, RSV mg).
gershom: 1. Moses’ son by Zipporah, born in Midian during Moses’ exile from Egypt.
gershon, gershonites: Levi’s oldest son (also spelled Gershom) who went into Egypt with Israel and was ancestor of a division of Levites (Gershonites) who came out of Egypt with Moses.
geruth-kimham: Plot of land (meaning “the lodging place of Kimham”) near Bethlehem. Geruth-kimham possibly was given to Kimham for the service that his father, Barzillai the Gileadite, had rendered to King David.
geshan: Jahdai’s son and a descendant of Judah through Caleb’s line.
geshem: Arab opponent of Nehemiah who derided those seeking to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. He was likely an inhabitant of the north Arabian Desert and has been identified with Gashmu son of Shahr in a Dedanite Arabian inscription.
geshur, geshurites: 1. District and its inhabitants east of the Jordan River, in the tribal allotment of the half-tribe of Manasseh.
gether: Aram’s son and the grandson of Shem. In 1 Chronicles 1:17 he is listed as one of the sons of Shem.
gethsemane: Place to which Jesus and his disciples walked after their Last Supper together in the upper room. In Gethsemane, Jesus underwent a great inner struggle, as he realized the hour of his betrayal was at hand.
geuel: Maki’s son from Gad’s tribe, and one of the 12 spies appointed by Moses to search out the Promised Land of Canaan.
gezer: Modern Tell Jezer (also known as Tell Abu Shusha), and an important ancient city in a strategic position in the north Shephelah hills.
gezrite: KJV spelling of Girzite in 1 Samuel 27:8. The Girzites were raided by David’s men while he was at Ziklag.
giah: Unidentified place along the descent from Gibeon to the Arabah to which Joab and Abishai pursued Abner.
giants: English translation of four different Hebrew words. One of these words occurs in Job 16:14, where the Hebrew word is translated “warrior” in the RSV, and “giant” in the KJV.
giants, valley of the: KJV translation for “valley of Rephaim” in Joshua 15:8 and 18:16.
gibbar: Forefather of a family that returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. The parallel list in Nehemiah 7:25 reads “sons of Gibeon,” suggesting that “Gibbar” may be a textual corruption.
gibbethon: City in the western part of central Palestine. It was located in the territory of Dan and allotted to the Levite clan of Kohath (21:23).
gibeah: 1. Town in the hill country of Judah.
gibeath: KJV spelling of the town Gibeah in Joshua 18:28.
gibeath-elohim: Place where Samuel foretold an event that would confirm Saul as Israel’s king (1 Sm 10:5, RSV; NLT mg).
gibeath-haaraloth: Place located between the Jordan River and Jericho, in the vicinity of Gilgal, where Joshua conducted the circumcision of the Hebrew males born in the wilderness during the 40 years of wandering. (Jos 5:3, NLT; KJV “hill of the foreskins”).
gibeathite: Inhabitant of the Benjamite town of Gibeah.
gibeon, gibeonites: Place and its inhabitants figuring prominently in the OT from the days of Joshua to the days of Nehemiah, though both were in existence outside these time limits.
giblite: KJV rendering of Gebalite, an inhabitant of Gebal, in Joshua 13:5.
giddalti: Heman’s son and a temple singer appointed by David to serve under the direction of his father. The 22d of the 24 divisions of service was appointed to Giddalti (1 Chr 25:29, NLT mg).
giddel: 1. Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile.
gideon: Judge of Israel, son of Joash, of the clan of Abiezer and the tribe of Manasseh. Of the 12 judges of Israel, more verses are devoted to Gideon than any other—Samson running a close second.
gideoni: Abidan’s father and leader of Benjamin’s tribe when the Israelites were roaming in the Sinai wilderness after their escape from Egypt. As leader, Gideoni presented his tribe’s offering at the consecration of the tabernacle (7:60-65).
gidom: Place to which the Benjamite army was driven during a civil war between Benjamin and the rest of Israel.
gier eagle: KJV translation for carrion vulture in Leviticus 11:18 and Deuteronomy 14:17.
gifts, spiritual: Phrase regularly used to translate two Greek words, charismata and pneumatika (the plural forms of charisma and pneumatikon). Both words are almost exclusively Pauline within the biblical writings; elsewhere in the NT, they appear only in 1 Peter 2:5 and 4:10.
gihon, spring of: Site in Jerusalem where Solomon was anointed as king.
gilalai: Musician present at the dedication of the Jerusalem wall, rebuilt during Ezra’s time.
gilboa, mount: Mountain on the east side of the plain of Esdraelon between Galilee on the north and Samaria on the south (modern Jebel Fuqu’ah). Mt Gilboa towers over the valley of Jezreel.
gilead (person): 1. Makir’s son from Manasseh’s tribe and head of the clan of his descendants (26:29; 27:1) during the time of Moses (36:1).
gilead (place): 1. Region east of the Jordan River.
gilead, balm of: Substance of uncertain identification and one of several resins used in the Near East for medicinal purposes. It did not grow in Gilead, but it may have received its name from being exported to Egypt and Phoenicia from Gilead.
gileadite: Name given to Israelites from the two and a half Transjordanian tribes.
gilgamesh epic: Popular legendary composition about a Sumerian hero’s life of adventure and acquisition of wisdom. Gilgamesh was king of Uruk, or Erech (Tell Obeid; modern Warka), at the end of the fourth millennium BC.
gilo, giloh, gilonite: Village, and the inhabitants, in the mountains of southern Judah. David’s counselor Ahithophel was a Gilonite.
gimzo: Town of Judah captured by the Philistines during King Ahaz’s reign. It is modern Jimzu, located southeast of Ludd (Lydda).
ginath: Tibni’s father. Tibni unsuccessfully attempted to gain the throne of Israel; Omri became king instead.
ginnethon: 1. Priest who set his seal on Ezra’s covenant during the postexilic period.
girdle: One of various articles of clothing worn about the waist.
girgashites: Canaanite tribe whose land was promised to Abraham and was ultimately acquired. The tribe’s location is unknown, though they may have lived in Karkisha, a city mentioned in Hittite texts, or in Kirkishati, an area east of the Tigris.
girzites: People living in southwest Canaan who were raided by David when at Ziklag (1 Sm 27:8, KJV “Gezrites”).
gishpa, gispa: Overseer of the temple servants in Nehemiah’s time (Neh 11:21, KJV “Gispa”); perhaps alternately called Hasupha in Ezra 2:43 and Nehemiah 7:46.
gittah-hepher: KJV form of the town Gath-hepher, in Joshua 19:13.
gittaim: Town in Benjamin to which the inhabitants of Beeroth fled, where they remained under civil protection. Nehemiah 11:33 lists Gittaim as one of the places where the returned exiles later settled.
gittite: Inhabitant of Gath, the Philistine city.
gittith: Obscure Hebrew term in the superscriptions of Psalms 8, 81, and 84 (NLT mg); perhaps a musical instrument or a musical cue, signaling a mood, to which the psalms were to be performed.
gizon, gizonite: Designation for Hashem (Jashen, NLT), one of David’s mighty men. Gizon may have been an ancient Canaanite settlement.
glass: Translation for “mirror” in Isaiah 3:23, 1 Corinthians 13:12, and James 1:23 (KJV). Since mirrors of Bible times were polished metal sheets, “glass” is incorrect.
glean, gleaning: Practice of allowing the poor to follow reapers in a field to pick up missed spears of grain (cf. Lv 19:9; 23:22; Dt 24:19; Ru 2:2-23).
glorification: The expression of God’s glory and splendor. The Hebrew word for “glory” originally meant “weighty, heavy, or important.” From there it moved to the idea of an influential, rich, or prominent person.
glory: The singular splendor of God and the consequences for humanity.
glossolalia: Transliteration of a Greek expression meaning “speaking in tongues.” See Tongues, Speaking in.
gnat: Small flying insect. The word as found in Matthew 23:24 is a general word for a small fly.
gnosticism: Religious thought distinguished by claims to obscure and mystical knowledge, and emphasizing knowledge rather than faith.
goad: Pointed rod, sometimes tipped with metal, used for driving or guiding cattle, especially oxen in plowing.
goah: Location mentioned in connection with the hill of Gareb, to which the restored city of Jerusalem will extend. Goah is situated south of Gareb (Jer 31:39, KJV “Goath”).
goat: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
goath: KJV spelling of Goah in Jeremiah 31:39.
gob: Location where David and his men twice encountered the Philistines in battle. In the parallel description of 1 Chronicles 20:4, Gezer is mentioned as the place of war instead of Gob.
god, being and attributes of: Inherent characteristics of God revealed in Scripture and displayed in God’s actions in biblical history. They are characteristics equally of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
god, names of: God’s self-identifications expressing various aspects of his being.
god-fearer: One who fears God. This can be a term of reverence, an emotional reaction of terror, or a dread of God’s vengeance.
gods and goddesses: Male and female deities worshiped by pagans. Although the Bible teaches that there is only one God, heathen people in ancient times quickly developed a belief in large numbers of so-called gods and goddesses.
goiim: 1. People or region mentioned in Genesis 14:1, 9 as ruled by a king named Tidal.
golan: City and a district in the territory given to Manasseh in Bashan. It was the northernmost city of refuge east of the Jordan River, given to the Levite family of Gershon.
golden calf: Calf-shaped idol fashioned at the Israelites’ request from their own gold jewelry. Under Aaron’s supervision, the idol was created while Moses was receiving the Ten Commandments on Mt Sinai.
goldsmith: Artisan who specialized in fine gold work. They fashioned costly and elegant idols for pagan worship and prepared items and gold plating for the tabernacle and Solomon’s temple.
golgotha: Place where Jesus and two thieves were crucified, in the vicinity of Jerusalem. The term appears in the NT only in the accounts of the Crucifixion.
goliath: Eleventh-century BC Philistine warrior from Gath, who challenged Israel to battle. He was subsequently felled and decapitated by the youthful David.
gomer: 1. Son of Japheth, who was a son of Noah (Gn 10:2; cf. 1 Chr 1:5).
gomorrah: One of the “cities of the valley” destroyed by God because of its wickedness.
goose: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
gopher wood: Material Noah used to build the ark.
gorgias: One of the three generals chosen by Lysias, who was “governor of the kingdom, as far as the bounds of Egypt, and of the Lower Asia, and reaching from the river Euphrates,” according to Josephus, early Jewish historian.
gortyna: A city of Crete mentioned in 1 Maccabees 15:23 in the list of places to which the Romans sent letters instructing the kings and countries that they should do the Jews no harm.
goshen: 1. Geographical region in Egypt occupied by the Israelites during their sojourn in Egypt from the time of Joseph to the exodus.
gospel: Word derived from the Anglo-Saxon godspell denoting “glad tidings” or “good news.”
gospels, apocryphal: One major class of apocrypha are the apocryphal gospels. These writings preserved stories about Christ and some teachings, but being mostly fanciful in nature they never became canonical.
gouging: Common practice among the Philistines, Amorites, Babylonians, and other nations surrounding Israel of forcibly removing the eyes. The practice was intended not only to disable but also to bring extreme disgrace upon the person.
governor: Biblical term translated from at least ten different Hebrew root words and five Greek roots.
goyim: Alternate rendering for people defeated by Joshua west of the Jordan.
gozan: City and district near the Euphrates River. The Habor River (modern Khabur) flowed through it.
grace: The gift of God as expressed in his actions of extending mercy, loving-kindness, and salvation to people.
grain: During Bible times agriculture took the same three main forms found in Palestine today. Emphasis on each of these has depended upon the social and technological status of the people.
granary: During Bible times agriculture took the same three main forms found in Palestine today. Emphasis on each of these has depended upon the social and technological status of the people.
grape: Smooth-skinned, juicy berry that grows in clusters on woody vines. Grapes are eaten fresh or dried, and are fermented for wine.
grasshopper: Plant-eating insect equipped with long hind legs for leaping.
grate, grating: Network of bronze surrounding the lower half of the altar of burnt offering in the tabernacle.
gratitude: Natural expression of thanks in response to blessings, protection, or love. In the Judeo-Christian tradition, gratitude is not a tool used to manipulate the will of God.
grave: The Bible makes frequent reference to burial practices. A society’s burial customs are a reflection of its views about death and the afterlife.
graveclothes: The Bible makes frequent reference to burial practices. A society’s burial customs are a reflection of its views about death and the afterlife.
graven image: Image or representation of a deity made of wood, stone, or metal.
great lizard: One of the reptiles that the Jewish law listed as ceremonially unclean.
great owl: Name of one of the great horned or eagle owls.
great sea, the: Alternate name for the Mediterranean Sea. It was given this name by the ancient Near Eastern peoples because of its great size in comparison to the other seas they knew.
greaves: Protective piece of armor worn over the shank of the leg.
greece, greek: The biblical references to Greece and the Greek people are often ambiguous. In the OT some references have been understood to mean Greece or the Greeks.
grief: Emotional suffering brought on by bereavement, mishap, or disaster. To grieve is either to cause or feel sorrow or distress.
grove: Mistaken KJV translation of a Hebrew word that was the name of a Canaanite goddess, Asherah. Often sacred trees were designated as symbols of that fertility goddess; sometimes wooden poles were erected.
guard, courtyard of the: Perhaps an emergency detention area in seventh-century BC Jerusalem, when the city was under Babylonian attack.
guard, gate of the: Gate located in the north or northwest part of Jerusalem (Neh 12:38-39, KJV “prison gate”), although unrelated to the courtyard of the guard (3:25), which was connected to the palace. Perhaps it was the same as the Muster Gate.
guardian: Servant whose responsibility was to accompany, protect, and sometimes discipline his master’s son until the boy reached maturity. These custodians supervised their charges’ moral conduct and general behavior.
guardian angel: Messenger of God or supernatural being, either good or evil, with powers greater than humans possess.
gudgodah: Alternate name for Hor-haggidgad, one of the stopping places in the wilderness wanderings of the Israelites.
guilt offering: Major ritual expressions of religious life with accompanying rites, such as libations, effusions, and sacred meals. The ideology expressed in Israel’s ritual complex made its religion unique in the ancient Near East.
gull: Any of a number of birds from the family Laridae. The NLT “seagull” (KJV “cuckow”) in Leviticus 11:16 and Deuteronomy 14:15 is uncertain.
gum: General name for tragacanth, used in trade and obtained from the sap of shrubs of the Astragalus genus. These shrubs grew widely in the Near East.
guni: 1. Naphtali’s son and the grandson of Jacob.
gur, ascent of: Elevated place near Ibleam where Ahaziah, king of Judah, was smitten by the soldiers of Jehu of the northern kingdom. From Gur, Ahaziah fled to Megiddo, where he died.
gurbaal: Town in the Negev occupied by Arabs, possibly in the neighborhood of Edom, which Uzziah of Judah conquered (2 Chr 26:7, NLT mg).
gymnasium: Ancient Greek institution devoted to physical education and intellectual development. By the Hellenistic period, gymnasiums had become centers for the propagation of Greek culture.
habaiah: Alternate spelling of Hobaiah in Nehemiah 7:63.
habakkuk (person): Author of the eighth book of the Minor Prophets. The meaning of Habakkuk’s name is uncertain.
habakkuk, book of: Eighth book of the Minor Prophets in the OT.
habazziniah: Jaazaniah’s grandfather. Jaazaniah was a leader of the Recabites, warriors tested by Jeremiah with regard to their forefather’s command not to drink wine.
habergeon: KJV translation for coat of mail, part of a soldier’s defensive armor (2 Chr 26:14; Neh 4:16; Jb 41:26, NLT “javelin”).
habor: Modern Habur (Chaboras) River. The Habor River runs from the mountains in north-central Assyria, in Gozan, into the Euphrates River at a junction about 250 miles (402 kilometers) south and west of Nineveh.
hachilah: Unidentified site in Horesh, near Hebron, to which David fled when Saul attempted to kill him.
hachmoni, hachmonite: Name of Jehiel’s family. Jehiel was David’s servant, apparently a companion or tutor of David’s sons.
hacmoni: Name of Jehiel’s family. Jehiel was David’s servant, apparently a companion or tutor of David’s sons.
hacmonite: Designation for Jashobeam (also named Josheb-basshebeth in 2 Sm 23:8), one of David’s personal guards. He is alternately called a Tahkemonite in 2 Samuel 23:8 (NLT mg), but this is probably a textual error.
hadad: 1. Eighth of the 12 sons of Ishmael, and thus a grandson of Abraham.
hadadezer: King of Zobah in Syria during David’s reign in Israel. He apparently ruled a region from Ammon in the south to the Euphrates in the east.
hadad-rimmon: Combination of two storm deities, Hadad (mentioned in the Ugaritic texts) and Rimmon (Babylonian storm god). Hadad-rimmon was formerly thought to be a place.
hadar: 1. KJV spelling of Hadad, Ishmael’s son, in Genesis 25:15.
hadarezer: KJV alternate spelling of Hadadezer, king of Zobah.
hadashah: Town in the lowlands of Judah, near Gath, in the vicinity of Zenan and Migdal-gad.
hadattah: Name of a city (KJV) incorrectly derived from the name of the town Hazor-hadattah in Joshua 15:25.
hades: Abode of the dead. In Greek mythology Hades was originally the god of the underworld (also named Pluto), a brother of Zeus.
hadid: City in Benjamin mentioned with Lod and Ono as the home of over 720 Benjamites returning from the Babylonian captivity. In 1 Maccabees 12:38 and 13:13 the place is identified with Adida, which was fortified by Simon Maccabeus and later by Vespasian.
hadlai: Amasa’s father from Ephraim’s tribe. Amasa opposed the taking of prisoners from Judah’s tribe after a battle.
hadoram: 1. Joktan’s fifth son; Hadoram and his brothers were the sixth generation from Noah.
hadrach: Settlement in northwest Lebanon mentioned only in association with Tyre, Sidon, Hamath, and Damascus (Zec 9:1, see NLT mg). The last two cities were listed in Assyrian records with Hatarivia, with which Hadrach is now identified.
haeleph: City given to Benjamin’s tribe for an inheritance after the initial conquest of Canaan.
hagab: Ancestor of a family of temple servants returning with Zerubbabel to Palestine following the exile.
hagaba, hagabah: Forefather of a family of temple servants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile (Neh 7:48; spelled “Hagabah” in Ezr 2:45).
hagar: Egyptian handmaid of Sarai, the wife of Abram. At Sarai’s insistence, Abram took Hagar as his concubine, and she became the mother of his son Ishmael.
hagarene, hagarite, hagerite: KJV alternate forms of Hagrite, the name of a member of an Arabian tribe descended from Hagar living east of Palestine; spelled Hagerite in 1 Chronicles 27:31.
haggadah: Method of Jewish interpretation that is homiletical in character. Haggadah is usually defined negatively, that is, as that part of rabbinic teaching that is not Halakah.
haggai (person): Prophet whose book is the 10th in a series of 12 brief prophetic books concluding the OT. Haggai’s name probably came from a word for “festival.” We have no information concerning his family or social background.
haggai, book of: Tenth of the 12 short prophetic books at the end of the OT.
haggedolim: Father of Zabdiel, overseer of 128 “mighty men of valor” (RSV) who lived in Jerusalem in Nehemiah’s day.
haggeri: KJV rendering of Hagri, Mibhar’s father, in 1 Chronicles 11:38.
haggi: Gad’s son and founder of the family of Haggites.
haggiah: Merarite Levite, Shimea’s son and the father of Asaiah.
haggith: One of David’s wives and the mother of Adonijah. She gave birth to Adonijah in Hebron while David maintained his capital there.
hagri: Mibhar’s father, according to 1 Chronicles 11:38. The parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:36, however, has “Bani, the Gadite” instead of “Mibhar, son of Hagri.” Due to some textual difficulties in the 1 Chronicles passage, the 2 Samuel reading is preferred.
hagrite: Arabian tribe descended from Hagar, Abraham’s concubine. Being nomads, the Hagrites roamed the desert east of Gilead.
hahiroth: Alternate form of Pi-hahiroth in Numbers 33:8.
hai: KJV form for the Canaanite city Ai in Genesis 12:8 and 13:3.
hairstyles and beards: In Palestine and throughout the Near East, women’s hairstyles were long. In NT times a woman who cut her hair might be mistaken for a pagan priestess and thus be disgraced (see 1 Cor 11:15).
