hakilah: Unidentified site in Horesh, near Hebron, to which David fled when Saul attempted to kill him.
hakkatan: Member of Azgad’s family, the father of Johanan, and one of the exiles who returned to Jerusalem with Ezra.
hakkoz: Name borne by a priestly family during the monarchy. In Ezra’s time, the family pedigree could not be documented properly; consequently, the privilege of priestly service was withdrawn (Ezr 2:61; Neh 3:4, 21; 7:63; KJV “Koz”).
hakupha: Forefather of a family of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile.
halah: Place in Assyria where the inhabitants of Samaria were taken after its fall in 722 BC (2 Kgs 17:6; 18:11; cf. 1 Chr 5:26).
halak, mount: Mountain listed as marking the southern boundary of Joshua’s conquests. It is located in the western Arabah and is probably identical with Jebel Halaq on the northwest side of the Wadi Marra.
halakah: Overall term for Jewish law. Halakah, which means literally “walking,” gives the authoritative Jewish way of life as contained in the Mishnah.
half-shekel tax: Tax on all adult Jews throughout the world, begun during intertestamental times for the support of the temple, and continued by Vespasian for its Roman replacement; the temple tax of Mt 17:24-25.
halhul: City assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance after the initial conquest of Canaan. It was located between Beth-zur and Beth-anoth, four miles (6.4 kilometers) north of Hebron.
hali: Town mentioned among those that formed the border of Asher’s tribe. Hali may have been located west of Mt Carmel, but this is uncertain.
halicarnassus: An important commercial city of Caria in Asia Minor, beautifully situated on a bay about 15 miles (24 kilometers) from the island of Cos.
hallel: Hebrew term describing a song of praise to God. It was later used in the Talmud and in rabbinical writings to refer to several groups of psalms of praise to God.
hallelujah: Important Christian acclamation used extensively in the church’s worship and liturgy from early times.
hallohesh, halohesh: Shallum’s father and one who set his seal on Ezra’s covenant (10:24).
ham (person): Second son of Noah. Ham had four sons whose names were Cush, Mizraim (Hebrew for Egypt), Put, and Canaan.
ham (place): Place where Chedorlaomer and his cohorts defeated the Zuzim. The name is probably preserved by Tell Ham, near the modern village on the Wadi er-Rejeilah.
haman: Son of Hammedatha the Agagite, a high official under King Ahasuerus (Xerxes) in Persia during the time of Esther. Haman became angry with Mordecai, the uncle of Esther the queen, because Mordecai would not bow down to him as all others did.
hamath: 1. City and district located about 125 miles (201 kilometers) north of Damascus (Syria), on the Orontes River.
hamath, entrance of: Place of uncertain identification, marking the northern border of the Canaanite territory promised to Israel by God, but only attained by the time of the monarchy.
hamath-zobah: City captured by King Solomon of Israel. Its identity is uncertain.
hammath (person): Ancestor of the house of Rechab, about whom nothing else is known.
hammath (place): Fortified outpost identified with the modern Hamman Tabariyeh. This place is located among hot springs on the western shore of Galilee and is probably identifiable with Hammon, Hammoth-dor, and perhaps the Emmaus of Josephus (Antiquities 18.2.3).
hammedatha: Father of Haman, a chief adviser to the Persian king Ahasuerus and a sworn enemy of the Jews, according to the book of Esther (3:1, 10; 8:5; 9:10, 24).
hammelech: Hebrew word meaning “the king,” taken to be a personal name by the KJV, but more correctly translated as “the king” by other versions.
hammon: 1. One of the cities of Asher mentioned in Joshua 19:28.
hammoth-dor: Alternate name for the Levitical town Hammath in Joshua 21:32.
hammuel: Member of Mishma’s family from Simeon’s tribe.
hammurabi, law code of: Law code devised by Hammurabi, the last great king of the first Babylonian dynasty (c. 1790–1750 BC), to safeguard the rights and define the responsibilities of Babylonian citizens.
hamonah: Name of site meaning “horde” in the Transjordan where the marauding armies of Gog will be destroyed by the Israelites.
hamon-gog: Valley in the Transjordan where the dead of the armies of Gog (Gog’s “hordes”) will be buried.
hamor: Hivite or Horite prince of the country about Shechem, from whom Jacob bought land when returning with his family from Paddan-aram. At this time Hamor’s son Shechem committed fornication with Dinah, the daughter of Jacob.
hamran: Alternate name for Hemdan, Dishon’s oldest son in 1 Chronicles 1:41 (see NLT mg).
hamuel: KJV spelling of Hammuel, the Simeonite, in 1 Chronicles 4:26.
hamul, hamulite: Perez’s younger son and founder of the Hamulite family.
hamutal: Daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, one of King Josiah’s wives, and the mother of two kings: Jehoahaz and Zedekiah.
hanamel: Shallum’s son, from whom Jeremiah bought a field in Anathoth. This purchase signified that God would restore the nation and that possession of the land would again be possible.
hanan: 1. Shashak’s son and one of the chief men of Benjamin.
hananel, tower of: Tower on the north wall of Jerusalem, located near the Sheep Gate (Neh 3:1; 12:39; KJV “Hananeel”). Later in Israel’s history John Hyrcanus erected a Maccabean fortress on this spot, which Pompey destroyed in 63 BC.
hanani: 1. Seer who rebuked King Asa for giving treasure to Ben-hadad of Syria to persuade him to attack Israel.
hananiah: 1. Zerubbabel’s son and a descendant of David.
hand: The terminal part of the forelimb that has the ability to grasp. “Hand” is used hundreds of times in the Bible to describe a physical part of one’s body.
handbreadth: Linear measure equivalent to one-sixth of a cubit or just under three inches (7.6 centimeters) in length. The fingers, up to four, made a handbreadth; three handbreadths made a handstretch or span.
handmaid, handmaiden: Female servants. They were familiar members among many households in biblical days.
hands, washing of: The terminal part of the forelimb that has the ability to grasp. “Hand” is used hundreds of times in the Bible to describe a physical part of one’s body.
hanes: City in Egypt included with Zoan (or Tanis) in Isaiah 30:4 as a center of Egyptian government to which ambassadors would be sent. This indicates that it was one of the dynastic centers.
hanging: The science or philosophy of law is called jurisprudence. Although modern jurisprudence bears little resemblance to biblical concepts of law, the Scriptures have played a definite role in its development.
haniel: KJV spelling of Hanniel, Ulla’s son, in 1 Chronicles 7:39.
hannah: Wife of Elkanah from Ephraim’s tribe and the mother of the prophet Samuel. The childless Hannah prayed annually at Shiloh for a son, whom she vowed to dedicate to the Lord.
hannathon: Northern border town of Zebulun, mentioned in the Amarna tablets (c. 1370 BC) and in the annals of Tiglath-pileser III (745–727 BC). Not yet precisely located, it has been identified with Kefr ‘Anau near Rimmon and with Tell el-Bedeiwiyah, north of Nazareth.
hanniel: 1. Ephod’s son and leader of Manasseh’s tribe who represented his tribe in apportioning land to Israel under Moses.
hanoch: 1. Midian’s third son, and grandson of Abraham by Keturah.
hanochite: Descendant of Hanoch, Reuben’s firstborn son.
hanukkah: Occasions of public or private rejoicing to commemorate some significant event or personage. The element of celebration has a special meaning in the cycle of religious occasions and the rites and ceremonies associated with these particular days.
hanun: 1. Nahash’s son and successor to the Ammonite throne.
hapharaim: Town included in the territory allotted to Issachar’s tribe for an inheritance. Some scholars have identified it with et-Taiyibeh, about ten miles (16 kilometers) northwest of Beth-shan.
happizzez: Head of a division of priests whom David assigned to official duties in the temple.
hara: Place where Tiglath-pileser of Assyria exiled Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
haradah: Twentieth wilderness encampment of the children of Israel, and the ninth from Sinai; listed between Mt Shepher and Makheloth. Its location is unknown.
haran (person): 1. Terah’s son, brother of Abraham, and the father of Lot.
haran (place): City of northern Mesopotamia, first mentioned in Genesis 11:31 as the destination of Terah, Abraham’s father, in migrating from Ur of the Chaldees, and his home until his death. At age 75, Abraham was commanded by God to move to a land that God had for him.
harar, hararite: Terms applied to several names that appear in the accounts of King David’s “mighty men.” Shammah, one of David’s mightiest men, and Jonathan’s father (a different Jonathan than Saul’s son and David’s friend) is called a Hararite (2 Sm 23:11, 33; 1 Chr 11:34 has “Shagee”), as is Agee, Shammah’s father.
harbona: One of King Ahasuerus’s seven personal attendants. They were ordered by Ahasuerus to parade Queen Vashti before a drunken banquet to satisfy his vanity.
hare: Small, swift, long-eared mammal similar to the rabbit.
hareph: Caleb’s descendant from Judah’s tribe and founder (or perhaps father) of Beth-gader.
hareth: KJV spelling of Hereth in 1 Samuel 22:5.
harhaiah: Father of Uzziel, a goldsmith who worked to rebuild the wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah’s time.
harhas: Shallum’s grandfather. Shallum’s wife was Huldah the prophetess (2 Kgs 22:14; spelled “Hasrah” in 2 Chr 34:22), who delivered an oracle for Josiah after the discovery of the Book of the Law by the high priest Hilkiah.
har-heres: Mountain in Aijalon of Dan’s territory.
harhur: Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile.
harim: 1. Priest whom King David appointed to official duties in the temple.
hariph: Ancestor of a family who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile. The name Jorah appears in the parallel list of Ezra 2:18.
harlot: Person guilty of illicit sexual relationships; figuratively, one who worships an idol. The term “prostitute” translates four different words found in the Bible.
harmon: Place mentioned by the prophet Amos to which the inhabitants of Bashan would be exiled (Am 4:3, NLT mg). Harmon occurs only once in the Bible, and there is no known place with such a name.
harod: 1. Spring beside which Gideon and his army camped before their encounter with the Midianites.
harodite: Designation for Shammah and Elika, two of David’s mighty men.
haroeh: Alternate name of Reaiah, Shobal’s son, in 1 Chronicles 2:52.
harorite: Alternate description of one of David’s mighty men.
harosheth-haggoyim: Town in Canaan that was the home of Sisera. This Canaanite general led his forces from Harosheth against Deborah and Barak (Jgs 4:2-13, KJV “Harosheth of the Gentiles”).
harrow: Agricultural term for implement or procedure, though no implement corresponding to the modern harrow is known from Palestine or Egypt.
harsha: Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile.
harumaph: Jedaiah’s father. Jedaiah helped repair the wall of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah.
haruph, haruphite: Name applied to Shephatiah, one of David’s ambidextrous warriors from Benjamin’s tribe who joined him at Ziklag. Whether the name refers to a family or a place is uncertain.
haruz: Maternal grandfather of Amon, king of Judah.
harvest: The gathering in of a crop, especially for food. There was no single harvesttime in ancient Israel.
hasenuah: KJV rendering of Hassenuah in 1 Chronicles 9:7.
hashabiah: 1. Ancestor of Ethan, a Levite and descendant of Merari.
hashabnah: One of the leaders who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God with Nehemiah and others after the exile.
hashbaddanah: Man, possibly of Levite origin, who stood on Ezra’s left when Ezra read the law to the people.
hashem: Warrior among David’s mighty men (1 Chr 11:34, NLT mg); alternately called Jashen in 2 Samuel 23:32.
hashmonah: One of the places where the Israelites stopped during the 40 years they wandered in the wilderness.
hashum: 1. Ancestor of a family who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel after the exile.
hashupha: KJV alternate spelling of Hasupha in Nehemiah 7:46.
hasideans, hasidim: Transliterations of a Hebrew word meaning “the pious.” The influence of Greek customs and ways threatened the preservation of Jewish patterns of life in the third and fourth centuries BC.
hasmonean: Family name of the Jews who instigated the Jewish revolt against the Greeks in 167 BC.
hasrah: Variant spelling of Harhas, Shallum’s grandfather, in 2 Chronicles 34:22 (NLT mg).
hassenaah: Alternate name for Senaah in Nehemiah 3:3.
hassenuah: Ancestor of a Benjamite family that returned to Judah with Zerubbabel after the exile (1 Chr 9:7; Neh 11:9, KJV “Senuah”); perhaps alternately called Senaah, and Hassenaah.
hasshub: 1. Merari clan leader of Levi’s tribe.
hassophereth: Ancestor of a family of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile (Ezr 2:55, NLT mg). He is perhaps identifiable with Sophereth in Nehemiah 7:57.
hasupha: Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile. He is perhaps the same person as Gishpa in Nehemiah 11:21.
hat: Something used to cover one’s head either for protection or for religious reasons.
hatach, hathach: Eunuch appointed by the Persian king Ahasuerus to wait on Esther. Hathach brought Esther messages from Mordecai.
hathath: Othniel’s son and the grandson of Kenaz.
hatipha: Ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the captivity.
hatita: Ancestor of a family of gatekeepers who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile.
hatred: Intense feeling of aversion or enmity, which could prompt a person to loathe someone or something, or even to seek revenge for having been wronged. The Scriptures forbid people to hate others because it leads to sin.
hattil: Forefather of a family of King Soloman’s servants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile.
hattush: 1. Shemaiah’s son and a descendant of David.
hauran: Region in northeastern Transjordan mentioned in Ezekiel’s description of the borders of the land. In biblical times it corresponded to the modern Jebel ed-Druze of the Leja.
havilah (place): Land in the neighborhood of Eden, now unknown but said to be watered by the river Pishon and containing supplies of gold, bdellium, and onyx stone. The location of Havilah has been a matter of much dispute.
havoth-jair, havvoth-jair: Series of settlements on the edge of Bashan across the Jordan captured by Jair, according to Numbers 32:41 (NLT mg). Because of their location, they fell into the allotment of the half-tribe of Manasseh.
hawk: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
hay: Dried grass used as animal fodder.
hazael: King of Syria (843?–796? BC) who came to power by assassinating his ruler, Ben-hadad, and establishing a new dynasty.
hazaiah: Maaseiah’s descendant from Judah’s tribe, who was one of the leaders in Jerusalem after the exile.
hazar-addar: Town that, with Azmon, defined the southern border of Judah, usually identified with Khirbet el-Qudeirat near Kadesh-barnea. The parallel passage in Joshua 15:3-4 lists four places—Hezron, Addar, Karka, and Azmon—instead of two.
hazar-enan, hazar-enon: Place describing the northeast corner of Israel’s border; alternately spelled Hazar-enon in Ezekiel 47:17-18 and 48:1 (RSV). It is identified with modern Hadr at the base of Mt Hermon.
hazar-gaddah: City in the southern extremity of the land assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance.
hazar-hatticon: KJV spelling of the place Hazer-hatticon in Ezekiel 47:16.
hazarmaveth: Descendant of Shem through Joktan whose progeny lived in southern Arabia in the Wadi Hadhramaut. Excavations there revealed a flourishing economy in the fifth century BC, based on frankincense trade.
hazar-shual: Simeonite city located in the southern section of Judah. It is also listed among those cities occupied by the Jews who returned from captivity.
hazar-susah, hazar-susim: City assigned to Simeon within the territory allotted to Judah for an inheritance; alternately called Hazar-susim.
hazazon-tamar: City identifiable with En-gedi in 2 Chronicles 20:2. During the time of Abraham, it was inhabited by Amorites who were subdued by Kedorlaomer as he and other eastern kings swept through the area.
hazel: KJV mistranslation for almond in Genesis 30:37.
hazelelponi: KJV spelling of Hazzelelponi, Etam’s daughter, in 1 Chronicles 4:3.
hazer-hatticon: Boundary marker along Israel’s northern perimeter. In conjunction with the use of Hazar-enan in this context, and in comparison with Numbers 34:9-10, it appears that Hazer-hatticon may represent a scribal error for Hazar-enan.
hazerim: KJV transliteration of the corresponding Hebrew word in Deuteronomy 2:23. Instead of the proper name for a city, it may be a generic term for “villages,” a rendering favored by the NLT.
hazeroth: Camp of the Israelites during their wanderings in the desert. It was the third camp from Mt Sinai.
hazezon-tamar: KJV spelling of the city Hazazon-tamar in Genesis 14:7.
haziel: Levite and son of Shimei during David’s time.
hazo: Nahor’s fifth son; probably used as the name for a Nahorite clan. It has been identified with the name Hazu, which designated a mountainous region in northern Arabia mentioned in an inscription telling of Esarhaddon’s Arabian campaign.
hazor: 1. City in northern Palestine in the territory of Naphtali, called “the capital of the federation of all these kingdoms [of Canaan]” in Joshua 11:10.
hazor-hadattah: One of the cities located in the southern extremity of Judah, near the border of Edom. The KJV translates the term as two different cities, “Hazor and Hadattah.” The Aramaic adjective “Hadattah” indicates this as a settlement from Hazor, but this is unsure.
head: Head
The uppermost portion of the body, containing the brain, major sense organs, and the mouth. It appears many times in the Bible as a physical description.
head covering: Something used to cover one’s head either for protection or for religious reasons.
heal, healing: To make well. The OT provides the proper background for a Christian understanding of the concept of healing.
healing, gift of: Phrase regularly used to translate two Greek words, charismata and pneumatika (the plural forms of charisma and pneumatikon). Both words are almost exclusively Pauline within the biblical writings; elsewhere in the NT, they appear only in 1 Peter 2:5 and 4:10.
heart: Vital bodily organ; emotional center of one’s being.
hearth: Israel’s early ancestors lived mostly in tents or temporary dwellings, but the Canaanites of the middle Bronze Age (into whose land the Israelites came) lived in substantial houses of several rooms built around a courtyard.
heath: Type of evergreen shrub; KJV mistranslation for shrub or bush in Jeremiah 17:6 and 48:6.
heaven: Realm (or realms) designated by a Hebrew term used to represent the sky and air and also heaven. The form of the word in Hebrew is dual (implying two of something).
heavenlies, the: Term unique to Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, also translated “heavenly places” or “realms,” and referring to the super earthly upper regions of the air.
heavens, new: Concept of a new or renewed universe first found in the book of Isaiah. God declares, “For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind. . . .
heave offering: Portions of the sacrifices and offerings set aside for the Lord and for the priests.
heber: 1. Descendant of Jacob through Asher and Beriah and father of the family of Heberites.
heberites: Descendants of Heber in the family of Jacob.
hebrew language: Language of the Jewish people. The name Hebrew is not applied by the OT to its own language, although the NT does use the name that way.
hebrews, letter to the: One of the most profound and enigmatic books in the NT. The identity of its author, the time of its writing, and the people and place to which it was sent are all shrouded in mystery.
hebron (person): 1. Third of Kohath’s four sons, Hebron was a descendant of Levi.
hebron (place): 1. City of antiquity still standing today.
hebronite: Descendant of Hebron from Levi’s tribe.
hedgehog: Small, insect-eating mammal with a coat of short spines and similar to the porcupine.
hegai, hege: Chamberlain of Ahasuerus and keeper of his harem when Esther was chosen as queen.
hegemonides: Principal Syrian officer appointed by Antiochus, king of Syria, to govern the territory from Ptolemais to Gerar.
heglam: Alternate name for Gera, Bela’s son, in 1 Chronicles 8:7.
heir: One who inherits something or who is entitled to a future inheritance; the one who receives the property of a deceased person, particularly on the basis of law and usually by means of a will.
helah: One of Ashhur’s wives who bore him Zereth, Izhar, and Ethnan from Judah’s tribe.
helam: Place east of the Jordan where David defeated the armies of Hadadezer, king of Syria.
helbah: One of the Canaanite strongholds that was not conquered by the tribe of Asher after they took possession of the land.
helbon: District north of Damascus, which produced choice wine; perhaps identifiable with modern Halbun, where the vine is still cultivated.
heldai: 1. Baanah’s son, described as a Netophathite in the line of Othniel.
heleb: Alternative name for Heldai, Baanah’s son, in 2 Samuel 23:29.
helech: Term mentioned in Ezekiel’s prophecy against the city of Tyre, perhaps referring to Cilicia or to mercenaries from Cilicia, which was southeast of Asia Minor. Assyrian texts indicate that Cilicia was once called Hilakku, but little is known about the people.
heled: Alternate name for Heldai, Baanah’s son, in 1 Chronicles 11:30.
helek, helekite: Gilead’s son from Manasseh’s tribe and founder of the Helekite family.
helem: 1. Member of Asher’s tribe, called Hotham in verse 32.
heleph: Village on Naphtali’s southern border, northeast of Mt Tabor. Its site may be modern Khirbet ‘Arbathah.
helez: 1. One of David’s valiant warriors, called a Paltite in 2 Samuel 23:26 and a Pelonite in 1 Chronicles 11:27.
heli: Ancestor of Joseph in Luke’s genealogy of Christ.
heliodorus: There is an inscription in the temple of Apollo at Delos that indicates that Heliodorus was prominent in the court of the Seleucid king Seleucus IV Philopator, who reigned from 187 to 175 BC.
heliopolis: Ancient Egyptian city famed as a center for worship of the sun god Re. Heliopolis (“city of the sun”) was located in the Nile River delta region of Lower Egypt, a few miles northeast of modern Cairo.
helkai: Head of Meraioth’s priestly house in the time of Joiakim the high priest.
helkath: First of 22 cities mentioned in the territory allotted to Asher’s tribe for an inheritance. Helkath was one of four cities in Asher given to the Levitical Gershonite families (21:31).
helkath-hazzurim: Area near the pool of Gibeon, where 12 champions from Joab’s army and 12 from Abner’s battled. All 24 died in the fight, each fighter killing his opponent.
hell: Place of future punishment for the lost, unrepentant, wicked dead.
hellenism: That unique blend of Greek cultural, philosophical, and ethical ideals that had a profound effect on the development of culture throughout the Mediterranean world.
hellenists: Name used in Acts 6:1, 9:29, and possibly 11:20 for a distinct branch of the early church that was characterized by Greek modes of thinking.
helmet: The location of Palestine at the crossroads of three continents gave it a strategic importance in the ancient world quite out of proportion to its size.
helon: Father of Eliab, prince of Zebulun’s tribe at the taking of the first census.
helps, gift of: Phrase regularly used to translate two Greek words, charismata and pneumatika (the plural forms of charisma and pneumatikon). Both words are almost exclusively Pauline within the biblical writings; elsewhere in the NT, they appear only in 1 Peter 2:5 and 4:10.
hemam: KJV spelling of Heman, Lotan’s son, in Genesis 36:22.
heman: 1. Lotan’s son, the brother of Hori and a descendant of Seir the Horite; alternately spelled Homam in 1 Chronicles 1:39, reflecting a later scribal error.
hemath: KJV form of Hammath, the Rechabite, in 1 Chronicles 2:55.
hemdan: Dishon’s son and a descendant of Seir the Horite. He is also called Hamran in 1 Chronicles 1:41 (KJV “Amram”).
hemlock: KJV mistranslation for poisonous weeds and for wormwood in Hosea 10:4 and Amos 6:12, respectively.
hemorrhage: Issue of blood, coming from any cut or nosebleed. However, in Scripture it almost always refers to vaginal bleeding.
hen: Domesticated poultry (Gallus gallus domesticus), probably derived from the red jungle fowl of India. They seem to have been known already in OT times.
hen (person): KJV alternate name for Josiah, Zephaniah’s son, in Zechariah 6:14.
hena: One of the six cities that the rabshakeh boasted fell before the armies of Sennacherib, in spite of their gods.
henadad: Head of a Levite family that participated in the rebuilding of the temple. Members of this family also helped to build the Jerusalem wall, and signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God together with Nehemiah (10:9).
henna: Fragrant, flowering shrub mentioned in Song of Songs 1:14 and 4:13.
henoch: 1. KJV form of Enoch, Jared’s son, in 1 Chronicles 1:3.
hepher (person): 1. Manassite and founder of the Hepherite family.
hepher (place): Canaanite city located northwest of Jerusalem. It was captured by Joshua and later used as an administrative district under Solomon.
hepherite: Descendant of Hepher from Manasseh’s tribe.
hephzibah: 1. Mother of Manasseh, king of Judah.
herb: Plant valued for its culinary, medicinal, or aromatic properties.
hercules: A Greek god, the son of Zeus, renowned for strength. Second Maccabees 4 records the Hellenizing fervor of Antiochus Epiphanes (175–164 BC), who succeeded Seleucus IV Philopator, as he “founded a gymnasium right under the citadel”.
herdsmen: Men who cared for domestic animals, such as cattle, sheep and goats. They also included shepherds.
heres: 1. Region from which the Amorites were not expelled by the Israelites, known as Mt Heres (Jgs 1:34-35, RSV “Har-heres”).
heresh: Levite who returned to Jerusalem following the exile.
heresy: A sectarian group or teaching that deviates from the norm. The Greek word (hairesis), literally meaning “choice,” designates a sect or faction.
hereth: Section of forested land in the territory of Judah where David and his men hid for a time as they fled from King Saul.
hermas: 1. Christian to whom Paul sent greetings in his letter to the Romans.
hermes: 1. Greek god and the son of Zeus by Maia.
hermogenes: Prominent Asian believer who “turned away” from Paul.
hermon, mount: Mountain often mentioned as the northern extremity of the territory conquered by Joshua and Moses in Transjordan; it is also the northern boundary of the inheritance of the half-tribe of Manasseh as well as of Israel in general.
hermonite: KJV mistranslation for Hermon (Mount) in Psalm 42:6. Mt Hermon, a sacred site since antiquity, lies on the northernmost boundary of Joshua’s conquest.
herod, herodian family: Political rulers during the lifetime of Christ. Christ was born when Herod the Great was ruling.
herodians: Jewish party mentioned three times in the Gospels in connection with two incidents (one in Galilee and one in Jerusalem) and associated with the Pharisees in their opposition to Christ.
herodias: Daughter of Aristobulus, the son of Herod the Great, and Berenice. Born between 9 and 7 BC, her older brother was Herod Agrippa I.
herodion: Christian of Jewish ancestry to whom Paul sent greetings at the conclusion of his Epistle to the Romans.
heron: Long-necked wading bird, considered unclean under Jewish law.
heshbon: Important Transjordanian city about 50 miles (80 kilometers) due east of Jerusalem. It had originally been Moabite but was conquered by Sihon, the Amorite king, and became the capital of his kingdom.
heshmon: Town mentioned only in Joshua 15:27. It was located near Beth-pelet in southern Judah.
heth: Progenitor of the Hittite people and a descendant of Canaan, in Ham’s line.
hethlon: Site mentioned by Ezekiel describing part of the northern boundary of the restored kingdom of Israel.
hexateuch: Name meaning “the sixfold book,” given to a grouping of the first six books of the Bible.
hezeki: KJV spelling of Hizki, Elpaal’s son, in 1 Chronicles 8:17.
hezekiah's tunnel: Pool mentioned in John 9. Jesus, after anointing with clay the eyes of a blind man, directed him to go and wash in the pool.
hezion: Tabrimmon’s father and the grandfather of Ben-hadad, king of Syria. Ben-hadad formed an alliance with King Asa of Judah (910–869 BC) and opposed Israel’s King Baasha (908–886 BC; 1 Kgs 15:18).
hezir: 1. Levite and head of the 17th of 24 divisions of priests for sanctuary service formed during David’s reign.
hezrai, hezro: One of David’s mighty warriors, a Carmelite by birth.
hezron (person): 1. Reuben’s son and founder of the Hezronite family in Reuben’s tribe.
hezron (place): Town on Judah’s border. In Numbers 34:4 it probably forms part of the name Hazar-addar.
hiddai: Name of one of King David’s mighty men (2 Sm 23:30, NLT mg).
hiddekel: Hebrew name for the Tigris River (Gn 2:14; Dn 10:4, KJV).
hiel: Bethelite in the days of King Ahab who fulfilled Joshua’s curse upon the city of Jericho. Joshua had said centuries before that anyone attempting to rebuild the city would suffer the loss of his oldest and youngest sons.
hierapolis: City of southwest Phrygia, strategically located between Colosse to the east and Laodicea to the south. The founding of the city is credited to Eumenes II of Pergamum (197–160 BC).
hieroglyphics: Early form of writing by using pictorial signs. The Egyptian, Hittite, Mayan, and Cretan civilizations—each one independently of the others—developed hieroglyphics.
hieronymus: Hellenistic ruler in intertestamental period. Hostile toward Palestinian Jews who refused to accept Greek ways, Antiochus Eupator sent his vice-regent Lysias with 80,000 troops to solicit compliance.
higgaion: Musical notation in text of Psalm 9:16, presumably cueing the instrumental accompaniment to play softly.
high council: Supreme judicial council (NLT “high council”) of Judaism with 71 members, located in Jerusalem.
high place: Phrase commonly translated from the Hebrew bamah, which apparently derived from a word originally meaning “the back (or ridge) of an animal.” Thus it came to refer to a height or hill or a stone burial cairn.
high priest: Servants of God in the OT. There were three basic classes of religious personnel in ancient Israel: prophets, wise men, and priests and Levites.
highway, king's: The road running north-south across the Transjordanian plateau. It appears in the OT only twice in requests by the Israelites to use this road when passing through Edom and the Amorite kingdom of Heshbon (21:22).
hilen: Alternate name for Holon, a city assigned to Levites, in 1 Chronicles 6:58.
hilkiah: 1. Father of Eliakim, an overseer in King Hezekiah’s household.
hillel: 1. Father of Abdon, one of the judges.
hin: Liquid measure equal to one-sixth of a bath, or about one gallon (3.8 liters).
hinnom, valley of: Deep, narrow ravine running south of Jerusalem that marked the boundary between Judah’s and Benjamin’s territories.
hippopotamus: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
hippos: One of the cities of the Decapolis (a loose confederation of 10 Greek cities) established in Palestine after the death of Alexander the Great (323 BC; also called Susitha); not mentioned in the Bible.
hirah: Adullamite and friend of Judah to whose house Judah went after he and his brothers sold Joseph. He accompanied Judah to the sheepshearing after Judah’s wife died (v 12), and he served as the messenger to carry a kid from Judah to Tamar (v 20).
hiram: 1. King of Tyre during the time of David and Solomon.
hittites: Biblical people who figure largely in the promises of a land for the descendants of Abram and the children of Israel.
hivites: Name of a pre-Israelite group living in Canaan. Though not yet discovered/rated archaeologically or from secular history as a people, they were regarded as emerging from a son of Canaan and as inhabiting areas of the Lebanon Mountains and Mt Hermon.
hizkiah: 1. Neariah’s son and a descendant of David through Rehoboam’s line.
hizkijah: KJV form of Hezekiah, Ater’s descendant, in Nehemiah 10:17.
hobab: Name associated with Moses’ father-in-law (Nm 10:29; Jgs 4:11, NLT mg), who was a priest of Midian and ancestor of the Kenites. He is usually called Jethro, but also Reuel.
hobah: Town to which Abraham pursued the armies under Chedorlaomer. Its location is uncertain, but various suggestions have been made.
hobaiah: Head of a priestly family who returned to Palestine with Zerubbabel after the exile. He was unable to prove his priestly genealogy and so was not allowed to do priestly service.
hodaiah: KJV spelling of Hodaviah, David’s descendant, in 1 Chronicles 3:24.
hodesh: Name given to Shaharaim’s wife from Benjamin’s tribe in 1 Chronicles 8:9 (a textually corrupt passage).
hodevah: Alternate spelling of Hodaviah in Nehemiah 7:43 (see NLT mg).
hodiah, hodijah: 1. A man of Judah mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:19.
hoglah: One of Zelophehad’s five daughters. Zelophehad, who was of Manasseh’s tribe, had no sons, so that his inheritance passed to his daughters.
hoham: Amorite king of Hebron, confederate with four other kings in reprisals against Gibeon for making peace with Joshua. They were defeated and put to death at the cave of Makkedah (vv 16-27).
holiness: Chief attribute of God and a quality to be developed in his people. “Holiness” and the adjective “holy” occur more than 900 times in the Bible.
holm tree: Tree mentioned in Isaiah 44:14 (KJV “ash”) whose wood was used for fuel and idol construction; its identity is uncertain.
holofernes: According to the book of Judith, the chief Assyrian general under King Nebuchadnezzar who was ordered by the king to “go and attack the whole west country” (v 6).
holon: 1. Town in the uplands of Judah’s inheritance given to the Levites (21:15).
holy of holies: Inner room of the tabernacle and temple in which the ark of the covenant was kept.
holy one of israel: God’s self-identifications expressing various aspects of his being.
holy place: Place of worship during the earliest years of the history of Israel.
holy spirit: Description of God in action, God in motion. The word “spirit” (Hebrew, ruach; Greek, pneuma) is the word used from ancient times to describe and explain the experience of divine power working in, upon, and around people.
holy war: Warfare as described in the book of Deuteronomy, especially in chapter 20.
homam: Alternate spelling of Heman, Lotan’s son, in 1 Chronicles 1:39 (NLT mg).
homer: Dry measure of capacity estimated to be anywhere from four to six and a half bushels.
homes and dwellings: Israel’s early ancestors lived mostly in tents or temporary dwellings, but the Canaanites of the middle Bronze Age (into whose land the Israelites came) lived in substantial houses of several rooms built around a courtyard.
homosexuality: Unlike some religious and philosophical systems, the Bible takes a positive view of human sexuality. According to the OT’s account of Creation, it was God himself who made people sexual beings.
honey: Sweet syrup produced by bees, either wild or domesticated (apparently so in 2 Chr 31:5). Sometimes, however, it may refer to thick grape syrup (as in Arabic) or date syrup (as described by Josephus).
hoopoe: Any of a number of Old World singing birds; considered unclean.
hope: An expectation or belief in the fulfillment of something desired. Present hurts and uncertainty over what the future holds create the constant need for hope.
hophni: Brother of Phinehas, with whom he served as a priest at Shiloh. He was an evil man who flouted the sacrificial rituals (2:12-17) and behaved immorally (v 22).
hophra: Son of Psammis, ruler over Egypt from 589–570 BC during the 26th dynasty. Called Pharaoh Hophra in Jeremiah 44:30, although he is alluded to several other times during the divided kingdom period.
hopping locust: Type of locust (KJV “cankerworm”) mentioned in Joel 1:4.
hor, mount: 1. Mountain located at the border of the land of Edom.
horam: King of Gezer who, while coming to the aid of Lachish, was defeated and killed by Joshua.
horem: Town set up for defense purposes in the uplands of Naphtali’s territory. Though its exact site is unknown, it must have been in northern Galilee.
horesh: Hebrew word translated as a place-name in 1 Samuel 23:15-19 (part of the wilderness of Ziph). David hid from Saul there, and met secretly with Jonathan.
hor-haggidgad: Camping place of the Israelites during their wilderness wanderings. It may be the Gudgodah of Deuteronomy 10:7, and has been identified with Wadi Ghadaghed.
horites: Cave dwellers of Mt Seir, according to tradition. These pre-Edomites were called the children of Seir.
hormah: Town near Beersheba in the Negev and on the border of the tribes of Judah and Simeon. Originally a Canaanite settlement, it became Judah’s according to Joshua 15:30 and then Simeon’s according to Joshua 19:4, 9.
horn: 1. Musical instrument frequently made from a ram’s horn.
horonaim: Moabite settlement of uncertain location, listed in prophetic oracles against Moab. It fell to Alexander Janneus, but the Hasmonean rule was subsequently returned to King Aretas by John Hyrcanus (Josephus’s Antiquities 13.15.4; 14.1.4).
horonite: Reference to either the residence or birthplace of Sanballat, who opposed Nehemiah’s restoration program. The name probably derives from the two cities of Upper and Lower Beth-horon.
horse: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
horse gate: Gate near the palace in Jerusalem, in the southeast part of the city wall. Here Queen Athaliah was put to death.
horus: All of Egyptian life was bound up with religious considerations. As the “gift of the Nile,” Egypt worshiped the great river as Hapi.
hosah (person): Merarite Levite who guarded the gate of the tent where the sacred ark was kept when David brought it to Jerusalem. His gatekeeping responsibilities were shared by his sons (26:10-16).
hosah (place): City south of Tyre on Asher’s border.
hosanna: Hebrew expression meaning “Save us, LORD,” taken from Psalm 118:25.
hosea (person): Prophet of ancient Israel whose sphere of activity was the northern kingdom. Little is known of him outside of the prophetic book that bears his name.
hosea, book of: First of the 12 minor prophets in the traditional arrangements of the OT books. It was written in the last part of the eighth century BC.
hoshaiah: 1. Prince of Judah who led a contingent of princes in procession at the dedication of the walls of Jerusalem after they were rebuilt.
hoshea: 1. Original name of Joshua, the son of Nun and Moses’ successor, before his name was changed by Moses.
hospitality: Biblical concept often used with the terms “guest,” “stranger,” and “sojourner.” It is useful to limit the meaning of “hospitality” to benevolence done to those outside one’s normal circle of friends, as is implied in the literal meaning of the Greek word…
host, host of heaven: Hebrew expressions found frequently in the OT and literally meaning “army” and “army of the skies.” “Host” is basically a military term, occurring nearly 500 times in the OT, and can mean “army”, “angels,” “heavenly bodies,” or “creation.”
hosts, lord of: Old Testament name for God found mostly in the prophets. The hosts are the heavenly powers and angels that act at the Lord’s command.
hotham: 1. Variant form of Helem in 1 Chronicles 7:32.
hothan: KJV spelling of Hotham in 1 Chronicles 11:44.
hothir: Levite and the head of the 21st of 24 divisions of priests for sanctuary service, formed during David’s reign.
hour: Most literally, a period of time delimited by the earth’s rotation around its axis, such as the period between two consecutive sunrises; also, the portion of that period in which the sun is visible, the other portion being called “night.” The word “day” occurs over 2,000 times in the OT, over 350 times in the NT.
house: Israel’s early ancestors lived mostly in tents or temporary dwellings, but the Canaanites of the middle Bronze Age (into whose land the Israelites came) lived in substantial houses of several rooms built around a courtyard.
household: Persons who live in the same place and compose a family or extended family. In biblical times a household included father, mother(s), children, grandparents, servants, concubines, and sojourners.
house of god: Common phrase used in the ancient Near Eastern world for a structure used to accommodate a deity or his servants. In the OT it referred to the tabernacle, Solomon’s temple, national shrines, or pagan temples.
house of the archives: Building used for storage of records, annals, and decrees; a common structure in Near Eastern nations in the second millennium BC.
house of the forest of lebanon: House of the Forest of Lebanon
Name for Solomon’s palace in Jerusalem, adjacent to the temple, given this designation because of the amount of Lebanese cedar used in its construction.
hozai: Author of annals describing the life of Manasseh, king of Judah, and included in the “Chronicles of the Seers”. The Septuagint renders Hozai as “seers,” which is preferred by many commentators and the NLT (see 2 Chr 33:19 mg).
hubbah: Alternative spelling for Shomer’s son from Asher’s tribe.
hukkok: Town near Naphtali and Zebulun’s boundary, listed next to Aznoth-tabor. It has been identified with Yaquaq, northwest of Gennesaret.
hukok: Alternate form of the Asherite town Helkath in 1 Chronicles 6:75.
hul: Son of Aram and grandson of Shem.
huldah: Prophetess living in Jerusalem; a contemporary of the prophets Jeremiah and Zephaniah. Huldah is introduced as the wife of Shallum, the wardrobe keeper in King Josiah’s court.
humility: A condition of lowliness or affliction in which one experiences a loss of power and prestige. Outside of biblical faith, humility in this sense would not usually be considered a virtue.
humtah: Settlement in the Judean uplands near Hebron, according to Joshua 15:54.
hunchback: Any obvious physical abnormality. In the OT sacrificial system both the animal to be sacrificed and the priest who performed the sacrifice (ch 21) had to be perfect physical specimens, without defect or blemish.
hundred, tower of the: Tower at the northernmost part of the Jerusalem wall (near where the wall crosses over the Tyropeon Valley). It stood west of the Sheep Gate near the Tower of Hananel (Neh 3:1; 12:39; KJV “tower of Meah”).
hundred-weight: Measure equal to about 1 talent or 75 pounds (34 kilograms), mentioned only in Revelation 16:21.
hunting: Practice of tracking and pursuing animals for food, animal products, or sport—a practice as old as man. In Bible times hunting was practiced all over the biblical world.
hupham, huphamite: Benjamite and the founder of the Huphamite family; he is perhaps identifiable with Huppim and Huram.
huppah: One of the chief men appointed in charge of the 13th division of priests in the time of David and Solomon.
huppim: Perhaps the son of Ir (Iri) and a descendant of Benjamin through Bela’s line. Huppim is probably an alternate spelling of Hupham, the father of the Huphamite family from Benjamin’s tribe.
hur: 1. Aaron’s assistant in supporting Moses’ hands until the Amalekites were defeated at Rephidim.
hurai: Alternate form of Hiddai in 1 Chronicles 11:32.
huram: 1. Bela’s son from Benjamin’s tribe; perhaps the same person as Hupham.
huram-abi: Alternate name for Hiram, Solomon’s temple craftsman, in 2 Chronicles 2:13 and 4:16.
huri: Abihail’s father from Gad’s tribe who inhabited Gilead in Bashan.
hurrians: People (also called Mitannians) who spoke a language different from Semitic and Indo-European and yet played a significant cultural role in the Near East during the second millennium BC, particularly in transmitting the culture of Sumer and Babylon to western Asia and to the Hittites.
husband: In Bible times, the family comprised members of a household, including not only parents and children, along with other relatives and concubines, but also servants, travelers, aliens, and anyone else who happened to be within the house and was therefore under the protection of the head of the family.
husbandman, husbandry: Occupation and practice of farming and animal production; KJV rendering of farmer, tenant farmer, plowman, tiller, and vinedresser.
hushah, hushathites: Ezer’s son or perhaps a town that Ezer founded. The warriors Sibbecai and Mebunnai were described as Hushathites.
hushai: Friend and adviser who remained faithful to David when his other adviser, Ahithophel, defected to join the rebelling Absalom. According to David’s instructions, Hushai pretended loyalty to Absalom and slipped information to David regarding Absalom’s plans.
husham: Temanite who succeeded Jobab as king of Edom.
hushim: 1. Dan’s son, alternately called Shuham in Numbers 26:42, where he is mentioned as the founder of the Shuhamite family.
huz: KJV rendering of Uz, Nahor’s son, in Genesis 22:21.
huzzab: Obscure Hebrew word found only in Nahum 2:7 (KJV). Scholars are uncertain whether the word is a verb meaning “it is decreed,” a noun personifying Nineveh, or a reference to an Assyrian queen.
hyacinth: Plant indigenous to the Holy Land yielding blue fragrant flowers.
hyena: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
hyksos: Term used by Egyptian historian Manetho (c. 280 BC) to designate the foreign rulers of the 15th and 16th dynasties in Egypt (1730?–1570? BC).
hymenaeus: Believer, probably of Ephesus, cited by Paul as one who “rejected conscience” and “swerved from the truth”. In the first instance, Hymenaeus (mentioned with Alexander) is viewed as having rejected correct beliefs and made a shipwreck of his faith.
hymn, hymnody: A natural human expression that probably began with speech-singing and developed into songs, which were then accompanied by instruments.
hypocrisy: The act of pretending to be what one is not, especially the false appearance of being religious or virtuous. Our modern understanding of the word “hypocrisy” is determined by its use in the NT, especially by Jesus.
“i am” sayings: Self-proclamations made by Jesus in the Gospel of John.
ibex: Species of wild goat, declared ceremonially clean in the Law.
ibhar: Son born to David during his reign in Jerusalem.
ibis: Wading bird with a long, slender bill, declared unclean in Leviticus 11:17.
ibleam: City in Manasseh’s territory, perhaps identifiable with Bileam, a Levitical city west of the Jordan River between Samaria and Jezreel.
ibnijah: Forefather of Meshullam from Benjamin’s tribe.
ibri: Merarite Levite and Jaaziah’s son, who lived during David’s time.
ibzan: Judge who ruled over Israel, or part of it, for seven years. Ibzan was a native of Bethlehem, probably of Zebulun, and was buried in his place of birth.
ichabod: Name given to Phinehas’s son (Eli’s grandson) to commemorate the glory that had departed from Israel, after the ark of God was taken by the Philistines.
iconium: City in the southwest part of central Asia Minor located about 95 miles (153 kilometers) from the Mediterranean coast. It is known today as Konya, a Turkish city, and capital of the province bearing the same name.
idalah: Town assigned to Zebulun’s tribe for an inheritance. It is generally identified with Khirbet el-Hawarah, northwest of Nazareth.
idbash: One of the descendants of Etam from Judah’s tribe.
iddo: 1. Father of Ahinadab, Solomon’s official at Mahanaim, who provisioned the royal household.
idols, idolatry: Man-made images or natural representations worshiped as deities; anything receiving worship other than the one true God. Idolatry is the spiritual worship of an idol.
idumaea, idumea, idumeans: Term derived from the Greek form of Edom (“red”). The change from Edomite to Idumean resulted from the conquests of Alexander the Great, which made Greek the common language of the area.
iezer, iezerites: Contractions of Abiezer and Abiezrite, the names of Gilead’s son and that son’s descendants.
igal: 1. Joseph’s son from Issachar’s tribe and one of the 12 spies sent by Moses to search out Canaan.
igdaliah: Hanan’s father. Hanan’s sons had a room adjacent to the temple during Jehoiakim’s reign.
igeal: KJV spelling of Igal, Shemaiah’s son, in 1 Chronicles 3:22.
ignatius and his epistles: Bishop of Antioch in Syria in the late first century, whose writings were very close to the thought of the NT writers. He wrote seven letters while en route under armed guard to Rome to suffer martyrdom (probably AD 107).
iim: 1. KJV rendering of Iyim, a shortened form of Iye-abarim, in Numbers 33:45.
ije-abarim: KJV spelling of Iye-abarim, one of Israel’s stopping places in the wilderness, in Numbers 21:11 and 33:44.
ijon: Town assigned to Naphtali’s tribe in the extreme north of Palestine. Some identify it with Tell ed-Dibbon between the Litani River and Mt Hermon, but this is disputed.
ikkesh: Man from Tekoa whose son Ira was one of David’s mighty men, and head of a division of 24,000 men during the sixth month of the year.
ilai: Alternate name for Zalmon, a renowned warrior, in 1 Chronicles 11:29 (see NLT mg).
illness: Term used in Scripture synonymously with sickness, infirmity, illness, plague, and pestilence. However, plague and pestilence are generally used when there are large numbers of victims, as in epidemics.
illyricum: Roman province northwest of Macedonia. During the height of the Roman Empire (c.
image of god: Likeness to God, the most basic affirmation to be made concerning the nature of human beings from a Christian perspective. Humans are unique among the creatures in that they are like God and therefore able to have communion and fellowship with God.
imalkue: An Arab chieftain who was in charge of Antiochus, the son of Alexander. Trypho, who had once supported Alexander, sought the aid of Imalkue to have Antiochus crowned king instead of Demetrius.
imlah: Father of Michaiah, a prophet during King Ahab’s reign, whom the king despised for speaking the truth.
immanuel: Hebrew masculine name that means “God with us.” It appears only twice in the OT and once in the NT, where it is sometimes transliterated “Emmanuel.” In the OT the name was given to a child born in the time of Ahaz as a sign to the king that Judah would receive relief from attacks by Israel and Syria.
immer (person): Priest in the time of David. He became the ancestral head of a house of priests: Pashhur, the priest who had Jeremiah arrested and placed in stocks, was a descendant of Immer.
immer (place): Place in Babylon. The Jews who returned from Immer had lost the record of their ancestry and could not prove their Jewish lineage.
immersion: Method of baptism whereby the believer is submersed under water.
imnah: 1. Asher’s son and founder of the Imnite family.
imnite: Descendant of Imnah from Asher’s tribe.
impalement: Driving of a pointed stake into a human body. It was apparently practiced in ancient Egypt, Assyria, Babylonia, Persia, and possibly also in Israel.
imprecatory psalms: Psalms that contain curses (imprecations, maledictions) against enemies.
imputation: Charging to an account, used in the Bible with legal reference to sin and salvation being recorded by God. The biblical teaching on imputation represents one of the principal doctrines of the Christian faith.
imrah: Zophah’s son, a chief of Asher’s tribe.
imri: 1. Ancestor of Uthai, one of the postexilic Jews of Judah’s tribe.
incarnation: Literally, “in flesh”; theologically, the doctrine that in Jesus of Nazareth God took on human flesh and became the God-man.
incense: Fragrant spices and oils or sacrifice that sends up perfumed smoke to God in order to please him.
india: Eastern land of uncertain geographical boundaries in Bible times. The only specific reference to the land of India in the Bible occurs in Esther 1:1 and 8:9, where the boundaries of the empire of Ahasuerus are said to have stretched from Hoddu to Kush.
infirmity: Term used in Scripture synonymously with sickness, infirmity, illness, plague, and pestilence. However, plague and pestilence are generally used when there are large numbers of victims, as in epidemics.
ingathering, feast of: One of the three great festivals of Israel, also called the Feast of Booths, or Tabernacles, which celebrated the completion of the agricultural year.
inheritance: Legacy or bequest. Inheritance plays an unusually significant role in the Scriptures when it is used to convey theological truths.
iniquity: Evildoing that is not only against humanity, society, others, or oneself, but against God. The concept of God, therefore, gives to the idea of sin its many-sided meaning.
ink, inkhorn: The process that goes into producing books.
inner man: The inner, invisible being of a human. This Pauline phrase resembles the “hidden man” (KJV) of 1 Peter 3:4 (cf.
innocents, slaughter of the: Herod the Great’s massacre of all the boys under two years old in Bethlehem and its vicinity. Herod slaughtered “the holy innocents” in an effort to destroy the child about whom the Magi had told him.
inscriptions: Term used to refer to writing in the ancient world that was done on a material of a permanent nature, such as stone or clay, rather than on ordinary and impermanent substances, such as papyri or parchment.
insect: Small invertebrates generally characterized by a segmented body (head, thorax, abdomen) and three pairs of legs.
inspiration: Theological term for the influence God exerted on the writers of Scripture, enabling them to transmit his revelations in writing.
installation offering: Major ritual expressions of religious life with accompanying rites, such as libations, effusions, and sacred meals. The ideology expressed in Israel’s ritual complex made its religion unique in the ancient Near East.
instruct, instructor: Teachers conserved the values and academia of a nation and passed them on to each new generation. In OT times the first teachers were often parents.
instruments, musical: Stringed, wind, and percussion instruments used to make music.
intercede, intercession: The addressing and petitioning of God. Prayer to a god or gods is a feature of many, if not all, religions, but here attention will be restricted to the biblical teaching and some of its implications.
intercession of christ: Theological term for Christ’s activity of petitioning God the Father to save, help, and sustain people on earth.
interest: Something owed to another person, such as goods, property, or money. In the Bible, righteous conduct is something one “owes” to God; hence, in theology, sin is described figuratively as being “in debt.”
intermediate state: State of the human person after death and before the final resurrection. Such teaching is more developed in the NT than in the OT, though it is a mistake to think that reference to it is totally absent in the OT.
interpreter: One who facilitates communication between people who speak different languages, or one who explains the meaning of dreams. Joseph pretended to need an interpreter to speak to his brothers.
intertestamental period: Portion of time extending from the close of OT history to the beginning of NT history. Much of this period is covered in the books of 1 and 2 Maccabees.
iob: Alternate name for Jashub, Issachar’s son, in Genesis 46:13.
iphtah: City of the Shephelah assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance, listed between Ashan and Ashnah.
iphtah-el: Valley on Asher and Zebulun’s border, possibly the modern Sahl el-Battof.
ir: Benjamite father of Shuppim and Huppim, perhaps identical with Iri (v 7). In Numbers 24:19, the name is translated “the city” (KJV, NIV; cf.
ira: 1. David’s priest or chief official in service at the time of Sheba’s revolt.
irad: Enoch’s son, a member of Cain’s line.
irijah: Benjamite guard who apprehended Jeremiah as he left Jerusalem to see property that was his by redemption and charged him before the princes with deserting to the Chaldeans; as a consequence, Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned (37:13-14).
ir-nahash: Son of Tehinnah, Eshton’s son from Judah’s tribe. Some translations note the alternate rendering, “city of Nahash” (mg NIV, KJV).
iron (place): KJV form of Yiron, a city in Naphtali’s territory.
ironsmith: An artisan who normally worked in iron; a blacksmith. The first worker in iron recorded in the Bible is Tubal-cain.
irpeel: City of inheritance allotted to Benjamin’s tribe, perhaps situated in the hill country several miles northwest of Jerusalem, near Gibeon.
ir-shemesh: City allotted to Dan’s tribe for an inheritance, probably identical with Beth-shemesh.
isaac: Son of Abraham and Sarah, father of Jacob and Esau, one of the patriarchs of Israel.
isaiah (person): Eighth-century BC prophet during the reigns of the Judean kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah; author of the biblical book of Isaiah. Isaiah was the son of Amoz and may have been a relative of King Amaziah.
isaiah, book of: The prophet Isaiah, whose name means “the Lord saves,” lived and ministered in Jerusalem. Because of his repeated contact with the kings of Judah, some scholars believed that Isaiah was related to the royal family, but this is not certain.
iscariot: 1. Simon’s son, surnamed Iscariot; one of the 12 disciples of Jesus.
ishbah: Mered’s son by Bithiah, the daughter of the pharaoh.
ishbak: One of the sons of Abraham by Keturah.
ishbi-benob: Giant who nearly killed David. During one of his many battles with the Philistines, David grew faint and was nearly killed by Ishbi-benob.
ishbosheth: Alternate name for Eshbaal, Saul’s son and successor to Israel’s throne.
ishi: 1. Appaim’s son, the father of Sheshan and a descendant of Judah through Jerahmeel’s line.
ishiah: KJV spelling of Isshiah, Izrahiah’s son, in 1 Chronicles 7:3.
ishijah: Harim’s son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife.
ishmael: 1. Abraham’s first son, born of Hagar, Sarah’s Egyptian handmaid, at the instigation of Sarah herself.
ishmaelite: Descendant of Ishmael, Abraham’s son by Hagar.
ishmaiah: 1. Warrior from Benjamin’s tribe who joined David at Ziklag in his struggle against King Saul.
ishmerai: Elpaal’s son and a chief in Benjamin’s tribe.
ishod: KJV spelling of Ishhod, Hammoleketh’s son.
ishpan: Shashak’s son and a leader in Benjamin’s tribe.
ish-tob: KJV translation for “men of Tob” in 2 Samuel 10:6-8.
ishuah: KJV spelling of Ishvah, Asher’s son, in Genesis 46:17.
ishuai: KJV spelling of Ishvi, Asher’s son, in 1 Chronicles 7:30.
ishui: KJV spelling of Ishvi, Saul’s son, in 1 Samuel 14:49.
ishvi: 1. Asher’s third son and founder of the Ishvite family.
ismaiah: KJV spelling of Ishmaiah, a warrior from Benjamin’s tribe who joined David at Ziklag in 1 Chronicles 12:4.
ismakiah: Levite overseer of things dedicated at the temple during Hezekiah’s reform.
ispah: KJV spelling of Ishpah, Beriah’s son, 1 Chronicles 8:16.
israel (person): Name meaning “one who struggles with God” or “God struggles” (Gn 32:28, NLT mg). It was given to Isaac’s son Jacob and to his descendants (35:9-12; cf.
israel (place): Country on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean Sea, also known as Canaan and Israel.
israel, history of: An account of God’s sovereign purpose in calling a people out of paganism and establishing them as witnesses for the true faith among the nations, of God’s sovereign power in protecting them from extinction, of his sovereign justice in dealing with their…
israelite: Descendant of the 12 sons of Israel (the name God gave to Jacob, Gn 32:28).
issachar, tribe of: Tribal inheritance of Issachar. The territory is defined in Joshua 19:17-23; detailed boundary descriptions are not included.
isshijah: Alternate rendering of Ishijah, Harim’s son in Ezra 10:31.
issue of blood: KJV rendering of “hemorrhage” in Matthew 9:20 and Mark 5:25.
isuah: KJV spelling of Ishvah, Asher’s son, in 1 Chronicles 7:30.
isui: KJV rendering of Ishvi, Asher’s son, in Genesis 46:17.
italian band, italian cohort, italian re: Italian Band, Italian Cohort, Italian Regiment
Roman military unit to which the centurion Cornelius belonged. The single biblical reference to a regiment (NASB “cohort”; KJV “ band”) is in Acts 10:1.
italy: Boot-shaped peninsula located between the Tyrrhenian and the Adriatic seas. Uplands and two major mountain ranges—the Alps, which form a northern boundary, and the Apennines, which form the backbone of the peninsula—occupy 77 percent of the land.
ithai: Alternate spelling of Ittai, a Benjamite warrior, in 1 Chronicles 11:31.
ithamar: Aaron’s fourth and youngest son, who served as a priest to the tribes of Israel during the wilderness period. After the death of two of his brothers, he was given the special duty of overseeing the moving of the tabernacle.
ithiel: 1. Ancestor of Sallu, a Benjamite who lived in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile.
ithlah: City given to Dan’s tribe for an inheritance, after the initial conquest of Palestine by Joshua.
ithmah: Warrior of Moabite origin and one of David’s mighty men.
ithra: Father of Amasa by Abigail, Zeruiah’s sister (2 Sm 17:25, NLT mg). He is called Jether in 1 Kings 2:5, 32 and 1 Chronicles 2:17.
ithran: 1. Dishon’s son, who was a Horite chief.
ithream: David’s sixth son, borne by his wife Eglah at Hebron.
ithrite: Family or clan that lived at Kiriath-jearim. Ira and Gareb, two of David’s mighty men, were Ithrites (2 Sm 23:38; 1 Chr 11:40; NLT “from Jattir”).
ittah-kazin: KJV form of the town Eth-kazin in Joshua 19:13.
ittai: 1. Philistine from Gath who, with 600 other Gittites, remained loyal to David and accompanied him on his flight from Absalom.
ituraea, iturea, itureans: Small province mentioned with Trachonitis as forming the tetrarchy of Philip, brother of Herod the Great, during the reign of Tiberius Caesar.
ivory: Opaque dentine substance, often mentioned along with precious metals and gems in the Bible and ancient Near Eastern writings.
ivvah: City that had already fallen along with others to the Assyrians. Sennacherib’s representative mocked Hezekiah’s belief that God would save Jerusalem.
iye-abarim, iyim: Israelite camping place on the southeast border of Moab during the wilderness wanderings. In verse 45 the town is called Iyim, which is a shortened form of Iye-abarim.
izehar, izeharites: KJV spelling of Izhar, Kohath’s son, and his descendants.
izhar: 1. One of Kohath’s sons from Levi’s tribe, and father of the Izharite family; alternately called Amminadab in 1 Chronicles 6:22.
izharite: Descendant of Izhar from Levi’s tribe.
izrahiah: Uzzi’s son and a leading member of Issachar’s tribe.
izrahite: Designation given to Shamhuth, one of David’s 12 monthly captains, meaning a man of a family or town called Izra. The word “Izrahite” is perhaps a corruption of “Zerahite,” a descendant of Zerah of Judah.
izri: Temple musician and head of the 4th of the 24 divisions of priests for service as musicians in the sanctuary (1 Chr 25:11, NLT mg). He is called Zeri in 1 Chronicles 25:3.
izziah: Parosh’s son, who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce the foreign woman he married during the postexilic period.
jaakan: Esau’s descendant and a son of Ezer the Horite (1 Chr 1:42, NLT mg); alternately called Akan in Genesis 36:27.
jaalah: Servant of King Solomon and head of a family who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile.
jaalam: KJV form of Jalam, Esau’s son, in Genesis 36:5, 14, 18 and 1 Chronicles 1:35.
jaanai: KJV form of Janai, a Gadite, in 1 Chronicles 5:12.
jaar: Most common word in Hebrew for “forest.” It refers to forests generally and to specific forests, such as the “forest of Ephraim” and the “forest of Hereth”, both associated with King David.
jaare-oregim: Textual corruption of Jair in 2 Samuel 21:19.
jaareshiah: Jeroham’s son, a Benjamite leader who lived in Jerusalem.
jaasau: KJV spelling of Jaasu, Bani’s son, in Ezra 10:37.
jaasu: Bani’s son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile.
jaazaniah: 1. Son of Hoshaiah, who was a Maacathite and a leader in the armies of Judah at the beginning of the exile.
jaazer: KJV alternate form of Jazer, an Amorite city in Gilead, in Numbers 21:32 and 32:35.
jaaziah: Descendant of Merari in a list of family leaders among Levites assigned to temple duty in David’s reign.
jaaziel: One of the eight men appointed to play harps or lyres when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem by David (1 Chr 15:18-20; and probably 16:5a, “Jeiel,” which is most likely a copyist’s error). He is called Aziel in verse 20.
jabal: Descendant of Cain and the first son of Lamech and Adah. He was the father of a nomadic people who dwelt in tents.
jabbok: Eastern tributary of the Jordan, the modern Nahr ez-Zerqa or Blue River. Its source is a spring near Amman, capital of modern Jordan (the Decapolis town of Philadelphia in Hellenistic times).
jabesh (person): Shallum’s father. Shallum assassinated Zechariah, king of Israel.
jabesh, jabesh-gilead (place): Town appearing in the closing chapters of the book of Judges (chs 19–21).
jabez (person): Member of Judah’s tribe who was noted for his godliness. He prayed for God’s protection, and his prayer was answered.
jabez (place): City that was probably located in Judah and was inhabited by scribes.
jabin: 1. King of Hazor who led a coalition against Joshua at Merom.
jabneel: 1. Alternate name for the town Jabneh in Judah’s tribe.
jabneh: Biblical city on the coastal plain between Joppa (modern Jaffa) and Ashdod, first mentioned as Jabneel, on the northern border of the tribe of Judah.
jacan, jachan: Member of Gad’s tribe who lived in Bashan during the reign of Jotham, king of Judah.
jachin: 1. Son of Simeon and leader of the Jachinites, who immigrated to Egypt with his grandfather Jacob.
jachin and boaz: Names of two pillars Solomon set up before the temple vestibule. He named the south pillar Jachin and the north pillar Boaz.
jacinth: Precious stone mentioned in Revelation 21:20 as a foundation stone in the new Jerusalem.
jackal: Wolflike mammal known for its distinctive wail.
jackal's well: Unknown location along the Jerusalem wall between the Valley Gate and the Dung Gate visited by Nehemiah during his night inspection of the wall. It is also called Dragon’s Well or Serpent’s Well.
jacob: 1. Younger of twin sons born to Isaac and Rebekah.
jacob's ladder: When Jacob left home after deceiving his father, Isaac, into giving him the blessing that Isaac had intended for Esau, he was not only desirous of finding a wife from among the daughters of his mother’s brother, but he was also literally fleeing for his life, because Esau had determined to kill him (v 41).
jacob's well: Place mentioned only in John’s Gospel. It was here that Jesus sat and talked with the unnamed woman of Samaria, who readily accepted Jesus’ words.
jaddai: Nebo’s descendant, who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife during the postexilic era.
jaddua: 1. Leader who set his seal on Ezra’s covenant during the postexilic era.
jadon: Workman on the Jerusalem wall after the return from exile. Jadon worked on the section near the Old Gate of the city with men from Gibeon and Mizpah.
jael: Wife of Heber. Though her husband was from the Kenite tribe, a longtime ally of Israel, he had chosen to side with Jabin, the Canaanite king.
jagur: Place in the extreme southern part of Israel, near Edom, inherited by Judah’s tribe soon after the Conquest.
jah: Abbreviation of the covenant name of God, YHWH or Yahweh (“Jehovah,” KJV; “LORD,” most modern translations). The fragment is often used in words and names (e.g., Hallelujah, Jahaziel).
jahath: 1. Reaiah’s son and the father of Ahumai and Lahad, Zorathites from Judah’s tribe.
jahaz: Town east of the Dead Sea (in modern Jordan) where the Israelites defeated Sihon, king of the Amorites, when he refused to permit them to pass through his land. According to Joshua 13:18, Moses gave the town to Reuben’s tribe as part of its allotment.
jahaziah: KJV rendering of Jahzeiah, Tikvah’s son, in Ezra 10:15.
jahaziel: 1. Warrior from Benjamin’s tribe who joined David at Ziklag in his struggle against King Saul.
jahdiel: One of the family heads of Manasseh’s tribe dwelling east of the Jordan following the allotment of the land. He was noted as one of the mighty warriors in his tribe.
jahdo: Gadite, son of Buz and a forefather of a number of valiant men who were registered during the reigns of King Jeroboam of Israel (793–753 BC) and King Jotham of Judah (750–735 BC; 1 Chr 5:14).
jahleel, jahleelite: Zebulun’s son and the founder of the Jahleelite family.
jahzah: Alternate form of Jahaz, a town east of the Dead Sea, in 1 Chronicles 6:78 (NLT mg) and Jeremiah 48:21 (NLT mg).
jahzeel, jahzeelite: Naphtali’s son and founder of the Jahzeelite family.
jahzeiah: Tikvah’s son and one of the persons named in connection with the divorce proceedings between the Israelites and their foreign wives. Opinions differ as to whether he was for or against the proceedings.
jahzerah: Ancestor of a priest who returned to Judah after the Babylonian exile. He is called Ahzai in Nehemiah 11:13.
jahziel: Alternate spelling of Jahzeel, Naphtali’s son, in 1 Chronicles 7:13 (NLT mg).
jair: 1. Descendant of Manasseh, who at the time of the Conquest took several villages in the Argob region of Bashan and Gilead and called them after his own name, Havvoth-jair, meaning “Towns of Jair” (Dt 3:14; cf.
jairite: Descendant of Jair from Manasseh’s tribe.
jairus: Leader of the synagogue, perhaps at Capernaum. Jairus sought Jesus among the crowds and petitioned him to come and heal his critically ill daughter.
jakan: KJV spelling of Jaakan, Esau’s descendant, in 1 Chronicles 1:42.
jakeh: Agur’s father. Agur authored a series of proverbs addressed to Ithiel and Ucal.
jakin: 1. Son of Simeon and leader of the Jachinites, who immigrated to Egypt with his grandfather Jacob.
jakin and boaz: Names of two pillars Solomon set up before the temple vestibule. He named the south pillar Jachin and the north pillar Boaz.
jalam: Esau’s son and chief of an Edomite clan.
jambres: Enemy of Moses, who, along with Jannes, is used by Paul as an example of the type of person to avoid.
jambri: Ancestor of an Arab tribe. During the Hasmonean (Maccabean) wars when Jonathan was ruler, the Jambrites captured a baggage train of the Jews when it was being sent to the Nabateans for safekeeping.
james (person): 1. James, brother of Jesus; leading elder in the church at Jerusalem; author of the epistle bearing his name.
james, letter of: First letter of the General Epistles.
jamin: 1. Simeon’s son and founder of the Jaminite family.
jaminite: Descendant of Jamin from Simeon’s tribe.
jamnia: Alternate name for Jabneh in Judith 2:28.
janai: Gadite chief who settled, along with his kinsmen, in the land of Bashan.
janim: City in the hill country of the territory assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance. Its location is presumably southwest of Hebron.
jannai: Ancestor of Jesus recorded in Luke’s genealogy.
jannes and jambres: Two of Pharaoh’s magicians, who opposed Moses and tried to show that they were as effective as he at working miracles. Jewish legend regarded Jannes and Jambres (somewhat improbably) as sons of Balaam, the Midianite prophet of Numbers 22–24.
janoah: 1. City defining the eastern border of Ephraim’s territory, located southeast of Shechem and northeast of Shiloh.
janohah: KJV spelling of Janoah, a town in Ephraim’s territory, in Joshua 16:6-7.
janum: KJV spelling of Janim, a town in Judah’s territory, in Joshua 15:53.
japheth: One of Noah’s three sons who, along with his wife, was among the eight human survivors of the great Flood.
japhia (person): 1. King of Lachish who joined an alliance of four other Amorite kings to punish Gibeon for its treaty with the Jews.
japhia (place): Town described as part of the southern border of Zebulun’s territory. It has been identified with modern Yafa, about two miles (3.2 kilometers) southwest of Nazareth.
japhlet: Heber’s son and chief in Asher’s tribe.
japhletites: People occupying an area that marked part of the southern border of Ephraim’s territory in the vicinity of Beth-horon.
japho: KJV form of Joppa in Joshua 19:46.
jar: The manufacture of clayware and earthenware.
jarah: Descendant of King Saul (1 Chr 9:42, NLT mg).
jareb: Name used by Hosea to designate an Assyrian king. Because no such name is to be found in the Assyrian king lists, some have conjectured that it designated Sargon, but this is mere speculation.
jared: Mahalalel’s son and a descendant of Seth. He was the father of Enoch.
jaresiah: KJV rendering of Jaareshiah, Jeroham’s son, in 1 Chronicles 8:27.
jarha: Egyptian servant of Sheshan, Jerahmeel’s descendant, who was given his master’s daughter in marriage. Sheshan did this because he had no sons.
jarib: 1. Alternate name for Jachin, Simeon’s son, in 1 Chronicles 4:24.
jarmuth: 1. Fortified city in the northern part of the Shephelah given to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance.
jashar, book of: This was an ancient Hebrew writing that is no longer extant. It was probably a national songbook containing songs praising the exploits of Hebrew heroes.
jashobeam: 1. Zabdiel’s son who was put in charge of David’s “Three” mightiest men and also appointed chief of a division (24,000 soldiers) on duty in the first month of the year.
jashub: 1. Issachar’s third son (1 Chr 7:1; alternately called Iob in Gn 46:13), and founder of the Jashubite family.
jashubi-lehem: Mentioned along with Moab in 1 Chronicles 4:22.
jashubite: Descendant of Jashub, Issachar’s third son.
jasiel: KJV form of Jaasiel the Mezobaite in 1 Chronicles 11:47.
jason: 1. Jewish high priest (174–171 BC) who brought about the decline of the priesthood by Hellenizing Jerusalem, making her inhabitants “citizens of Antioch” (2 Macc 4:9ff.).
jathan: One of the sons of Shemaiah, who had accompanied Tobit to Jerusalem to worship (Tb 5:14, NLT mg).
jathniel: Fourth son of Meshelemiah the Korahite and doorkeeper of the temple in David’s time.
jattir: Town in the hill country of Judah given to the Levites. David sent spoils from his victory over the Amalekites to Jattir.
javan (person): Japheth’s son whose seafaring descendants migrated to the north and west of Canaan.
javan (place): Location commonly identified with Greece. The name is linguistically associated with Ionia, a region in westernmost Asia Minor that was colonized by Greeks.
jazer: Town east of the Jordan River in southern Gilead, taken with its surrounding villages by the Israelites under Moses. The tribes of Gad and Reuben asked for the lands of Jazer and Gilead.
jaziz: One of David’s royal stewards in charge of the flocks.
jealousy, ordeal of: Numbers 5:11-28 contains a provision by which a man who suspected his wife of adultery could bring her to the priest to determine her guilt or innocence.
jearim, mount: Mountain on the northwest border of Judah’s territory between Beth-shemesh and Kiriath-jearim. Kesalon was located on its northern slope.
jeaterai, jeatherai: Zerah’s son, a Gershonite Levite, called Ethni in 1 Chronicles 6:41.
jeberechiah, jeberekiah: Father of Zechariah the scribe. Zechariah, with Uriah the priest, witnessed Isaiah’s prophecy of the Assyrian conquest of Israel.
jebus, jebusite: Walled city, lying on the boundary between Judah and Benjamin, conquered by David; thereafter, it was known as the “city of David,” or ancient Jerusalem. Its occupants were Jebusites.
jecamiah: KJV spelling of Jekamiah, King Jehoiachin’s son, in 1 Chronicles 3:18.
jecholiah: KJV spelling of Jecoliah, King Azariah’s mother, in 2 Kings 15:2.
jechoniah: Alternate form of Jehoiachin, a Judean king, in Matthew 1:11-12.
jechonias: KJV form of Jechoniah, an alternate name of Jehoiachin, king of Judah, in Matthew 1:11-12.
jecoliah: Mother of King Azariah, or Uzziah.
jeconiah: Alternate name for King Jehoiachin of Judah, who was carried into Babylonian exile.
jedaiah: 1. Shimri’s son and the father of Allon.
jediael: 1. Benjamin’s son, whose descendants were warriors, numbering 17,200 by David’s time.
jedidah: Adaiah’s daughter, the wife of King Amon of Judah and the mother of King Josiah.
jedidiah: Name meaning “beloved of the LORD [Yahweh].” God told Nathan the prophet to give Solomon, David’s second son by Bathsheba, this name soon after his birth.
jeduthun: Member of the Levitical family of Merar who, along with Asaph and Heman, presided over the music in the sanctuary in David’s reign (1 Chr 25:1; 2 Chr 5:12; called “Ethan” in 1 Chr 6:44; 15:17). Jeduthun is mentioned in the titles of Psalms 39, 62, and 77.
jeezer, jeezerite: KJV forms of Iezer and Iezerite, contractions of Abiezer and Abiezerite, the names of Gilead’s son and his descendants.
jegar-sahadutha: Aramaic name given by Laban to the heap of stones that he and Jacob piled up as a memorial to their covenant; Jacob called it “Galeed”. The name means “heap of witness.”
jehallelel: 1. Descendant of Judah who had four sons.
jehdeiah: 1. Shubael’s son, a Levite in David’s time.
jehezkel: Levite assigned to temple duty in David’s time; leader of the 20th division.
jehiah: Levite who, along with Obed-edom, was appointed as doorkeeper for the ark when David brought it to Jerusalem.
jehiel: 1. KJV spelling of Jeiel, King Saul’s ancestor, in 1 Chronicles 9:35.
jehieli, jehielite: Alternate spelling of Jehiel, a Levite and founder of the Jehielite family, in 1 Chronicles 26:21-22.
jehizkiah: Shallum’s son and a chief of Ephraim during the reign of Ahaz in Judah. He opposed the enslavement of the men of Judah by victorious Israel.
jehoadah, jehoaddah: Ahaz’s son and a descendant of King Saul through Jonathan’s line; alternately called Jarah in 1 Chronicles 9:42.
jehoaddan, jehoaddin: Mother of Amaziah, king of Judah.
jehoahaz: 1. Twelfth king of Israel, succeeding his father, Jehu, and ruling from 814 BC to 798 BC.
jehoash: Name of two OT kings, occurring only in the book of 2 Kings. The name means “the LORD is strong” or “the LORD hath bestowed.” Joash, the shorter form of the name, frequently appears in the Kings and Chronicles narratives.
jehohanan: 1. Korahite Levite who was a gatekeeper of the sanctuary during David’s reign.
jehoiachin: King of Judah for a very brief time (598–597 BC). He was the son of Jehoiakim and Nehushta, the daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem (possibly the Elnathan mentioned by Jeremiah, cf.
jehoiada: 1. Father of Benaiah, a high military officer during the reigns of David and Solomon.
jehoiakim: Second son of Josiah by Zebidah who became king of Judah in 609 BC. He replaced his younger brother Jehoahaz as king when he was deposed and exiled by Pharaoh Neco after a three-month reign.
jehoiarib: 1. Alternate form of Joiarib, a priestly family in Jerusalem, in 1 Chronicles 9:10.
jehonadab: Alternate name for Jonadab, Recab’s son.
jehonathan: 1. KJV spelling of Jonathan, Uzziah’s son, in 1 Chronicles 27:25.
jehoram: 1. Jehoshaphat’s son and Judah’s fifth king (853–841 BC; also called Joram).
jehoshabeath: Alternate name for Jehosheba, daughter of Judah’s King Jehoram, in 2 Chronicles 22:11.
jehoshaphat (person): 1. The fourth king of Judah (872–848 BC), son and successor of Asa (910–869 BC).
