jehoshaphat, valley of: Valley mentioned in prophecy as the place of future judgment, sometimes called the valley of decision (v 14). Its exact location is disputed.
jehosheba: Daughter of King Jehoram of Judah (853–841 BC) and Queen Athaliah, sister of King Ahaziah (841 BC), and wife of Jehoiada the high priest.
jehoshua, jehoshuah: Alternate KJV names for Joshua, son of Nun, in Numbers 13:16 and 1 Chronicles 7:27, respectively.
jehovah: Name for God formed by adding the vowels of the Hebrew word ’Adonai to the consonants of the Hebrew divine name, YHWH.
jehovah-tsidkenu: Name of the righteous king of David’s line who God promised would rule over his people. The name means “The LORD (Yahweh or Jehovah) is our righteousness.” It was also applied to the king’s subjects, who will profit by his reign (33:16).
jehozabad: 1. Shomer’s son, who was a servant of King Joash and later, with another assailant, murdered the king at Millo.
jehozadak: Alternate name for Jozadak, Seraiah’s son.
jehu: 1. Prophet and son of the “seer” Hanani, who denounced Baasha for following in the ways of Jeroboam.
jehucal: Son of Shelemiah who was sent by King Zedekiah to request Jeremiah’s prayers for Judah.
jehud: One of the towns given to Dan’s tribe after the Conquest. It has been variously identified with the village of el-Yehudiyeh, about seven miles (11.3 kilometers) southeast of Joppa, and with Yazur, about five miles (8 kilometers) southeast of Joppa.
jehudi: Son of Nethaniah and a messenger of King Jehoiakim of Judah. He was sent by a number of princes to summon Baruch to read Jeremiah’s scroll privately to them.
jehudijah: Not a proper name; KJV mistranslation for “Jewish,” a descriptive term distinguishing Mered’s Jewish wife from his other wife, who was an Egyptian princess.
jehush: KJV spelling of Jeush, Eshek’s son, in 1 Chronicles 8:39.
jekabzeel: Alternate name for Kabzeel, a city in southern Judah, in Nehemiah 11:25.
jekameam: Hebron’s son from the Kohathite division of Levi’s tribe.
jemimah: First of the three daughters born to Job when he was restored after his affliction.
jemuel: Simeon’s first son. He is called Nemuel in 1 Chronicles 4:24 and is the founder of the Nemuelite family.
jephthah: Illegitimate son of Gilead and a leader in the period of the judges. The son of a harlot, Jephthah was dispossessed by his father’s other sons and refused a share in their father’s home.
jephunneh: 1. Father of Caleb, one of the 12 spies sent by Moses to search out the land of Canaan.
jerah: Son of Joktan and nephew of Peleg, during whose lifetime the earth was divided, probably a reference to the dispersion following Babel. Jerah is likely also the name of an Arabian tribe or district.
jerahmeel: 1. Firstborn of Hezron’s three sons, the father of six sons and a descendant of Judah through Perez’s line.
jered: 1. KJV spelling of Jared in 1 Chronicles 1:2.
jeremai: Hashum’s son who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his foreign wife after the exile.
jeremiah (person): 1. Prophet to Judah before its fall in 586 BC; his name is also spelled “Jeremias” and “Jeremy” in the KJV.
jeremiah, book of: OT prophetic book, second in the canonical order of the Prophets.
jeremiah, letter of: The Letter of Jeremiah is a book accepted as part of the Deuterocanonical works. It was originally written in Hebrew or Aramaic by an unknown Jewish author.
jeremias: KJV spelling of Jeremiah in Matthew 16:14.
jeremoth: 1. One of Beker’s nine sons and a leader in Benjamin’s tribe.
jeremy: KJV spelling of Jeremiah in Matthew 2:17 and 27:9.
jeriah: Levite of the family of Kohath and head of Hebron’s house. David organized Jeriah and other Levites to manage the religious and civil affairs of the kingdom (26:31).
jeribai: Elnaam’s son and one of David’s mighty men.
jericho: Ancient city on the west side of the Jordan River. The name Jericho may be connected to the ancient name of the Canaanite moon god.
jerijah: Alternate spelling of Jeriah, a Kohathite Levite, in 1 Chronicles 26:31 (NLT mg).
jerimoth: 1. One of Bela’s five sons and a leader in the tribe of Benjamin.
jerioth: One of Caleb’s wives, according to 1 Chronicles 2:18.
jeroboam: Name of two kings who reigned in the northern kingdom of Israel: Jeroboam I (930–909 BC), the originator and first monarch of the 10 tribes of Israel, and Jeroboam II (793–753 BC), the 14th king of the northern kingdom.
jeroham: 1. Levite of the family of Kohath, father of Elkanah and a forefather of the prophet Samuel and Heman the singer.
jerubbaal: Name given to Gideon after he destroyed an altar to Baal. The name means “let Baal contend against him.” See Gideon.
jerubbesheth: An alternate name for Gideon See Gideon.
jeruel: Wilderness lying southeast of Tekoa near En-gedi, just above and west of the cliff of Ziz. Some identify it with el-Hasasah.
jerusalem: Historic city sacred to Christians, Jews, and Muslims; the chief city of ancient Palestine and of the modern state of Israel.
jerusalem, new: Phrase appearing only twice in the Bible, once near the beginning and once near the end of the book of Revelation. In the first of the great visions of that book, the risen Christ speaks to his people in the midst of their conflict in this world.
jerusalem council: Meeting described in Acts 15:6-29, held about AD 50. Acts records that the conference was held to deal with the question of the requirement for gentile salvation raised by Jews first in Antioch (14:26–15:1) and later in Jerusalem (15:3-5).
jerusha, jerushah: Zadok’s daughter, wife of King Uzziah of Judah and mother of King Jotham (2 Kgs 15:33; 2 Chr 27:1, alternately spelled “Jerushah”).
jeshaiah: 1. Hananiah’s son; the father of Rephaiah and a descendant of David through Zerubbabel’s line, who lived in postexilic Palestine.
jeshanah: Border city in the hill country of Ephraim that King Abijah of Judah (913–910 BC) seized from King Jeroboam I (930–909 BC) and the northern kingdom during a civil war.
jesharelah: A variant for Asharelah or Asarelah, the name of a Levite musician, in 1 Chronicles 25:14 (KJV; NIV “Jesarelah”).
jeshebeab: Levite family leader assigned to temple duty during David’s reign.
jeshimon: 1. Desolate wilderness at the end of the Dead Sea, not far from Pisgah and Peor.
jeshishai: Descendant of Gad in the days of Jotham, king of Judah.
jeshohaiah: One of the 13 Simeonite princes in the days of Hezekiah who participated in the invasion of the valley of Gedor; they killed the inhabitants of the territory and took the land for the pasture of their sheep.
jeshua (person): 1. Levite and head of the ninth of 24 divisions of priests formed during David’s reign.
jeshua (place): Town in the Negev listed before Moladah among the towns where Judeans returned after exile (Neh 11:26; cf. v 20). It may be identical with the Shema mentioned next to Moladah in Joshua 15:26.
jeshuah: KJV spelling of Jeshua, a priest during David’s time, in 1 Chronicles 24:11.
jeshurun: Poetical name for Israel, possibly derived from the Hebrew root meaning “upright,” but according to many scholars a diminutive of Israel. The name Jeshurun is mentioned in Deuteronomy 32:15 and 33:5, 26 (see NLT mg).
jesiah: 1. KJV rendering of Isshiah, one of David’s ambidextrous archers, in 1 Chronicles 12:6.
jesimiel: One of the 13 Simeonite princes who participated in the invasion of the valley of Gedor in King Hezekiah’s day, killing the inhabitants and taking the land for the pasture of their sheep.
jesse (person): Son of Obed and grandson of Ruth and Boaz. Jesse was a shepherd from Bethlehem.
jesse, root of: Figure of speech used by Isaiah to express the hope of a messianic king from the line of David. The “root” of a family is its progenitor.
jesui, jesuite: KJV forms of Ishvi and Ishvite, one of Asher’s descendants and his family, in Numbers 26:44.
jesurun: KJV spelling of Jeshurun, a poetical name for Israel, in Isaiah 44:2.
jesus: 1. Name meaning “savior” or “Jehovah [Yahweh] is salvation” given to the Messiah.
jesus christ: Messiah, Savior, and founder of the Christian church.
jesus christ, teachings of: Because of the wide variety of forms in which the teachings of Jesus have been preserved, it is difficult to bring out the essence of that teaching in a systematic way. Jesus did not present us with a theological system.
jether: 1. Firstborn son of Gideon who, because of his youth, was afraid to execute the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna at his father’s request.
jethlah: KJV form of the Danite city Ithlah in Joshua 19:42.
jethro: Father-in-law of Moses. Zipporah, Jethro’s daughter, became Moses’ wife while he was a fugitive in the wilderness.
jetur, jeturites: Son of Ishmael and his descendants; the Israelite tribes who settled east of the Jordan had to fight them. Also called Itureans, they survived into NT times, giving their name to Iturea, an area northeast of Galilee.
jeuel: 1. Descendant of Judah residing in postexilic Jerusalem.
jeush: 1. Eldest of three sons born to Esau by Oholibamah, daughter of the Canaanite Anah, and a chief among Esau’s descendants in Edom.
jeuz: From Benjamin’s tribe, Shaharaim’s son by his wife Hodesh.
jew: Judean, belonging to Judah. The short form of the English word was developed from the French.
jewelry, jewels: Decorated adornments. In the Bible, jewelry was used by both men and women.
jewish literature, extrabiblical: Series of interpretations of the meaning of the law; according to rabbinic tradition, they were given when Moses received the law from God on Mt Sinai, and they were to be passed down in oral form.
jezaniah: Alternate form of Jaazaniah, one of the Judean captains in Jerusalem during the exile (Jer 40:8 NLT mg; 42:1) See Jaazaniah #1.
jezebel: Daughter of Ethbaal, king of Sidon. She became the wife of Ahab, king of the northern kingdom of Israel.
jezer: Naphtali’s third son and the founder of the family of Jezerites.
jeziah: KJV form of Izziah, Parosh’s descendant, in Ezra 10:25.
jeziel: Warrior from Benjamin’s tribe who joined David at Ziklag in his struggle against King Saul. Jeziel was one of David’s ambidextrous archers and slingers.
jezliah: KJV form of Izliah, Elpaal’s son, in 1 Chronicles 8:18.
jezoar: KJV rendering of Izhar, Helah’s son, in 1 Chronicles 4:7.
jezrahiah: Leader of the temple singers who participated in the dedication of the rebuilt Jerusalem wall.
jezreel (person): 1. Descendant of Etam from the tribe of Judah.
jezreel (place): 1. Town originally founded by the tribe of Issachar to the south of Shunem, a site that was abandoned in the el-Amarna period by earlier settlers.
jezreel valley: Largest and richest valley in the land of Israel. It was named after Jezreel, and it was apparently the only town on the plain where the Israelites had gained a foothold in the early stages of their conquest (cf.
jezreelite: Inhabitant of one of two cities named Jezreel. Two such persons are specifically named:
jibsam: KJV form of Ibsam, Tola’s son, in 1 Chronicles 7:2.
jidlaph: Seventh son of Nahor and Milcah.
jimna, jimnah, jimnite: KJV forms of Imnah and Imnite, Asher’s son and his family, in Genesis 46:17 and Numbers 26:44.
jiphtah: KJV rendering of Iphtah, a village in Judah, in Joshua 15:43.
jiphthah-el: KJV rendering of Iphtah-el, a valley on Zebulun’s border, in Joshua 19:14, 27.
joab: 1. Son of Zeruiah, the half sister of David, who, along with his brothers Abishai and Asahel, was well known for his military valor in Judah (2 Sm 2:18; cf. 1 Sm 26:6).
joah: 1. Asaph’s son and a court official under King Hezekiah.
joahaz: 1. Variant spelling or contraction of Jehoahaz, Jehu’s son, in 2 Kings 14:1.
joanan: Ancestor of Jesus mentioned in Luke’s genealogy.
joanna: 1. KJV form of Joanan in Luke 3:27.
joarib: Ancestor of Mattathias, and according to 1 Chronicles 24:7 (there spelled Jehoiarib), head of the first of the 24 courses of priests in David’s time.
joash: 1. Abiezrite who lived at Ophrah and the father of Gideon.
joatham: KJV spelling of Jotham, king of Judah (750–735 BC), in Matthew 1:9.
job (person): 1. KJV rendering of Iob, an alternate form of Jashub, Issachar’s third son, in Genesis 46:13.
job, book of: Old Testament book belonging to the scriptural category called the Writings.
jochebed: Amram’s wife and the mother of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.
joda: Joanan’s son, the father of Josech, and a forefather of Jesus Christ living in Palestine during the postexilic era.
joed: Descendant of Benjamin living in Jerusalem during the days of Nehemiah. His name, meaning “Yahweh is witness,” does not appear in a parallel list in 1 Chronicles 9:7.
joel (person): 1. Levite from the family of Kohath.
joel, book of: Old Testament book; second of the Minor Prophets.
joelah: Warrior who joined David at Ziklag in his struggle against King Saul. Joelah was one of David’s ambidextrous archers and slingers.
joezer: Warrior who joined David at Ziklag in his struggle against King Saul. He was one of David’s ambidextrous archers and slingers.
jogbehah: City in Gilead (Transjordan) built and fortified by Gad’s tribe. During the period of the judges, Gideon, in his pursuit of the Midianites, circled to the east of Jogbehah in order to attack the unsuspecting camp of Midian at Karkor.
jogli: Father of Bukki, a Danite leader who helped oversee the distribution of the Promised Land west of the Jordan River.
joha: 1. Benjamite and one of Beriah’s nine sons.
johanan: Name meaning “Yahweh has been gracious.” It occurs also in the alternate form of Jehohanan. The name John is derived from these names.
johanan ben zakkai: Leading Jewish sage at the end of the second temple period. His place of birth is not known; he went to Jerusalem to study, and after 18 years there spent some time in Galilee.
john (person): 1. Father of Simon Peter and Andrew.
john, the apostle: The apostle known as “the disciple whom Jesus loved”; author of the fourth Gospel, three epistles, and probably Revelation.
john, gospel of: At the end of this Gospel we are told that it was written by “the disciple whom Jesus loved”, but unfortunately the book nowhere tells us who this disciple was. Evidence shows that the most probable identification is with the apostle John.
john, letters of: Three brief epistles ascribed to John. Their brevity is deceiving, for they deal with profound and critical questions about the basic nature of Christian spiritual experience.
john, the revelation of: Last book of the Bible, containing revelations concerning the events of the last days.
john hyrcanus: Hasmonean ruler of the Jewish people from 135 to 105 BC.
john mark: Cousin of Barnabas; companion to both Paul and Peter; author of the second Gospel.
john of gischala: Leader in the first Jewish revolt, from Gischala (Gush-halab) in Galilee. He was a rival of Josephus Flavius, who had been appointed commander of Galilee by the Jews.
john the baptist: Forerunner of the Messiah who prepared the people for Jesus’ coming, proclaimed the need for forgiveness of sins, and offered a baptism symbolizing repentance.
joiada: 1. Paseah’s son who, with Meshullam, repaired the Old Gate in the Jerusalem wall during the days of Nehemiah.
joiakim: Levite high priest in a family of high priests. Jeshua’s son and the father of Eliashib the high priest, a contemporary of Nehemiah.
joiarib: 1. One of the Jewish leaders whom Ezra sent to Iddo at Casiphia to gather Levites and temple servants for the caravan of Jews returning to Palestine from Babylon.
jokdeam: One of the cities located in the hill country allotted to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance, mentioned between Jezreel and Zanoah.
jokim: Descendant of Judah through Shelah’s line.
jokmeam: 1. City mentioned in 1 Kings 4:12 (KJV “Jokneam”); seemingly close in proximity and perhaps the same as Jokneam.
jokneam: Royal Canaanite city belonging to Carmel, mentioned also by Thutmose III as “the Well of Q.” The border of Zebulun touched on the stream near Jokneam (19:11); the town became a Levitical city in Zebulun (21:34).
jokshan: Son of Abraham and Keturah, and the father of Sheba and Dedan.
joktan: Eber’s son and younger brother of Peleg. A number of Arabian groups descended from him.
joktheel: 1. Town in the Shephelah of Judah near Lachish.
jona: KJV form of John, father of Simon Peter and Andrew, in John 1:42.
jonadab: 1. King David’s nephew, the son of David’s brother Shimeah.
jonah (person): Prophet of Israel; Amittai’s son of the Zebulunite city of Gath-hepher. The historian who wrote 2 Kings recorded that Jonah had a major prophetic role in the reign of King Jeroboam II (793–753 BC).
jonah, book of: Fifth book of the 12 Minor Prophets in the traditional arrangement of the books of the OT.
jonam, jonan: Ancestor of Jesus mentioned in Luke’s genealogy.
jonas: 1. KJV form of Jonah in Matthew 12:39-41 and Luke 11:29-32.
jonathan: 1. Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, a descendant of Gershom, son of Moses (cf. 1 Chr 23:14-15); he was a priest first to Micah in Ephraim and later to Dan’s tribe during the period of the judges.
jonath-elem-rechokim: Hebrew phrase in the title of Psalm 56 (KJV), translated “To be sung to the tune, ‘Dove on Distant Oaks’ ” (NLT); perhaps a familiar ancient melody to which the psalm was performed.
joppa: City about 35 miles (56.3 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem that served as Jerusalem’s seaport.
jorah: Alternate name for Hariph in Ezra 2:18 and Nehemiah 7:24.
joram: 1. Toi’s son and king of Hamath.
jordan river: River lying in the bottom of a great canyon called the Jordan Rift, an elongated depression stretching from lower southwest Asia Minor (Syria) to the Gulf of Aqaba.
jorim: Ancestor of Jesus listed in Luke’s genealogy.
jorkeam, jorkoam: Identified with Raham, a descendant of Judah through Caleb’s line (1 Chr 2:44; KJV “Jorkoam”), the name should perhaps be understood as a place-name and be identified with Jokdeam.
josabad: KJV spelling of Jozabad, a Benjamite warrior, in 1 Chronicles 12:4.
josaphat: KJV spelling of Jehoshaphat, Asa’s son, in Matthew 1:8.
jose: KJV spelling of Joshua, Eliezer’s son, in Luke 3:29.
josech: Ancestor of Jesus mentioned only in Luke’s genealogy.
josedech: KJV spelling of Jozadak, Joshua’s father, in Haggai 1:1, 12, 14; 2:2, 4; and Zechariah 6:11.
joseph: 1. Jacob’s 11th son and the firstborn son of Rachel.
joseph barsabbas: 1. Jacob’s 11th son and the firstborn son of Rachel.
joseph of arimathea: 1. Jacob’s 11th son and the firstborn son of Rachel.
joses: 1. Alternate spelling for Joseph, Mary’s son, in Mark 6:3 (NLT mg).
joshaphat: 1. Mithnite (NLT “from Mithna”) and one of David’s mighty men.
joshaviah: Elnaam’s son, the brother of Jeribai and one of David’s 30 valiant warriors.
joshbekashah: Heman’s son and head of the 17th of 24 divisions of priestly musicians for ministry in the sanctuary during David’s reign.
josheb-basshebeth: Alternate spelling of Jashobeam, commander of David’s mighty men, in 2 Samuel 23:8 (NLT mg).
joshibiah: Simeonite prince, Seraiah’s son, and the father of Jehu.
joshua (person): 1. Son of Nun, Moses’ assistant and successor, and the military leader whom God chose to lead the Israelites in the conquest of Canaan (Nm 13:16, KJV “Jehoshua”; also spelled “Jehoshuah” in 1 Chr 7:27 and “Jeshua” in Neh 8:17).
joshua, book of: First of the historical books in the English Bible and the first of the Former Prophets (including Judges, the books of Samuel, and the books of Kings) in the Hebrew Bible.
josiah: 1. Sixteenth king of the southern kingdom of Judah (640–609 BC).
josias: KJV spelling of Josiah, Jehoiachin’s father, in Matthew 1:10-11.
josibiah: KJV spelling of Joshibiah, Jehu’s father, in 1 Chronicles 4:35.
josiphiah: Father of Shelomith, leader of a family of which 160 members accompanied Ezra back to Palestine.
jotbah: Hometown of Haruz, the father of Meshullemeth, who was the mother of King Amon of Judah.
jotbathah: Temporary camping place of the Israelites during their wilderness wanderings, located between Hor-haggidgad and Abronah. Later, following the death of Aaron, Israel journeyed from Gudgodah to this place, noted for its streams of water.
jotham: 1. Youngest of Gideon’s 70 sons and the only survivor of Abimelech’s slaughter of Jotham’s brothers at Ophrah.
jot or tittle: An expression Jesus used in the Sermon on the Mount. In Matthew 5:18 jot is a transliteration of the Greek letter iota.
joy: Positive human condition that can be either feeling or action. The Bible uses “joy” in both senses.
jozabad: 1. Benjamite from Gederah and one of the military men who came to David’s support at Ziklag.
jozacar, jozachar: Son of Shimeath the Ammonitess and one of the royal servants who conspired against the murdered King Joash of Judah. He is alternately called Zabad in 2 Chronicles 24:26.
jozadak: Seraiah’s son and one of the exiles transported by Nebuchadnezzar to Babylonia. He was the father of Jeshua (also called Joshua), the high priest in postexilic Jerusalem during the days of Zerubbabel.
jubal: Son of Adah, wife of Lamech, a descendant of Cain. He is crredited with being the first musician, the inventor of the harp and flute.
jubilee year: Year of emancipation and restoration to be kept every 50 years. For Israel, the seventh year expressed at length the values of the seventh day Sabbath.
jucal: Alternate name for Jehucal, Shelemiah’s son, in Jeremiah 38:1 (NLT mg).
juda (person): 1. Alternate KJV spelling of Judas, Jesus’ brother, in Mark 6:3.
juda (place): Alternate KJV spelling for Judah’s territory (or “Judea”) in Luke 1:39.
judaea: “Land of the Jews,” particularly after the Captivity. Since most of the Israelites who returned from the exile were from the tribe of Judah, they were called Judeans or Jews and their land, Judea.
judah (person): 1. Fourth of Jacob’s 12 sons and the fourth son born to Jacob by Leah, who, overjoyed with the thought of bearing Jacob another son, named him Judah, meaning “praise”.
judah, tribe of: One of the 12 tribes of Israel.
judaism: Religion and culture of the Jewish people from the beginning of the postexilic period (538 BC) to modern times. The term “Judaism” is derived from “Judah,” the name of the southern kingdom of ancient Israel, while “Jew” is a shortened form of “Judeans.”
judaizers: Christian Jews who, during the apostolic and early postapostolic periods, attempted to impose the Jewish way of life on gentile Christians.
judas: 1. Simon’s son, surnamed Iscariot; one of the 12 disciples of Jesus.
judas barsabbas: 1. Simon’s son, surnamed Iscariot; one of the 12 disciples of Jesus.
judas iscariot: 1. Simon’s son, surnamed Iscariot; one of the 12 disciples of Jesus.
judas maccabeus: Third son of Mattathias; leader of the Jewish insurrection against Rome in 166 BC. His surname, Maccabeus (perhaps from an Aramaic word meaning “the Hammerer”), was later applied to all of the Hasmonean family.
judas of galilee: 1. Simon’s son, surnamed Iscariot; one of the 12 disciples of Jesus.
jude (person): Brother of James and author of the general epistle named Jude. Jude is the English form of the Greek name Judas (Hebrew Judah).
jude, letter of: Short, hard-hitting letter to a church being infiltrated by teachers who practiced all types of moral evil. Jude reveals the inner situation of a Jewish-Christian community and also presents some great difficulties for the Christian interpreter.
judea, judeans: “Land of the Jews,” particularly after the Captivity. Since most of the Israelites who returned from the exile were from the tribe of Judah, they were called Judeans or Jews and their land, Judea.
judge: An official authorized to decide matters brought before a court. The judge undertook a variety of tasks, mostly in legal and judicial areas, but at times in political areas.
judges, book of: Old Testament book named after the prominent leaders raised up by the Lord to deliver his people. The word “judge” in Hebrew also denotes the activity of governance, including warfare.
judges, period of: Old Testament book named after the prominent leaders raised up by the Lord to deliver his people. The word “judge” in Hebrew also denotes the activity of governance, including warfare.
judgment: Concept in Scripture closely related to the concept of God’s justice. In all his relationships God acts justly and morally.
judgment, hall of: KJV translation in Jn 18:28, 33; 19:9; Acts 23:35 of a NT word also translated “Praetorium” and “common hall”.
judgment seat: Place before which people will one day stand to give an account of their lives to God.
judith (person): 1. Daughter of Beeri the Hittite and one of Esau’s wives.
judith, book of: A deuterocanonical book, named from its leading character.
julia: 1. Woman greeted by the apostle Paul.
julius: Roman centurion of the Augustan cohort who escorted the apostle Paul and other prisoners from Palestine to Rome. Jewish leaders in Jerusalem accused Paul of teaching false doctrine and defiling the temple.
junia: A Jew who, along with Andronicus, was greeted by Paul in his letter to the church in Rome—according to the reading of some manuscripts. Paul recognized Junia as an apostle who had been a prisoner with Paul for the sake of the gospel.
juniper: KJV mistranslation for “broom,” a desert shrub.
jupiter: Supreme Roman deity, equivalent to Zeus in Greek mythology. He was Saturn’s son and Juno’s husband and brother.
jushab-hesed: One of Zerubbabel’s seven sons. Jushab-hesed means “lovingkindness is returned.”
just: The establishment of a right relationship—primarily between God and people, secondarily between people themselves. Righteousness is the fulfillment of just expectations in any relationship, whether with God or other people.
justification, justified: The act of God in bringing sinners into a new covenant relationship with himself through the forgiveness of sins. It is a declarative act of God by which he establishes persons as righteous—that is, in right and true relationship to himself.
juttah: One of the cities of refuge assigned to Aaron’s descendants. It was in the hill country of Judah’s territory and in the district of Maon (15:55).
kab: According to Josephus, a dry measure equaling about a quart. Other authorities think the kab was larger (see 2 Kgs 6:25, NASB mg).
kabzeel: City located in the extreme south of Judah’s territory adjacent to neighboring Edom (Jos 15:21; also called Jekabzeel in Neh 11:25). Benaiah, one of David’s valiant warriors, came from there.
kadesh, kadesh-barnea: Home of the wandering Israelites for nearly 38 years. In the vast area of the Sinai there are two main oases: in the south is Wadi Feiran, near the mountain of Moses (Mt Sinai or Horeb); in the north is Kadesh, or Kadesh-barnea.
kadmiel: Head of a Levite family who returned from the exile with Zerubbabel. His name appears in the list of those who supervised the temple rebuilding project, participated in sealing the covenant, and were prominent in the praise service (9:4-5; 12:24).
kadmonites: Semitic tribe whose land was promised to Abraham’s descendants. The name of the tribe is the same as the Hebrew adjective “eastern” and suggests that references to peoples or lands of the east may be synonymous with the tribal name.
kain (place): Town in the Judean hill country. Its place in the same district as the known cities of Maon, Carmel, Ziph, and Juttah (v 55) favors its identification with Khirbet Yuqim, southwest of Hebron.
kain (tribe): Clan name synonymous with the Kenites. The name is Hebrew for “spear,” suggesting a tribe of metalworkers.
kaiwan: Mesopotamian astral deity, called “Chiun” in the KJV and “Kiyyun” in the NASB.
kallai: Priest and the head of Sallu’s (Sallai’s) priestly family during the days of Joiakim the high priest.
kamon: City in Gilead where Jair the judge was buried. While the place has not been identified with certainty, modern Kameim, a small village southeast of the Sea of Galilee, probably reflects the original name, if not the exact location.
kanah: 1. Brook forming Ephraim’s northern border and the southern border of Manasseh’s tribe.
kanatha: One of the original 10 Greek cities rebuilt by Rome after Pompey’s conquest of Palestine and Syria around 63 BC. The region of these cities became known as the Decapolis.
kareah: Father of Jonathan and Johanan. After Jerusalem fell to Nebuchadnezzar’s army, his sons joined Gedaliah at Mizpah.
karka: Unidentified town marking a part of Judah’s southern boundary. It was located in the southwest section of Palestine between Kadesh-barnea and Wadi el-Arish (Besor Brook).
karkor: City in the Transjordan where Gideon attacked the armies of the two Midianite kings, Zebah and Zalmunna. Indications of its location are sketchy.
karnaim: Town situated along the King’s Highway and along one of the northeastern tributaries of the Yarmuk River, 22 miles (35.4 kilometers) east of the Sea of Galilee on the Transjordan Plateau.
kartah: Levitical city in Zebulun’s territory. The list of cities assigned to the Merarite clan of Levites in Joshua 21:34 mentions Kartah, but the parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 6:77 (in the Hebrew) does not.
kartan: Levitical town assigned to the Gershonites from the tribe of Naphtali. It is called Kiriathaim in 1 Chronicles 6:76.
kattath: Town assigned to Zebulun, perhaps the same as the Kitron of Judges 1:30.
kebar: Canal in Babylonia. The prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles from the southern kingdom of Judah, received visions from God while living in the area of the Kebar Canal.
kedar: 1. Second son of Ishmael, Abraham’s son.
kedemah: Son of Ishmael who gave his name to the tribe he fathered.
kedemoth: City east of the Jordan, probably located on the upper course of the Arnon River. From the wilderness of Kedemoth, Moses sent messengers to Sihon, king of Heshbon, asking permission to pass peaceably through his land.
kedesh: 1. Town in the Judean Negev; its appearance alongside Adadah (Aroer) argues against its identification with Kadesh-barnea.
kedorlaomer: King of Elam who participated with three other kings in a campaign against five cities near the southern end of the Dead Sea plain. Although Kedorlaomer is initially third in the list (v 1), he was evidently the leader of the four kings.
kehelathah: One of the places where the Israelites encamped on their journey from Egypt to Mt Sinai, located somewhere between Rissah and Mt Shepher.
keilah (person): Caleb’s descendant from Judah’s tribe, called the Garmite in 1 Chronicles 4:19. Some identify this reference with the city in Judah instead of a person.
keilah (place): City assigned to Judah’s tribe, located in the southeast Shephelah near the Philistine border. It is identified with modern Khirbet Qila, eight and a half miles (13.7 kilometers) northwest of Hebron.
kelaiah: A Levite who was guilty of marrying a pagan wife. According to verse 23 Kelaiah is also called Kelita.
kelal: Pahath-moab’s son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile. Also spelled Kelal.
kelita: A Levite sometimes thought to be the same as Kelaiah.
kelub: 1. Shuhah’s brother and the father of Mehir from Judah’s tribe.
kelubai: Hezron’s son and the brother of Jerahmeel; alternately called Caleb in 1 Chronicles 2:18, 42.
keluhi: One of Bani’s sons, who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife after the exile.
kemuel: 1. Third son of Nahor (Abraham’s brother) and the father of Aram.
kenaanah: 1. Father of Zedekiah, the false prophet who incorrectly prophesied victory for kings Ahab and Jehoshaphat over the Syrians.
kenan: Fourth-generation descendant of Adam; alternately called Cainan in Luke’s genealogy of Christ (Lk 3:37, RSV).
kenani: Levite who participated in Ezra’s public reading of the law after the exile.
kenaniah: 1. Levite chief who led processional singing when King David brought the ark of the covenant to the new tabernacle in Jerusalem.
kenath: Town in the Hauran taken by Nobah but later lost to Geshur and Aram. It was a Canaanite city known from Egyptian execration texts of the 19th and 18th centuries BC and from the conquest by Thutmose III and the Amarna letters.
kenaz: Singular form of the name of the Kenizzite tribe, whose land was promised to Abraham’s descendants.
kenezite: KJV spelling of Kenizzite in Numbers 32:12 and Joshua 14:6, 14.
kenites: One of 10 tribes living in Canaan during Abraham’s time. The Kenites, however, are not included in the parallel statement from Moses’ day.
kenizzites: A people related to Kenaz, grandson of Esau. The Kenizzites were of Edomite stock and resided to the southeast of Judah in the vicinity of the Kenites.
kephar-ammoni: City allotted to Benjamin’s tribe for an inheritance after the initial conquest of Canaan by Joshua.
kephirah: Hivite city included in a treaty with Joshua that the Gibeonites secured by deception. When the Israelites conquered the land of Canaan, Kephirah became the property of Benjamin’s tribe (18:26).
keran: Dishon’s son, a member of the Horite tribe during Esau’s time.
keren-happuch: Job’s third daughter and the sister of Jemimah and Keziah. She was listed as a member of Job’s family at the time of his restoration.
kerethites: Members of a tribal group that lived in southern Judah near Hebron, mentioned along with the Pelethites. The Kerethites were associated with the Philistines, according to Ezekiel 25:15-17 (cf.
kerioth: 1. Town in the Negev of Judah, called Kerioth-hezron.
kerith, the brook: Also rendered the “Kerith Ravine” (NIV), it was the place where the Lord told the prophet Elijah to hide from King Ahab during a famine Elijah had predicted. There he had sufficient water to drink and was fed by ravens each morning and evening.
keros: One of the temple servants whose descendants returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel.
kerub: One of five Babylonian cities from which Israelites who could not trace their ancestry returned after the exile.
kerygma: Basic evangelistic message proclaimed by the earliest Christians.
kesalon: City in northern Judah near the border of Dan, situated on the northern slope of Mt Jearim; usually identified with modern Kesla, about nine miles (14.5 kilometers) west of Jerusalem.
kesed: Son of Milcah and Nahor, Abraham’s brother.
kesil: City situated along the borders of Edom in the Negev, allotted to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance. In parallel lists of towns Kesil is replaced by Bethul, Bethuel, and perhaps Bethel—not to be confused with the Bethel north of Jerusalem.
kesulloth: Town in Issachar; also called Kisloth-tabor in Joshua 19:12. It is probably to be identified with the modern Iksal, about three miles (4.8 kilometers) southeast of Nazareth.
keturah: Second wife of Abraham. It is unclear whether he married her before or after Sarah’s death.
keys of the kingdom: Symbolic description of the authority given by Jesus to Peter in Matthew 16:19: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (RSV).
keziah: Job’s second daughter, born after his restoration.
kezib: Alternate name for Aczib, a city in Judah’s territory, in Genesis 38:5.
keziz, valley of: KJV rendering of Emek-keziz, a city allotted to Benjamin’s tribe for an inheritance, in Joshua 18:21.
kibroth-hattaavah: Location in the wilderness where the Israelites who were killed by plague for craving meat from Egypt were buried. It was situated between Mt Sinai and Hazeroth, but its exact site is unknown.
kibzaim: One of several cities in Ephraim given to the Levitical family of Kohath after the conquest of Canaan. It is probably the same as the Jokmeam of 1 Chronicles 6:68.
kidney: One of the body parts of sacrificial animals used for offerings to God. The kidneys, along with their fat, were to be burned on the altar and represented the blood that the Israelites were not permitted to eat.
kidon: Threshing floor where Uzzah was struck down by God as he attempted to steady the ark of the covenant (1 Chr 13:9, NLT mg).
kidron: Valley and streambed running below the southeast wall of Jerusalem and separating the city from the Mt of Olives on the east. It then turns southeast from Jerusalem and follows a winding course to the Dead Sea.
kileab: David’s second son, and the first born to him by Abigail; alternately called Daniel in 1 Chronicles 3:1.
kilion: One of the two sons of Elimelech and Naomi. He married a Moabite girl named Orpah (v 4) and eventually died in Moab (v 5).
killing: Civil law deals with private disputes between individuals occasioned by debt, divorce, inheritance, or other relationships. In contrast, criminal law deals with crimes such as murder, treason, or theft.
kilmad: Mesopotamian city listed with Haran, Canneh, Eden, and Asshur as traders with Tyre.
kiln: Large furnace used in firing pottery.
kimham: Son of Barzillai (according to Josephus), a very wealthy man who supplied David and his men with food while they were in Mahanaim during their flight from Absalom.
kinah: Town in the Negev of Judah, perhaps named after the Kenites who lived in the area. According to a letter discovered at Arad, troops were sent from Kinah to reinforce Ramoth-negev against an Edomite attack.
kindness: State of being that includes the attributes of loving affection, sympathy, friendliness, patience, pleasantness, gentleness, and goodness. Kindness is a quality shown in the way a person speaks and acts.
king: The word melek (king) occurs more than 2,000 times in the Hebrew OT. It may refer to God or to human rulers.
kingdom of god, kingdom of heaven: Kingdom of God, Kingdom of Heaven
The sovereign rule of God, initiated by Christ’s earthly ministry and consummated when the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ.
kings, books of first and second: Kings, Books of First and Second
Books continuing the history of the covenant people as recorded in Joshua, Judges, and the books of Samuel. The record in Kings begins with the events at the end of David’s reign.
king's dale: KJV name for the King’s Valley near Salem, the city of Melchizedek, in Genesis 14:17.
king's garden: Probably an area of the royal estates, situated outside the walls of Jerusalem near the pool of Siloam in the Kidron Valley, near where the Kidron meets the valley of Hinnom.
king's highway: The road running north-south across the Transjordanian plateau. It appears in the OT only twice in requests by the Israelites to use this road when passing through Edom and the Amorite kingdom of Heshbon (21:22).
king's pool: Reservoir in the king’s garden in Jerusalem, also called the pool of Siloam (3:15).
king's valley: Valley near Salem, the city of Melchizedek, where Abraham encountered the king of Sodom and rejected his offer of a morally compromised truce; also called the valley of Shaveh.
kinnereth: 1. Fortified town in the territory allotted to Naphtali’s tribe.
kinsman: A relative of the same family. In ancient Israel the tribe was the largest social and political unit.
kios: Rocky, mountainous island in the east-central area of the Aegean Sea. On his third missionary journey, Paul’s ship anchored opposite Kios between stops at Mitylene and Samos en route to Jerusalem.
kir: 1. Mesopotamian city from which the Syrians migrated to Damascus and back to which they were later exiled by the Assyrians.
kir-hareseth: Fortified city often identified with the ancient capital of Moab.
kiriathaim: 1. Town on the Moabite plateau, mentioned in the march of the four kings against the five where the indigenous Emim were attacked.
kiriath-arba: Ancient name of Hebron, near which is the cave of Machpelah, the burial place of the patriarchs.
kiriath-arim: Alternate name for Kiriath-jearim in Ezra 2:25 (NLT mg).
kiriath-baal: Alternate name for Kiriath-jearim in Joshua 15:60 and 18:14.
kiriath-huzoth: Town in Moab to which Balak and Balaam went before going to Bamoth-baal.
kiriath-jearim: Village on the road from Jerusalem to Tel Aviv, about 10 miles (16 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem. Excavations by the French revealed a settlement 7,000 years old in which the residents changed from grazing to farming.
kiriath-sannah: Alternate name for Debir, a Judean city, in Joshua 15:49.
kiriath-sepher: Older name for the Judean city Debir in Joshua 15:15.
kirioth: KJV alternate spelling of Kerioth, the Moabite city, in Amos 2:2.
kirjath: KJV spelling of Kiriath, an abbreviation of Kiriath-jearim, in Joshua 18:28.
kirjath-arba: KJV form of Kiriath-arba, the ancient name of Hebron.
kirjath-arim: KJV form of Kiriatharim, an alternate name for Kiriath-jearim, in Ezra 2:25.
kirjath-baal: KJV spelling of Kiriath-baal, an alternate name for Kiriath-jearim, in Joshua 15:60 and 18:14.
kirjath-huzoth: KJV spelling of Kiriath-huzoth, a Moabite town, in Numbers 22:39.
kirjath-sannah: KJV spelling of Kiriath-sannah, in Joshua 15:49.
kirjath-sepher: KJV spelling of Kiriath-sepher in Joshua 15:15-16 and Judges 1:11-12.
kish: 1. Benjamite of Gibeah, father of King Saul and a man of some position in the community.
kishi: Levite of Merari’s family whose son Ethan was a singer and musician in the sanctuary during David’s reign. He is also known as Kushaiah in 15:17.
kishion: City allotted to Issachar’s tribe and given to the Gershonite Levites.
kishon: 1. KJV variant of Kishion in Joshua 21:28.
kislev: Month in the Hebrew calendar, about mid-November to mid-December; also spelled Chislev or Chisleu.
kislon: Father of Elidad, leader of Benjamin’s tribe during the Israelites’ wilderness wanderings and one of those appointed by Moses to divide the land of Canaan among the tribes.
kison: KJV spelling of the river Kishon in Psalm 83:9.
kiss, kiss of peace: Common salutation symbolizing love and fellowship. In the Bible, kissing is referred to in a wide variety of contexts.
kitchen: Substances required by the body to sustain life, and the methods of making them edible. Food consumed in Bible times included bread, milk products, fruit, meat, and fish.
kite: Bird of prey declared unclean by the law.
kithlish, kitlish: City assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance.
kitron: City allotted to the tribe of Zebulun from which the Canaanite inhabitants could not be driven out. It has been identified with Kattath, Tell el-Far, and Tell Qurdaneh.
kittim: Ancient Hebrew name for the island of Cyprus.
kneeling: Position often denoting worship, respect, or submission. A strong knee symbolically implied a man with strength of faith and purpose, and thus bowing the knee indicated submission to a superior.
knife: Small, handheld, single- or double-edged cutting instrument, usually made of flint or metal.
knowledge: Observation and recognition of objects within the range of one’s senses; acquaintance of a personal nature that includes a response of the knower.
koa: People probably living northeast of Babylonia. They are named along with Babylon, Pekod, and Shoa as people who would come against Jerusalem as instruments of God’s judgment on Israel.
kohath, kohathites: Son of Levi, father of Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, and progenitor of the Kohathite branch of Levitical families who were responsible for the tabernacle service. Moses, Aaron, and Miriam were descendants of Kohath.
koheleth: Hebrew title for the book of Ecclesiastes, translated “the Preacher” or “the Teacher”; also spelled “Koheleth.” Derived from a word meaning “to call an assembly,” it came to mean “to address an assembly.” The author of the book calls himself Qoheleth in numerous passages.
koine greek: Type of Greek that was “common” (koine) to the Near Eastern and Mediterranean lands in Roman times. It is the Greek in which the NT was written.
kola: Kola is mentioned in the book of Judith as a place-name. It may be identified with Holon.
kolaiah: 1. Benjamite; forefather of a family who lived in Jerusalem after the exile.
kona: Town referred to in the apocryphal book of Judith.
kor: Dry commodity measure equivalent to one homer (about 3.8 to 7.5 bushels).
korah: 1. Third son of Esau by Oholibamah, daughter of Anah.
korahite, korathite: Member of Levi’s tribe, of the division of Kohath. Their ancestor, Izhar, was a member of the priestly family and was related to Moses and Aaron.
korazin: Palestinian city on which Jesus pronounced woe. It was in Korazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum that “most of his miracles” had been done, but the people were generally unresponsive and had not repented.
kore: 1. Kohathite Levite who, with his brothers, was responsible for the service at the entrance to the tent of meeting in David’s time.
korhite: KJV alternate spelling of Korahite, a descendant of Korah, Hebron’s son, in 1 Chronicles 12:6.
koz: 1. Descendant of Judah and possibly an ancestor of the priestly house of Hakkoz.
kub: A place in Ezekiel 30:5 identified as Libya (NLT mg).
kue: Name of Cilicia in OT times. From there Solomon imported horses (1 Kgs 10:28; 2 Chr 1:16, NLT mg).
kushaiah: Alternate name for Kishi, a Merarite Levite, in 1 Chronicles 15:17.
laadah: Shelah’s son and the father of Mareshah from Judah’s tribe.
laadan: 1. KJV spelling of Ladan, Joshua’s ancestor, in 1 Chronicles 7:26.
laban (person): Bethuel’s son, brother of Rebekah (vv 15, 29), father of Leah and Rachel (29:16), and the uncle and father-in-law of Jacob.
laban (place): Israelite camping place in Sinai. Some equate it with the Libnah of Numbers 33:20-21.
lachish: Place first mentioned in the Bible in connection with Joshua and the Israelite conquest of Palestine. At that time, its king and army were among the coalition of southern Palestinian towns that faced Joshua at Gibeon.
lachish letters: Collection of letters, sometimes described as “a supplement to Jeremiah,” which was J. L.
ladan: 1. Member of Ephraim’s tribe who was Joshua’s ancestor.
lael: Levite of the family of Gershon and father of Eliasaph.
lahai-roi: KJV form of Beer-lahairoi, the name of a well mentioned in Genesis 24:62 and 25:11.
lahmam: Judahite town in the Shephelah district of Lachish, usually identified with modern Khirbet el-Lahm; alternately spelled Lahmas in some versions (NIV, NASB).
lahmi: Brother of Goliath the Gittite. According to 1 Chronicles 20:5, he was killed by Elhanan.
laish (person): Father of Paltiel (Palti), to whom Saul gave his daughter Michal, who was formerly David’s wife.
laish (place): 1. Early name for the city of Dan.
laishah: Town in Benjamin mentioned between Gallim and Anathoth. Its site is possibly Khirbet el-’Isawiyeh.
lake of fire: Final abode of Satan, his servants, and unrepentant human beings.
lakkum, lakum: Fortified border town within the territory of Naphtali. Its site is identifiable with Khirbet el-Mansurah, about three miles (4.8 kilometers) southwest of Khirbet Kerak, at the head of Wadi Fejjas.
lamb: Domestic animal, Ovis orientalis, referred to directly or by some term such as ewe, lamb, ram, or by some fact concerning them over 700 times in Scripture.
lamb of god: General term used twice by John the Baptist, adding on the first instance “who takes away the world’s sin!” He does not explain what the term means. Christians use the term freely, but what do they mean by it?
lamech: 1. Methushael’s son, a descendant of Cain, and the husband of Adah and Zillah.
lament, lamentation: Established ritual for grieving, observed by a dead person’s relatives and friends. It began with the closing of the eyes of the dead, the embracing of the body (50:1), and its preparation for burial.
lamentations, book of: Book consisting of five poems that constitute a formal dirge lamenting the fall of Jerusalem.
lamp, lampstand: Israelite lamps developed from those in general use among the Canaanites in the second millennium BC. Their shape was similar to a shell or saucer with a lip.
land: The relationship of humans to the land is a prominent theme in the OT. In Genesis the earth with its dry land was created as a place for humans to dwell in fellowship with God.
landmark: Inscribed stone that denoted a boundary of fields, districts, or nations. In most Near Eastern countries the removal of a landmark was a serious crime; in Israel it was a violation of the law of Moses.
laodicea, laodiceans: Largest of three cities and its residents in the broad valley area on the borders of Phrygia, Laodicea stood where the Lycus Valley joined the Meander. Significantly, the western entrance to the city was called the Ephesian Gate.
lapis lazuli: Semiprecious stone (silicate) known for its rich blue color.
lapwing: KJV translation for hoopoe, an unclean bird according to the Law, in Leviticus 11:19 and Deuteronomy 14:18.
lasciviousness: Extreme indulgence in sensual pleasures. Modern Bible translations commonly use the words “licentiousness,” “debauchery,” or “sensuality” instead.
lasea: Seaport city on the island of Crete, about five miles (8 kilometers) east of Fair Havens. Paul’s ship passed Lasea on its way to Italy.
lasha: Place-name, otherwise unknown, used in an ancient description of the southern boundary of the territory occupied by the Canaanites. In this passage Lasha is associated with other cities usually located near the southern end of the Dead Sea.
lasharon: Town in Canaan conquered by Joshua. Another early manuscript reads “the king of Aphek in Sharon,” perhaps indicating that Lasharon was not the name of a town but part of a phrase distinguishing this city from the other Apheks mentioned in the Bible.
last days: Expression used in Scripture to describe the final period of the world as we now know it.
last judgment: Time at the end of history when God will judge the deeds of all humankind.
last supper: The supper Jesus shared with his disciples a few hours before he was arrested and taken to his trial and death (thus often called “The Last Supper”); the ceremony of partaking of the bread and wine that Christians have come to call the Lord’s Supper, the…
last times: Expression used in Scripture to describe the final period of the world as we now know it.
latin: One of the primary languages of the Greco-Roman world. The supremacy of Rome, and the ramifications of its official relations with the people under its control, made the widespread use of Latin, Rome’s vernacular, inevitable.
latter days: Expression used in Scripture to describe the final period of the world as we now know it.
latter rain: Annual spring rainfall in Palestine from late March to early April, following the citrus harvest and preceding the wheat and barley harvests. The spring rains normally conclude the rainy season until the resumption of the fall (early) rains in October.
laughter: Expression of a variey of emotions. Laughter can express overjoyed happiness when circumstances change for the better, as for the Jews in returning from exile.
laver: Basin filled with water that the priests used to wash their hands and feet before entering the Holy Place and before returning to serve at the altar.
law, biblical concept of: God’s means of consecrating his people to himself. The nature and content of “law” may change, but the goal remains the same: maturity and conformity to the image of God.
lawless one: Name Paul used for the Antichrist.
lawyer: Term used primarily by Luke in his Gospel in reference to those learned in the law of Moses.
laying on of hands: The terminal part of the forelimb that has the ability to grasp. “Hand” is used hundreds of times in the Bible to describe a physical part of one’s body.
leah: Laban’s daughter, the wife of Jacob, and the older sister of Rachel.
leather: Prepared animal hide, used extensively in Bible times for a wide variety of purposes. It was used as clothing in early times.
leaven: Any substance that produces fermentation when added to dough.
lebana, lebanah: Head of a family who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel following the exile.
lebanon: Region mentioned only in the OT, although its towns, including Tyre and Sidon, are named in the NT. The name Lebanon generally refers to the double range of mountains that commences near Tyre and runs northeast following the Mediterranean coast.
lebaoth: Town in the Negev of Judah occupied by the tribe of Simeon under the name Beth-lebaoth (19:6). The parallel list of Simeonite towns has Beth-biri in this place.
lebbaeus: Alternate name given to Thaddaeus, one of the 12 disciples, in Matthew 10:3 (KJV only). Most versions omit the name, which comes from a textual variant followed by the KJV translators.
lebo-hamath: Town on the Orontes River below Riblah; perhaps the correct reading for the phrase “entrance of Hamath” in numerous OT passages.
lebonah: Town located between Shiloh and Shechem. It is usually identified with modern Lubban, about three miles (4.8 kilometers) northwest of Shiloh.
lecah: Either a person, descendant of the Judahite Er, or an otherwise unknown place in Judah settled by Er, depending on one’s understanding of “father”.
leech: Blood-sucking, segmented worm, mentioned only in Proverbs 30:15.
lees: Thick substance, or dregs, that forms at the bottom of a wine container as fermentation takes place.
legion: A unit of the Roman army. In NT times the standard size of the legion was 6,000 men, to which some 120 cavalry were added.
lehabim, lehabites: One of several peoples associated with Egypt. The Lehabim are either an unidentified people near Egypt or—as many scholars hold, probably correctly—identical with the Lubim (Libyans).
lehi: Place in Judah where the Philistines assembled to capture Samson.
lemuel: King credited with writing Proverbs 31:1-9. In these verses he sets forth teachings given him by his mother on good government, sexual relations, and wine.
lentils: Pealike vegetable; specifically, the seeds of the lentil plant.
leopard: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
leper, leprosy: One afflicted with a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae, a bacterium similar to the tuberculosis bacillus. The disease is manifested by changes in the skin, mucous membranes, and peripheral nerves.
leshem: Alternate name for Laish, the early name for the city of Dan, in Joshua 19:47 (NLT mg).
lethech: Dry measure equaling about two to three measures.
letter of jeremiah: The Letter of Jeremiah is a book accepted as part of the Deuterocanonical works. It was originally written in Hebrew or Aramaic by an unknown Jewish author.
letter writing, ancient: A communication, especially from a king or high official, usually containing commands, promulgations, or reports.
letushim, letushites: Tribe founded by the second of Dedan’s three sons, a descendant of Abraham and Keturah through Jokshan’s line. Some suggest that the tribe eventually settled in northern Arabia.
leummim, leummites: Tribe founded by the third of Dedan’s three sons, a descendant of Abraham and Keturah through Jokshan’s line. The tribe probably settled in northern Arabia.
levi, tribe of: Israelite tribe taking its name from the third son of Leah and Jacob. The meaning of the name (“attached”) is a pun on Leah’s position as an unloved wife: now that she has borne three sons to Jacob, surely he will be “attached” to her.
leviathan: Great sea monster or large aquatic reptile.
levirate marriage: Israelite custom in which a man, upon the death of his brother, marries his brother’s widow and raises up children for his brother.
levitical cities: Special areas set aside for the tribe of Levi in place of a regular territorial inheritance. The Levites were allotted 48 cities, including the six cities of refuge.
leviticus, book of: Third book of the OT, largely concerned with the duties of the Levitical priests.
libation: Ritual of pouring a liquid such as oil or wine upon the ground as a sacrifice.
libertines: Freedmen of Jewish extraction. The only reference to Libertines in the NT is Acts 6:9 (KJV).
liberty: Quality or state of being free. In the ancient world slavery was universal.
libnah: 1. One of the stations at which the Israelites encamped during the wilderness journey.
libni: 1. Gershon’s son, the grandson of Levi, and Shimei’s brother.
libnite: Descendant of Libni, Gershon’s son, from Levi’s tribe.
libya, libyans: Country and its inhabitants to the west of Egypt.
lice: KJV translation for some sort of small insects, probably gnats; the third plague in Egypt.
licentiousness: Extreme indulgence in sensual pleasures. Modern Bible translations commonly use the words “licentiousness,” “debauchery,” or “sensuality” instead.
life: In biblical perspective, life flows from the living Father through the Son (his agent in creation and redemption) into a world thirsting for “real” life (see Jn 6:57).
life, book of: Term used to refer to a heavenly record. The phrase appears seven times in the NT: Philippians 4:3; Revelation 3:5; 13:8; 17:8; 20:12, 15; 21:27.
life everlasting: Mode of existence referred to in Scripture characterized by either timelessness or immortality; kind of life attributed to God and distributed to believers.
lightning: The flashing of light. When the Bible speaks of lightning, it usually has to do with God making an appearance.
lign aloes: KJV translation for aloes in Numbers 24:6.
ligure: KJV translation for jacinth in Exodus 28:19 and 39:12.
lilith: Hebrew for the night creature referred to in Isaiah 34:14. According to Hebrew mythology, Lilith was Adam’s first wife, who was replaced by Eve; subsequently, Lilith became a female demon.
lily: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
lily-work: Design of a lily or lotus used on ancient pillars, inspired by the large water lily found along the Nile.
lime: White substance (calcium oxide) obtained by applying heat to materials containing calcium carbonate, such as limestone or shells.
lintel: Horizontal beam placed above a doorway, supported by structures called “jambs” or simply “doorposts.”
linus: Christian at Rome who joined Paul in sending salutations to Timothy. According to Irenaeus and Eusebius, the apostles Peter and Paul made a man named Linus bishop of Rome.
lion: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
lion of the tribe of judah: Lion of the Tribe of Judah

A title of the Messiah that appears only in Revelation 5:5: “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the heir to David’s throne, has conquered” (NLT). This is an allusion to the messianic promise of Genesis 49:9-10, “Judah is a young lion. . . .
litter: Large couch used for carrying dignitaries; it is also translated as “carriage” or “palanquin.” See Travel.
liver: Large abdominal organ that performs many functions necessary for life. The writer of Proverbs understood the critical nature of the liver when he noted that an arrow injury to the liver (NLT “heart”) was fatal.
lizard: Small reptile with scaly skin, four legs, and a long tail.
lo-ammi: Symbolic name, meaning “Not My People”, given by the prophet Hosea to his son.
locusts: Various insects known especially for their swarming, mass migration, and tremendous destruction of vegetation.
lod: City on the coastal plain of Palestine. The modern city, called Ludd, is located 10 miles (16.1 kilometers) southeast of Tel Aviv.
lo-debar: Alternate name for Debir, the Gadite city, in 2 Samuel 9:4 and Amos 6:13.
log: Liquid measure mentioned only in Leviticus 14. The log was equal to one-twelfth of a bath or one-half pint (236.6 milliliters).
logia: Term used for many of Jesus’ sayings as collected and later employed by the Gospel writers.
logos: English transliteration of a Greek term for “word.” The term is significant because in John’s writings it refers to Jesus.
loins: Region of the body from the chest to the lower part of the hip; an expression in the KJV (“out of his loins”) for that part of the body that involved procreation.
lois: Maternal grandmother of Timothy, whose family, including Timothy’s mother, Eunice, lived at Lystra. Lois was a deeply committed Jew who probably converted to Christianity during Paul’s first missionary trip (ch 14).
longsuffering: Word denoting long and patient endurance. This is a word used in the KJV four times in the OT and 13 times in the NT.
lord: “Lord” in English is the rendering of the Hebrew ‘adonai or of the Greek kurios. The Hebrew YHWH is usually rendered “LORD”; See Yahweh (YHWH).
lord of hosts: Old Testament name for God found mostly in the prophets. The hosts are the heavenly powers and angels that act at the Lord’s command.
lord's day, the: Expression occurring once in the NT, where John says, “On the Lord’s Day I was in the Spirit” (NIV); synonym for “Sunday” in modern usage.
lord's prayer, the: Pattern for prayer Jesus gave his followers to use. There are two versions of the Lord’s Prayer.
lord's supper, the: The supper Jesus shared with his disciples a few hours before he was arrested and taken to his trial and death (thus often called “The Last Supper”); the ceremony of partaking of the bread and wine that Christians have come to call the Lord’s Supper, the…
lo-ruhamah: Symbolic name, meaning “Not pitied”, given by the prophet Hosea to his daughter, indicating God’s rejection of Israel.
lot: Abraham’s nephew; progenitor of both the Moabites and the Ammonites. Like Abraham, he was born in Ur.
lotan: Seir’s eldest son and a chief of the native Horite inhabitants of Edom (vv 22, 29). Lotan had two sons, Hori and Homam.
lots, casting of: Practice common in the OT, less common in the NT prior to Pentecost, and absent in the biblical narrative after Pentecost.
lotus: Water plant common in the Near East, mentioned only in Job 40:21-22.
love: Prominent virtue in Christian theology and ethics.
lubim: KJV form of Libyan, an inhabitant of Libya, in 2 Chronicles 12:3, 16:8, and Nahum 3:9.
lucas: KJV spelling of Luke in Philemon 1:24.
lucifer: Appellation from a Latin word meaning “light bearer.” The Latin term refers to the planet Venus appearing in the evening and the morning, which is the brightest object in the sky except for the sun and moon. Others have identified it with the crescent moon.
lucius: 1. Man from Cyrene, listed among the prophets and teachers in Antioch.
lud, ludim, ludites: Names occurring in the table of nations in Genesis 10. Ludim is listed as the first son of Mizraim, and Lud is listed as the fourth son of Shem.
luhith: Moabite city mentioned in connection with the flight of the Moabites to Zoar. Since it was also listed with Horonaim, it was perhaps situated between these two cities in the southeastern area around the Dead Sea.
luke (person): Companion of the apostle Paul; author of the third Gospel and Acts.
luke, gospel of: Third book of the NT; also the third of the synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke).
lute: Guitarlike musical instrument with strings stretched along a neck and over a sounding box, usually plucked or strummed.
luz: 1. Original Canaanite name of the city of Bethel.
lycaonia: Region in the southern interior of the Roman province of Asia (also called Asia Minor), north of the Taurus Mountains.
lycia: Country located in the southwest part of the Roman province of Asia (commonly known as Asia Minor), bounded on the northwest by Caria, on the north by Phrygia and Pisidia, on the northeast by Pamphylia, and on the west, south, and east by the Mediterranean Sea.
lydda: New Testament name for Lod, a town located southwest of Jerusalem in the Shephelah.
lydia (person): Gentile woman who was converted under the preaching of Paul in Philippi. Lydia was a dealer in purple cloth and came from the city of Thyatira in the region of Lydia in the western part of the Roman province of Asia (commonly known as Asia Minor).
lydia (place): Name designating a geographical area occurring in Jeremiah 46:9, Ezekiel 27:10, and 30:5 in the NLT. In other versions, it is listed as “Lud” (see NLT mg) or “Ludim.” But the identification of Lydia with Lud or Ludim in the OT is not certain.
lye: Strong alkaline substance (probably potassium carbonate) used for cleaning purposes.
lyre: Stringed instrument consisting of a body, crossbar, and sometimes a sounding box.
lysanias: Tetrarch of Abilene (the area west of Damascus) in AD 27–28. The Gospel of Luke mentions Lysanias as among those who ruled at the beginning of John the Baptist’s ministry.
lysias: 1. Roman commander who wrote a letter to Felix concerning the apostle Paul.
lysimachus: 1. According to the Additions to Esther, the son of Ptolemy of Jerusalem and translator of the book of Esther into Greek.
lystra: City in the region of Lycaonia in the Roman province of Galatia. Events in the town in the NT are confined to the book of Acts (and referenced in 2 Tm 3:11).
maacah, maachah (person): Common Hebrew name, often spelled Maachah in the KJV.
maacah, maachah (place): Small kingdom in northern Transjordan alternately named Aram-Maacah in 1 Chronicles 19:6 (KJV “Syria-maachah”). According to Joshua 13:11, the states of Geshur and Maacah were between Gilead and Mt Hermon and they bordered the kingdom of Og, ruler of Bashan.
maacathite, maachathi, maachathite: People of Maacah who held the territory neighboring the Geshurites and the boundary of land granted to the half-tribe of Manasseh. It was taken over by Jair, who with his companions were unable to dislodge the Maacathites and Geshurites living among them.
maadai: Bani’s son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile.
maadiah: Head of a priestly family who returned to Jerusalem after the exile (Neh 12:5, NLT mg) and whose house was headed by Piltai in the next generation during the days of Joiakim the high priest. He is called Moadiah in v 17.
maai: Priestly musician who participated in the dedication of the rebuilt Jerusalem wall.
maaleh-acrabbim: KJV rendering of “ascent of Akrabbim,” a site on Canaan’s southern border, in Joshua 15:3.
ma'aneh: Unit of measure equivalent to the length of a furrow (20–30 yards, or 18.3–27.4 meters).
maarath: One of Judah’s cities of inheritance located in the hill country, perhaps modern Biet Ummar, seven miles (11.3 kilometers) north of Hebron. It may be the same as Maroth, mentioned in Micah 1:12.
maasai: Priest who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile.
maaseiah: 1. One of the singers appointed by the Levites to accompany David when he brought the ark from Obed-edom’s house to Jerusalem.
maasiai: KJV spelling of Maasai, a postexilic priest, in 1 Chronicles 9:12.
maath: Ancestor of Jesus in Luke’s genealogy.
maaziah: 1. Levite who served in the temple during David’s reign.
macbannai: Warrior from Gad’s tribe who joined David at Ziklag in his struggle against King Saul.
macbenah: Evidently a place-name among the geographical names in the genealogy of Caleb and Judah.
maccabaeus, judas: Third son of Mattathias; leader of the Jewish insurrection against Rome in 166 BC. His surname, Maccabeus (perhaps from an Aramaic word meaning “the Hammerer”), was later applied to all of the Hasmonean family.
maccabean period: Period of Israel’s history when the Maccabeans fought for Israel’s freedom and governed the country.
maccabees, 1 and 2: Two deuterocanonical books that cover the period of Israel’s history from 167 BC to 100 BC. The books are named after Judas Maccabeus, who initiated the Jewish revolt in 166 BC against Rome.
maccabees, 3 and 4: The writings of the Old and New Testaments tended to attract certain additional compositions in the form of books, parts of books, letters, “gospels,” apocalypses, and so on.
maccabeus, judas: Third son of Mattathias; leader of the Jewish insurrection against Rome in 166 BC. His surname, Maccabeus (perhaps from an Aramaic word meaning “the Hammerer”), was later applied to all of the Hasmonean family.
macedonia: Roman province in NT times, beginning as a kingdom in the seventh century BC.
machaerus: Fortified castle where John the Baptist was imprisoned and later beheaded by Herod Antipas (according to Josephus’s Antiquities 18.5.2).
machbanai, machbannai: Warrior from Gad’s tribe who joined David at Ziklag in his struggle against King Saul.
machbenah: Evidently a place-name among the geographical names in the genealogy of Caleb and Judah.
machi: Father of Geuel from Gad’s tribe. Geuel was one of the 12 spies sent to search out the land of Canaan.
machir: 1. Joseph’s grandson and the firstborn son of Manasseh through his Aramean concubine.
machirite: Descendant of Machir, Joseph’s grandson from Manasseh’s tribe.
machnadebai: A son of Bani (Binnui), who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his foreign wife during the postexilic era.
machpelah: Small field of trees and a cave with two chambers near Mamre in the district of Hebron, which was purchased by Abraham as a burial place for Sarah. The seller was Ephron, a Hittite, and the price was 400 shekels of silver.
macnadebai: A son of Bani (Binnui), who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his foreign wife during the postexilic era.
madian: KJV spelling of Midian, a geographical region in northwest Arabia, in Acts 7:29.
madmannah (person): Shaaph’s son and a grandson of Caleb.
madmannah (place): Alternate name for Beth-marcaboth, a city in southern Judah, in Joshua 15:31.
madmen: Town in Moab, according to Jeremiah’s oracle. It may be a form created by dittography from an original Dimon, as in the oracle against Moab by Isaiah.
madmenah: Benjamite town positioned north of Jerusalem along the route taken by the Assyrian army during Sennacherib’s military incursion into Judah (c. 701 BC) against King Hezekiah (715–686 BC) and the Holy City.
madon: One of the many Canaanite cities allied against Joshua in a vain attempt to stop the progress of the Israelites into Palestine. A disastrous battle fought at Meron brought these cities under Israelite control.
magadan: Locality visited by Jesus after he crossed the Sea of Galilee. The correct spelling was most likely Magdala.
magbish: Town reoccupied after the exile by 156 descendants of its former residents.
magdala: KJV place-name used in Matthew 15:39. Recent versions and translations have the name Magadan.
magdalene, mary: Name of one of several Marys who followed Jesus. This Mary was the first to see the risen Christ.
magdiel: One of the chiefs of Edom.
magi: “Wise men” (NLT, KJV) appearing in Matthew 2:1-12 who, following a star, came to Jerusalem and then to Bethlehem in order to pay homage to the newborn “king of the Jews.” Matthew’s account forms a significant introduction to his Gospel by drawing attention to…
magic: Attempt to influence or control people or events through supernatural forces. These forces are called upon by means of ceremonies, the recitation of spells, charms, incantations, and other forms of ritual.
magistrate: Title of a public official who acted as judge and administrator of a given municipality. King Artaxerxes ordered Ezra to select magistrates along with judges to govern the people when they returned to Palestine.
magnificat: The song of Mary found in Luke 1:46-55. This poem is in the style of the OT psalms and is strongly reminiscent of the prayer of Hannah in 1 Samuel 2:1-10.
magog: Term found only five times in the Bible but significant because of its use in the well-known prophetic passages of Ezekiel 38–39 and Revelation 20.
magor-missabib: Name given by Jeremiah to Pashhur, the chief officer in the house of the Lord. Jeremiah did this because Pashhur put him in stocks for prophesying judgment upon Judah.
magpiash: Political leader who signed Ezra’s covenant during the postexilic period.
mahalab: Reconstructed name of a town in Asher’s tribe (Jos 19:29, NLT “Mehebel”); the Hebrew text has a transposition of the last two consonants, but the town is probably the same as Ahlab and Helbah of Judges 1:31.
mahalah: KJV rendering of Mahlah, Hammoleketh’s son, in 1 Chronicles 7:18.
mahalaleel, mahalalel: 1. Kenan’s son and the father of Jared in Seth’s line, also mentioned in Luke’s genealogy.
mahalath (music): Musical cue, perhaps meaning “sadness,” listed in the title of Psalm 53 (see RSV), which would designate the way in which and/or the melody to which the psalm should be sung.
mahalath (person): 1. Daughter of Ishmael, Nebaioth’s sister, Esau’s third wife, and Reuel’s mother; alternately called Basemath (KJV “Bashemath”) in Genesis 36:3-17.
mahalath leannoth: Hebrew phrase in the title of Psalm 88, translated “The Suffering of Affliction”; perhaps a familiar ancient melody to which the psalm was performed.
mahali: KJV form of Mahli, Merari’s son, in Exodus 6:19.
mahanaim: Settlement east of the Jordan in Gilead. Jacob met angels there and named the place “God’s camp.” He divided his household and possessions into two camps (Mahanaim means “two camps” in Hebrew) to keep from losing everything when he confronted Esau.
mahaneh-dan: Place west of Kiriath-jearim between Zorab and Eshtaol, where the Spirit of the Lord began to stir in Samson and where Dan’s tribe encamped on the way to the hill country of Ephraim (18:12).
maharai: One of David’s mighty men and a Zerahite from Netophah in the hill country of Judah. He was appointed commander of a division (24,000 soldiers) during the 10th month of the year.
mahath: 1. Levite, son of Amasai, and ancestor of Heman the temple singer in David’s time.
mahavah, mahavite: Term used in 1 Chronicles 11:46 to designate Eliel, one of David’s mighty men. The word was probably added to indicate where he came from so as to distinguish him from the Eliel in verse 47.
mahazioth: One of the 14 sons of Heman the Kohathite, and head of the 23d course of tabernacle musicians who ministered with cymbals, harps, and lyres.
maher-shalal-hash-baz: Name of Isaiah’s son, meaning “swift to plunder and quick to spoil” (NLT mg), which prophetically described the imminent destruction to befall Damascus and Samaria by the hand of the Assyrians.
mahlah: 1. Manassite; one of Zelophehad’s five daughters.
mahli: 1. Merari’s son and Levi’s grandson, and the founder of the Mahlite family.
mahlite: Descendant of Mahli, Merari’s son from Levi’s tribe.
mahlon: Son of Elimelech and Naomi, and Chilion’s brother. While with his family in Moab, he married Ruth, the Moabitess.
mahol: Father of three famous wise men (Heman, Calcol, and Darda) during the Solomonic era (970–930 BC; 1 Kgs 4:31).
mahseiah: Forefather of Baruch and Seraiah (51:59), spelled Maaseiah in the KJV.
maid, maiden: Young unmarried woman, often of the servant class. In the OT, five Hebrew words with varying shades of meaning are translated by the English word “maiden.”
mail, coat of: Body armor consisting of small interlaced metal plates sewn onto a leather jacket.
makaz: One of the 12 cities that provided food one month out of the year for King Solomon and his household. Situated in northwest Judah, it may be identified with Khirbet el-Mukheizin, south of Ekron.
makheloth: One of the stopping places of the Israelites on their way to Canaan, situated between Haradah and Tahath.
maki: Father of Geuel from Gad’s tribe. Geuel was one of the 12 spies sent to search out the land of Canaan.
makir: 1. Joseph’s grandson and the firstborn son of Manasseh through his Aramean concubine.
makirite: Descendant of Machir, Joseph’s grandson from Manasseh’s tribe.
makkedah: One of the Shephelah towns conquered during the southern campaign led by Joshua. It belonged to the same district as Lachish (15:41).
maktesh: Locality within the topography of Jerusalem. Since the word means “mortar,” the expression here should refer to some basinlike depression.
malachi (person): Author of the last book of the OT. The prophet Malachi lived about 500–460 BC.
malachi, book of: Last prophetic book of the Jewish canon; last book of the Old Testament.
malcham: 1. KJV form of Malcam in 1 Chronicles 8:9.
malchiah: 1. KJV spelling of Malchijah, Gershon’s descendant, in 1 Chronicles 6:40.
malchiel, malchielite: Beriah’s son, a grandson of Asher, and the founder of the Malchielite family.
malchijah: 1. Gershon’s descendant, appointed by David, along with the rest of his family, to serve as a temple musician (1 Chr 6:40, KJV “Malchiah”).
malchiram: Son of Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), and a descendant of David.
malchi-shua: King Saul’s third son. He was killed by the Philistines at the battle of Gilboa.
malchus: Name of a slave of the high priest in John 18:10. At the time of Jesus’ arrest, Peter struck Malchus with a sword, cutting off his right ear.
maleleel: KJV form of Mahalaleel, an ancestor of Jesus, in Luke’s genealogy.
malkiel, malkielite: Beriah’s son, a grandson of Asher, and the founder of the Malchielite family.
malkijah: 1. Gershon’s descendant, appointed by David, along with the rest of his family, to serve as a temple musician (1 Chr 6:40, KJV “Malchiah”).
malkiram: Son of Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), and a descendant of David.
malkishua: King Saul’s third son. He was killed by the Philistines at the battle of Gilboa.
mallothi: One of Heman’s 17 children, who became leader of the 19th of 24 divisions of singers for service in the sanctuary during David’s reign (v 26).
malluch: 1. Merarite Levite and ancestor of Ethan the singer in Solomon’s temple.
malluchi: Father of a house headed by Jonathan during the days of the high priest Joiakim in the postexilic period (Neh 12:14, NLT mg). Possibly the same person as Malluch #6.
malta: Island in the Mediterranean Sea, south of Sicily. The name Malta occurs only once in the Bible (Acts 28:1, KJV “Melita”), in connection with the shipwreck that occurred on Paul’s voyage to Rome (25:11-12).
mammon: Aramaic word, meaning wealth or property, transliterated by the Gospel writers in Greek letters.
mamre (person): Owner of a parcel of land called “the plain of Mamre.” He was an Amorite and is recorded as having two brothers: Aner and Eshcol. These became confederates of Abraham when he fought to save his nephew Lot.
mamre (place): Important oak grove near which Abraham lived, and named for an Amorite who helped him defeat Chedorlaomer and rescue Lot. Abraham erected an altar under the oak of Mamre (13:18).
man: Human being, whether male or female.
man, natural: Expression occurring in 1 Corinthians 2:14 (RSV mg). The adjective translated there by “natural” is also found in 1 Corinthians 15:44 (twice), 46; James 3:15; and Jude 1:19.
man, old and new: Biblical terms used to describe the state of man in relation to Christ. Human beings are created in the image of God and are made to have fellowship with him.
man, son of: Messianic title used by Jesus to express his heavenly origin, earthly mission, and glorious future coming. It does not refer merely to his human nature or humanity, as some church fathers or contemporary scholars believe.
manaen: One of the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch, identified as a close companion of Herod the tetrarch. The name is a Greek form of the Hebrew name Menahem.
manahath (place), manahathite: Evidently a place in the Judean hills near the Benjamite border. The Manahathites, the people of Manahath, had connections with the Judean and Calebite clans in northern Judea.
manasseh (person): 1. Firstborn son of Joseph and his Egyptian wife, Asenath.
manasseh, tribe of: Geographically, the largest of the 12 tribes of Israel, and unique in having two territories, a half-tribe in each. Isolated from each other by the Jordan River valley, they developed separately.
manasses: 1. KJV form of Manasseh, king of Judah, in Matthew 1:10.
manassite: Descendant of Manasseh, Joseph’s firstborn son.
mandrake: Mediterranean herb believed to have had aphrodisiac properties and noted for its fragrance.
maneh: KJV rendering of mina, a weight in Ezekiel 45:12.
manger: Feeding trough for domesticated animals. The Greek term for manger is found only four times in the NT.
manius, titus: Roman legate who wrote to the Jews concerning political concessions.
