manna: Miraculous food the Lord provided for the Israelites in the desert. It originally appeared in the form of thin flakes, like frost on the ground, around the Israelite camp.
manoah: Danite from Zorah whose wife was barren. Through encounters with the Angel of the Lord, the couple learned that God was about to give them a son who would judge the Philistines and deliver Israel from its oppression.
man of lawlessness, man of sin: Man of Lawlessness, Man of Sin
Expression used by the apostle Paul of the Antichrist in 2 Thessalonians 2:3.
manual of discipline: Book of community rules of conduct belonging to the Essenes at Qumran.
maoch: Father of Achish, the Philistine king of Gath. David sought refuge with this king in order to escape Saul’s plots to kill him.
maon (person), maonite: Son of Shammai, and Bethzur’s father. He was either the founding father of the people of Bethzur and/or the founder of the city.
maon (place): Chief town in the hill country of Judah, about nine miles (14.5 kilometers) south of Hebron. David and his men hid in this area while fleeing from Saul, and David’s wife Abigail was from this town (25:2-3).
mara: A name, meaning “bitter,” which Naomi gave to herself when she returned as a widow to Judah from Moab.
marah: Spring of water in the wilderness of Etham, the first camping place of the Israelites after crossing the Red Sea.
maralah: KJV and NLT rendering of Mareal, a site on Zebulun’s western border, in Joshua 19:11.
maranatha: Aramaic expression used by Paul in 1 Corinthians 16:22, meaning either “Our Lord, come!” or “Our Lord has come.”
marble: A “mineral” is a naturally occurring substance, normally an ore that must be mined and treated before the metal can be extracted. A “metal” is a chemical element such as iron or copper, which is free from contamination by other materials.
marcion, gospel of: Heretical gospel of the early second century.
marduk: Supreme Babylonian deity, worshiped as the god of creation and destiny. Marduk (also called Bel) was originally the local city god of Babylon.
mareal: Town defining part of the western border of the land allotted to Zebulun’s tribe for an inheritance. It was positioned between Sarid and Dabbesheth (Jos 19:11, NLT “Maralah”).
mareshah (person): 1. Caleb’s firstborn son and the father of Hebron (1 Chr 2:42; RSV, based on the Greek text).
mareshah (place): City (Greek Marisa; Josephus, “Marissa”) on the road from the coastal plain of Judah toward Hebron and Jerusalem. Remains of Jewish pottery indicate occupation from at least 800 BC.
mari: Influential city-state, located in eastern Syria, which became important in the early second millennium BC.
mariner: Men trained in sailing ships at sea. The people of Israel were not generally seafaring and confined their activities on the water to the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan River.
marjoram: Small mint growing as high as three feet (.9 meter) tall. It was perhaps the “hyssop” of the OT.
mark, gospel of: Second book of the NT, probably written by John Mark of Jerusalem sometime between AD 60 and 68.
mark, john: Cousin of Barnabas; companion to both Paul and Peter; author of the second Gospel.
market, marketplace: Place for the buying and selling of goods in antiquity. Generally, the marketplaces of the ancient Near East would be much like the open air bazaars one can still see in any city throughout Israel, Greece, and Turkey.
mark of god, mark of the beast: Mark of God, Mark of the Beast
Ensignia placed on people either by God or by the Antichrist. Though the phrase is limited to the book of Revelation, a mark was used in Ezekiel 9:4-6.
maroth: City in Palestine, mentioned only by Micah. It may be the same as the Maarath in Joshua 15:59; if so, it would be an ancient Canaanite city, part of the inheritance of Judah’s tribe.
marriage, levirate: The joining together of male and female in matrimony, as practiced by various cultures.
marriage, marriage customs: The joining together of male and female in matrimony, as practiced by various cultures.
marsena: One of the seven princes of Persia and Media who served Ahasuerus, ranking next to him in authority in the kingdom.
marsh hen: Alternate name for water hen in Leviticus 11:18 and Deuteronomy 14:16.
mars' hill: Alternate KJV translation for Areopagus, the name of a small hill northwest of the Acropolis in Athens and the site of Paul’s address to the Athenians.
martha: Sister of Mary and Lazarus, and friend of Jesus. Martha’s family lived in Bethany, a small town on the eastern slope of the Mt of Olives.
mary: Popular feminine name among first-century Jews, borne by six (or seven) women in the NT.
mary magdalene: Popular feminine name among first-century Jews, borne by six (or seven) women in the NT.
masada: Rock fortress on the western shore of the Dead Sea, opposite the Lisan, about 10 miles (16.1 kilometers) south of En-gedi where the Jewish Zealots made their last stand against the Romans in AD 73.
maschil: KJV rendering of maskil, a musical cue in the titles of numerous psalms.
mash: Aram’s fourth son, a descendant of Shem. He is called Meshech in 1 Chronicles 1:17.
mashal: Alternate spelling of Mishal, a Levitical town in Asher, in 1 Chronicles 6:74.
maskil: Hebrew term in the superscriptions of 13 psalms; perhaps a musical cue denoting the manner in which the designated psalms were to be performed.
mason, masonry: Worker in and craft of brick and stonework. The mason prepared stone from the quarry for use in building.
masora, masoretes: Oral tradition concerning the pronunciation and accuracy of the Hebrew text of the OT, and the scholars who were responsible for putting those traditions into writing.
masoretic text: Oral tradition concerning the pronunciation and accuracy of the Hebrew text of the OT, and the scholars who were responsible for putting those traditions into writing.
masrekah: Home of an Edomite king named Samlah.
massa: Ishmael’s seventh son and Abraham’s grandson. His descendants inhabited northwestern Arabia.
massah and meribah: Two Hebrew words meaning, respectively, “to put to the test” and “to find fault, quarrel.” According to Exodus 17:7, after Moses got water from the rock at Rephidim, he called the place by these two names to memorialize the Israelites’ “testing” of God’s faithful provision.
master: Word used to translate five different Hebrew words and seven different Greek terms with root meanings of owner, elder, sovereign, teacher, superintendent, lord, sir, rabbi, and captain; often used to describe Jesus.
mastic: Small Mediterranean tree that exudes a gum used to make numerous products.
mathusala: KJV rendering of Methuselah, Enoch’s son, in Luke 3:37.
matred: Mother of Mehetabel, the wife of King Hadad (Hadar) of Edom.
matri, matrites: Family of Benjamin’s tribe. Saul, the first king of Israel, came from this family.
mattan: 1. Priest of Baal killed at the time when Jehoiada the priest had Queen Athaliah killed and Joash placed on the throne of Judah.
mattanah: Place of encampment for Israel following the exodus as the company moved east of the Dead Sea from the Arnon River northward into the territory of Sihon, king of the Amorites.
mattaniah: 1. Last king of Judah, whom King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon enthroned in place of his nephew Jehoiachin; his name subsequently was changed to Zedekiah, and as such he was known in the other references to him in 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, and Jeremiah.
mattatha: Ancestor of Jesus, according to Luke’s genealogy.
mattathah: KJV spelling of Mattattah, Hashum’s son, in Ezra 10:33.
mattathias: 1. Member of the priestly family of Joarib (his genealogy can be traced in 1 Macc 2:1 and in Josephus’s Antiquities 12.6.3).
mattattah: Hashum’s son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile.
mattenai: 1. Hashum’s son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile.
matthan: Ancestor of Jesus; perhaps identifiable with Matthat in Luke 3:24.
matthat: 1. Ancestor of Jesus, perhaps the same as Matthan.
matthew (person): Son of Alphaeus; a tax collector by occupation; chosen by Jesus to be one of the 12 apostles; credited with the authorship of the Gospel of Matthew.
matthew, gospel of: First Gospel and first book of the NT.
matthias: Disciple of Jesus, mentioned by name only in Acts 1:23-26, chosen to take the place of Judas Iscariot.
mattithiah: 1. Levite and Shallum’s firstborn son, who was in charge of making the baked cakes that accompanied the offerings in the temple.
mattock: Agricultural tool used for grubbing or breaking up the soil (1 Sm 13:20-21, NLT “pick”).
maul: KJV translation for “war club” (NLT “ax”) in Proverbs 25:18.
mayor: An official in municipal administration whose duties included those of scribe or secretary. He published the decrees of the civic authority but also acted as a liaison officer between the administration of a city and the Roman provincial government.
mazzaroth: Word appearing in Job 38:32 that may refer to a constellation. The Hebrew form is feminine in Job 38:32 and masculine in Job 9:9, where it has usually been thought to refer to the Hyades.
meah, tower of: KJV translation for “Tower of the Hundred” in Nehemiah 3:1 and 12:39.
meal offering: An offering of grain or fine flour. It has also been translated “grain offering” (NLT, NIV), “cereal offering” (RSV) and “meat offering” (KJV).
meals, significance of: The meal played a significant role in family, social, and religious life. The evening meal was the time when all family members normally were gathered together, and was thus an important time of fellowship.
mearah: Region of Palestine that the Israelites had not possessed (Jos 13:4, NIV “Arah”). Its location is uncertain.
measure: Units of measure in the ancient world were largely based on practical standards: the length of an arm, a day’s journey, how much a donkey could carry, and so forth. While this was a convenient system, it also suffered from a lack of standardization.
meat: Substances required by the body to sustain life, and the methods of making them edible. Food consumed in Bible times included bread, milk products, fruit, meat, and fish.
mebunnai: Alternate name (probably a textual corruption) of Sibbecai, a warrior among David’s “mighty men,” in 2 Samuel 23:27 (NLT mg).
mecherathite: Designation for Hepher in 1 Chronicles 11:36. The parallel passage in 2 Samuel 23:34 calls him “the son of the Maachathite” (KJV) or “from Maacah” (NLT).
meconah: Settlement mentioned beside Ziklag and presumably in the western Negev.
medad: Elder of Israel who, with Eldad, prophesied in the wilderness to Joshua’s consternation. Moses, however, defended Medad’s right to speak in God’s name.
medan: Third son of Abraham by his second wife, Keturah.
medeba: Moabite town in the fertile plain northeast of the Dead Sea, about 25 miles (40.2 kilometers) south of Philadelphia (modern Amman). It was situated 6 miles (9.7 kilometers) south of Heshbon on the Roman road to Kerak.
medes, media, median: Indo-European-speaking people appearing in the highland area of the ancient Asian country called Media.
mediate, mediator: The act of an intermediary, go-between, or expert in divine things, not to negotiate agreement or compromise but to approach God on behalf of others, and so to convey desired knowledge and reassurance with divine authority.
medicine and medical practice: The field of knowledge dealing with the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of diseases, as well as the actual substances used to diagnose, treat, or prevent disease.
mediterranean sea: Body of water often called the Great Sea, bordering Palestine on the west.
medium: Person who acts as a channel of communication between human beings and the spirit world.
megiddo, megiddon: City standing at the southwest edge of the plain of Esdraelon on the main route between Mesopotamia and Egypt. It overlooks the historic route where a pass through the Mt Carmel range led from the plain of Sharon into the plain of Jezreel.
megiddo, waters of: Scene of the battle between Sisera and Barak, mentioned in the victory song of Deborah (Jgs 5:19, NLT “Megiddo’s springs”). It refers to a perennial stream near Megiddo, probably the Wadi el-Lejjun, which drained the basin behind Megiddo.
megilloth: Plural form of the Hebrew word for scroll. The word occurs several times in Jeremiah 36, where King Jehoiakim, rejecting the word from God, burned the scroll that the prophet sent to him.
mehetabel: 1. Matred’s daughter and the wife of Hadar, king of Edom in pre-Israelite times.
mehida: Head of a family of temple servants in Ezra’s time.
meholah, meholathite: Location used to describe Adriel the son of Barzillai, who was the husband of Merab, Saul’s eldest daughter. He was probably from Abel-meholah, an important city of Gilead.
mehujael: Irad’s son and the father of Methushael in Cain’s line.
mehuman: One of the seven chamberlains King Ahasuerus sent to bring Queen Vashti to the royal banquet.
mehunim, mehunims: KJV forms of Meunim and Meunites in Ezra 2:50 and 2 Chronicles 26:7, respectively.
me-jarkon: Topographical designation in the description of Dan’s inheritance.
mekerah, mekerathite: Designation for Hepher in 1 Chronicles 11:36. The parallel passage in 2 Samuel 23:34 calls him “the son of the Maachathite” (KJV) or “from Maacah” (NLT).
mekonah: KJV spelling of Meconah, a Judean city, in Nehemiah 11:28.
melatiah: Descendant of Gideon who helped repair the Jerusalem wall next to the Old Gate during Nehemiah’s time.
melchi: 1. Jannai’s son, according to Luke’s genealogy.
melchiah: KJV spelling of Malchiah, Pashhur’s father, in Jeremiah 21:1.
melchisedec: KJV rendering of Melchizedek, the priest and king of Salem who blessed Abraham, in Hebrews 5–7.
melchi-shua: KJV alternate form of Malchi-shua, King Saul’s third son, in 1 Samuel 14:49.
melchizedek: Mysterious biblical personality whose name means “king of righteousness.” The historical record about this priest-king is contained in Genesis 14:18-20, and he is spoken of in Psalm 110:4 and Hebrews 5:10; 6:20; 7:1-17.
melea: Ancestor of Jesus, according to Luke’s genealogy.
melicu: KJV form of Malluchi the priest in Nehemiah 12:14.
melita: KJV form of Malta, an island south of Sicily, in Acts 28:1.
melki: 1. Jannai’s son, according to Luke’s genealogy.
melkon: Name that tradition has given to one of the wise men (also called Melchior) who brought gifts to Jesus.
melon: Generic name for many-seeded fruit of the gourd family.
melzar: Steward responsible for the food given to Daniel. The KJV translates the word as a proper name, but the RSV translates the word as a title.
memorial: Something that keeps remembrance vivid. The ideas represented by the words “remember,” “remembrance,” and “memorial” are closely connected in common parlance as well as in biblical usage.
memphis: City located about 15 miles (24.1 kilometers) southwest of Cairo, once the sprawling capital of Egypt; now, for all practical purposes, it does not exist.
memucan: One of the seven princes of Persia and Media under King Ahasuerus. He brought charges against Vashti, the Persian queen, who had refused to make a royal appearance that the king had commanded (v 16).
menahem: King of Israel who ruled from 752–742 BC. He was the son of Gadi, a name not attested in the OT except in 2 Kings 15:14-22.
menan: KJV form of Menna, an ancestor of Jesus in Luke’s genealogy.
mene, mene, tekel, parsin: Mysterious prophetic words in Daniel 5:25 pointing to the judgment of God against Babylon and her king. A decade or so following the death of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon (562 BC), a man of lesser moral stature, Belshazzar, became monarch of the empire.
menelaus: It is thought that this conscienceless, conniving high priest was the leader of the Jewish supporters of the Seleucid kings during the reign of Antiochus IV Epiphanes.
meni: Pagan god of destiny or luck worshiped by apostate Jews. The name is rendered “destiny” in NASB, NIV, NLT; “fortune” in NEB; and “unto that number” in KJV, reflecting the meaning of the Hebrew word “to count, apportion,” as it were, by fate.
menna: Ancestor of Jesus, according to Luke’s genealogy.
menorah: Lamp or lampstand in the tabernacle. It refers to the seven-branched lamp (candelabrum) that was to lighten the tabernacle: these seven lamps gave light in front of the lampstand.
menuhoth: People descended from Judah through Shobal, mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 2:52 (rendered Manahethites in NEB, KJV; Manahathites in NIV, NASB, NLT).
meonenim, plain of: KJV mistranslation for the diviners’ oak, a place near Shechem, in Judges 9:37.
mephaath: One of the cities of Reuben’s tribe on the plain near Heshbon, which was allotted to the Merari family of Levites. Later, it was numbered among Moabite towns during Jeremiah’s ministry.
merab: Eldest of Saul’s two daughters, who was promised as a wife to David (18:17-18). Saul unexplainedly did not keep the agreement, instead giving him Michal.
meraiah: Head of Seraiah’s priestly family during the priesthood of Joiakim in postexilic Jerusalem.
meraioth: 1. Levite, six to seven generations removed from Aaron.
merari, merarite: Transliteration of a Hebrew word meaning “bitter,” “bitter drink,” or “to be bitter.” It means the same in Arabic and Akkadian, but in Ugaritic it means “to strengthen, to bless.” Traditionally, the word has been understood to be derived from the Hebrew and…
merathaim: Name that Jeremiah uses in reference to God’s judgment upon Babylon. Though it means “double rebellion” or “twofold rebel,” it is a wordplay on the name for southern Babylonia, Marratu.
merchant: A person who buys and sells commodities for profit. The barter system of trade gave way in time to a system where professional merchants facilitated the exchange of goods.
mercy: A divine quality by which God faithfully keeps his promises and maintains his covenant relationship with his chosen people despite their unworthiness and unfaithfulness.
mercy seat: Gold slab placed on top of the ark of the covenant with cherubim attached to it on either end, termed the “mercy seat” in many English versions of the Bible (cf. Ex 25:17-22).
mered: Ezrah’s son from Judah’s tribe, who had two wives. One wife, Bithiah, was the daughter of Pharaoh, and one was a Jewess.
meremoth: 1. Priest, son of Uriah, grandson of Hakkoz.
meres: One of the seven princes of Persia and Media who acted as personal adviser to King Ahasuerus.
meribah: 1. Noun meaning “strife,” named for a place at Horeb, near Rephidim (Wadi Feiran), where Israel contended with Moses for water near the beginning of the wilderness wanderings.
meribah-kadesh, meribath-kadesh: Alternate names for Kadesh-barnea, a place for lengthy encampment by the Israelites during the wilderness wanderings.
meribbaal: Original name for Mephibosheth, the handicapped son of Jonathan. The name means “Baal contends” and is displaced by the later name (Mephibosheth, meaning “idol breaker”) in 2 Samuel 4:4 and 9:6.
merodach: Hebrew pronunciation of Marduk, the chief Babylonian deity.
merodach-baladan: Name meaning “Marduk has given a son!” Second Kings 20:12-19 and Isaiah 39 present a parallel account of Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sending envoys to King Hezekiah of Judah.
merom, waters of: Site of Joshua’s victory over Jabin, king of Hazor, and his allies, mentioned only twice in the Bible.
meronoth: The hometown of Jehdeiah and Jadon.
meroz: Town in northern Palestine whose inhabitants were cursed for not assisting Deborah and Barak in their war against Sisera and the Canaanites.
mesech: KJV spelling of Meshech, Noah’s grandson, in Psalm 120:5.
mesha (person): 1. King of Moab in the ninth century BC whose name is derived from a root meaning “to save or deliver.” According to 2 Kings 3:4-5, Mesha was a sheep breeder who paid heavy tribute to Israel during the time of Ahab but rebelled after Ahab’s death.
mesha (place): Place in southern Arabia defining the western boundary of the territory in which the descendants of Joktan settled. Its location is unknown.
meshach: One of the three companions of the prophet Daniel who was thrown into the fiery furnace.
meshech: 1. Son of Japheth and Noah’s grandson.
meshelemiah: Korahite Levite, Kore’s son from the house of Asaph, and a gatekeeper of the sanctuary with his sons in the time of David; alternately called Shelemiah in 1 Chronicles 26:14.
meshezabeel, meshezabel: 1. Ancestor of Meshullam who helped repair the Jerusalem wall.
meshillemith: Alternate spelling of Meshillemoth in 1 Chronicles 9:12.
meshillemoth: 1. Father of Berekiah, a chief of Ephraim.
meshobab: Prince of Simeon’s tribe in the days of Hezekiah, who, with 12 other princes, moved to Gedor, dispossessed its pagan people (the Meunim), and settled his family there.
meshullam: 1. Forefather of Shaphan, the royal secretary to King Josiah of Judah.
meshullemeth: Mother of Amon, king of Judah (642–640 BC) and the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah.
mesobaite: KJV spelling of Mezobaite, a title given to Jaasiel, in 1 Chronicles 11:47.
mesopotamia: Name given by the Greeks to the land between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers, an area today called al-Jazira, “the island,” by the Arabs.
messenger: One who carries a message, a herald. The word “messenger” is used in the Bible in four ways.
messiah: Title derived from the Hebrew, mashiach, a verbal adjective meaning “anointed one.” Along with its NT equivalent, christos (Christ), it refers to an act of consecration whereby an individual is set apart to serve God and then anointed with oil.
metheg-ammah: Place (whose name means “Bridle of the Mother City”) conquered by David (2 Sm 8:1, NLT mg). Most likely it refers to the Philistine capital, Gath.
methusael: KJV spelling of Methushael, Mehujael’s son, in Genesis 4:18.
methuselah: Son of Enoch, Lamech’s father, and the grandfather of Noah through Seth’s line. Living 969 years, Methuselah is the oldest recorded person in the Bible.
methushael: Mehujael’s son and the father of Lamech in Cain’s line.
meunim, meunites: People living in Edom (Mt Seir, 1 Chr 4:41-42) who were dispossessed of their rich pasturelands by the Simeonites. Later, Meunites from Edom attacked Judah’s King Jehoshaphat; later still, King Uzziah of Judah defeated them (26:7).
mezahab: Matred’s father and the grandfather of Mehetabel, the wife of the Edomite king Hadar (or Hadad).
mezobaite: Designation for Jaasiel, one of David’s “mighty men”. The meaning is unknown, though some suggest “from Zobah” (NLT).
mezuzah: A Hebrew word, used about 20 times in the OT, that means the upright framework of a door or gate. The blood of the Passover lamb was smeared on the “mezuzah” of the house.
miamin: 1. KJV rendering of Mijamin, Parosh’s son, in Ezra 10:25.
mibhar: Warrior among David’s mighty men, who were known as “the thirty”.
mibsam: 1. One of Ishmael’s sons and the founder of a tribe named after him.
mibzar: Chief of Edom. The name means “fortress.” Eusebius connects Mibzar with Mibsara, a large town in Edom.
mica: Common name interchangeable with Micah and probably a contracted form of Micaiah.
micah (person): 1. Ephraimite judge who had idols made and then hired a Levite to become his priest.
micah, book of: Sixth in the order of the books of the 12 minor prophets.
micaiah: 1. Prophet and Imlah’s son, called by Ahab to forecast the result of projected battles against the Syrians.
micha: 1. KJV spelling of Mica, Mephibosheth’s son, in 2 Samuel 9:12.
michael: Name meaning “Who is like God?” used of 10 men in Scripture and also of one who is described as an archangel.
michah: KJV spelling of Micah, Uzziel’s son, in 1 Chronicles 24:24-25.
michaiah: 1. KJV spelling of Micaiah, Acbor’s father, in 2 Kings 22:12.
michal: Younger daughter of Saul. She fell in love with David after his defeat of Goliath (18:20).
michmash: Town in southern Mt Ephraim near the edge of the wilderness that descends eastward toward the Jordan Valley. Though it must have been an Israelite settlement in the territory of Benjamin, it is absent from the list of Benjamite towns.
michmethath: Geographical location describing part of the boundary dividing the territory assigned to Ephraim and Manasseh’s tribes (17:7), situated in the mountains west of the Jordan, midway between the Dead Sea and the Sea of Galilee.
michri: Ancestor of a family who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian captivity. Also spelled Michri.
michtam: KJV rendering of miktam, a musical cue, in the titles of Psalms 16, 56, 57, 58, 59, and 60.
micmash: Town in southern Mt Ephraim near the edge of the wilderness that descends eastward toward the Jordan Valley. Though it must have been an Israelite settlement in the territory of Benjamin, it is absent from the list of Benjamite towns.
micmethath: Geographical location describing part of the boundary dividing the territory assigned to Ephraim and Manasseh’s tribes (17:7), situated in the mountains west of the Jordan, midway between the Dead Sea and the Sea of Galilee.
micri: Ancestor of a family who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian captivity. Also spelled Michri.
middin: One of the six cities in the wilderness west of the Dead Sea allotted to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance, located between Beth-arabah and Secacah.
midian, midianite: Person, place, or people, the latter living on the eastern edge of Gilead, Moab, and Edom south into northwest Arabia. They had few, if any, permanent settlements.
midrash: Transliteration into English of a Hebrew word that occurs twice in 2 Chronicles. Second Chronicles 13:22 refers to the literary source used for recording the reign of King Abijah of Judah (913–910 BC) as the “midrash” of the prophet Iddo.
migdal-el: One of the fortified cities belonging to Naphtali’s tribe.
migdal-gad: Village in Judah located in the Shephelah district of Lachish. It is perhaps identifiable with Khirbet el-Mejdeleh, southeast of Tell el-Nuweir.
migdol: Town in the eastern delta of Lower Egypt. In the narrative of the exodus it appears between the place called Pi-hahiroth and Baal-zephon.
migron: Site where Saul rested under a pomegranate tree, near Gibeah; also mentioned as part of the line of march of the Assyrians. The first reference is to a site south of Michmash, the second is probably north of Michmash.
mijamin: 1. Priest who ministered during the time of David.
mikloth: 1. Resident of Gibeon, son of the Benjamite Jeiel, and father of Shimeah.
mikneiah: Levite of the second order who was a gatekeeper and musician during David’s reign.
miktam: Title in Psalms 16 and 56–60 (see NIV), possibly also of Hezekiah’s recovery psalm, Isaiah 38:9. The precise meaning of the term is uncertain.
milalai: Participant in the dedication of the rebuilt Jerusalem wall.
milcah: 1. Daughter of Haran and half sister of Nahor who became Nahor’s wife.
milcom: National god of the Ammonites, better known as Molech or Moloch. Worship of this deity, which was accompanied by sacrificing children in the fire, was strictly prohibited to Israel.
mildew: Superficial growth produced on organic matter or living plants by fungi. Mildew was caused by a common fungus in Palestine, Puccinia graminis, and was regarded as divine punishment for disobedience.
mile: Measurement of distance. A Roman mile was somewhat shorter than the English mile.
miletum, miletus: Important Greek city located at the mouth of the Meander River. It was settled by Crete as early as 1339–1288 BC.
milk: Substances required by the body to sustain life, and the methods of making them edible. Food consumed in Bible times included bread, milk products, fruit, meat, and fish.
mill: Two circular stones (millstones) used in the grinding of grain.
millennium: Biblical term (taken from the Latin word meaning “a thousand”) referring to the thousand-year reign of Christ. The primary biblical context for the doctrine of the millennium is found in Revelation 20:1-6 (where the Greek word for thousand is used five times).
millet: Small-seeded grass grown for food and foliage.
millo: 1. Earthen embankment or fortification mentioned in Judges 9:6, 20.
mina: A twenty-ounce weight used in the measure of precious metals as well as other substances.
mind: One’s intellectual processes in a narrow sense or, more broadly, the sum total of a person’s mental and moral state of being. To the Hebrew way of thinking, there is no distinctive terminology for the concept of the mind.
minerals and metals: A “mineral” is a naturally occurring substance, normally an ore that must be mined and treated before the metal can be extracted. A “metal” is a chemical element such as iron or copper, which is free from contamination by other materials.
miniamin: 1. Levite who assisted Kore, the son of Imnah, with the distribution of the “contribution reserved for the Lord” among the priests in the cities of Judah.
minister, ministry: Official in the church whose qualifications are listed in 1 Timothy 3:2-7 and Titus 1:6-9.
minni: People mentioned in Jeremiah 51:27, along with Ararat and Ashkenaz, as aggressors against Babylon. The Minni first appear in Assyrian inscriptions during the reign of Shalmaneser III (858–824 BC), who pillaged and subdued the people.
minnith: One of the 10 cities conquered by Jephthah in his defeat of the Ammonites. The city was a center for the wheat trade.
mint: Sweet-smelling herb used in cooking and medicine.
miphkad, gate of: KJV translation for Muster Gate (“Inspection Gate,” NLT), a city gate in northeast Jerusalem, in Nehemiah 3:31.
miracle: A divine act by which God reveals himself to people. The classical definition of miracle assumes that it is contrary to natural law, but this is a misnomer for two reasons.
miriam: 1. Daughter of Amram and Jochebed and the sister of Aaron and Moses.
mirma, mirmah: Son of Shaharaim and Hodesh from Benjamin’s tribe.
mirror: Smooth surface for reflecting images. The word does not occur in the KJV, but the idea is there, translated from the Hebrew or Greek as “glass,” “glasses” or “looking glass.” Modern translations use the word “mirror.”
miscarriage: Spontaneous abortion of a nonviable fetus. It occurs in both human and animal pregnancies.
misgab: KJV translation for a place in Moab, rendered “the fortress” in the NLT.
mishael: 1. Uzziel’s son, who, with his brother Elzaphan, was summoned by Moses to remove the bodies of Nadab and Abihu after they were killed for defiling the altar of the Lord.
misham: Elpaal’s son from the tribe of Benjamin, who helped to build Ono and Lod with its towns.
misheal: KJV spelling of the Levitical town Mishal in Joshua 19:26.
mishma: 1. Son of Ishmael, Abraham’s grandson, and the father of an Arabian tribe.
mishmannah: Warrior from Gad’s tribe who joined David at Ziklag in his struggle against King Saul.
mishnah: Series of interpretations of the meaning of the law; according to rabbinic tradition, they were given when Moses received the law from God on Mt Sinai, and they were to be passed down in oral form.
mishraite: Descendant of Caleb and a member of Kiriath-jearim’s family from Judah’s tribe.
mispar, mispereth: One of the men who returned with Zerubbabel to Palestine following the Babylonian captivity; alternately called Mispereth in Nehemiah 7:7.
misrephoth-maim: One of the northernmost places to which the Israelites pursued the fleeing Canaanite armies defeated at the waters of Merom.
mite: Small bronze or copper coin worth only a fraction of a cent (Mk 12:42, KJV).
mithcah, mithkah: One of the temporary camping places of the Israelites during their wilderness wanderings. It was mentioned between Terah and Hashmonah.
mithna: Town of Joshaphat, one of David’s mighty warriors (1 Chr 11:43, NLT). Other translations describe him as “the Mithnite.”
mithredath: 1. Name of the treasurer of King Cyrus of Persia, who was given charge of the sacred vessels to give to the Judean prince Sheshbazzar as the exiles prepared to return to Jerusalem.
mitre: KJV translation for turban, a kind of headdress, worn by the high priest of Israel, in Exodus 28:4.
mitylene: Main city on the island of Lesbos in the Aegean Sea near the northwestern coast of Asia Minor. Mitylene was a seaport with two harbors.
mixed marriage: Marriages between Jews and Gentiles. Marriages to the original inhabitants of Canaan were forbidden lest Israel become idolatrous (Dt 7:1-5; cf. 2 Cor 6:14).
mizar: Small hill apparently situated in northern Palestine on the Transjordan plateau near Mt Hermon.
mizpah: Name meaning “watchtower” in Hebrew (alternately spelled Mizpeh) used to designate a number of different locations mentioned in the OT and Apocrypha.
mizpar: KJV spelling of Mispar in Ezra 2:2.
mizraim: Hebrew word for the land of Egypt and/or its people, though some scholars suggest that Mizraim refers to a site either on the Edomite border or in northern Syria.
mizzah: Reuel’s son and a chief of an Edomite clan.
mnason: Name of a Christian in Jerusalem. He is identified as a native of the island of Cyprus and a disciple of long standing.
moab, moabites: Name of a small kingdom in central Transjordan and also its inhabitants. The land of Moab was situated on the high plateau immediately east of the Dead Sea; the escarpment of the Jordan Rift formed an effective boundary between Moab and Judah.
moabite stone: Longest literary source outside the OT dealing with the history of the region of Palestine and Transjordan during the period of 1300–600 BC.
moadiah: Head of a family of postexilic priests, whose house was headed by Piltai during the days of Joiakim the high priest; alternately called Maadiah in verse 5.
modius: Dry measure equivalent to about one peck.
moladah: One of the cities belonging to Judah’s tribe, later assigned to Simeon. The people of Judah resettled that area after the exile.
molech: Ammonite god worshiped with human sacrifice.
molid: Son of Abishur and Abihail from Judah’s tribe.
moloch: Alternate spelling of Molech, an Ammonite god.
molten sea: Alternate name for the laver in King Solomon’s temple in 1 Kings 7:23.
money: Medium of exchange, measurement of value, means of payment.
money changer: Ancient profession that undertook many of the services performed by the modern banker, particularly in the area of exchanging the currency of one country or province into that of another, or of exchanging small coins for coins of greater value or vice versa.
monotheism: Belief that there is only one God.
monster: Term designating various creatures of the water.
month: Systematic arrangements showing the beginning and length of each year and its division into days, weeks, and months. The modern calendar is usually taken for granted.
moon: Lesser luminary of the heavens. Many Semitic languages use the same word for moon as the Hebrew.
moon, new: Systematic arrangements showing the beginning and length of each year and its division into days, weeks, and months. The modern calendar is usually taken for granted.
morasthite: KJV designation for the prophet Micah, taken from the name of the town Moresheth.
moreh, hill of: Hill close to the valley of Jezreel, near which the Midianites camped when they were attacked by Gideon. It was probably called by this name because it was the location of a sanctuary where divination was practiced.
moreh, oak of: Abraham’s first recorded stopping place upon entering Palestine after leaving Mesopotamia. Here he built an altar to God.
moresheth-gath: Town in the lowland country of Judah included in Micah’s lament; perhaps the same as Moresheth, Micah’s hometown. The “gath” in Moresheth-gath suggests that the town was in close proximity to the major Philistine city by that name.
moriah: Name used twice in the OT. Abraham was sent to sacrifice his son Isaac in “the land of Moriah”.
morning sacrifice: Major ritual expressions of religious life with accompanying rites, such as libations, effusions, and sacred meals. The ideology expressed in Israel’s ritual complex made its religion unique in the ancient Near East.
morning star: Literally, Venus. The phrase is closely related to the idea of the “dayspring” and the “daystar”.
mortar, the: Name given by Zephaniah to a hollow place or depression resembling a mortar in Jerusalem. The “mortar” (Hebrew, Maktesh) was a place of business whose merchants were soon to grieve for their loss of trade.
moserah, moseroth: Temporary camping place of the Israelites during their wilderness wanderings. It was positioned between Hashmonah and Bene-jaakan.
moses: Great leader of the Hebrew people who brought them out of bondage in Egypt to the Promised Land in Canaan; also the one who gave them the law at Mt Sinai that became the basis for their religious faith through the centuries.
moses, books of: Fifth book of the OT, and last of the Pentateuch (the five books of the Law). In it Moses restated to the people of Israel various laws and precepts of the covenant that God had revealed to them at Mt Sinai.
moses, law of: Arrangement between two parties involving mutual obligations; especially the arrangement that established the relationship between God and his people, expressed in grace first with Israel and then with the church.
moses, song of: One of two archaic poems: the Blessing of Moses and the Song of Moses (ch 32). The Song of the Sea is set at a much earlier period of Moses’ life, while these two poems are virtually his “last will and testament.”
moses' seat: Biblical expression occurring only in Matthew 23:2, where Jesus speaks of the scribes and the Pharisees as having sat down on the seat of Moses.
most holy place: Inner room of the tabernacle and temple in which the ark of the covenant was kept.
mote: Term used in the KJV to describe a small particle lodged in the eye of a “brother”. More recent translations prefer the term “speck.”
moth: Winged insect noted for its destruction of clothes while it is in the larval stage.
mount, mountain: Elevated topographical feature. In Israel, as in surrounding countries, mountains were places where people expected to meet God.
mount ebal: Mountain just over 3,000 feet (914.4 meters) high in the central hill country of Israel. Mt Gerizim is usually mentioned with it.
mount gaash: 1. Mountain about 20 miles (32.2 kilometers) southwest of Shechem.
mount gerizim: Mountain (modern Jebel et-Tor) from which the blessings were to be pronounced, just as the cursings were to come from Mt Ebal.
mount hermon: Mountain often mentioned as the northern extremity of the territory conquered by Joshua and Moses in Transjordan; it is also the northern boundary of the inheritance of the half-tribe of Manasseh as well as of Israel in general.
mount hor: 1. Mountain located at the border of the land of Edom.
mount horeb: Name of the mountain where God met Moses and gave him the Ten Commandments and the rest of the law.
mount nebo: Name of a high mountain on the east side of the Jordan River opposite the city of Jericho. The Israelites encamped near it on the last stage of their journey to the Promised Land.
mount of assembly: KJV translation for “mount of assembly,” the name of a mountain that figured in Babylonian and Canaanite mythology, in Isaiah 14:13.
mount of corruption: Southern end of the Mt of Olives, called “corruption” because King Solomon built idols there for his foreign wives.
mount of olives: Prominent ridge running north-south in the Judean mountains, lying due east of Jerusalem and the Kidron Valley. Three summits with two intervening valleys distinguish the mountain.
mount of the amalekites: An area near Pirathon in Ephraim, probably about six miles (9.6 kilometers) west of Shechem. It is mentioned in the Hebrew Bible but not in the Greek manuscripts of the OT.
mount of the amorites: Central mountainous region between the plains of Philistia, Sharon, and Phoenicia on the west and the valley of the Jordan on the east.
mount of the beatitudes: Place where Jesus delivered the Sermon on the Mount.
mount of the congregation: KJV translation for “mount of assembly,” the name of a mountain that figured in Babylonian and Canaanite mythology, in Isaiah 14:13.
mount sinai: Name of the mountain where God met Moses and gave him the Ten Commandments and the rest of the law.
mount tabor: Important hill in lower Galilee located in the northeast area of the Jezreel Valley. About six miles (9.7 kilometers) east of Nazareth, Tabor rises abruptly from the valley floor.
mourning: Established ritual for grieving, observed by a dead person’s relatives and friends. It began with the closing of the eyes of the dead, the embracing of the body (50:1), and its preparation for burial.
mouse: Small rodent considered unclean by the law.
moza: 1. Caleb’s son by his concubine Ephah.
mozah: Town in the territory assigned to Benjamin’s tribe; tentatively identified with the village of Qalunyah. It has been suggested that the name is preserved in the modern Khirbet beit Mizza, a small village about four miles (6.4 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem.
mulberry: Tree with a darkish blue edible berry.
mule: Offspring of a male ass and a female horse.
muppim: One of Benjamin’s 10 sons. He is elsewhere called Shephupham and Shuppim and is perhaps identifiable with Shephuphan.
murder, murderer: Civil law deals with private disputes between individuals occasioned by debt, divorce, inheritance, or other relationships. In contrast, criminal law deals with crimes such as murder, treason, or theft.
mushi, mushite: Son of Merari, the grandson of Levi, and Mahli’s brother. He was the father of Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth and the founder of the family of Mushites.
music: A natural human expression that probably began with speech-singing and developed into songs, which were then accompanied by instruments.
musical instruments: Stringed, wind, and percussion instruments used to make music.
musician: A natural human expression that probably began with speech-singing and developed into songs, which were then accompanied by instruments.
mustard: Herb noted especially for its small seed.
muster gate: RSV translation for the Jerusalem gate located opposite the house of the temple servants and the merchants during the days of Nehemiah (Neh 3:31; KJV “Miphkad Gate”; NIV “Inspection Gate”). Its exact location is uncertain.
muteness: The inability to speak. Muteness, or aphasia, can be a momentary phenomenon or a permanent handicap.
myra: Port city on the southern coast of Asia Minor in the province of Lycia, identified with the modern Demre in Turkey.
myrrh: Fragrant gum resin obtained from various shrubs.
myrtle: Evergreen shrub with small leaves and scented flowers.
mysia: Region in northwest Asia Minor (modern Turkey). It had a long history, leading up to its annexation into the Roman Empire in 133 BC as part of the province of Asia.
mystery: Counsel, or secret plan, that God shares only with his people. In most biblical passages it relates to the wise counsel of God in his guidance of history to its destiny.
mystery of lawlessness: Phrase used by the apostle Paul to describe a lawless power or force threatening the world. The expression is found only in 2 Thessalonians 2:7 and must be considered in the light of its context.
naamah (person): 1. Daughter of Zillah and Lamech in the list of Cain’s descendants.
naamah (place): One of the 16 cities located in the Shephelah assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance, mentioned between Beth-dagon and Makkedah.
naaman: 1. Grandson of Benjamin and son of Bela, who gave his name to the Naamite clan.
naamathite: Resident of Naamah in northwest Arabia. Zophar, one of Job’s friends, was a Naamathite.
naamite: Descendant of Naaman, Bela’s son from Benjamin’s tribe.
naarah (person): One of Ashhur’s two wives, who bore him four sons.
naarah (place): City on the eastern border of Ephraim’s tribe, just north of Jericho; alternately called Naaran in 1 Chronicles 7:28. Josephus locates it near Jericho and associates it with abundant water supply in Archelaus’s day (Antiquities 17.13.1).
naarai: One of David’s mighty men (1 Chr 11:37, NLT mg); perhaps the same as Paari.
naaran: Alternate name for Naarah, an Ephraimite border town, in 1 Chronicles 7:28.
naarath: KJV spelling of Naarah, an Ephraimite border town, in Joshua 16:7.
naashon: KJV spelling of Nahshon, Amminadab’s son, in Exodus 6:23.
naasson: KJV form of Nahshon, Amminadab’s son, in Matthew 1:4 and Luke 3:32.
nabal: Wealthy, successful farmer of Maon in the southern wilderness of Judah. Unlike his godly forefather, Caleb, Nabal was hard of heart and wicked in all his ways.
nabataeans, nabateans: Inhabitants of an independent kingdom bordering Judea, which existed from 169 BC to AD 106.
naboth: Owner of a vineyard that Ahab, king of Israel, coveted (see the story in 1 Kgs 21). Ahab’s request was perhaps not unreasonable, and Naboth’s refusal may have been a little curt.
nachon: KJV spelling of Nacon in 2 Samuel 6:6.
nachor: KJV form of Nahor, Abraham’s ancestor, in Joshua 24:2 and Luke 3:34.
nacon: A place David passed when he brought the ark from Baale-judah (Kiriath-jearim) to Jerusalem. At the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah was struck dead for touching the ark.
nadab: 1. Eldest son of Aaron and Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab, who became one of Israel’s first priests together with his brothers and father.
naggai, nagge: Ancestor of Jesus, according to Luke’s genealogy (Lk 3:25, KJV “Nagge”).
nag hammadi manuscripts: A collection of 12 Coptic codices containing 52 tractates, or Gnostic documents.
nahalal: City in Zebulun’s territory, given to the Levites for an inheritance (21:35). Zebulun’s tribe was unable to drive the Canaanites from the city, so they forced them into hard labor (Jgs 1:30, “Nahalol”).
nahaliel: Temporary camping place for the Israelites during their wilderness wanderings, situated east of the Dead Sea in the vicinity of Moab between Mattanah and Bamoth.
nahallal: KJV spelling of Nahalal, a city of Zebulun, in Joshua 19:15.
nahalol: A city of Zebulun, in Judges 1:30.
naham: Judahite chief and the brother of Hodiah’s wife.
nahamani: One of the leading officials who returned with Zerubbabel to Palestine following the exile. His name is omitted in the parallel list of returning officials in Ezra 2:2.
naharai: One of David’s mighty warriors, who was also Joab’s armor bearer. Naharai was from the city of Beeroth.
nahash: 1. King of the Ammonites who laid siege to Jabesh-gilead during the days of Saul.
nahath: 1. Chief of a clan in Edom and Reuel’s firstborn son.
nahbi: Son of Vophsi; the head of Naphtali’s tribe and one of the 12 spies sent to search out the land of Canaan.
nahor (person): 1. Abraham’s grandfather; also an ancestor of Jesus according to Luke’s genealogy (Lk 3:34, where some English translations follow the Greek spelling, Nachor).
nahor (place): Northwestern Mesopotamian city; home of Rebekah, Isaac’s wife, and Nahor, Abraham’s brother. Nahor is frequently mentioned in the Mari documents (18th century BC) as the town of Nakhur, located near Haran in the Balikh River Valley.
nahshon: Amminadab’s son; brother of Elisheba and Salmon’s father. Nahshon, the prince of Judah’s tribe at the start of Israel’s wilderness wanderings, represented his kinsmen at the altar’s dedication (7:12).
nahum (person): 1. A prophet of Judah whose name means “consolation” or “consoler.” This name fits his message, as he wrote to encourage the people of Judah while they were being oppressed by the Assyrians.
nahum, book of: Seventh book in the canonical grouping of the 12 Minor Prophets. Its significance and importance lie in the strategic place it holds in delineating the plan and program of God in relationship to both Judah and the nations of the world.
nain: Village in southern Galilee near the border of Samaria. It is the location of the miracle in which Jesus brought a dead man back to life.
naioth: Place where David was given refuge from Saul. Here Samuel supervised a group of prophets.
names of god: God’s self-identifications expressing various aspects of his being.
names, significance of: In biblical times names were given in order to express something about a person, or to express something through him, and not simply to hang a convenient label around his neck. At least seven motivations appear in the choice of names:
nanea: Persian goddess mentioned in 2 Maccabees 1:13. In a temple to her in Elymais, a certain Antiochus was assassinated.
naomi: Wife of Elimelech and the mother of Mahlon and Chilion. A member of Judah’s tribe, she lived in Bethlehem during the period of the judges.
naphath-dor: Region or town identified with Dor, a site on the Mediterranean coast, in Joshua 12:23 and 1 Kings 4:11.
naphish: Eleventh of Ishmael’s 12 sons and the founder of a tribe that later went to war against the tribes of Israel living east of the Jordan.
naphoth-dor: Alternate form of Naphath-dor, a site on the Mediterranean coast, in Joshua 11:2.
naphtali (person): One of Jacob’s 12 sons. He was the second of two sons borne to Jacob by Bilhah, Rachel’s maid.
naphtali, mount of: Hill country comprising the majority of Naphtali’s territory, in which the town of Kedesh was set apart as a city of refuge.
naphtali, tribe of: One of the 12 tribes of Israel that migrated from Egypt to Canaan, ultimately settling in northern Canaan in the high country of Galilee.
naphtuhim, naphtuhites: Egyptian descendants of Noah through Ham’s line, listed between the Lehabim and Pathrusim tribes. Some scholars suggest that the Naphtuhim were the inhabitants of Middle Egypt, situated between the Libyans of Lower Egypt and the Pathrusim of Upper Egypt.
narcissus (person): Christian whose household knew the Lord and received greetings from Paul in his letter to Rome.
narcissus (plant): Fragrant plant growing profusely on the plains of Sharon.
nard: Perennial herb with strong, fragrant roots.
nathan: 1. Son of David by Bathsheba, the third son to be born in Jerusalem.
nathanael: Jew from Cana of Galilee whom Jesus called to be a disciple.
nathan-melech: Official during King Josiah’s reign. Horses for sun worship were kept near his quarters but were removed by Josiah.
nations: Groups formed on the basis of political or social interests or on kinship. Generally, the word “nations” implies peoples of the world other than the Hebrews, although it can also include the Jews.
natural man: Expression occurring in 1 Corinthians 2:14 (RSV mg). The adjective translated there by “natural” is also found in 1 Corinthians 15:44 (twice), 46; James 3:15; and Jude 1:19.
naum: KJV spelling of Nahum, an ancestor of Jesus.
nazarene: Native or inhabitant of Nazareth, a NT town in lower Galilee.
nazarenes: Name given to those who followed Jesus of Nazareth. Since Jesus was known as Jesus of Nazareth or Jesus the Nazarene, it was easy to transfer that title to his followers.
nazareth: Village in the Roman province of Galilee, the home of Joseph, Mary, and Jesus. Always small and isolated, Nazareth is not mentioned in the OT, the Apocrypha, intertestamental Jewish writings, or the histories of Josephus.
nazarite, nazirite: Person who was either chosen or consecrated for life or for a set period of time to complete a vow to God. The Nazirite (Nazarite) devoted himself to self-imposed discipline in order to perform some special service.
neapolis: Port city of Philippi, identified with modern Kavalla. Neapolis, whose name comes from a Greek word meaning “new city,” existed as early as the fifth century BC, and in Roman times was clearly dependent upon the city of Philippi.
neariah: 1. One of Shemaiah’s six sons and a descendant of David.
nebai: Political leader who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God with Nehemiah and others after the exile.
nebaioth: Firstborn of Ishmael’s 12 sons whose sister, Mahalath (also called Basemath, cf. Gn 36:3) later married Esau.
neballat: Town situated in the hills overlooking the southeastern region of the plain of Sharon, settled by Benjamites after the exile. It is identified with modern Beit Nebala, four miles (6.4 kilometers) east of Lod and two miles (3.2 kilometers) north of Hadid.
nebat: Ephraimite of Zeredah in the Jordan Valley, a servant to Solomon, and the father of King Jeroboam.
nebo (deity): Marduk’s son and a chief god among the Babylonian pantheon. Nebo (Hebrew spelling; pronounced Nabu in Akkadian) was the patron deity of wisdom, education, and literature.
nebo (person): Forefather of 52 descendants who returned with Zerubbabel to Judah following the exile, 7 of whom were encouraged by Ezra to divorce their foreign wives.
nebo (place): 1. City located on the pastoral tablelands of the Transjordan and desired by the sons of Gad and Reuben.
nebo, mount: Name of a high mountain on the east side of the Jordan River opposite the city of Jericho. The Israelites encamped near it on the last stage of their journey to the Promised Land.
nebuchadnezzar, nebuchadrezzar: Babylonian king (605–562 BC) who captured and destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC. He was the son of Nabopolassar and the foremost ruler of the Neo-Babylonian Empire (612–539 BC); his name is alternately spelled Nebuchadrezzar in Jeremiah and Ezekiel (see NLT mg).
nebushasban, nebushazban: Babylonian officer among those ordered to provide safety for Jeremiah after the Babylonians conquered Jerusalem.
nebuzaradan: Chief Babylonian official and captain of the bodyguard during Nebuchadnezzar’s reign (605–562 BC). Nebuzaradan was one of the officials whom Nebuchadnezzar authorized to oversee Jerusalem and Judah and the deportations of Jewish exiles to Babylon.
necklace: Decorated adornments. In the Bible, jewelry was used by both men and women.
necho, nechoh, neco, necoh: Pharaoh of the 26th dynasty of the Saite kings, who succeeded his father, Psammetichus, in 610 BC. Psammetichus had ruled 54 years over Egypt and was instrumental in the renewal of archaic art forms and in the revival of religious fervor.
necromancer, necromancy: Practice of communicating with the dead; a practice strictly forbidden by the law.
nedabiah: Son of Jeconiah (NLT “Jehoiachin”), king of Judah.
needle: Object used in Jesus’ lesson about the rich man and entrance into God’s kingdom.
negeb, negev: Southernmost region of Palestine. The name comes from the root “to be dry, parched,” although its basic meaning is “south country, south.” It is an area with no precise geographical boundaries.
neginah, neginoth: Hebrew terms in the superscriptions of Psalms 4, 6, 54–55, 61, 67 and 76 (KJV); musical cues, meaning “stringed instruments,” describing the kind of musical accompaniment for the performance of the designated psalms.
nehelamite: Ancestral name or the geographical designation for Shemaiah the false prophet. Its derivation is unknown.
nehemiah (person): Name of three men mentioned in the OT after the period of the exile. The name means “the Lord comforts” and was appropriate for this time of hope and fulfillment.
nehemiah, book of: One of the last of the Jewish historical books.
nehiloth: Hebrew term in the superscription of Psalm 5 (KJV); musical cue, meaning “flutes,” describing the kind of musical accompaniment for the performance of the psalm.
nehum: One of the men listed in Nehemiah 7:7 who returned with Zerubbabel to Palestine following the Babylonian captivity. His name is alternately spelled Rehum in Ezra 2:2.
nehushta: Mother of Jehoiachin, king of Judah, who was deported with her son to Babylon.
nehushtan: Name given to the bronze serpent that Moses made during the wilderness wanderings. At the time of King Hezekiah’s reforms, it was destroyed.
neiel: Border town in Asher’s territory. Its site is perhaps identifiable with modern Khirbet Ya’nin, on the east end of the plain of Acco.
neighbor: Concept apparently limited in the OT period and late Judaism to one’s fellow Israelite, or member of the covenant, and extended by Jesus to include anyone encountered in life.
nekeb: KJV rendering of a town defining the boundary of the territory allotted to Naphtali’s tribe for an inheritance, positioned between Za-anannim and Jabneel.
nekoda: 1. Father of a family of temple servants who returned to Jerusalem following the exile.
nemuel: 1. Reubenite and the son of Eliab.
nemuelite: Member of Nemuel’s family from Simeon’s tribe (Nm 26:12; alternately called Jemuel in Gn 46:10).
nepheg: 1. Levite of the family of Kohath and the second of Izhar’s three sons.
nephilim: Early group of the human race, mentioned only twice in the OT (Gn 6:4; Nm 13:33; NLT mg). The Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures (the Septuagint) rendered the name “Nephilim” as “giants,” and other versions followed this rendering, including the KJV.
nephish: KJV spelling of Naphish, Ishmael’s son.
nephishesim, nephisim: A group of people who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile, counted among the temple servants.
nephthalim: KJV rendering of Naphtali’s tribe in Matthew 4:13, 15.
nephtoah, waters of: Geographical landmark situated between Mt Ephron to the west and the valley of Hinnom to the east, defining part of the boundary separating the tribes of Judah and Benjamin.
nephushesim, nephusim, nephussim: Alternate spellings of Nephisim in Ezra 2:50, Nehemiah 7:52.
nepthalim: KJV rendering of Naphtali’s tribe in Revelation 7:6.
ner: Benjamite, father of Abner and brother of Kish; he was probably the uncle of Saul. Although Ner’s father’s name was given as Abiel, disputed readings put Ner among the sons of Jeiel.
nereus: Roman Christian to whom Paul sent greetings in the salutation of his letter to Rome.
nergal: Heathen deity worshiped by the men of Cuth after the fall of Israel in 722 BC. Nergal, lord of the netherworld and associated with the sun god, was the city god of the northern Babylonian city of Cuthah (cf. v 24).
nergal-sharezer: Babylonian prince who held the title “Rabmag.” Nergal-sharezer participated with Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldean army in conquering Jerusalem after a three-year siege from 588 to 586 BC and later entrusted Jeremiah to Gedaliah’s care (v 13).
neri: Ancestor of Jesus in Luke’s genealogy.
neriah: Father of Baruch the scribe and Seraiah the quartermaster (51:59), both of whom served Jeremiah the prophet.
net: Those who caught fish for a living. Fishing was carried on by fishermen in the Holy Land from early times and is referred to in both the OT and the NT.
netaim: Habitation of the potters who were employed in the king’s service.
nethaneel, nethanel: Common OT name spelled Nethaneel in the KJV.
nethaniah: 1. Elishama’s son, father of Ishmael and a member of the royal family of Judah.
nethinim: Term appearing only in the books written after Israel’s return from exile (1 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah).
netophah, netophathite: Home and designation for two of David’s thirty mighty men. Seraiah, one of the captains who came to Gedaliah, the governor in Jerusalem after its fall to Babylon in 586 BC, was a Netophathite.
nettle: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
new: That which has just been made or come into existence—often replacing that which already existed, thereby turning the old into new.
new birth: Spiritual rebirth producing a new beginning. It describes the new life of the believer in Christ and the new order that will begin at Christ’s return.
new commandment: Expression used by Jesus to designate his teaching concerning the love of Christians for each other.
new covenant: Expression used by Jesus (Lk 22:20; cf. Jer 31:31) to designate the meaning of his death.
new creation, new creature: Concept of redemption developed throughout the OT and NT to its final consummation in the second coming of Jesus Christ.
new gate: One of the gates of the temple during Jeremiah’s ministry.
new heavens and new earth: Concept of a new or renewed universe first found in the book of Isaiah. God declares, “For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind. . . .
new jerusalem: Phrase appearing only twice in the Bible, once near the beginning and once near the end of the book of Revelation. In the first of the great visions of that book, the risen Christ speaks to his people in the midst of their conflict in this world.
new man, new person: Expression used by the apostle Paul to refer to Jesus Christ and his body, the church.
new moon: Monthly celebration involving grain offerings, burnt sacrifices, and trumpet blasts.
new testament: Derived from the Greek biblia (“books”), which, though plural, came to be used as a singular noun and to stand for the collection of books known as the Scriptures. The idea of a collection of holy writings developed early in Hebrew-Christian thought.
new testament canon: Those books in the Jewish and Christian Bible considered to be Scripture and therefore authoritative in matters of faith and doctrine.
new testament chronology: Branch of biblical studies that attempts to discover the sequence of NT events and the amount of time that elapsed between them. Chronology is essential to historians, whose task it is to determine the causes and effects of past events.
neziah: Forefather of a family of temple servants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel following the Babylonian captivity.
nezib: One of the cities in the lowland allotted to Judah for an inheritance. Its site is identified with modern Khirbet Beit Nesib, east of Lachish.
nibhaz: The name of a god worshiped by displaced Avvites after they were forcibly resettled in Samaria by the Assyrians in 722 BC. They brought the worship of this idol, as well as that of Tartak, with them at that time.
nibshan: One of the six cities in the wilderness allotted to Judah for an inheritance.
nicanor: 1. The son of Patroclus, “one of the king’s chief friends” and a Syrian general under Antiochus IV Epiphanes and Demetrius Soter.
nicodemus: Pharisee and member of the Sanhedrin mentioned only in John’s Gospel. According to John 3, Nicodemus came to Jesus at night and acknowledged him as a teacher sent by God.
nicolaitans: Heretical sect in the early church that is mentioned by name twice in the book of Revelation.
nicolas, nicolaus: One of the seven men named in Acts 6:5, who was enlisted for service in the Jerusalem church in its early days. His duty as specified in Acts 6:1-4 was to direct the fair and equal distribution of food.
nicopolis: Name meaning “Victory City,” a popular choice in the Roman Empire when a newly founded city required a name, especially when a newly built town was created to commemorate some military victory in days of warfare.
niger: Surname of Simeon, one of the leaders in the church at Antioch.
night: Word in Scripture denoting that time of darkness from dusk until dawn when no light of the sun is visible. For example, Joseph took Mary and Jesus to Egypt by night.
night hag: Designation for a bird of the wasteland.
night hawk: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
night monster: Designation for a bird of the wasteland.
nile river: Life-giving river of Egypt in northeast Africa. Perhaps no other river has been so vital to the history of the nation through which it flows.
nimrah: Alternate rendering of Beth-nimrah, a city in Moab, in Numbers 32:3.
nimrim, waters of: One of the places in the southern extremity of Moab denounced by Isaiah and Jeremiah in their oracles of judgment against the nation.
nimrod: Cush’s son and grandson of Ham the son of Noah. He is described as “the first man of might on earth” and “a mighty hunter”.
nimshi: Father of Jehoshaphat and grandfather of Jehu, who was king of Israel.
nineveh, ninevite: One of the capitals of the Assyrian Empire and, at the height of that empire, one of the great cities of the world.
nisan: Babylonian name for a Hebrew month.
nisroch: The god of King Sennacherib, in whose temple at Nineveh the king was assassinated by Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons. Nisroch was the city god of Nineveh, the chief capital of the Assyrian Empire; he was perhaps identical with the Assyrian god Nusku.
no: KJV form of Thebes in Nahum 3:8.
noadiah: 1. Binnui’s son and one of the two Levites present when the temple treasure that was brought back to Jerusalem by Ezra was weighed and recorded.
noah: 1. Son of Lamech and the grandson of Methuselah, a descendant of Seth, third son of Adam.
no-amon: Alternate reading for No, the Hebrew name for Thebes, capital of upper Egypt (Na 3:8, NLT mg).
nob: City located on the eastern slopes of Mt Scopus opposite the Mt of Olives and northeast of Jerusalem. An important religious center, 86 priests resided there, as did the ephod.
nobah (person): Manassite who conquered and settled the town of Kenath, east of the Jordan, and subsequently renamed it after himself.
nobah (place): 1. Town east of the Jordan, previously named Kenath, allotted to Nobah the Manassite for an inheritance, at which time he called it Nobah after his own name.
nod: Land east of Eden to which Cain went after he murdered his brother Abel.
nodab, nodabites: Forefather of an Arabian tribe that joined forces with the Hagarites to fight against the tribes of Israel who were living east of the Jordan. Though not included in the list of Ishmael’s sons (cf.
noe: KJV rendering of Noah in Matthew 24:37-38 and Luke 3:36; 17:26-27.
nogah: One of 13 sons of David born in Jerusalem after David established his kingdom.
nohah (place): Place west of Gibeah in Benjamin’s territory (Jgs 20:43, RSV). Other translations consider Nohah (meaning “quiet”) an adverb and translate it accordingly, “with ease” (KJV), because no town by that name is known.
non: KJV form of Nun, Joshua’s father, in 1 Chronicles 7:27.
noph: KJV translation of the Hebrew word for Memphis (Egypt).
nophah: Place delineating the boundaries between Israel and the Moabites and Amorites. Some scholars equate Nophah with the Nobah of Judges 8:11.
north, north country: Cardinal point on a compass opposite the south, often having the connotation of “dark,” perhaps because the north side is often in shadow.
northeaster: Name given to the stormy wind of Acts 27:14, encountered by Paul on his journey to Rome. Against his advice, the ship weighed anchor from a harbor near Lasea.
not loved, not pitied: Symbolic name given by the prophet Hosea to his daughter as a warning of the coming judgment of God upon Israel.
not my people: Symbolic name given by the prophet Hosea to his third son as a warning of the coming judgment of God upon Israel.
numbers and numerology: Individual numbers have a symbolic as well as a literal sense in the Bible. In Daniel, and to a lesser extent in Revelation, there is a developed system of numerology where interrelated systems of numbers are used in a definite pattern.
numbers, book of: Fourth book of the English Bible. Its title is the English translation of the Latin Vulgate title, Numeri.
numenius: Son of Antiochus, a Jewish diplomat sent first by Jonathan, and later by Simon the Hasmonean to Rome and Sparta to strengthen alliances.
nun: Ephraimite, Elishama’s son, and the father of Joshua, the great leader of Israel.
nurse: A woman who took care of an infant that did not belong to her, or a man who took care of young children. The work was limited to the nursing and caring of an infant.
nurture: KJV rendition of a Greek word (paideia, Eph 6:4) better translated as “discipline.” See Discipline.
nut: Substances required by the body to sustain life, and the methods of making them edible. Food consumed in Bible times included bread, milk products, fruit, meat, and fish.
nuzi, nuzi tablets: Town in northeastern Mesopotamia, about nine miles (14.5 kilometers) southwest of present-day Kirkuk. In ancient times the site was called Gasur, but the modern name is Yorgan Tepe.
nympha: Christian woman living in Laodicea (or perhaps Colossae), in whose house believers gathered for worship. Paul sent greetings to her and the church (Col 4:15, KJV uses the masculine form “Nymphas”).
oak: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
oak of the pillar: Sacred meeting place in Shechem where the citizens of that city and the inhabitants of Beth-millo made Abimelech king (Jgs 9:6, ASV, NAS). It is perhaps identifiable with the Oak of Moreh.
oak of weeping: Tree near Bethel under which Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, was buried, hence called Allon-bacuth, meaning “Oak of Weeping.”
oak of zaanannim: Site regarded as a border point in the territory of Naphtali.
oaks of mamre: Site associated with Abraham and Isaac.
oath: Solemn vow or promise to fulfill a pledge. There are two terms in Hebrew that mean “oath”: ‘ala and sebu’a.
obadiah, book of: Fourth book of the Minor Prophets; shortest book in the OT.
obal: Alternate spelling of Ebal, Joktan’s descendant, in Genesis 10:28.
obed: 1. Ruth and Boaz’s first child, listed among the ancestors of Jesus.
obed-edom: 1. Man under whose care David placed the ark of the covenant when he was transferring it from Gibeah to Jerusalem.
obedience: Act or instance of submitting to the restraint or command of an authority; compliance with the demands or requests of someone over us. The general words for obedience in both Hebrew and Greek refer to hearing or hearkening to a superior authority.
obil: Ishmaelite steward of King David’s camels.
oblation: Major ritual expressions of religious life with accompanying rites, such as libations, effusions, and sacred meals. The ideology expressed in Israel’s ritual complex made its religion unique in the ancient Near East.
oboth: Temporary camping place of the Israelites during their wilderness wanderings, mentioned between Punon and Iye-abarim.
ochran: Father of Pagiel, the leader of Asher’s tribe during the wilderness journeys.
ocina: A town on the coast south of Tyre. Its location is uncertain, and it has been identified with both Sandaliam and Acco.
ocran: Father of Pagiel, the leader of Asher’s tribe during the wilderness journeys.
offend, offense: Words used two ways in the Bible: doing what is wrong oneself, or causing someone else to do wrong or to stumble.
offerings and sacrifices: Major ritual expressions of religious life with accompanying rites, such as libations, effusions, and sacred meals. The ideology expressed in Israel’s ritual complex made its religion unique in the ancient Near East.
officers in the church: Official in the church whose qualifications are listed in 1 Timothy 3:2-7 and Titus 1:6-9.
og: King whose fame partly came from his being a giant. “King Og of Bashan was the last of the giant Rephaites.
ohad: Simeon’s son, whose name does not appear in the list of Numbers 26:12-14.
ohel: Descendant of Jehoiakim and King David.
oholah and oholibah: Names given to the northern kingdom (KJV “Aholah”), with its capital at Samaria, and to the southern kingdom (KJV “Aholibah”), with its capital at Jerusalem, respectively, by Ezekiel in his allegory depicting the unfaithfulness of God’s people.
oholiab: Man assigned by Moses to assist Bezalel, the master craftsman, in the construction and ornamentation of the tabernacle. Son of Ahisamach and member of Dan’s tribe, Oholiab was specifically noted as a designer and embroiderer.
oholibamah: 1. Esau’s wife, the daughter of Anah the Hivite (Gn 36:2, 5, 14, 18, 25, KJV “Aholibamah”), who bore to him Jeush, Jalam, and Korah before Esau left Canaan for Seir.
oil: Substance most commonly produced from the olive berry, although the word could also apply to oil of myrrh.
oil, anointing: To pour oil or ointment onto a person or object in a ritualistic fashion.
oil tree: Small tree bearing an olivelike fruit that yields a medicinal oil.
ointment: Various preparations, generally of a spicy nature with an oil base. In Palestine, olive oil was the chief base of ointments and was itself considered an ointment.
old gate: Jerusalem gate repaired by Joiada and Meshullam under Nehemiah’s supervision, and subsequently mentioned in the northerly route traveled by one of the companies of celebrants during the Jerusalem wall’s dedication (12:39).
old man: Biblical terms used to describe the state of man in relation to Christ. Human beings are created in the image of God and are made to have fellowship with him.
old testament: Derived from the Greek biblia (“books”), which, though plural, came to be used as a singular noun and to stand for the collection of books known as the Scriptures. The idea of a collection of holy writings developed early in Hebrew-Christian thought.
old testament canon: Those books in the Jewish and Christian Bible considered to be Scripture and therefore authoritative in matters of faith and doctrine.
old testament chronology: Branch of biblical studies that attempts to assign dates and sequences to OT events. Chronology is a science.
old testament quotations in the new test: Old Testament Quotations in the New Testament
OT passages cited or alluded to in the NT writings.
olive, olive tree: During Bible times agriculture took the same three main forms found in Palestine today. Emphasis on each of these has depended upon the social and technological status of the people.
olives, mount of: Prominent ridge running north-south in the Judean mountains, lying due east of Jerusalem and the Kidron Valley. Three summits with two intervening valleys distinguish the mountain.
olivet: Prominent ridge running north-south in the Judean mountains, lying due east of Jerusalem and the Kidron Valley. Three summits with two intervening valleys distinguish the mountain.
olympas: Member of the church in Rome to whom Paul sent personal greetings.
olympian zeus, temple of: Name given to the temple of Jerusalem by Antiochus Epiphanes in 168 BC when he turned the holy place into a shrine for the chief of the pagan gods of Greece. Jews were forced to abandon ancestral customs and could no longer observe God’s law.
omar: Second son of Eliphaz, grandson of Esau and the great-grandson of Abraham; an Edomite clan chief.
omega: English spelling of the name of the last letter of the Greek alphabet.
omen: Natural sign or occurrence prefiguring the outcome of a future event. Augury was listed among the abominable pagan practices forbidden to Israel.
omer: Measuring unit used in gathering manna.
omnipotence: God’s unlimited authority to bring into existence or cause to happen whatsoever he wills.
omnipresence: Aspect of God’s infinity in which he transcends the limitations of space and is present in all places at all times.
omniscience: God’s infinite knowledge and understanding of things past, present, and future.
omri: 1. King of Israel who first appears in Scripture as general of the army during the reign of Elah, king of Israel.
on (person): Reubenite, Peleth’s son who joined Korah’s rebellion against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness.
on (place): Hebrew name for Heliopolis, an Egyptian city.
onam: 1. Grandson of Seir and Shobal’s fifth son.
onan: Second son of Judah and a Canaanitess named Shua. Judah forced him to enter into a levirate marriage with Tamar, the wife of his deceased brother, Er.
onesimus: Slave on whose behalf Paul wrote the Letter to Philemon. A slave of Philemon, he had robbed his master and run away from him.
onesiphorus: Christian who took care of Paul during his confinement in Ephesus. After Paul’s transfer to Rome, Onesiphorus eagerly sought him out and ministered to him there.
onias: Onias is the family name of four high priests in the intertestamental period. They were descendants of Zadok, the high priest in Solomon’s reign.
onion: Substances required by the body to sustain life, and the methods of making them edible. Food consumed in Bible times included bread, milk products, fruit, meat, and fish.
only begotten: Phrase deeply entrenched in Christian language as descriptive of Jesus. The word traditionally translated “only begotten” does not carry the idea of birth at all.
ono: Benjaminite town built by Shemed. Some of its inhabitants returned to Palestine with Zerubbabel following the exile.
onycha: One of the sweet spices used in the sacred incense of the tabernacle. Its identification is uncertain.
onyx: Semiprecious stone used on the breastplate of the high priest.
ophel: 1. Hill or mound in Samaria where Elisha’s house stood.
ophir (person): Joktan’s son and a descendant of Shem through Arphaxad’s line.
ophir (place): Place to which Solomon sent a fleet of merchant ships to bring back gold and all sorts of precious and exotic products. The location of Ophir is not certain; most scholars place it in southwest Arabia.
ophni: Village allotted to Benjamin after Israel had taken possession of Palestine. Its precise location is unknown, but some early writers suggest the town of Gophna (modern Jifna) on the highway from Samaria to Jerusalem, a day’s march north of Gibeah.
ophrah (place): 1. City in Benjamin, probably identical with Ephraim (2 Sm 13:23; 2 Chr 13:19, “Ephron”; Jn 11:54).
oracle: Divine revelation communicated through God’s spokesperson (prophet, priest, or king), usually pronouncing blessing, instruction, or judgment. Contrary to Balak’s request for Balaam to curse Israel, Balaam spoke an oracle of blessing.
ordain, ordination: The act of officially investing someone with religious authority.
oreb: One of two Midianite chieftains (the other being Zeeb) put to death by men from Ephraim’s tribe. The occasion for this execution was Gideon’s surprise attack on the Midianite encampment at the hill of Moreh in the valley of Jezreel.
oreb, rock of: Place where the Ephraimites killed the Midianite chieftain Oreb.
oren: Descendant of Judah and the third son of Jerahmeel.
organ: KJV mistranslation for pipe in Genesis 4:21, Job 21:12, 30:31, and Psalm 150:4.
orion: Septuagint name for a constellation widely believed to resemble a giant hunter, belted or fettered.
ornan: Alternate rendering of Araunah, the Jebusite, in 1 Chronicles 21:15 (NLT mg).
orontes: River of the Great Rift Valley, flowing northward from the watershed and reaching the Mediterranean at Seleucia Pieria, the harbor city for Antioch.
orpah: Woman of Moab who married Chilion, son of Elimelech and Naomi. After her husband and sons died, Naomi decided to return to Judah.
orphan: Word coming from a Hebrew root meaning “to be alone” or “bereaved,” often rendered as “fatherless.” The idea describes any person who is without legal standing in the covenant community of Israel, who is unprotected or needy, and who is especially exposed to oppression.
orthosia: A city north of Tripolis in Phoenicia to which the Syrian usurper Trypho fled after being defeated by Antiochus VII Sidetes during the time of Simon Maccabeus.
oshea: KJV form of Hoshea, the alternate name for Joshua, in Numbers 13:8, 16.
osiris: Egypt figured significantly as a stage on which the biblical narrative was enacted. Here Abraham lived in time of famine.
osnapper: Aramaic name for the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal (Ezr 4:10, NLT mg).
ospray, osprey: Large predatory bird, also known as the black vulture, considered unclean (Lv 11:13; Dt 14:12, NLT).
ossifrage: Largest of the vulture family, also known as the bearded vulture, considered ceremonially unclean (Lv 11:13; Dt 14:12, KJV).
ossuary: A small stone coffin (Latin, ossuarium), vase, or casket for the reception of the calcined remains of the dead, or a sepulchral house, where the bones of the dead were deposited. Sarcophagus was the name given by the Greeks and Romans to a big stone coffin.
ostrich: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
othni: Levite; Shemaiah’s son and a gatekeeper in Solomon’s temple.
