othniel: Judge of Israel, mentioned as the son of Kenaz and Caleb’s nephew (or perhaps brother), who delivered Israel from the tyranny of Cushan-rishathaim, and who earlier distinguished himself by capturing Debir.
outcast: English translation of two related Hebrew terms whose primary meanings are to push away, banish, or cast out. In five of seven passages the term refers to exiles from Israel who are to be regathered by the Lord.
outward man: Part of a person outwardly observed.
oven: Substances required by the body to sustain life, and the methods of making them edible. Food consumed in Bible times included bread, milk products, fruit, meat, and fish.
ovens, tower of the: Structure in the Jerusalem wall restored by Nehemiah and his workmen after the exile. Malkijah, son of Harim, and Hasshub, son of Pahath-moab, are named as its builders.
overseer: Word appearing 12 times in the OT (KJV) and once in the NT.
owl: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
ox: Domestic animals of the bovine species (Bos primigenius). The OT often emphasized the beauty of cattle.
ox (person): Descendant of Israel, grandfather of Judith, the heroine of Maccabean times.
ozem: 1. Sixth son of Jesse and a descendant of Hezron.
ozias: KJV rendering of Uzziah, king of Judah in Matthew 1:8-9.
oziel: Ancestor of Judith, the heroine of Maccabean times.
ozni, oznite: Alternate names for Ezbon and his descendants.
paarai: One of David’s mighty men, said to be from Arba, in Judah; perhaps the same as Naarai the son of Ezbai.
pace (measure): Linear measure equivalent to the average distance of a man’s stride, or about one yard (.9 meter).
paddan, paddan-aram: Northwestern Mesopotamian district whose name means “Field of Aram,” distinguishing this flatland from the mountainous regions to the north and east.
padon: Forefather of a family of temple servants who returned with Zerubbabel to Palestine following the Babylonian captivity.
pagans: The non-Jewish nations, known as goyim in Hebrew and ethnoi in Greek. According to the OT perspective, there are but two categories of people, the Jews (God’s elect) and the nations.
pagiel: Ocran’s son from Asher’s tribe, who was appointed by Moses to help number the people in the wilderness. He also served as leader of his tribe during that time.
pahath-moab: Head of a family of Israelites who returned with Zerubbabel to Palestine after the Babylonian captivity. Other members of his family, about 200 men, came with Ezra.
pai: Alternate form of Pau, an Edomite city, in 1 Chronicles 1:50 (see NLT mg).
palace: Residence for royalty. Excavations suggest that any city that enjoyed royal patronage would boast of a building that could be described as a palace.
palace of the forest of lebanon: Palace of the Forest of Lebanon
Name for Solomon’s palace in Jerusalem, adjacent to the temple, given this designation because of the amount of Lebanese cedar used in its construction.
palaestra: Greek word designating a place for athletic exercise.
palal: Uzai’s son, who helped rebuild the Jerusalem wall in Nehemiah’s day.
palestina: KJV rendering of Philistia, a country along the southwest coast of Canaan, in Exodus 15:14 and Isaiah 14:29-31.
palestine: Country on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean Sea, also known as Canaan and Israel.
pallu, palluite: Reuben’s son, father of Eliab and the founder of the Palluite family.
palm: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
palmerworm: KJV designation for the cutting locust in Joel 1:4, 2:25, and Amos 4:9.
palms, city of: Designation for Jericho in Deuteronomy 34:3 and 2 Chronicles 28:15.
palsy: Symptom of an organic disease of the central nervous system affecting the temporary or permanent loss of sensation and/or voluntary muscle control. This degenerative condition was usually incurable.
palti: 1. One of the 12 spies Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan before the Israelite conquest.
paltiel: 1. Son of Azzan and a leader of Issachar’s tribe.
paltite, the: Designation for Helez, one of David’s mighty men and possibly a descendant of Palti (2 Sm 23:26, NLT mg). He may have lived in Beth-pelet.
pamphylia: Coastal region on the southern shore of Asia Minor (Turkey) stretching 80 miles (128.7 kilometers) from Lycia on the west to Cilicia on the east, and about 20 miles (32.2 kilometers) wide from the seacoast to the Taurus Mountains.
pannag: KJV rendering of millet, an annual grass whose seeds are used in making bread.
panther: Called Panthera pardus tulliana, it is the most widespread of all the large wildcats. In rocky areas it lives in caves, but in forested regions it lives in thick vegetation.
paper: Word in English translations of the Bible better understood as papyrus.
paphos: Originally a Phoenician settlement in southwest Cyprus.
papias: Early church leader of Hierapolis; chronicler of early Christianity. The information we have about Papias (AD 60–130) and his work was given by Eusebius of Caesarea and Irenaeus of Lyons.
papyrus: Ancient Egyptian writing material derived from the papyrus plant.
parable: A particular form of Jesus’ teaching in the Gospels.
paraclete: Transliteration of a Greek word meaning “one who is called to someone’s aid” or “one who advocates for another.” Thus, the term may be used technically for a lawyer.
paradise: Term borrowed from Persian that means “garden of god.” The Hebrews originally used a word that they applied not only to ordinary gardens but also to God’s garden in Eden.
paradox: Form of expression that seems to be either self-contradictory or absurd but at another level expresses fundamental truth. It is often employed to get hearers to think at a deeper and more critical level.
parah: City belonging to Benjamin’s inheritance. It is undoubtedly Khirbet el-Farah, approximately five and a half miles (8.8 kilometers) northeast of Jerusalem.
paralysis, paralytic, paralyzed: Symptom of an organic disease of the central nervous system affecting the temporary or permanent loss of sensation and/or voluntary muscle control. This degenerative condition was usually incurable.
paran: Desert region in the northeast Sinai Peninsula west of the Arabah (Rift Valley). The settlement of Kadesh-barnea is its northernmost limit.
parapet: Protective barrier around the circumference of house roofs. The parapet was required by the Law since flat roofs were widely used.
parchment: The process that goes into producing books.
pardon: Pardon, involving restoration of broken relationships; ceasing to feel resentment for wrongs and offenses. Primarily, forgiveness is an act of God, releasing sinners from judgment and freeing them from the divine penalty of their sin.
parent: In Bible times, the family comprised members of a household, including not only parents and children, along with other relatives and concubines, but also servants, travelers, aliens, and anyone else who happened to be within the house and was therefore under the protection of the head of the family.
parmashta: One of the 10 sons of Haman killed by the Jews.
parmenas: One of the seven men full of the Spirit and of wisdom chosen by the Jerusalem church to minister to the widows.
parosh: Head of a family who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile. One of his descendants, Pedaiah, participated in rebuilding the Jerusalem wall; other descendants are mentioned as having taken foreign wives.
parousia: Transliteration of a Greek word meaning “presence,” “arrival,” “appearance,” or “coming.” While it is used often with reference to people and once with reference to the Antichrist, the word is employed most frequently with reference to Christ.
parshandatha: One of the 10 sons of Haman slain by the Jews.
parthia, parthians: Land (roughly corresponding to modern Iran) lying beyond the eastern boundaries of the Roman Empire, and so almost outside the world of the NT.
partridge: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
paruah: Father of Jehoshaphat from Issachar’s tribe. Jehoshaphat was appointed to provide food for King Solomon and his household one month out of the year.
parvaim: Geographical area from which Solomon obtained gold for use in the temple.
pas-dammim: Alternate form of Ephes-dammim, a place in Judah’s tribe, in 1 Chronicles 11:13.
paseah: 1. Eshton’s son, the brother of Beth-rapha and a descendant of Kelub from Judah’s tribe.
pashhur, pashur: 1. Forefather of a family of priests who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile.
passion: A derivative from Latin meaning “suffering.” It is used in some translations (KJV and RSV) in Acts 1:3 to refer to the sufferings of Jesus. Throughout the centuries Christians have referred to Jesus’ sufferings as his Passion.
passover: Important Jewish festival celebrating Israel’s redemption from Egypt.
pastor: Word literally meaning “shepherd,” used in both the OT and NT in a figurative sense for rulers and leaders.
pastoral letters: Descriptive phrase used in modern biblical study to designate the letters known as 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus. In Christian tradition these three writings have been grouped together since the second century.
patara: Seaport of the ancient region of Lycia, now located in modern Turkey. The ancient city, one of the largest and most prosperous of the region, was a center of trade and commerce.
pathros: The region of Upper Egypt, mentioned five times in the Hebrew OT. Each time it occurs in conjunction with a city in Lower Egypt (Noph = Memphis, or Zoan = Tanis).
pathrusites: Inhabitants of Pathros, a region of southern Egypt.
patience: Ability to take a great deal of punishment from evil people or circumstances without losing one’s temper, without becoming irritated and angry, or without taking vengeance.
patmos: Small island in the Aegean Sea, located about 35 miles (56.3 kilometers) west of the city of Miletus off the coast of Asia Minor.
patriarchs, period of the: Period of time during which the biblical fathers of Israel lived. The Bible tells of long-lived patriarchs before the Flood, of Noah (chs 6–9), and of a line of patriarchs after the Flood (chs 10–11).
patrimony: Inheritance from a father or ancestor.
patrobas: One of the Christians in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings.
patroclus: Father of Nicanor, the Syrian general whose 20,000 soldiers were routed by a numerically inferior band led by Judas Maccabeus. Patroclus is mentioned only in connection with his embarrassed and dishonored son.
pau: City located in Edom, in which King Hadar reigned; alternately called Pai in 1 Chronicles 1:50.
paul, the apostle: Prominent leader of the first-century church; apostle to the Gentiles; author of 13 NT epistles.
paulus, sergius: Proconsul of Cyprus, described as a “man of intelligence”. Paul and Barnabas, on their first missionary journey, evangelized the Cyprian city of Paphos, Sergius Paulus’s residence.
pavement: Term occurring ten times in the Bible, usually alluding to the stone floor of the temple(s). Particular interest focuses on the reference in John 19:13 to the pavement on which Jesus stood trial before Pilate.
pavilion: A translation of the Hebrew word sukkah and sokoh in the KJV. The word sukkah is also translated as “booth”, “tabernacle”, and “tent”.
peace: Total well-being, prosperity, and security associated with God’s presence among his people. Linked in the OT with the covenant, the presence of peace was conditional, based on Israel’s obedience.
peace offering: Major ritual expressions of religious life with accompanying rites, such as libations, effusions, and sacred meals. The ideology expressed in Israel’s ritual complex made its religion unique in the ancient Near East.
peacock: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
pearl: Gem formed within the shell of certain mollusks. The word appears only once in the OT.
pedahel: Ammihud’s son from Naphtali’s tribe, appointed to work with Joshua and Eleazar in distributing Canaanite territory west of the Jordan River among the Israelites.
pedaiah: 1. Maternal grandfather of Judah’s King Jehoiakim.
pekah: Son of Remaliah and 18th king of Israel.
pekahiah: Son of Menahem, king of Israel. Pekahiah (whose name means “Yahweh has opened [his eyes]”) was among the 20 kings who ruled Israel from Samaria following its decline consequent to the fracture of the Solomonic monarchy in the tenth century BC.
pekod: Place mentioned as the location of an Aramean tribe living in southern Babylonia between Babylon and Elam and more exactly on the eastern bank of the Lower Tigris by modern Kut-el-Amara and the confluence of the Kerkha.
pelaiah: 1. Elioenai’s son and a remote descendant of David.
pelaliah: Forefather of Adaiah, a priest living in Jerusalem during Ezra’s day.
pelatiah: 1. Hananiah’s son, in a list of King Solomon’s descendants.
peleg: Son of Eber and father of Reu. During his lifetime, the earth was divided (Peleg means “division” or “watercourse”).
pelethites: Bodyguards of David, and loyal mercenaries during the king’s political setbacks.
pelican: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
pella: City located east of the Jordan River in the Decapolis region. There is no reference to this city in the Bible, but records show that it was an important Canaanite city, influenced by Egypt and later by Greece and Rome.
pelonite: Designation given to two of David’s mighty men, Helez and Ahijah (1 Chr 11:27, 36; 27:10, NLT “from Pelon”). No sources for the designation are known, which has led some scholars to consider it a textual corruption.
pelusium: City known for its flax and wine, but also a strategic fortified town on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast, situated on the trade route between Egypt and Mesopotamia.
pence: KJV form of denarius in Matthew 18:28, Mark 14:5, Luke 7:41, 10:35, and John 12:5.
pencil: A carpenter’s outlining tool named in RSV in connection with the manufacture of idols. Other translations are “line” (KJV), “red chalk” (NASB), “a scriber” (NEB), “a marker” (NIV).
peniel: Alternate form of Penuel, the Palestinian city where Jacob wrestled with the “angel” of God, in Genesis 32:30.
peninnah: One of Elkanah’s two wives, the other and more favored being Hannah. Peninnah’s fortune in bearing children was the source of much domestic friction for the childless Hannah, especially at the time of the annual sacrifice at Shiloh.
penknife: Iron tool used to sharpen reed pens, cut papyrus, and carve letters in stone. It is mentioned by name only in Jeremiah 36:23 (RSV), but it is referred to elsewhere as a pen or tool of iron.
pentateuch: Word formed by two Greek words, pente (“five”) and teuchos (“case”) and commonly used to refer to the first five books of the OT (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy), which were encased together, as in one book.
pentecost: Word derived from the Greek word pentekoste (“fiftieth”), which stood for the festival celebrated on the 50th day after Passover.
penuel (person): 1. Descendant (possibly son) of Hur and father (in the sense of progenitor) of Gedor from Judah’s tribe.
penuel (place): Name given to the place near the Jabbok River where Jacob strove all night with God; alternately called Peniel in verse 30.
people of god: Designation for the collective group that believes in God. It is a common strand of Israel’s faith that it became the people of God because he chose it to be his own possession.
people of the east: Tribes located east and northeast of Canaan, many of them overtly hostile to the Jews. Genesis 29:1 provides the first reference to these peoples.
people of the land: OT phrase also known by its Hebrew transliteration, ‘Am-Ha’arets.
peoples: Groups formed on the basis of political or social interests or on kinship. Generally, the word “nations” implies peoples of the world other than the Hebrews, although it can also include the Jews.
peor (deity): Contraction for the Canaanite god of Baal-peor, or for the place itself.
peor (place): 1. Mountain east of the Jordan and north of the Dead Sea where Balak led Balaam in a final effort to evoke a curse on Israel.
peraea: Term not occurring in the NT except in the fourth-century manuscript Codex Sinaiticus and the fifth-century manuscript Codex Washingtonianus, where it appears in Luke 6:17 and is treated as a variant reading by most editors of the Greek NT.
perazim, mount: Mountain mentioned in Isaiah 28:21, apparently near Baal-perazim, the “Baal of Breaches,” where David defeated the Philistines. From the context of 2 Samuel 5:20, this battleground was evidently located in the valley of Rephaim, southwest of Jerusalem.
perdition: Term used eight times in the KJV NT to express the eternal aspect of the destruction of life and self.
perea: Term not occurring in the NT except in the fourth-century manuscript Codex Sinaiticus and the fifth-century manuscript Codex Washingtonianus, where it appears in Luke 6:17 and is treated as a variant reading by most editors of the Greek NT.
peresh: Son of Maachah and Makir from Manasseh’s tribe, and the grandson of Manasseh.
perez, perezite: Son of Judah whose name is derived from a Hebrew word meaning “he who bursts forth”; his name refers to the manner in which he unexpectedly came first from Tamar’s womb before his twin brother, Zerah.
perez-uzzah: Alternate name given to the site associated with the threshing floor of Nacon in 1 Chronicles 13:11 and 2 Samuel 6:8, respectively.
perfume: Term covering a wide range of materials prepared from ground-up minerals, vegetable oils, and roots, which were used from the earliest times to enhance one’s personal presentation or to produce pleasing fragrances both for secular and religious purposes.
perfumer: Also known as an “apothecary” (Ex 30:25, KJV) or a “confectionary” (1 Sm 8:13, KJV). This person prepared oils, powders, and mixtures for medicinal use, for perfumes and cosmetics, and for religious use in incense.
perga: City probably of very early Greek origin and the religious capital of ancient Pamphylia. In the second century BC, the Romans overthrew a Syrian garrison there, and thereafter the city apparently had a substantial degree of independence from external control.
pergamos, pergamum: City just north of the Caicus River, in the southern part of Mysia (western Turkey), and one of the greatest cultural centers of the Hellenistic era. The early geographer Strabo (63 BC–AD 24?) called the area around Pergamum the richest land in Mysia.
perida: Alternate rendering of Peruda, the ancestor of a family of servants who returned to Jerusalem after the exile (Neh 7:57, NLT mg).
perizzite: One of several population segments occupying the land of Palestine prior to and subsequent to the Israelite conquest. The enumeration of these peoples throughout the OT serves a variety of purposes, none of which is strictly historical or geographical.
persecution: Infliction of suffering, injury, or death on others because of their identity or beliefs. The Bible begins with an account of the persecution of the righteous by the unrighteous (Gn 4:3-7, “regard for Abel”; Mt 23:35; Heb 11:4).
perseus: Last king of Macedonia. Perseus was the illegitimate son of Philip III of Macedonia.
perseverance: Action or condition of steadfastness. OT Israel waited generations for fulfillment of promises that many believers never lived to see.
persia, persians: Country lying just to the east of Mesopotamia (modern Iraq) and covering virtually the same territory as present-day Iran. It was known in ancient times by various forms of Fars or Pars, which came down to us as Persia.
persis: Christian woman in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings.
peruda: Head of a family of Solomon’s servants; alternately called Perida in Nehemiah 7:57. His descendants formed part of the remnant of Israel that returned to Jerusalem after the exile.
pestilence: Derivative of a Hebrew word referring to a contagious epidemic disease of devastating proportions. Pestilence is never portrayed in the Bible as an aimless, naturally occurring phenomenon.
peter, first letter of: First of two general epistles authored by Peter.
peter, second letter of: The second, general epistle authored by Peter.
peter, the apostle: One of the 12 disciples; rose to prominence both among the disciples during Jesus’ ministry and among the apostles afterwards.
pethahiah: 1. Levite and ancestor of one of the postexilic priestly families.
pethor: Hometown of Balaam. Pethor is located in Upper Mesopotamia at the confluence of the Sajur River and the Euphrates.
petra: Capital of the Nabateans, who first appeared in history in 312 BC. The Nabateans were of Arabic origin, though their ancestry is uncertain.
peullethai, peulthai: Obed-edom’s son, who was a Levite gatekeeper in the sanctuary during David’s reign.
phalec: KJV rendering of Peleg, a descendant of Shem and an ancestor of Jesus, in Luke 3:35.
phallu: KJV spelling of Pallu, Reuben’s second son, in Genesis 46:9.
phalti: KJV spelling of Palti, Laish’s son, in 1 Samuel 25:44.
phaltiel: KJV spelling of Paltiel, an alternate name for Palti, Laish’s son, in 2 Samuel 3:15.
phanuel: Father of Anna the prophetess. Anna prophesied in connection with the presentation of the infant Jesus at the temple.
pharaoh: Ruler over Egypt also known as “the King of Upper and Lower Egypt.” He lived in a palace known as the “great house,” which was the symbol of his authority.
pharaoh hophra: Fourth king of the 26th dynasty (Egypt), he ruled 589–570 BC.
pharaoh necho, pharaoh nechoh, pharaoh n: Pharaoh Necho, Pharaoh Nechoh, Pharaoh Neco, Pharaoh Necoh
Alternate names for Neco, pharaoh of the 26th dynasty (Egypt), who ruled 609–594 BC.
pharaoh's daughter: 1. Egyptian princess who rescued the infant Moses and adopted him as her own son.
phares, pharez: KJV forms of Perez, Judah’s elder son by Tamar.
pharisees: Religious sect active in Palestine during the NT period. The Pharisees are consistently depicted in the Gospels as Jesus’ antagonists.
pharosh: KJV spelling of Parosh, the ancestor of a postexilic family, in Ezra 8:3.
pharpar: One of two rivers named by Naaman as in or near Damascus. Its exact identity is uncertain.
pharzite: KJV form of Perezite, a member of Perez’s family, in Numbers 26:20.
phaseah: KJV spelling of Paseah, the head of a family of temple servants, in Nehemiah 7:51.
phasiron: Victims of a raid by Jonathan. The tribe, situated near Bethbasi, is otherwise unknown.
phebe: KJV spelling of Phoebe, a Christian woman, in Romans 16:1.
phenice: 1. KJV form of Phoenicia, the country on the east Mediterranean coast and north of Palestine, in Acts 11:19 and 15:3.
phenicia: KJV spelling of Phoenicia in Acts 21:2.
phichol, phicol: Commander of Abimelech’s army, mentioned in connection with his ruler’s treaty negotiations with Abraham and Isaac.
philadelphia: 1. City of the Decapolis, not specifically mentioned in any NT writing.
philemon (person): Christian known only from the letter addressed to him by the apostle Paul. He is mentioned nowhere else in the NT.
philemon, letter to: The shortest of Paul’s Prison Epistles.
philetus: False teacher who, along with his companion Hymenaeus, held an erroneous view of the resurrection of believers—that the resurrection had already happened (2 Tm 2:17; cf. v 11).
philip: 1. Apostle whose name is placed fifth in each of the lists of the twelve after the two pairs of brothers, Simon Peter and Andrew, and James and John.
philippi: Minor village of Thrace (known in antiquity as “The Springs”) until about 357 BC, when the father of Alexander the Great, Philip II of Macedon, conquered the site and rebuilt it.
philistia, philistines: Small country situated in southwestern Palestine, along the Mediterranean coast (also called “Palestina” in KJV, Ex 15:14; Is 14:29-31); Aegean people who settled on the maritime plain of Canaan.
philo, judaeus: Hellenistic Jewish philosopher (c. 25 BC–AD 40) whose thought presents the first major confrontation of biblical faith with Greek thought.
philologus: Early Christian acquaintance or friend of the apostle Paul to whom he sent greetings. In the series of greetings, he seems to be paired with a woman named Julia.
philometor: Name of Ptolemy VI, ruler in Egypt.
philosophy: Logically disciplined, self-critical inquiry into the basic questions of life. “Philosophy” itself means “love of wisdom.” This “love” treasures pursuing, discovering, analyzing, and justifying wisdom.
phinehas: 1. Eleazer’s son, grandson of Aaron, and Abishua’s father.
phlegon: Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings.
phoebe: Christian woman of the church at Cenchrea, the eastern port for the city of Corinth. In Romans 16:1-2, Paul commended Phoebe to the recipients of the letter on the basis of her valuable service to other Christians.
phoenicia, phoenicians: Group of city-states (and their residents) that occupied a strip of the Syrian coastal plain at the foot of the Lebanon Mountains.
phoenix: Harbor town on the southern coast of Crete, where Paul and his shipmates hoped to spend the winter during their voyage to Rome (Acts 27:12, KJV “Phenice”). Phoenix was situated west of Fair Havens near the island of Cauda.
phrygia: Area in western Turkey on the Anatolian plateau, the boundaries of which cannot be defined precisely. The Phrygians were originally Europeans, called Phryges by the Greeks, who crossed the Hellespont from Macedonia and Thrace and settled here.
phurah: KJV spelling of Purah, Gideon’s servant, in Judges 7:10-11.
phut: 1. KJV spelling of Put, Ham’s third son, in Genesis 10:6.
phuvah: KJV spelling of Puvah, Issachar’s son, in Genesis 46:13.
phygellus, phygelus: Asian Christian who, along with others, abandoned Paul. Phygelus is mentioned with Hermogenes, also otherwise unknown.
phylactery: Small prayer case containing Scripture passages worn at times of prayer by pious Jews. Orthodox Jewish males wear two small, black leather cubes or boxes, with Scripture inside, at the time of prayer.
physician: One trained in medicine. The physician tended to and repaired wounds and administered medicines to the sick.
pi-beseth: City mentioned together with Thebes, Memphis, and On in Ezekiel’s oracle about Egypt’s fall (Ez 30:17, NLT mg).
pig: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
pigeon: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
pi-hahiroth: Stopping place of the Israelites on their journey from Egypt to the Promised Land. It was here that the pursuing Egyptians overtook them (v 9), which led to the deliverance at the Red Sea.
pilate, pontius: Appointed by Tiberius as the fifth prefect of Judea, Pilate served in that capacity from AD 26–36. He appears prominently in the trial narratives of the Gospels as the Roman governor who authorized Jesus’ crucifixion.
pildash: Sixth son of Nahor and Milcah; nephew of Abraham.
pileha, pilha: Political leader who set his seal on Ezra’s covenant during the postexilic era.
pillar of fire and cloud: One of the most frequent modes of God’s appearing to humans in the OT; a visual manifestation of the presence of God common in the narratives of the exodus, Sinai covenant, the wilderness wanderings, and the dedication of the temple.
piltai: Priest and head of Modiah’s house during the days of Joiakim the high priest in the postexilic period.
pim: Weight measurement equivalent to about two-thirds of a shekel.
pine tree: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
pinon: One of the “chiefs” (NLT “leaders”) descended from Esau.
pipe: English word that translates a number of Hebrew and Greek words designating various tubular wind instruments.
piram: King of Jarmuth, a Canaanite city located southwest of Jerusalem. After joining an alliance with four Amorite kings against Joshua, Piram—along with other kings—was defeated and killed.
pirathon: Home of Abdon, one of the minor judges. It is described as being in the land of Ephraim and in the hill country of the Amalekites.
pisgah, mount: Mountain located at the northeast end of the Dead Sea near the ancient city of Jericho. Balak took Balaam to the top of Pisgah, and Moses was told to go to its summit to view the Promised Land.
pishon: First of four divisions of the river that flowed out of the Garden of Eden. Suggestions for its identity include the Rion, the Indus, the Ganges, a canal connecting the Tigris and Euphrates, and a symbol of the Milky Way.
pisidia: Region included in the Roman province of Galatia at the time of the visit of Paul and Barnabas about AD 48.
pison: KJV translation for the Pishon River in Genesis 2:11.
pistachio: Substances required by the body to sustain life, and the methods of making them edible. Food consumed in Bible times included bread, milk products, fruit, meat, and fish.
pit: Word used frequently in the OT to denote the grave, the abode of the dead, or Sheol—that is, a shadowy existence that the living feared because it cut them off from light, joy, and vitality.
pitch: Brown or black tarlike substance, a variety of bitumen, obtained in ancient times from natural oil seeps and used for mortar and caulking. Mortar, pitch, slime, and tar are other translations of the related terms in Hebrew.
pitcher: The manufacture of clayware and earthenware.
pithom: One of the store cities (along with Rameses) built by the Israelites during their Egyptian captivity. There has been considerable debate among Egyptologists for over a century as to the identification of these sites.
pithon: Benjaminite, Micah’s son and a descendant of Jonathan.
pity: A divine quality by which God faithfully keeps his promises and maintains his covenant relationship with his chosen people despite their unworthiness and unfaithfulness.
plague: Word used to refer to a disease, disaster, or pestilence. Although there is a specific disease known as plague, the term “plague” as used in Scripture is not restricted to a single disease.
plagues upon egypt: Unprecedented series of disasters striking Egypt, probably culminating in spring or early summer (c. 1400 BC). They struck particularly the Nile Delta, although apparently not affecting the area called Goshen.
plain of the pillar: KJV for “oak of the pillar,” a sacred tree at Shechem, in Judges 9:6.
plane tree: Large spreading tree having a wide trunk and scaly bark, indigenous to Palestine.
plants: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
pledge: A person who engages in loaning, exchanging, and issuing money. The development of interstate and international trade made it imperative to devise a method of banking to facilitate the transfer of funds.
pleiades: Name of a constellation in the eastern sky composed of six bright and many other less visible stars. Telescopic photography has captured the appearance of these stars as being strung together by currents of matter.
plow, plowman, plowshare: During Bible times agriculture took the same three main forms found in Palestine today. Emphasis on each of these has depended upon the social and technological status of the people.
plumb line, plummet: Cord with a weight attached, used to ensure the straightness of a wall.
pochereth-hazzebaim, pochereth of zebaim: Head of a family of Solomon’s servants who returned from the exile with Zerubbabel. The KJV renders the name Pochereth of Zebaim, making the latter part a place-name.
pokereth-hazzebaim: Head of a family of Solomon’s servants who returned from the exile with Zerubbabel. The KJV renders the name Pochereth of Zebaim, making the latter part a place-name.
pollux: Son of Zeus and Castor’s twin brother in Greek mythology. The twin brothers are also called the Dioscuri.
polycarp: Early Christian leader and martyr in the postapostolic era.
polygamy: The joining together of male and female in matrimony, as practiced by various cultures.
pomegranate: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
pommel: KJV for “bowl,” part of the capitals of the temple pillars.
pontius pilate: Appointed by Tiberius as the fifth prefect of Judea, Pilate served in that capacity from AD 26–36. He appears prominently in the trial narratives of the Gospels as the Roman governor who authorized Jesus’ crucifixion.
pontus: Roman province in northeastern Asia Minor, located along the southern coast of the Black Sea. Galatia, Cappadocia, and Armenia bordered Pontus.
pools of solomon: Water-storage pools, whose construction has been attributed to Solomon. Solomon made pools for watering his vineyards, gardens, parks, and orchards, but their location is uncertain.
poplar: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
poratha: One of the ten sons of Haman killed by the Jews.
porch: Court associated with the temple or palace. In the KJV, it is the translation of several Hebrew words.
porcius festus: Roman procurator (governor) of Judea, who succeeded Felix Antonius and who was succeeded by Albinus. The precise date of Porcius Festus’s accession to power is debatable but has been narrowed to sometime between AD 55 and 60.
porcupine: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
portico, solomon's: Court associated with the temple or palace. In the KJV, it is the translation of several Hebrew words.
posidonius: Ambassador for Nicanor. Posidonius was sent with Theodotus and Mattathias by Nicanor to arrange a truce with Judas the Maccabee after having engaged in battle with Judas and realizing that it was better to negotiate a settlement.
possession, demon: Fallen angel who, under the leadership of Satan, rebelled against God.
postexilic period: A period in the Jews’ history after their exile to Babylon. This period extends from 539–c. 331 BC.
pot: The manufacture of clayware and earthenware.
potentate: A term used in 1 Timothy in the KJV and the ASV to translate the royal title ascribed to God in this passage. Most recent versions use the terms “Sovereign” or “Ruler.”
potiphar: Officer who purchased Joseph when he arrived in Egypt after being sold by his brothers to the Ishmaelites or Midianites. The word translated “officer” is derived from an Akkadian word for a court official.
potiphera: Priest of On whose daughter, Asenath, was given to Joseph as his wife by Pharaoh. On (or Heliopolis) was the center of the sun-god cult, and Potiphera was likely a high-ranking priest in the cult.
potsherd: Piece of broken pottery used in OT times to carry hot coals or to dip water. Potsherds were also used as lids for storage containers or cooking kettles, as a medium for written communication, or to add grit to waterproofing compounds.
potsherd gate: Gate in the south section of the preexilic Jerusalem wall. It led to the valley of Hinnom and to the Potter’s Field.
pottage: Red-colored vegetable stew commonly served in the OT. Pottage was made of lentils, herbs, onions, and sometimes meat.
potter: The manufacture of clayware and earthenware.
potter's field: Name of a burial ground outside Jerusalem.
pottery: The manufacture of clayware and earthenware.
pound: 1. KJV for “mina,” a weight equivalent of about one pound or half a kilogram.
power: Ability to do things, by virtue of strength, skill, resources, or authorization. In the Hebrew of the OT and the Greek of the NT, there are several different words used for power.
powers: Phrase familiarized by the KJV, occurring several times in Paul’s writings, and expressed by means of three Greek synonyms. The concept of principalities is signified by exousia and archai, while powers is represented by dunamis.
praetorium, praetorian guard: Term appearing in the Greek NT in Mark 15:16; Matthew 27:27; John 18:28, 33; 19:9; Acts 23:35; and Philippians 1:13. It is a Latin word borrowed from the Romans, who dominated the Mediterranean world in NT times.
prayer: The addressing and petitioning of God. Prayer to a god or gods is a feature of many, if not all, religions, but here attention will be restricted to the biblical teaching and some of its implications.
prayer, lord's: Pattern for prayer Jesus gave his followers to use. There are two versions of the Lord’s Prayer.
prayer of azariah: Part of the Deuterocanonical works, consists of three supplementary sections to the book of Daniel. This additional material is in the Greek translation of the OT book of Daniel, but not in the ancient Hebrew-Aramaic texts.
prayer of manasseh: This short prayer, ascribed to King Manasseh of Judah, is often regarded as the finest composition in the entire English Apocrypha. During the Reformation, Protestants highly valued its piety.
precious stones: A lengthy list of the precious stones used in OT times occurs in Exodus 28:17-20 and 39:10-13, where four rows of three stones, each engraved with the name of one of the 12 tribes of Israel, were set in the high priest’s breastplate.
predestination: In modern English, terms referring to the selection of a leader or representative by a group of people. An element of choice is involved, since usually there are several candidates out of whom one must be chosen.
preparation, day of: Term used in Scripture for the day before the Sabbath.
presbyter: NT term referring to an elder in the church. Following the OT pattern of synagogues governed by a council of elders, the church of the NT had officers (presbuteroi, “older persons”) whose task was to tend the flock of God that was under their care.
presence, bread of the: Loaves of bread placed on a special table in the sanctuary or Holy Place of the tabernacle and later in the temple. Two other terms in the OT are used to describe the “bread of the Presence,” which means bread that has been set before the Lord’s face.
presence of god, the: God’s manifestation of his spiritual being. Since God is spirit, believers experience him by sensing his invisible presence.
pride: A reasonable or justifiable self-respect; or improper and excessive self-esteem known as conceit or arrogance. The apostle Paul expressed a positive kind of pride when speaking of confidence in Christians or of strength in the Lord (12:5, 9).
priest, high: Servants of God in the OT. There were three basic classes of religious personnel in ancient Israel: prophets, wise men, and priests and Levites.
priesthood: Office or function of a priest. The modern word “priest” (in French prêtre and in German priester) is used of a clergyman in episcopalian churches (Roman, Orthodox, and Anglican).
priests and levites: Servants of God in the OT. There were three basic classes of religious personnel in ancient Israel: prophets, wise men, and priests and Levites.
primogeniture: Word not found in the Bible; derived from the Greek translation of the Hebrew word for “firstborn.” Primogeniture refers specifically to the exclusive right of inheritance that belonged to the firstborn male.
principalities and powers: Phrase familiarized by the KJV, occurring several times in Paul’s writings, and expressed by means of three Greek synonyms. The concept of principalities is signified by exousia and archai, while powers is represented by dunamis.
prisca: KJV rendering of the name of Priscilla, Aquila’s wife, in 2 Timothy 4:19.
priscilla and aquila: Christian couple who were friends and possibly converts of the apostle Paul during his ministry at Corinth. They are always mentioned together in the NT.
prison: The science or philosophy of law is called jurisprudence. Although modern jurisprudence bears little resemblance to biblical concepts of law, the Scriptures have played a definite role in its development.
prison, court of the: KJV rendering of “Court of the Guard,” an open court where the prophet Jeremiah was kept prisoner, in Jeremiah 32:2.
prison, spirits in: Term used in 1 Peter 3:18-20a. There is little agreement among scholars as to what “spirits in prison” really refers to or why Jesus would have gone to preach to them.
prison gate: KJV rendering of “Gate of the Guard,” a gate in Jerusalem, possibly in the palace complex, in Nehemiah 12:39.
prize: Reward given the winner of a contest. In the ancient Greek games (the Olympian and Isthmian), the prize usually consisted of a simple wreath woven with olive branches.
prochorus, procorus: One of the seven men appointed by the apostles in Jerusalem for service in the early days of the church. They were to oversee the fair distribution of food in the Christian community.
proconsul: Governor (NLT; KJV “deputy”) appointed by the senate of Rome to govern a province.
procurator: Financial officer of Rome (NLT “governor”), usually from the equestrian rank, whose responsibilities included the supervision and collection of imperial revenues in an assigned province.
promise: Declaration by one person to another that something will or will not be done, giving the person to whom it is made the right to expect the performance of whatever has been specified.
prophecy: Term, along with its English cognates (“prophet,” “to prophesy,” “prophetism,” and “prophetic”), derived from a group of Greek words that, in secular Greek, mean “speak forth,” “proclaim,” “announce.” In biblical Greek, however, these terms always carry the…
prophet, prophetess: A man or woman chosen by God to speak for him and to foretell events in the divine plan.
prophets, false: Spokesmen, heralds, or messengers falsely speaking for, or on behalf of, someone else. The false prophet was often motivated not by loyalty to God but by a desire for popularity.
propitiation: The act of appeasing another person’s anger by the offering of a gift. The word was often used by the pagans in antiquity, for they thought of their gods as unpredictable beings, liable to become angry with their worshipers for any trifle.
proselyte: Gentile who converted to Judaism by being circumcised, baptized, and offering a sacrifice in the temple.
prosperity: Pronouncement of the favor of God upon an assembled congregation. Worship services, especially observances of Holy Communion in Eastern Orthodox, Roman Catholic, and most Protestant churches, usually end with a blessing spoken by the senior clergyman present.
prostitute, prostitution: Person guilty of illicit sexual relationships; figuratively, one who worships an idol. The term “prostitute” translates four different words found in the Bible.
protevangelium: The word means first (protos) gospel (evangelion). Theologians have used the word in reference to the message of redemption God spoke after the fall of man.
proverbs, book of: Third poetical book in the OT. A collection of striking, epigrammatic expressions concerning practical wisdom by example, warning, or precept.
providence: God’s activity throughout history in providing for the needs of human beings, especially those who believe in him.
psalm 151: A noncanonical psalm that, prior to the Qumran discoveries, was known only through ancient translations (LXX, Latin, and Syriac). At Qumran the psalm was included in the Hebrew Psalm Scroll (11Q).
psalms, book of: Poems sung to musical accompaniment, originally the harp. The alternative title, the Psalter, refers to a collection of songs sung to harp accompaniment.
psychics: People who have contact with supernatural forces and who claim to be able to interpret their intentions. In the OT, such people are grouped with “mediums”—that is, people who claim to mediate between supernatural forces and human beings.
ptolemaic empire: Empire named from Ptolemy I Soter, a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great who got himself appointed satrap, or governor, of Egypt shortly after Alexander died in 323 BC.
ptolemais: Alternate name for Acco, a city in northern Palestine, in Acts 21:7.
pua: KJV form of Puvah, Issachar’s son, in Numbers 26:23.
puah: 1. One of two Hebrew midwives ordered by Pharaoh to kill Hebrew males at birth.
publius: Name of a resident of the island of Malta, mentioned in Acts 28:7-8. He hosted Paul and others briefly after a shipwreck had stranded them on the island as they journeyed to Rome.
pudens: Companion of Paul mentioned in 2 Timothy 4:21. At the close of the letter his personal greetings are communicated to the recipient.
puhite: KJV spelling of Puthite, a member of a family of Judah’s tribe, in 1 Chronicles 2:53.
puite: Member of family in Issachar’s tribe headed by Puvah.
pul: 1. Name given to Tiglath-pileser, the Assyrian ruler (745–727 BC), when he became king of Babylon (729–727 BC; 2 Kgs 15:19; 1 Chr 5:26).
pulse: KJV translation of a Hebrew word perhaps better rendered as “vegetable”. Not wishing to defile themselves with the king’s food, Daniel and his friends requested permission to live on a diet of vegetables and water.
punishment: The intentional infliction of pain or loss (e.g., loss of liberty or money) by an authorized individual on another because of an offense committed. There can be no punishment without authority, and none without a guilty party.
punishment, eternal: Place of future punishment for the lost, unrepentant, wicked dead.
punite: Member of family in Issachar’s tribe headed by Puvah.
punon: Town identified with the modern Feinan, lying on the eastern side of the Arabah in the hill country of Edom. Punon lay conveniently on the road from Edom through the Negev to Egypt.
pur: Hebrew word, meaning “lot,” from which the name of the Jewish festival Purim, celebrating their deliverance from Haman, was derived.
purah: Gideon’s servant, who accompanied his master on a secret night visit to the Midianite camp, where they were encouraged by the Lord.
purgatory: According to the Roman Catholic Church, the place of temporal punishment and cleansing before entry into heaven.
purification: Aspect of Hebrew religion having physical, ceremonial, moral, and spiritual significance.
purim: Hebrew name, meaning “lots,” for the Jewish festival celebrating their deliverance from Haman.
purple: Highly prized dye extracted from sea snails. Purple was used for dyeing fabrics in the tabernacle and making the clothes of wealthy people.
purse: A small bag or receptacle in which money and often other small objects would be carried. There are basically three Hebrew words and three Greek words referring to such a purse or pouch.
put (person): Third of Ham’s four sons, who most likely settled in northern Africa and is perhaps the forefather of the peoples of Egypt and Libya.
put (place): Ancient nation, descended from a man of the same name. It is commonly identified as Libya, although it has been argued that it was the Punt of Egyptian records, somewhere along the northeast coast of Africa, perhaps Somalia.
puteoli: Italian seaport town on the Bay of Naples. It was a normal stopping place for seafaring travelers and cargo going to Rome.
puthite: Family of Judah’s tribe from Kiriath-jearim mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 2:53.
putiel: Father of Eleazer’s wife and the grandfather of Phinehas.
puvah: Issachar’s son, who went with Jacob and his household to Egypt, where they sought refuge from the severe famine in Palestine (Gn 46:13; NLT “Puah”). Puvah founded the Punite family and is alternately called Puah in 1 Chronicles 7:1.
pygarg: KJV translation for antelope in Deuteronomy 14:5.
pyramids: Egypt figured significantly as a stage on which the biblical narrative was enacted. Here Abraham lived in time of famine.
pyrrhus: Father of Sopater of Berea, who, with others, accompanied Paul on his return trip through Macedonia.
qere: An anglicized Aramaic word meaning “what is to be read.” Until the time of the Masoretes, the Hebrew Bible was written only with consonants.
qesitah: Weight of unknown value (Gn 33:19; Jos 24:32; Jb 42:11, RSV mg).
qoheleth: Hebrew title for the book of Ecclesiastes, translated “the Preacher” or “the Teacher”; also spelled “Koheleth.” Derived from a word meaning “to call an assembly,” it came to mean “to address an assembly.” The author of the book calls himself Qoheleth in numerous passages.
quadratus, apology of: An early Christian apology was written by Quadratus (c. AD 125) to the emperor Hadrian as a defense of Christianity.
quail: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
quart: Occurring only in Revelation 6:6 (see NLT mg), the choinix is a little more than a quart (1.1 liters). In Greek literature it was considered the amount of one man’s daily allowance of corn.
quartus: Christian who joined the apostle Paul in sending greetings to the church in Rome.
queen: Word used to describe a reigning monarch, a queen consort, or a queen mother.
queen of heaven: Goddess mentioned by Jeremiah in his denunciations of Judah’s idolatry. The women of Judah were especially involved in worshiping the Queen of Heaven.
quirinius: Roman governor of Syria at the time of Jesus’ birth. According to the Roman historian Tacitus (Annals 3.48), Publius Sulpicius Quirinius was elected consul of Syria in 12 BC.
qumran: Ancient Jewish religious community near the site where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found in 1947.
quotations of the old testament in the n: Quotations of the Old Testament in the New Testament
OT passages cited or alluded to in the NT writings.
raama, raamah: One of Cush’s five sons and a descendant of Ham’s line. He was the father of Sheba and Dedan.
raamiah: One who returned with Zerubbabel to Palestine following the Babylonian captivity (Neh 7:7, NLT mg). Raamiah is alternately spelled Reelaiah in Ezra 2:2.
raamses: Alternate spelling of Ramses and Rameses.
rabbah: One of the towns in the hill country assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance. Its location is uncertain.
rabbah of the ammonites: Capital of the ancient Ammonite kingdom.
rabbi: Title of respect, meaning “my great one” or “my superior one,” used in Jesus’ day for Jewish religious teachers.
rabbith: Town defining the border of Issachar and perhaps identifiable with the Levitical town called Daberath. If so, its site is near Mt Tabor at modern Deburiyeh.
rabboni: Variant of rabbi in Mark 10:51 and John 20:16.
rabmag: Title given to a certain Babylonian officer, Nergal-sharezer, who was in charge of Jeremiah’s safety during the fall of Jerusalem. The meaning of the title in uncertain.
rabsaris: Title of a high-ranking Assyrian and Babylonian court official, usually a eunuch and sometimes supervisor of the royal harem.
rabshakeh: High Assyrian official, originally a cupbearer or chamberlain, but later a powerful palace official.
raca: Derogatory expression used by Jews of the first century AD to show open contempt for another.
racal: One of the towns in southern Judah in which David distributed the spoils taken from the defeated Amalekites. The city is named Carmel in the Septuagint.
rachab: KJV form of Rahab in Matthew 1:5.
rachal: KJV form of Racal, a Judean town, in 1 Samuel 30:29.
rachel: Beautiful younger daughter of Laban; she was the favorite wife of Jacob. He first met her as he arrived at Haran in Paddan-aram.
rachel's tomb: Landmark set up by Jacob at the site of Rachel’s grave that was still in existence at the time of Samuel. Two persisting traditions make its original location still questionable.
raddai: Fifth of Jesse’s seven sons and the brother of David from Judah’s tribe.
ragau: KJV rendering of Reu, Peleg’s son, in Luke 3:35.
raguel: 1. KJV spelling of Reuel, an alternate name for Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, in Numbers 10:29.
rahab (monster): Mythological sea monster that poetically represented Egypt. “For Egypt’s help is worthless and empty, therefore I have called her ‘Rahab who sits still’ ” (Is 30:7, RSV).
rahab (person): Heroine of the battle of Jericho. Soon after Moses’ death, God told Joshua that he and the people were to cross the Jordan and occupy the land of promise.
raham: Son of Shema, and father of Jorkeam. He was a descendant of Judah.
rahel: KJV spelling of Rachel, Jacob’s wife, in Jeremiah 31:15.
rain: It has been said that the climate of Palestine is more varied than that of any other area of comparable size in the world.
rainbow: Sign of God’s covenant with Noah following the flood. The normal Hebrew word for “war bow” is used.
raisin: Staple food in biblical lands made by drying grapes on housetops. Raisins were used as gifts, sometimes offered to false gods, and considered a source of nourishment.
raisin cake: Culinary delicacy of ancient peoples. The cakes resisted deterioration and thus were useful for soldiers and travelers.
rakkath: One of 19 cities allotted to Naphtali’s tribe for an inheritance. The city served as a buffer against military attack on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee.
rakkon: One of the cities assigned to Dan’s tribe. It is identified today with Tell er-Ragguat, one and a half miles (2.4 kilometers) north of the mouth of the Yorkon River.
ram: Domestic animal, Ovis orientalis, referred to directly or by some term such as ewe, lamb, ram, or by some fact concerning them over 700 times in Scripture.
ram (person): 1. Ancestor of King David, listed in Matthew’s genealogy of Christ (Mt 1:3-4; called Arni in Lk 3:33).
rama: KJV spelling of Ramah, a Benjaminite city, in Matthew 2:18.
ramah: 1. One of the cities located in the territory allotted to Benjamin’s tribe for an inheritance, listed between Gibeon and Beeroth.
ramah of the negev, ramah of the south: Ramah of the Negev, Ramah of the South
Alternate names for Baalath-beer, a town in Simeon’s territory, in Joshua 19:8.
ramathaim: Alternate translation of Greek “Rathamin” (1 Macc 11:34, NLT mg).
ramathaim-zophim: Alternate name for Ramah, Samuel’s hometown, in 1 Samuel 1:1.
ramathite: Inhabitant of Ramah, though which Ramah is uncertain.
ramath-lehi: Place where Samson routed the Philistines with an ass’s jawbone (Jgs 15:17, NLT mg).
ramath-mizpeh: Alternate name for Mizpah, a town in Gad’s territory, in Joshua 13:26.
ramath of the south: KJV rendering of Ramah of the Negev, an alternate name of Baalath-beer, in Joshua 19:8.
rameses (person): Alternate form of the Egyptian Ramses of the 19th and 20th dynasties.
rameses (place): Place (also called Ra’amses or Ramses) mentioned with Pithom in Exodus 1:11 (KJV “Raamses”) as one of the locations where the Hebrews were engaged in a building program for the pharaoh. Here they were afflicted with heavy burdens by the pharaoh’s officers.
ramiah: Parosh’s son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his foreign wife after the exile.
ramoth (person): KJV form of Jeremoth, Bani’s son, in Ezra 10:29.
ramoth-gilead: City lying in the Transjordan area of Gilead and probably identifiable with Tell Ramith, although the site of Tell el-Husn has also been suggested. Initially, biblical references pertain to Ramoth in Gilead, while later it is called Ramoth-gilead.
ramoth of the negev, ramoth of the south: Ramoth of the Negev, Ramoth of the South
Alternate names for Baalath-beer, an unknown site in Simeon’s territory, in 1 Samuel 30:27.
ramses (person): Name of 11 kings of the 19th and 20th Egyptian dynasties (also spelled Rameses). Ramses II reigned for some 67 years (c. 1290–1224 BC).
ramses (place): Alternate form of the Egyptian place-name Rameses.
ram's horn: Primitive musical instrument made from an animal horn.
ransom: Price for redeeming or liberating slaves, captives, property, or life. Jesus described his entire ministry as one of service in giving his life as a ransom for many.
rape: The act of a man forcing a woman to have sexual intercourse against her will. Two instances are recorded in the OT: Shechem the son of Hamor, a Hivite, raped Dinah (see Gn 34:2-7), and Amnon raped his sister Tamar.
raphael: Major character in the deuterocanonical book of Tobit. When God heard the prayers of Tobit and Sarah, the angel Raphael was sent to their aid.
raphah: Alternate form of Rephaiah, Binea’s son, in 1 Chronicles 8:37.
raphanah: One of the original 10 Greek cities rebuilt by Rome after Pompey’s conquest of Palestine and Syria around 63 BC. Raphanah (also spelled Raphana) was situated in the Decapolis region.
raphon: A town where Judas Maccabeus and his troops defeated the Syrian commander Timothy. It was near Carnaim, and since Carnaim is the same as Ashteroth-karnaim (the modern Sheikh Sa’ad), Raphon is probably er-Rafeh on the Nahr el-Ehreir.
raphu: Benjaminite and the father of Palti, one of the 12 spies sent to search out the land of Canaan.
rapture: Christian term used to denote the ascension (or lifting up) of Christians at the time of Christ’s second coming.
rassis, rassisites: A place and its people, probably in Cilicia, which was devastated by the army of Holofernes.
rathamin: A territory transferred from the dominion of Samaria to Judah by Demetrius of Syria. A letter from Demetrius to his adjutant Lasthenes authorizing the transfer is mentioned in 1 Maccabees 11:34.
raven: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
ravenous birds: KJV translation for “birds of prey” in Isaiah 46:11 and Ezekiel 39:4.
razis: A fiercely patriotic Jewish elder sought by the Syrian general Nicanor for opposition to Hellenism. He committed suicide, throwing his own innards at spectators, rather than face arrest by Syrian soldiers.
razor: A sharp tool used for shaving off the beard or hair. Use of the razor was proscribed for those under the Nazirite vow.
reaia: KJV spelling of Reaiah, Micah’s son, in 1 Chronicles 5:5.
reaiah: 1. Shobal’s son and the father of Jahath from the tribe of Judah, perhaps identifiable with Haroeh (2:52).
reaper, reaping: During Bible times agriculture took the same three main forms found in Palestine today. Emphasis on each of these has depended upon the social and technological status of the people.
reba: One of the five Midianite kings killed by Moses at the Lord’s command for seducing the Israelite settlers to idol worship.
rebecca, rebekah: Daughter of Bethuel and the wife of the patriarch Isaac. Her name, which means “well fed” or “choice,” appears 31 times in Genesis (primarily in chs 24–27) and once in Romans 9:10.
rebirth: Spiritual rebirth producing a new beginning. It describes the new life of the believer in Christ and the new order that will begin at Christ’s return.
recab: 1. Rimmon’s son who, with his brother Baanah, commanded bands of raiders under Saul’s son Ishbosheth.
recah: Town in Judah occupied by Eshton, Beth-rapha, Paseah, Tehinnah, Ir-nahash, and their families.
rechah: KJV spelling of Recah, a Judean town, in 1 Chronicles 4:12.
reconciliation: Restoration of friendly relationships and of peace where there had previously been hostility and alienation. Ordinarily, it also includes the removal of the offense that caused the disruption of peace and harmony.
recorder: The title of a high public official from David’s reign until the end of the Israelite monarchy.
red: The OT and NT have no exact word for “color,” although the word appears several times in our English Bibles. The words translated “color” have quite different meanings in the original languages.
redeemer, redemption: English words derived from a Latin root meaning “to buy back,” thus meaning the liberation of any possession, object, or person, usually by payment of a ransom. In Greek the root word means “to loose” and so to free.
red heifer: Domestic animals of the bovine species (Bos primigenius). The OT often emphasized the beauty of cattle.
red sea: Arm of the Indian Ocean, extending to the northwest and lying between the continents of Africa and Asia. It is a long, narrow body of water, some 1,350 miles (2,172.2 kilometers) long and averaging 180 miles (289.6 kilometers) in width.
reed: Tall grass that grows in damp places and beside bodies of water.
reeds, sea of: Hebrew designation for the body of water crossed by the Israelites during the exodus from Egypt.
reelaiah: Head of a family who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile; alternately called Raamiah.
refuge, cities of: Six cities, three in Canaan and three in Transjordan (area east of the Jordan River), designated as places of safety for persons suspected of manslaughter. The six cities were among the 48 assigned to the Levites.
regem: Jahdai’s son and a descendant of Caleb.
regemmelech: One of the delegation sent to inquire whether fasting to commemorate the temple destruction should continue. The name may refer to a person or could be a title meaning “friend of the king.”
regeneration: Spiritual rebirth producing a new beginning. It describes the new life of the believer in Christ and the new order that will begin at Christ’s return.
rehabiah: Levite, son of Eliezer the priest and Moses’ grandson.
rehob (person): 1. King of Zobah whose son, Hadadezer, was defeated by David at the Euphrates River.
rehob (place): 1. Northernmost territory explored by the Israelite spies prior to occupation of Canaan.
rehoboam: King (930–913 BC) especially remembered for his part in perpetuating the split of the Hebrew kingdom and for being the first king of the separate kingdom of Judah.
rehoboth: 1. KJV name for Rehoboth-Ir, a city built by Nimrod, in Genesis 10:11.
rehoboth-ir: Name meaning “broad places of the city.” It was the second city built by Nimrod the hunter (KJV “Asshur”) in Assyria (Gn 10:11; KJV “Rehoboth”).
rehum: 1. One of the 12 Jewish leaders who returned from captivity with Zerubbabel (Ezr 2:2; Neh 7:7, where “Nehum” is apparently a copyist’s error).
rei: Officer who supported Solomon when Adonijah attempted to become king near the end of David’s reign.
rekem (person): 1. Prince or king of Midian killed with his four accomplices in a battle waged by Moses at the Lord’s command.
rekem (place): One of 26 cities assigned to Benjamin’s tribe for an inheritance.
religion: The service and worship of God; an institutionalized system of religious beliefs and practices. The Israelites’ service and worship of God had become institutionalized by the time Jesus lived.
remaliah: Father of King Pekah of Israel (737–732 BC). Pekah, through treachery, claimed Israel’s throne and later terrorized Jerusalem.
remeth: Border town in Issachar’s territory, and probably the same as Ramoth, also called Jarmuth.
remission of sins: KJV phrase synonymous with “forgiveness of sins.” The NT uses a variety of terms to describe a single truth.
remmon: KJV form of En-rimmon, a town in Simeon’s territory, in Joshua 19:7.
remmon-methoar: KJV translation for “Rimmon it ends toward Neah,” in Joshua 19:13.
remnant: Group of people who survive a catastrophe brought about by God, ordinarily in judgment for sin.
remphan: KJV form of Rephan, a pagan deity, in Acts 7:43.
repentance: Literally a change of mind, not about individual plans, intentions, or beliefs, but rather a change in one’s attitude about God. Such repentance accompanies saving faith in Christ.
rephael: Shemaiah’s son and a temple gatekeeper in David’s time.
rephaiah: 1. Jeshaiah’s son and a descendant of Solomon.
rephaim: 1. A Hebrew word referring to shades or departed spirits whose dwelling place was the habitation of Sheol.
rephaim, valley of: Geographical landmark forming part of the common boundary of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin (KJV “the valley of the giants” in Jos 15:8; 18:16); a broad valley in the southwestern outskirts of Jerusalem thought to be frequented by giants like the Anakim and the Nephilim.
rephan: Pagan deity mentioned by Stephen in Acts 7:43 (KJV “Remphan”; NASB “Rompha”) when he cited the text of Amos 5:26 (NLT “Kaiwan,” see mg) to portray the paganism of the wandering Israelites.
rephidim: Camping place of Israel in the wilderness of Paran, following their exodus from Egypt. Exodus 17:1 lists Rephidim as Israel’s stopping place after the wilderness of Sin.
reptile: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
resen: City built by Nimrod between Nineveh and Calah. It was part of the complex known as “the great city” and could have been a suburb of Nineveh.
resheph: Rephah’s son, a descendant of Ephraim and an ancestor of Joshua, son of Nun.
rest: Freedom from work or activity. The source of the Christian doctrine of rest is the rest of God himself, who, after completing the work of Creation in six days, “rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done”.
resurrection: Act of being raised from the dead, used in the Bible in three different contexts: (1) It refers to miraculous raising of the dead back to earthly life, such as when Elijah raised a boy, Elisha raised the Shunammite’s son, Jesus raised both Jairus’s daughter…
reu: Peleg’s son, the father of Serug, and a descendant of Shem, listed in Luke’s genealogy of Christ.
reuben (person): Eldest son of Jacob and Leah and forefather of one of the 12 tribes of Israel. Reuben was involved in the mandrake incident (30:14) and had sexual relations with Bilhah, his father’s concubine (35:22).
reuben (place): Territory east of the Jordan given to Reuben’s tribe on the condition that they assist in taking Canaan west of the Jordan. Moses agreed to the Reubenites’ request for lands suitable for cattle grazing.
reuben, tribe of: Tribe descended from Reuben, the eldest of Jacob’s sons. The tribe of Reuben usually receives the place of honor in lists of the tribes, being named first.
reuel: 1. Son of Esau by his wife Basemath, and the father of four sons: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah.
reumah: Nahor’s concubine. Her four sons became the ancestors of the Aramean tribes living north of Damascus.
revelation: Term from the Latin revelatio, referring to either (1) the act of revealing for the purpose of making something known or (2) the thing that is revealed.
revelation, book of: Last book of the Bible, containing revelations concerning the events of the last days.
revenge, revenger: Person who performed the duty of pursuing and ultimately executing the murderer of a close relative. Such a “redeemer” was expected to act in instances of deliberate murder but not of accidental manslaughter.
reward: Recompense for good or evil; most often it suggests a benefit for favorable compensation. Both good and evil are rewarded or punished, and man’s responsibility and accountability are involved in an ethical sense.
rezeph: City destroyed by the Assyrians. It was mentioned in a derisive letter sent from Sennacherib, king of Assyria, to Hezekiah of Judah.
rezia: KJV spelling of Rizia, Ulla’s son, in 1 Chronicles 7:39.
rezin: 1. Syrian monarch who ruled in Damascus during the earlier part of Isaiah’s prophetic ministry and during the last years that the northern 10 tribes existed as a nation.
rezon: Son of Eliada, who set himself up as ruler of Damascus and Syria following David’s killing of Hadadezer, king of Zobah. Rezon was a God-appointed adversary who despised Israel and was a constant problem to Solomon during his reign.
rhegium: Important Italian harbor visited by Paul in his journey to Rome. From Malta, Paul’s ship traveled north to the Sicilian capital of Syracuse.
rhesa: Descendant of Zerubbabel and an ancestor of Jesus Christ.
rhoda: Maid in the home of Mary the mother of John Mark in Jerusalem. Rhoda reported to those in the house that Peter was standing outside the door.
rhodes: Port of call on Paul’s return trip to Jerusalem from his third missionary journey. The mention of Rhodes in Genesis 10:4, Ezekiel 27:15, and 1 Chronicles 1:7 is not based on the Hebrew text of the OT but on its Greek translation.
rhodocus: A Jewish traitor who gave military information to the Syrians regarding the fortification of Beth-zur by Judas Maccabeus. When discovered, he was found guilty and imprisoned.
ribai: Benjaminite of Gibeah and the father of Ittai, one of David’s mighty men.
riblah: 1. Town along the Orontes River located some 35 miles (56.3 kilometers) northeast of Baalbek, identifiable with modern Ribleh in Syria.
riches: Wealth measured by money or the amount of property owned, whether land and buildings, livestock, or slaves (8:11-18). Great riches brought great influence and power, as the Hebrew word for wealth implies.
riddle: Word puzzle widely used and esteemed in the ancient world, both as an everyday amusement and as a test of wisdom at a more serious level. The point of a riddle was the discovery of a concealed meaning.
rie: KJV rendering of spelt, a common form of wheat in Bible times, in Exodus 9:32.
righteousness: The establishment of a right relationship—primarily between God and people, secondarily between people themselves. Righteousness is the fulfillment of just expectations in any relationship, whether with God or other people.
right hand: The word “right” in the Bible is often used in the sense of “being straight”; it is used to describe that which is just or righteous (cf. Gn 18:25).
rimmon (person): 1. Benjaminite of Beeroth, whose two sons, Baanah and Recab, assassinated Ishbosheth.
rimmon (place): 1. Alternate name for En-rimmon, a town in southern Judah, in Joshua 15:32 and 1 Chronicles 4:32.
rimmono: A town in the territory of Zebulun.
rimmon-perez: Temporary camping place of the Israelites during their wilderness wanderings, mentioned between Rithmah and Libnah.
riphath: Gomer’s son and the brother of Ashkenaz and Togarmah, non-Semitic descendants of Noah through Japheth’s line. First Chronicles 1:6, a parallel passage, reads Diphath instead of Riphath, undoubtedly a latter copyist’s misspelling that was never corrected.
rissah: Stopping place for Israel in the wilderness between Libnah and Kehelathah.
rithmah: Stopping place for Israel in the wilderness between Hazeroth and Rimmon-perez.
river of egypt: 1. Alternate name for the border of Egypt (possibly the Nile River) in Genesis 15:18.
river of the wilderness: KJV reading for an unidentifiable brook in the Arabah in Amos 6:14; called brook of the Arabah in the RSV (NLT “valley of the Arabah”).
rizia: Capable leader and mighty warrior, Ulla’s son from Asher’s tribe.
rizpah: Daughter of Aiah and a concubine of Saul. She bore two sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth, to Saul.
robber, robbery: The science or philosophy of law is called jurisprudence. Although modern jurisprudence bears little resemblance to biblical concepts of law, the Scriptures have played a definite role in its development.
roboam: KJV rendering of Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, in Matthew 1:7.
rock badger: Small hoofed mammal. What the KJV calls a “coney,” modern translations name “rock badger”.
rodanim: Fourth son of Javan and a descendant of Noah through Japheth’s line. An alternate spelling in Genesis 10:4 reads Dodanim, possibly a copyist’s error.
roe, roebuck: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
rogelim: Home of Barzillai the Gileadite, who served David at Mahanaim, where David sought refuge from Absalom. Rogelim was situated in the highlands east of the Jordan River.
romamti-ezer: Heman’s son and a musician appointed by King David to serve in the sanctuary.
romans, letter to the: Written in the first person (Rom 1:5, 10, etc.), this epistle was authored by the apostle Paul.
rome, city of: City in Italy founded, according to tradition, in 753 BC on seven hills about 15 miles (24.1 kilometers) from the mouth of the Tiber River. It was of no biblical interest until NT times.
root of jesse: Figure of speech used by Isaiah to express the hope of a messianic king from the line of David. The “root” of a family is its progenitor.
rose: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
rosetta stone: The fame of this stone rests upon the part it played in providing the clue for deciphering ancient Egyptian inscriptions. Rosetta is the European name for the town Rashid in the vicinity of which the stone was discovered.
ruby: A lengthy list of the precious stones used in OT times occurs in Exodus 28:17-20 and 39:10-13, where four rows of three stones, each engraved with the name of one of the 12 tribes of Israel, were set in the high priest’s breastplate.
rue: Perennial shrub whose leaves were used for medicinal purposes.
rufus: 1. One of the sons of Simon of Cyrene.
ruhamah: One of two symbolic names showing God’s altered perspective toward Israel from one of hostility to one of mercy. God’s attitude of displeasure was symbolized by the name Lo-ruhamah (meaning “Not pitied”), which Hosea named his daughter.
ruler: The term represents a number of different functions and translates 13 Hebrew and 3 Greek words. In a political sense, a ruler was one who exercised political control over a state, or a state that exercised control over a subject people.
ruler of the synagogue: Senior official in a synagogue of NT times. It is generally understood that there was only one such official in any one synagogue.
rumah: Home of Pedaiah, the father of Zebidah, Jehoiakim’s mother. Some identify it with Arumah, near Shechem (cf.
rush: KJV form of reed in Job 8:11 and Isaiah 9:14.
ruth (person): Moabitess and the widow of Mahlon, the son of Naomi and Elimelech, who were Ephrathites from Bethlehem living in Moab because of a severe famine in Judah.
ruth, book of: The author of the book is unknown. The question of authorship has particular connection with the date of writing, and a few clues provide at least an educated guess.
sabachthani: One of the final words Jesus spoke during his crucifixion; it is Aramaic.
sabaoth: Hebrew word meaning “hosts” or “army,” as in the expression “Lord of hosts.” See God, Names of.
sabbath: Derivation of a Hebrew word that means “cease” or “desist.” The Sabbath was a day (from Friday evening until Saturday evening in Jesus’ time) when all ordinary work stopped.
sabbath, covert for the: Covered place in the court of the temple reserved for the king who stood there with his attendants on a Sabbath or feast day (2 Kgs 16:18, KJV; NLT “canopy”).
sabbath day's journey: Regulation derived from Jewish literature limiting travel on the Sabbath. The prohibition against work on the Sabbath was interpreted to exclude extensive travel.
sabbath year, sabbatical year: Last year of the seven-year cycle established for keeping time in the Mosaic law.
sabeans: Inhabitants of Sheba (Saba), a country in southwest Arabia. The Sabeans were noted as men of stature and for their murder and theft of Job’s servants and property.
sabta, sabtah: One of Cush’s five sons and a descendant of Noah through Ham’s line. Sabtah presumably settled along the southern coast of Arabia, where several cities bear his name.
sabteca: One of Cush’s five sons and a descendant of Noah through Ham’s line. Sabteca settled in Arabia.
sachia, sachiah: NASB and NKJV, respectively, for Sakia (NLT, NIV).
sackbut: KJV rendering of trigon, a triangular-shaped harp, in Daniel 3:5-15.
sackcloth: Poor quality material or a garment of goat hair usually worn as a symbol of mourning, but also worn by some prophets and captives.
sacrifice: In Christian thought, the act by which God and man are brought together in personal relationship.
sadducees: Jewish sect cited 14 times in the NT, not referred to in the OT.
sadoc: KJV form of Zadok, an ancestor of Christ, in Matthew 1:14.
saffron: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
sage: Plant growing three feet (.9 meter) tall and indigenous to Palestine. When pressed flat, the inflorescence of this plant provides the pattern for the seven-branched lampstand used by the Jews.
sailors: Men trained in sailing ships at sea. The people of Israel were not generally seafaring and confined their activities on the water to the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan River.
saints: Name for believers meaning “holy ones” (which is the rendering in some modern versions—see NLT). The OT believers were called to be “holy,” or consecrated to God.
sakia: Son of Shaharaim and Hodesh from Benjamin’s tribe.
sakkuth: Name of the Babylonian Saturn, an astral deity in Mesopotamian religion. Some suggest that Sakkuth reflects a corruption of sukkah, meaning “shrine” (NIV) or “tabernacle” (KJV), within which an image would be placed.
sala: 1. Alternate name for Salmon, Boaz’s father, in Luke 3:32 (see NLT mg).
salah: KJV form of Shelah, Eber’s father, in Genesis 10:24 and 11:12-15.
salamis: Seaport on the eastern shore of Cyprus where Barnabas and Saul landed near the beginning of their first missionary journey. They proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews in this town.
salathiel: KJV alternate spelling of Shealtiel, King Jehoiachin’s son, in 1 Chronicles 3:17, Matthew 1:12, and Luke 3:27.
salcah, salchah, salecah: City or district that formed the northeastern extremity of the Amorite kingdom of Og in Bashan, east of the Jordan River. Salecah (variously spelled Salcah and Salchah in the KJV) was located near the city of Edrei.
salem: City from which the priest-king Melchizedek came. Salem is believed to be an ancient name of Jerusalem.
salim: Location near Aenon on the west side of the Jordan River. Aenon was known for its many springs and was used by John as a place for baptism.
sallai: 1. One of 928 Benjaminites who lived in the city of Jerusalem during the postexilic period.
sallu: 1. Son of Meshullam and a Benjaminite, who resided in the city of Jerusalem during the postexilic period.
salmon (person): Nahshon’s son and an ancestor of David from Judah’s tribe. Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab and is listed in Matthew’s genealogy as a forefather of Jesus Christ; in the Greek his name is spelled Sala in Luke’s genealogy.
salmon (place): KJV spelling of Zalmon, a mountain in Bashan, in Psalm 68:14.
salmone: Promonotory on the east side of Crete.
salome: Name deriving from the Hebrew greeting shalom (peace), with the additional letter being a Greek suffix.
salt, city of: City located near the Dead Sea, assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance.
salt, covenant of: Biblical phrase for a two-way agreement, the inviolability of which was symbolized by salt. A Middle Eastern saying, “There is bread and salt between us,” meant that a relationship had been confirmed by sharing a meal.
salt, valley of: Valley in the southern vicinity of the Dead Sea. The Valley of Salt was the scene of two major military campaigns recorded in the OT.
salt sea: A large saltwater lake into which the river Jordan empties.
saltwort: Family of bushy shrubs, of which numerous species can be found along the coasts of the Mediterranean Sea.
salu: Zimri’s father from Simeon’s tribe. Zimri, head of his father’s household, was killed by Phinehas.
