salvation: God’s way of providing people deliverance from sin and death. Scripture reveals God but it also reveals his plan to save the human race.
samaria: Capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, identified with the hill on which the village of Sebastieh is located.
samaritans: Schismatic group from the Jews. The group resided north of Judea and south of Galilee in hostile tension with its Jewish neighbors.
samgar-nebo: Babylonian prince who took part with Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldean army in conquering Jerusalem after a three-year siege from 588–586 BC.
samlah: King of the Edomites from the town of Masrekah. Samlah came to power before any king ruled in Israel.
samos: Small Greek island located off the coast of Asia Minor in the Aegean Sea near the promontory of Trogyllium. This Ionian island was positioned southwest of Ephesus and northwest of Miletus.
samothrace: Island in the northeastern part of the Aegean Sea off the coast of the Roman province of Thrace. It was named Samothrace, or “Samos of Thrace,” to distinguish it from the other Samos (cf.
samson: Manoah’s son, from Dan’s tribe. His mother, whose name is not given in the Bible, had been barren.
samuel (person): Last of the judges, his name means “name of God” or “his name is El” (El is the name of the God of strength and power). The play on words in 1 Samuel 1:20 (cf.
samuel, books of first and second: Samuel, Books of First and Second
First and Second Samuel derive their names from the individual whom God used to establish kingship in Israel. Samuel is the most prominent figure in the early narratives of 1 Samuel.
sanballat: Leading political official of Samaria residing at Beth-horon in Ephraim. In a letter from Elephantine of Egypt, Sanballat was named as the governor of Samaria in 407 BC.
sanctification: Term meaning “being made holy, or purified.” It is used broadly of the whole Christian experience, though most theologians prefer to use it in a restricted sense to distinguish it from related terms, such as “regeneration,” “justification,” and “glorification.”
sanctuary: Translation of two Hebrew words, kodesh and midkosh, both of which are derived from the verb “to be clean” and/or “to be holy.” It appears approximately 60 times in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers where the building, moving, and initial use of the tabernacle is reported.
sandalwood: The precious wood imported by King Solomon and used in making the pillars for the temple and for making harps and psalteries. This timber was brought by sea from Ophir to Ezion-geber, near Elath.
sand lizard: Reptiles of the suborder Lacertilia. Their skin is covered with scales.
sanhedrin: Supreme judicial council (NLT “high council”) of Judaism with 71 members, located in Jerusalem.
sansannah: One of 29 cities at the southern extremity of the land inherited by the sons of Judah. It is possibly the same city as Hazar-susah mentioned in a parallel description of the territory allotted to Simeon within Judah’s inheritance (19:5).
saph: Descendant of the giants, killed by Sibbecai the Hushathite (one of David’s warriors) at Gad in a battle between Israel and Philistia; alternately called Sippai.
saphir: KJV spelling of Shaphir, a place mentioned in Micah 1:11.
sapphira: Member of the Jerusalem church and wife of Ananias.
sapphire: A lengthy list of the precious stones used in OT times occurs in Exodus 28:17-20 and 39:10-13, where four rows of three stones, each engraved with the name of one of the 12 tribes of Israel, were set in the high priest’s breastplate.
sara: KJV rendering of Sarah, Abraham’s wife, in Hebrews 11:11 and 1 Peter 3:6.
sarah: 1. Wife of Abraham whose name was originally Sarai.
sarai: Original name for Sarah, Abraham’s wife.
saraph: Shelah’s son from Judah’s tribe. Saraph ruled in Moab and later returned to Lehem.
sardine stone: KJV form of carnelian in Revelation 4:3.
sardis: Important city in the Roman province of Asia, once the capital of the ancient kingdom of Lydia. It lay astride great highways linking it to the coastal regions to the west and to eastern Asia Minor.
sardite: KJV form of Seredite, a member of Sered’s family, in Numbers 26:26.
sardius: KJV form of carnelian in Ezekiel 28:13.
sardonyx: KJV form of onyx in Revelation 21:20.
sarepta: KJV form of Zarephath, a Phoenician town, in Luke 4:26.
sargon: Assyrian monarch from 722–705 BC, whose military campaigns are historically well documented. Excavations have revealed his palace at what was probably Nineveh as well as an incomplete palace at Khorsabad.
sarid: Town located in the region of Zebulun near its southern border, situated between Maralah to the west and Kisloth-tabor to the east. Some suggest that this town is the same as Tell Shadud, a town near the valley of Jezreel.
saron: KJV spelling of Sharon, the large coastal plain in northern Palestine, in Acts 9:35.
sarsechim, sarsekim: Personal name or title of an official who participated with Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldean army in conquering Jerusalem (see Jer 39:3, NLT mg). Some modern translations read “Nebo-sarsekim.”
saruch: KJV rendering of Serug, an ancestor of Jesus, in Luke 3:35.
satan: Spirit being who opposes God and seeks to frustrate his plans and lead his people into rebellion.
saton: Greek word in Matthew 13:33 for a dry commodity measure equivalent to the OT seah, equaling about one peck (8.8 liters). The plural is sata (NASB mg).
satrap: Governor who held jurisdiction over a number of provinces within the king’s domain. This official represented the authority of the king in both civil and military matters, and supplied the means for maintaining the king’s sovereignty over the whole empire.
satyr: Creature of uncertain identification, possibly referring to a demon, a goat, or a deity that resembles a goat.
saul: Name meaning “asked,” with the implication being “asked of God.” A name with a usage extending far back into prebiblical times, it is attested in third-millennium texts from Tell Mardikh in Syria (ancient Ebla) and appears also to have been used in the second millennium in the city of Ugarit on the coast of Syria.
savior: One who delivers or rescues. The term “savior” is most frequently applied to God and Jesus Christ in the Bible.
scab: Any localized abnormality of the skin. It was a well-demarcated skin abnormality with a definite border between the inflamed or abnormal skin and the normal skin.
scall: KJV rendering for an eruption, a skin rash, in Leviticus 13:30-37 and 14:54.
scapegoat: Goat that, on the Day of Atonement, is sent into the wilderness, symbolically bearing away the sins of the people.
scarlet: The OT and NT have no exact word for “color,” although the word appears several times in our English Bibles. The words translated “color” have quite different meanings in the original languages.
scepter: Long staff with an ornamental head and other decorations used to represent royal authority; a shorter staff was used as a battle mace to symbolize royal military power.
sceva: Father of seven sons and a Jewish chief priest in Ephesus at the time of Paul’s visit on his third missionary journey. Sceva’s sons attempted to imitate Paul’s exorcism of evil spirits in the name of Jesus.
school: The act or process of educating or being educated. The original purpose of Jewish education was to teach children to know and understand their special relationship with God, to teach them to serve him, and to educate them in holiness.
scorpion: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
scourge: The science or philosophy of law is called jurisprudence. Although modern jurisprudence bears little resemblance to biblical concepts of law, the Scriptures have played a definite role in its development.
screech owl: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
scribe: Reference in early OT times to those employed for their ability to transcribe information. After the exile, scribes were a class of scholars who taught, copied, and interpreted the Jewish law for the people.
scripture, scriptures: The holy writings of Judaism and Christianity. Jews recognize 39 books as comprising their Scriptures.
scroll: Roll of papyrus, leather, or parchment used as a writing document.
scrolls, dead sea: Copies of the OT books produced by scribes and editions made from these copies. The ancient manuscripts of the OT are the basic working material used to seek out the original text of the Bible with as great a degree of accuracy as possible.
scurvy: Term used three times in the Bible (Lv 21:20 and 22:22, KJV; Dt 28:27, NLT). In none of the instances does it refer to the modern disease by the same name, which results from severe vitamin C deficiency.
scythopolis: The Greek name for Beth-shan in 2 Maccabees 12:29.
sea: A great body of salty water covering much of the earth.
sea, dead: A large saltwater lake into which the river Jordan empties.
sea, molten: Alternate name for the laver in King Solomon’s temple.
sea, red: Arm of the Indian Ocean, extending to the northwest and lying between the continents of Africa and Asia. It is a long, narrow body of water, some 1,350 miles (2,172.2 kilometers) long and averaging 180 miles (289.6 kilometers) in width.
sea, the great: Body of water often called the Great Sea, bordering Palestine on the west.
sea of chinnereth, sea of chinneroth: Sea of Chinnereth, Sea of Chinneroth
Early names for the Sea of Galilee.
sea of galilee: A large body of water in Palestine. It has had many names in its history.
sea of glass: A body of water in the vision of heaven described by John in the book of Revelation. It appears again later, in a different vision (15:2), and is perhaps connected with other “sea” references in the same book (13:1; 21:1).
sea of kinnereth: Early name for the Sea of Galilee.
sea of reeds: Hebrew designation for the body of water crossed by the Israelites during the exodus from Egypt.
sea of the arabah: Alternate name for the Dead Sea.
sea of tiberias: Alternate name for the Sea of Galilee.
seagull: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
seah: Unit of dry measure mentioned twice in the Bible.
seal: Small engraved object widely used in the ancient Near East to produce an image in soft clay.
seasons: Systematic arrangements showing the beginning and length of each year and its division into days, weeks, and months. The modern calendar is usually taken for granted.
seat, moses': Biblical expression occurring only in Matthew 23:2, where Jesus speaks of the scribes and the Pharisees as having sat down on the seat of Moses.
seba: Semitic people descended from Cush and possibly to be identified with the people of Sheba.
sebam: City located on the pastoral tablelands of the Transjordan and desired by the sons of Gad and Reuben. Reuben was apportioned this area but eventually lost it to the marauding Moabites.
sebat: KJV spelling of Shebat, the Hebrew month extending from about mid-January to about mid-February, in Zechariah 1:7.
secacah: One of six cities situated in the wilderness region immediately west of the Dead Sea in the valley of Achor and included in the territory allotted to Judah, mentioned between Middin and Nibshan.
sechu: KJV spelling of Secu in 1 Samuel 19:22.
second adam: Analogy that compares and contrasts the first man with the one he is seen to typify, the Lord Jesus Christ.
second coming of christ: The return of Jesus Christ to earth to complete the work of salvation.
second death, the: Term used in the NT only in the book of Revelation, to describe God’s eternal judgment on sin. Originally a rabbinic expression, the second death will be experienced by those whose names are not written in the “Book of Life”.
second jewish revolt: This Bar-Kochba Revolt, so-called after its leader, lasted from AD 131 to 135.
second temple, period of the: Time interval from the dedication of the rebuilt Jerusalem temple in 516 BC to its destruction by the Romans in AD 70.
secu: Town or topographical landmark where Saul stopped to ask the whereabouts of Samuel and David, located between Gibeah and Ramah. It was especially noted for its large well—a natural place to go for information.
secundus: A Thessalonian believer; traveling companion of Aristarchus. Secundus accompanied Paul on his third missionary journey through Macedonia and Greece and awaited him at Troas in Asia Minor.
seer: Term, along with its English cognates (“prophet,” “to prophesy,” “prophetism,” and “prophetic”), derived from a group of Greek words that, in secular Greek, mean “speak forth,” “proclaim,” “announce.” In biblical Greek, however, these terms always carry the…
segub: 1. Youngest son of Hiel the Bethelite.
seir (person): Father of seven sons and a descendant of Abraham through Esau’s line. Originally a Horite tribe dwelling in the land of Edom, the nation descended from Seir was first dispossessed by, but later intermarried with, Esau’s descendants.
seir (place): 1. Mountain range of Edom extending from the Dead Sea southward to the Gulf of Aqaba.
seirah: Place where Ehud sought refuge after murdering Eglon, the king of Moab, and from where he summoned Israel to war against the Moabites.
sela: 1. Unidentified site on the border of the Amorites.
selah: Musical notation, perhaps designating a pause in performance, occurring over 70 times in psalm texts and in Habakkuk 3:3, 9, 13.
sela-hammahlekoth: Cliff in the wilderness of Maon, meaning “the Rock of Escape.” Saul, in his desire to kill David, attempted to catch him in the steep-ravined mountains of Judah, where David had fled.
seleucia: Name of several ancient Near Eastern cities, all founded by Seleucus I Nicator (312–281 BC).
sem: KJV form of Shem, Noah’s son, in Luke 3:36.
semachiah, semakiah: Korahite Levite, Shemaiah’s son and a gatekeeper in the temple.
semei, semein: Descendant of Josech and an ancestor of Jesus Christ.
senaah: Father of a family of Israelites who returned with Zerubbabel to Palestine following the exile. They helped Nehemiah rebuild part of the Jerusalem wall (Neh 3:3; Hassenaah is an alternate spelling for Senaah).
seneh: Name of one of the two rocky crags at a pass across the Wadi es-Suweinit over which Jonathan and his armor bearer crossed in their skirmish against the Philistines. The crag opposite Seneh was called Bozez and faced the town of Micmash to the north.
senir: Amorite name for Mt Hermon in Deuteronomy 3:9 and Song of Songs 4:8.
sennacherib: King of the Assyrian Empire from 705 to 681 BC. His name, meaning “son has replaced brothers,” may refer to a specific family situation by means of which he, a younger son of Sargon II, came to succeed his father.
senuah: KJV form of Hassenuah in Nehemiah 11:9.
seorim: Levite and head of the fourth of 24 divisions of priests formed during David’s reign.
separation, water of: KJV translation of “the water for the purification ceremony,” a water denoting cleansing from sin or impurity, in Numbers 19:9, 13, 20-21; 31:23.
sephar: Geographical landmark defining one of the boundaries of the territory settled by the sons of Joktan.
sepharad: Place of exile for the Jews of Jerusalem (Ob 1:20, NLT mg). Its location is not certain; however, good evidence is available to support Sardis, the capital of Lydia, in Asia Minor as the place of captivity.
sepharvaim, sepharvites: One of five cities and its inhabitants who were transported to Samaria after the fall of Israel to Sargon II, king of Assyria, in 722 BC.
septuagint: To get a picture of how the Bible has come to different peoples in the world, spread out a map of the eastern hemisphere and imagine Palestine as the center of a pool.
sepulcher: The Bible makes frequent reference to burial practices. A society’s burial customs are a reflection of its views about death and the afterlife.
seraiah: 1. Royal secretary of King David; alternately called Sheva in 2 Samuel 20:25, Shisha in 1 Kings 4:3, and Shavsha in 1 Chronicles 18:16.
seraph, seraphim: Angelic beings mentioned only twice in the Bible, both occurring in the same chapter of Isaiah. The word seraphim is plural in number, but it is impossible to say from Isaiah’s vision just how many he saw.
sered, seredite: One of Zebulun’s sons and the father of the Seredite family.
sergius paulus: Proconsul of Cyprus, described as a “man of intelligence”. Paul and Barnabas, on their first missionary journey, evangelized the Cyprian city of Paphos, Sergius Paulus’s residence.
sermon on the mount: Term derived from Latin beatitudo; it is not used in the English Bible. Technically it means “blessedness” as described in the OT and NT.
serpent: A snake or sea monster. Various words are used in the Bible for serpents or snakes.
serpent, bronze: Piece of sculpture that God commanded Moses to make when the Israelites were being bitten by “fiery serpents”. The serpents had been sent as a judgment because the people were grumbling against God and against Moses.
serpent's stone: Place where Adonijah, the son of David, sacrificed sheep and oxen and attempted to secretly set himself up as king (1 Kgs 1:9, NLT mg). The serpent’s stone was located near En-rogel, a spring in the Kidron Valley located just south of Jerusalem.
serug: Reu’s son from Shem’s line, Abraham’s forefather and an ancestor of Jesus Christ (Lk 3:35; KJV “Saruch”).
servant: A person under obligation to serve a master, who in turn would provide a measure of protection. Some servants were slaves under legal bondage; others were servants voluntarily.
servant of the lord: Title applied to a variety of persons in the Bible. The basic term, “servant,” covers a range of meanings.
seth: Third son of Adam and Eve, replacing Abel, whom Cain murdered. He appears as the firstborn son of Adam in the genealogies of Genesis 5:3-8, 1 Chronicles 1:1 (KJV “Sheth”), and Luke 3:38.
sethur: Asherite, Michael’s son and one of the 12 spies sent by Moses to search out the land of Canaan.
seven: Individual numbers have a symbolic as well as a literal sense in the Bible. In Daniel, and to a lesser extent in Revelation, there is a developed system of numerology where interrelated systems of numbers are used in a definite pattern.
seven last sayings of jesus: Recorded words of Jesus between the time he was crucified and the time he died. These seven sentences (quoted below from the KJV) are not found in any one Gospel.
sex, sexuality: Unlike some religious and philosophical systems, the Bible takes a positive view of human sexuality. According to the OT’s account of Creation, it was God himself who made people sexual beings.
shaalabbin, shaalbim, shaalbon: Amorite city known by three names, assigned to Dan’s tribe for an inheritance, mentioned between Ir-shemesh and Aijalon. The Danites, however, were unable to defeat the Amorites and take possession of the city.
shaalim: Region within the land of Ephraim or Benjamin where Saul searched for his father’s donkeys.
shaaph: 1. Jahdai’s sixth son, included in the genealogy of Caleb, Jerahmeel’s brother.
shaaraim: 1. One of 14 cities in the lowland region of the territory allotted to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance, listed between Azekah and Adithaim.
shaashgaz: Eunuch of King Ahasuerus, in charge of the concubines.
shabbethai: 1. Levite who opposed Ezra’s suggestion that the sons of Israel should divorce the foreign women they had married upon returning to Palestine from exile.
shaddai: Part of the Hebrew name El Shaddai for God, meaning “God Almighty”.
shadrach, meshach, and abednego: Babylonian names of three Hebrew youths, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, who along with Daniel and others were taken to Babylon as hostages by Nebuchadnezzar in 605 BC.
shagee: Hararite and Jonathan’s father. Jonathan was one of David’s mighty men.
shaharaim: Benjaminite living in Moab, father of nine sons, who divorced two of his three wives.
shahazumah: Town situated between Tabor and Beth-shemesh on the border of the land allotted to Issachar’s tribe for an inheritance.
shalisha, shalishah: One of the regions (mentioned between the hill country of Ephraim and the district of Shaalim) through which Saul traveled in search of his father’s lost donkeys.
shallecheth, shalleketh, gate of: Gate located on the western side of the temple, which was guarded by Shuppim and Hosah (1 Chr 26:16, NLT mg).
shallum: 1. Son of Jabesh and Israel’s 16th king (752 BC).
shallun: KJV and NIV spelling of Shallum, Col-hozeh’s son, in Nehemiah 3:15.
shalmai: Alternate rendering of Shamlai in Ezra 2:46 and Nehemiah 7:48.
shalman: Unknown conqueror whose brutal destruction of Beth-arbel was descriptive of Israel’s approaching judgment.
shalmaneser: Name of several Assyrian rulers, two of whom had direct contact with the people of Israel. However, only Shalmaneser V is known by name in the Bible.
shama: One of the mighty men of David’s army, son of Hotham the Aroerite and the brother of Jeiel.
shamariah: KJV spelling of Shemariah, King Rehoboam’s son, in 2 Chronicles 11:19.
shamed: KJV spelling of Shemed, one of El-paal’s sons, in 1 Chronicles 8:12.
shamer: 1. KJV spelling of Shemer, Bani’s son, in 1 Chronicles 6:46.
shamgar: Son of Anath from Beth-anath; a judge of Israel. Two brief references in the OT tell us little of the man except for his one major exploit: the killing of 600 Philistines with an oxgoad.
shamhuth: Alternate form of Shammah the Izrahite in 1 Chronicles 27:8.
shamir (place): 1. One of the 11 towns in the hill country allotted to Judah.
shamlai: Father of a family of temple servants returning to the land of Canaan with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian captivity; alternately spelled Shalmai in Ezra 2:46 and Nehemiah 7:48.
shammah: 1. One of Reuel’s four sons, the grandson of Esau and a chief in the land of Edom.
shammai: 1. Onam’s son, brother of Jada and the father of Nadab and Abishur from Judah’s tribe.
shammoth: The plural form of Shammah the Harodite in 2 Samuel 23:25; 1 Chronicles 11:27 (NLT mg).
shammua: 1. Reubenite, Zaccur’s son and one of the 12 spies sent by Moses to search out the land of Canaan.
shamsherai: Jeroham’s son and a chief in Benjamin’s tribe.
shapham: Leader in Gad’s tribe. He is believed to have lived in Bashan and served during the days of Jotham, king of Judah (v 17).
shaphan: 1. Son of Azaliah and the father of Ahikam, Elasah, and Gemariah.
shaphat: 1. Simeonite, Hori’s son and one of the 12 spies sent by Moses to search out the land of Canaan.
shapher: KJV form of Shepher, the name of an unidentified mountain, in Numbers 33:23-24.
shaphir: One of the towns spoken against by Micah the prophet. Its exact location is not certain.
sharai: One of Binnui’s sons who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife during the postexilic era.
sharaim: KJV spelling of Shaaraim, a city in Judah’s territory, in Joshua 15:36.
sharar: Alternate name for Sachar, Ahiram’s father, in 2 Samuel 23:33.
sharezer: 1. One of the sons of Sennacherib, the king of Assyria.
sharon: 1. Section of the plain on the Mediterranean coast of Israel.
sharonite: Designation for Shitrai, a royal steward in charge of David’s flocks in the plain of Sharon.
sharuhen: Alternate name for Shaaraim, a city in Simeon’s territory, in Joshua 19:6.
shashai: Binnui’s son, who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife during the postexilic era.
shashak: Benjaminite, Elpaal’s son and the father of 11 sons.
shaul: 1. Alternate name for Saul, an Edomite king, in Genesis 36:37-38 and 1 Chronicles 1:48-49.
shaulite: Descendant of Shaul from Simeon’s tribe.
shaveh, valley of: Alternate name for the King’s Valley near Jerusalem in Genesis 14:17.
shaveh kiriathaim: Plain east of the Dead Sea near the city of Kiriathaim and occupied by the people of Emim. The Emimites in Shaveh Kiriathaim are listed with a number of other tribes and nations that King Kedorlaomer and his allies defeated (Gn 14:5; NLT, “Kiriathaim”).
shavsha: Alternate name for Seraiah, the secretary to King David, in 1 Chronicles 18:16 (see NLT mg).
sheal: One of Bani’s sons who was told by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife.
shealtiel: Son of King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) of Judah (598–597 BC) and the father of Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel led the Jews back to Palestine and there ruled as governor of Judah during the postexilic period.
sheariah: One of Azel’s six sons, a descendant of Jonathan, son of King Saul, from Benjamin’s tribe.
shearing house: KJV translation for Beth-eked, a place on the road between Jezreel and Samaria, in 2 Kings 10:12-14.
shear-jashub: Isaiah’s son whose name, meaning “a remnant shall return,” symbolized the prophecy that, although Israel and Judah would be destroyed, a remnant would be saved and later return.
sheba (person): 1. Son of Raamah, the brother of Dedan and a descendant of Noah through Ham’s line.
sheba (place): 1. One of 14 cities listed in Joshua 19:2 that were assigned to Simeon’s tribe within the southern portion of Judah’s inheritance.
sheba, queen of: 1. One of 14 cities listed in Joshua 19:2 that were assigned to Simeon’s tribe within the southern portion of Judah’s inheritance.
shebah: KJV rendering of Shibah, a well near Beersheba, in Genesis 26:33.
shebam: KJV spelling of Sebam, a city in Reuben’s territory, in Numbers 32:3.
shebaniah: 1. One of the seven priests assigned to blow a trumpet before the ark of God in the procession led by David, when the ark was moved to Jerusalem.
shebarim: Location between Ai and Jericho to which the men of Ai pursued the fleeing Israelites. This region was evidently situated near the place of descent from the hill country to the lowlands (Jos 7:5, see NLT mg).
shebat: Name of the Hebrew month extending from about mid-January to about mid-February in Zechariah 1:7.
sheber: Caleb’s son by his concubine Maacah.
shebna: Eighth-century official of the kingdom of Judah.
shebuel: 1. Gershon’s son and Moses’ grandson from Levi’s tribe; father of Jehdeiah (24:20, “Shubael”).
shecaniah, shechaniah: 1. Descendant of David through the line of Zerubbabel living in postexilic Palestine.
shechem (place): Town in the center of western Palestine, near the watershed that separates the waters that flow to the Jordan from those that descend to the Mediterranean.
shechem, tower of: Fortress erected on the acropolis of Shechem, housing the temple of Baal-berith and situated inside the city walls. The city of Shechem was located in the hill country of the tribe of Ephraim near Mt Gerizim.
shechemite: Descendant of Shechem, Gilead’s son from Manasseh’s tribe.
shedeur: Elizur’s father. Elizur represented Reuben’s tribe in Moses’ census of the men capable of bearing arms, and in the dedication of the altar (7:30-35).
sheep: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
sheep gate: Jerusalem gate repaired by Eliashib and the priests under Nehemiah’s supervision during the postexilic era.
sheerah: Daughter or granddaughter of Ephraim. Her offspring built lower and upper Beth-horon and Uzzen-sheerah, named after her.
shehariah: Jehoram’s son and a chief of Benjamin’s tribe in Jerusalem after the exile.
shekel: Weight, and later also a coin.
shekinah: Transliteration of a Hebrew word meaning “the one who dwells” or “that which dwells.” The term enters Christian theology from its use in the Targums and rabbinic literature to describe the immanent presence in the world of the transcendent Deity.
shelah: 1. Arphaxad’s son and the father of Eber.
shelah, pool of: Reservoir in the King’s Garden in Jerusalem.
shelemiah: 1. Korahite from the tribe of Levi and a gatekeeper who was chosen by lot to guard the east gate of the sanctuary during David’s reign; also named Meshelemiah (vv 1-2).
sheleph: Joktan’s son and the founder of an Arabian tribe living in Yemen.
shelesh: Helem’s son and a chief of Asher’s tribe.
shelomi: Ahihud’s father. Ahihud represented Asher’s tribe in the division of the land of Canaan among Israel’s ten tribes west of the Jordan.
shelomith: 1. Dibri’s daughter and the mother of a man from Dan’s tribe who blasphemed the Lord’s name, for which he was subsequently stoned to death.
shelomoth: 1. Gershonite Levite and one of Shimei’s sons serving in the sanctuary during David’s reign.
shelters, festival of: Alternate name for the Festival of Tabernacles.
shelumiel: Simeonite, Zurishaddai’s son and one of the leaders who assisted Moses in taking a census of Israel in the wilderness. He is the forefather of the apocryphal Judith (Jdt 8:1, where his name is Salamiel and his father’s Sarasadai).
shem: Eldest son of Noah and the ancestor of the Semitic peoples. Shem lived 600 years (11:10-11).
shema (person): 1. Judahite, Hebron’s son and a descendant of Caleb.
shema (place): One of the 29 cities located near the border of Edom in the southern extremity of the land inherited by Judah, mentioned between the cities of Amam and Moladah.
shema, the: The declaration “Hear, O Israel, Yahweh our God is one Yahweh”. Shema comes from the first Hebrew word of the verse, shema, “hear.” Verses 4-9 make up the whole of this foundational biblical truth.
shemaah: Father of Ahiezer and Joash, two bowmen who joined David at Ziklag.
shemaiah: 1. Prophet during the reign of Rehoboam, king of Judah (930–913 BC).
shemariah: 1. Warrior from the tribe of Benjamin who joined David at Ziklag in his struggle against King Saul.
shemeber: King of Zeboiim, who joined a confederacy with four other kings in rebellion against Kedorlaomer and his allies. Abraham rescued Lot from captivity after Shemeber, along with Sodom and Gomorrah, was defeated.
shemed: Elpaal’s son and a descendant of Benjamin through Shaharaim’s line. Shemed rebuilt the towns of Ono and Lod after the Babylonian exile.
shemer: 1. Owner of the hill of Samaria, which Omri, king of Israel, bought as the site of his new capital city and named after Shemer.
shemida, shemidah, shemidaite: Father of the family of Shemidaites in Manasseh’s tribe.
sheminith: Obscure Hebrew term, meaning “the eighth,” in 1 Chronicles 15:21 and the superscriptions of Psalms 6 and 12 (see RSV and NLT mg), whose function as a musical cue or instrument is uncertain.
shemiramoth: 1. One of the Levites whom David commanded to play the harp when the ark of God was brought from the house of Obed-edom to Jerusalem, and who retained a permanent position under Asaph as one of the ministers of the ark (16:4-5).
shemuel: 1. Ammihud’s son and the representative of Simeon’s tribe in the division of the land of Canaan among Israel’s 10 tribes west of the Jordan.
shen: Alternate form of Jeshanah, a town near which the prophet Samuel set up the Ebenezer stone, in 1 Samuel 7:12.
shenazar, shenazzar: Fourth son of Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), captive king of Judah.
shenir: KJV alternate spelling of Senir, the Amorite name for Mt Hermon, in Deuteronomy 3:9 and Song of Songs 4:8.
sheol: Hebrew term for the place of the dead. In ordinary usage it means “ravine,” “chasm,” “underworld,” or “world of the dead.” In the OT it is the place where the dead have their abode, a hollow space underneath the earth where the dead are gathered in.
shepham: One of the places used by Moses to establish the eastern border of the Promised Land, mentioned between Hazar-enan, which marked the northeastern corner of the land, and Riblah.
shephathiah: Alternate KJV spelling of Shephatiah, Meshullam’s father, in 1 Chronicles 9:8.
shephatiah: 1. One of six sons born to David during his seven-year reign at Hebron.
shephelah: Lowlands or foothills of Julah (see NLT mg, Jos 15:33; 1 Chr 27:28).
shepher, mount: Temporary camping place for the Israelites during their wilderness wanderings. Mt Shepher was located between Kehelathah and Haradah.
shepherd: One who took complete care of a flock of sheep.
shepherd of hermas: Volume composed by Hermas. Not much is known of Hermas other than the details he includes of himself in his work The Shepherd.
shephi, shepho: One of Shobal’s five sons and a descendant of Seir the Horite. Shepho is listed in the genealogy of Abraham through Esau’s contact with the nation; his name is alternately spelled Shephi (1 Chr 1:40; see NLT mg).
shephupham: Benjamin’s fourth son (called “Muppim” in Gen 46:21) and the father of the Shuphamite family (Nm 26:39; see NLT mg). In the corresponding genealogy of Benjamin he is called Shuppim, appearing as Benjamin’s great-grandson.
shephuphan: Bela’s son from Benjamin’s tribe. Bela was the firstborn of Benjamin’s sons.
sherah: Daughter or granddaughter of Ephraim. Her offspring built lower and upper Beth-horon and Uzzen-sheerah, named after her.
sheresh: Makir’s son and the brother of Peresh from Manasseh’s tribe.
sheshach: Term that is probably a cryptic name for “Babel” (Babylon) found in Jeremiah 25:26 and 51:41 (NLT mg).
sheshai: Descendant of Anak who was at Hebron when the 12 spies searched out the land of Canaan; he was defeated and displaced by Israel.
sheshan: Descendant of Judah through Jerahmeel, whose family line is traced in 1 Chronicles 2:25-41 to Elishama, evidently a contemporary of the writer. In verse 31 Sheshan’s son Ahlai is named, but verse 34 says that Sheshan had no sons.
sheshbazzar: Jewish leader who found favor with Cyrus the Great, king of Persia. In the first year of his reign, Cyrus issued a decree that the temple in Jerusalem should be rebuilt (Ezr 1:1-4; cf. 6:1-5).
sheth: 1. Reference to the sons of Moab, who were the cause of tumult and war to Israel.
shethar: One of Ahasuerus’s seven counselors who, when Queen Vashti defied the king’s command, advised him to deprive her of her title and to seek a new queen, as an example of domestic discipline.
shethar-bozenai, shethar-boznai: Persian official in a province west of the Euphrates River, who joined with Tattenai and his colleagues in writing a letter to Darius Hystaspeis, king of Persia, protesting the rebuilding of the temple and walls of Jerusalem under Zerubbabel.
sheva: 1. Scribe or personal secretary of David.
shibah: Name of the fourth well dug by Isaac’s servants, so named for the covenant made between Isaac and Abimelech, king of Gerar. The city at the location of the well was called Beersheba (Gn 26:33, NLT mg).
shibboleth: Term used by Jephthah to detect the Ephraimites at the banks of the Jordan River. After the battle, many Ephraimites tried to escape by crossing the Jordan and returning to their own land.
shibmah: KJV form of Sibmah, an alternate name for Sebam, a city in Reuben’s territory, in Numbers 32:38.
shicron: KJV form of Shikkeron, a city in Judah’s tribe, in Joshua 15:11.
shield, shield bearer: Protective armor and the soldier or servant who carried the shield and weapons of a warrior.
shiggaion, shigionoth: Hebrew words in the titles of Psalm 7 and Habakkuk 3, respectively, perhaps denoting a hymn, a psalm of distress, or a psalm accompanied with instruments.
shihor: Body of water in Egypt. The name is Egyptian and is given as a boundary of the land to be possessed by the Hebrews.
shihor-libnath: Place defining the southern boundary of Asher’s tribe. Some have identified it with the Nahal Tanninim (Crocodile River), which flows into the Mediterranean Sea.
shikkeron: Town near the Mediterranean Sea on the northern border of the land allotted to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance, mentioned between Ekron and Mt Baalah. Its locality is uncertain, though perhaps identifiable with Tell el-Ful.
shilhi: Grandfather of King Jehoshaphat of Judah.
shilhim: Alternate name for Shaaraim, a town in southern Judah, in Joshua 15:32.
shillem, shillemite: Fourth son of Naphtali, and father of the Shillemites; alternately called Shallum in 1 Chronicles 7:13.
shiloah: Name of an aqueduct in Jerusalem (Is 8:6; see NLT mg).
shiloh: Town identified with Tell Seilun, located 10 miles (16.1 kilometers) northeast of Bethel, 12 miles (19.3 kilometers) southeast of Shechem, and 3 miles (4.8 kilometers) east of the road between Shechem and Jerusalem, precisely fitting the description of its location in Judges 21:19.
shiloni: 1. Inhabitant of Shiloh, the hometown of Ahijah the prophet.
shilonite: 1. Inhabitant of Shiloh, the hometown of Ahijah the prophet.
shilshah: Zophah’s son and a chief of Asher’s tribe.
shimea: 1. Alternate name for Shammah, Jesse’s third son, in 1 Chronicles 2:13 and 20:7.
shimeah: 1. Alternate name for Shammah, David’s brother, in 2 Samuel 13:3, 32.
shimeam: Alternate spelling of Shimeah, Mikloth’s son, in 1 Chronicles 9:38.
shimeath: Ammonitess mother or perhaps father of one of the royal servants who conspired against and murdered King Jehoash of Judah (835–796 BC).
shimeathite: One of three families of scribes living at Jabez in Judah. They were perhaps Kenites and descendants of Hammath.
shimei: 1. Son of Gershon, the grandson of Levi, and the brother of Libni.
shimeite: Family of Levites founded by Shimei, Gershon’s descendant.
shimeon: Harim’s fifth son, who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife whom he had married during the postexilic era.
shimhi: KJV form of Shimei, an alternate name for Shema, in 1 Chronicles 8:21.
shimi: KJV spelling of Shimei, Gershon’s son, in Exodus 6:17.
shimma: KJV spelling of Shimea, an alternate name for Shammah, Jesse’s son, in 1 Chronicles 2:13.
shimri: 1. Simeonite, Shemaiah’s son and the father of Jedaiah.
shimrith: Moabitess mother of Jehozabad, a royal servant, who along with Zabad conspired against and murdered King Joash of Judah (2 Chr 24:26, NLT mg). She is alternately called Shomer in 2 Kings 12:21; Shimrith is the feminine form of Shomer.
shimron (person): Issachar’s fourth son and the founder of the Shimronite family.
shimron (place): Canaanite town whose king joined the confederacy of King Jabin of Hazor in unsuccessful resistance to the Israelites under Joshua. Its site is uncertain, though it was in Zebulun’s territory (19:15-16).
shimronite: Family founded by Shimron, Issachar’s son.
shimron-meron: Canaanite city destroyed by Joshua on his northern military campaign in Palestine. The king of Shimron-meron was one of 31 kings defeated by Joshua.
shimshai: Persian government official whose territory included Palestine. With another official (Rehum), he wrote a letter to Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of the temple by the Jews returned from exile.
shinab: King of Admah, who joined an alliance with four neighboring rulers against King Kedorlaomer. Kedorlaomer defeated this confederation of kings in the valley of Siddim—the southern region of the Dead Sea.
shinar: Name for a district of Babylonia mentioned exclusively in the Bible. The plain of Shinar comprised the region approximately from modern Baghdad to the Persian Gulf.
shion: One of 16 cities in the territory allotted to Issachar’s tribe for an inheritance, mentioned between Hapharaim and Anaharath.
shiphi: Ziza’s father and a prince in Simeon’s tribe.
shiphrah: One of two Hebrew midwives who refused to kill Hebrew male infants at Pharaoh’s command.
shiphtan: Father of Kemuel, a prince of Ephraim appointed by Moses to help divide the land among Israel’s 10 tribes west of the Jordan.
ships and shipping: In biblical times travelers found roads bad and often impassable. Sea voyages were made in comparatively small ships, usually by military and commercial personnel, and hardly ever for simple tourist traffic.
shisha: Alternate name for Seraiah, King David’s scribe, in 1 Kings 4:3.
shishak: Egyptian pharaoh, descendant of a powerful family of Libyan chieftains, and founder of Egypt’s 22d dynasty. His Egyptian name was Sheshonk.
shitrai: David’s chief shepherd in charge of his flocks in Sharon.
shittah tree: KJV rendering of acacia, a common desert tree, in Isaiah 41:19.
shittim (place): Site on the plains of Moab where the Israelites made their final Transjordan encampment after defeating Sihon and Og and prior to their crossing of the Jordan (25:1).
shiza: Reubenite and the father of Adina, one of David’s select warriors.
shoa: Assyrian people listed with the Babylonians, Chaldeans, and other Assyrian tribes, who were used by the Lord to punish Judah.
shobab: 1. Second of David’s four sons by Bathsheba.
shobach: Commander of the army of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, who led the Ammonite-Syrian campaign against Israel.
shobai: Ancestor of a group of people who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile.
shobal: 1. One of the seven sons of Seir the Horite in Edom.
shobek: Leader who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God during the postexilic era.
shobi: Ammonite prince, son of King Nahash, who, along with Makir of Lo-debar and Barzillai of Rogelim, generously supplied David with food and equipment at Mahanaim during Absalom’s rebellion.
shocho, shochoh, shoco: KJV variant spellings of the city listed in Jos 15:35; 1 Sm 17:1; 2 Chr 11:7; 28:18.
shoham: Merarite Levite, and Jaaziah’s son in David’s reign.
shomer: 1. Father, or perhaps the Moabite mother, of Jehozabad, a royal servant, who, with Jozacar, conspired against and murdered Joash, king of Judah.
shophach: Alternate form of Shobach in 1 Chronicles 19:16-18 (NLT mg).
shophar: Primitive musical instrument made from an animal’s horn.
shoshannim, shoshannim-eduth: Hebrew word and phrase in the superscriptions of Psalms 45, 69 and 80 (KJV), translated “according to Lilies” (RSV; see also NLT); perhaps a familiar ancient melody to which the psalms were performed.
showbread: Bread that was kept in the Holy Place of the temple.
shrub: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
shuah: 1. One of six sons borne to Abraham by Keturah.
shual (person): Zophah’s son and a leader in Asher’s tribe.
shual (place): Region that included the town of Ophrah and was perhaps situated in the territory of Benjamin and Ephraim. Shual was located to the north of Micmash.
shubael: 1. Alternate form of Shebuel, Gershon’s son, in 1 Chronicles 24:20.
shuham, shuhamite: Alternate name for Hushim, Dan’s son, and his descendants in Numbers 26:42-43.
shuhite: Arab tribe, apparently descended from Shuah, the son of Abraham by Keturah. They were located near the land of Uz.
shulammite: Name or title of Solomon’s lover in his Song. Her identity is not certain.
shumathite: Family of Judah, descended from Shobal of Kiriath-jearim. Shobal was the son of Hur from Caleb’s line.
shunammite: Inhabitant of Shunem; hometown of Abishag.
shunem: Village of Issachar’s tribe strategically located in the Jezreel Valley. Shunem (modern Sulem) is about three and a half miles (5.6 kilometers) north of Jezreel, situated on the outer hills of Mt Moreh.
shuni, shunite: Third of Gad’s seven sons and the family he founded.
shupham, shuphamite: Benjamin’s son and descendants. Shupham is the KJV spelling of Shephupham in Numbers 26:39.
shuppim: 1. Son of Ir and a great-grandson of Benjamin.
shur: Wilderness region located in the Sinai Peninsula east of Egypt’s Nile Delta and west of the Negev. In antiquity, a caravan route passed through this region from Egypt to Palestine.
shushan: KJV form of Susa, the Persian capital.
shushan eduth: Hebrew phrase in the superscription of Psalm 60, translated “To [the tune] of ‘The Lily of the Covenant’ ” (NIV), perhaps a familiar ancient melody to which the psalm was performed.
shuthelah: 1. Ephraim’s son, the brother of Beker and Tahan, and the father of Eran and Bered.
sia, siaha: Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel following the exile (Neh 7:47, NLT mg); spelled Siaha in Ezra 2:44.
sibbecai, sibbechai: Zerahite from the town of Hushah and one of David’s “mighty men”. He is credited with killing the giant Saph when Israel fought Philistia at Gob.
sibboleth: Spelling of the Gileadite password as mispronounced by the Ephraimites.
sibmah: Alternate rendering of Sebam, a city in Reuben’s territory, in Numbers 32:38 and Joshua 13:19.
sibraim: Geographical landmark between Damascus and Hamath, marking the northern boundary of Israel.
sichem: KJV form of Shechem in Genesis 12:6.
sickle: Seeding was done at the beginning of the rainy season and harvesting was begun at the end. Harvesting lasted at least seven weeks.
sickness: Term used in Scripture synonymously with sickness, infirmity, illness, plague, and pestilence. However, plague and pestilence are generally used when there are large numbers of victims, as in epidemics.
siddim valley: Location of the battle between four kings from Mesopotamia and five allied kings living near the Dead Sea. The precise location of the battle in the vicinity of the Dead Sea has proved impossible to determine; one is left with conjectures.
sidon (person): Canaan’s firstborn son; Canaan was the son of Ham and grandson of Noah. Sidon founded a city (bearing his name) that set the northern boundary of the land of Canaan and later played a dominant role in Palestinian history.
sidon (place), sidonian: City on the Phoenician coast, between Beirut and Tyre; frequently called Zidon in the KJV. The present town, Saida, is not regarded as a direct continuation of the ancient city but rather a development of post-Crusader times.
siege: The means by which one nation seeks to impose its will upon another by force. An index to the importance of warfare in antiquity is provided by the amount of technical skill directed to perfecting devices for destruction and defense.
sign: Word connoting a visible event intended to convey meaning beyond that which is normally perceived in the outward appearance of the event.
signet: Small engraved object widely used in the ancient Near East to produce an image in soft clay.
sihon: King of the Amorites who ruled in Heshbon, about 14 miles (22.5 kilometers) east of the north end of the Dead Sea. His defeat by Israel under Moses, together with that of Og, king of Bashan, is frequently mentioned in OT prose and poetry, in narrative and song.
sihor: KJV form of Shihor, a body of water in northeast Egypt, in Joshua 13:3, Isaiah 23:3, and Jeremiah 2:18 (NLT mg).
sikkuth: Name of the Babylonian Saturn, an astral deity in Mesopotamian religion. Some suggest that Sakkuth reflects a corruption of sukkah, meaning “shrine” (NIV) or “tabernacle” (KJV), within which an image would be placed.
silas: Respected leader in the Jerusalem church, also called Silvanus. “Silas” is most likely the Aramaic form of the Hebrew name “Saul,” which when given a Latin form became Silouanos (Silvanus).
silk: Fine, delicate thread extracted from the cocoon of the silkworm. Originating in China, silk may have been introduced into Palestine as early as Solomon’s reign (970–930 BC), or perhaps not until the conquests of Alexander the Great (336–323 BC).
silla: Geographical landmark defining the whereabouts of “the house of Millo,” the place of King Joash’s murder. Its exact location is unknown, though it was probably in the vicinity of Jerusalem.
siloah: KJV rendering of Shelah, an alternate name for the pool of Siloam, in Nehemiah 3:15.
siloam, pool of: Pool mentioned in John 9. Jesus, after anointing with clay the eyes of a blind man, directed him to go and wash in the pool.
siloam, tower of: Edifice that collapsed, killing 18 people. Jesus compared those killed by the fallen tower to the rest of the people living in Jerusalem.
siloam inscription: Hebrew inscription in the Siloam tunnel, also known as Hezekiah’s tunnel, which marked the progress of the tunnel as it was being built.
siloam tunnel: Conduit, also known as Hezekiah’s tunnel, built by Hezekiah at the time of the Assyrian invasion to bring water into Jerusalem.
silvanus: Latin name for Silas, a companion of Paul and Peter.
silver: Pieces of metal used and accepted as a medium of exchange. A coin has a specific weight and bears some type of authentication to make it easily recognizable.
silversmith: One who refined silver-bearing ore and then cast it or beat it into the desired shape.
simeon (person): 1. Second of the 12 sons of Jacob and the second son borne to him by Leah.
simeon, tribe of: One of the 12 tribes of Israel descended from Jacob’s second son. Because of Simeon’s evil deed at Shechem, Jacob foretold that Simeon’s descendants would be dispersed among the other tribes of Israel.
simon: Greek form of a Hebrew/Aramaic name meaning “God has heard.” Nine men in the NT had this name:
simon maccabeus: The second son of Mattathias was successor to his brother Jonathan. In 142 BC Simon (d. 135 BC) negotiated a treaty with Syria by supporting Demetrius II against the plunderer Trypho.
simon magus: Sorcerer of Samaria apparently converted by Philip.
simon of cyrene: Man who was ordered to carry Jesus’ cross on the road to Golgotha.
simon peter: One of the 12 disciples; rose to prominence both among the disciples during Jesus’ ministry and among the apostles afterwards.
simon the canaanite: KJV rendering for Simon the Zealot in Matthew 10:4; Mark 3:18.
simon the cananaean: RSV rendering for Simon the Zealot in Matthew 10:4; Mark 3:18.
simon zelotes: KJV rendering for Simon the Zealot in Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13.
simri: KJV spelling of Shimri, Hosah’s son, in 1 Chronicles 26:10.
sin: Evildoing that is not only against humanity, society, others, or oneself, but against God. The concept of God, therefore, gives to the idea of sin its many-sided meaning.
sin (place): Hebrew name for an Egyptian city named Pelusium (Ez 30:15-16, KJV).
sin desert: Arid, sandy region in the southwestern part of the Sinai peninsula, described in the Bible as being “between Elim and Sinai”. It is mentioned only four times in the Bible in itineraries of the exodus from Egypt.
sin, man of: KJV rendering of an inferior textual variant in the Textus Receptus in 2 Thessalonians 2:3. The correct reading is “man of lawlessness,” an expression used by Paul of the Antichrist.
sin, wilderness of: Arid, sandy region in the southwestern part of the Sinai peninsula, described in the Bible as being “between Elim and Sinai”. It is mentioned only four times in the Bible in itineraries of the exodus from Egypt.
sina, sinai: Name of the mountain where God met Moses and gave him the Ten Commandments and the rest of the law.
singer: The professional singer was important in temple worship. David first organized singers for worship in the tabernacle.
sinite: Canaanite tribe, possibly located in northern Lebanon, whose ancestry is traced to Canaan, Ham’s son.
sinlessness of christ: The Scripture (quoted here from the RSV) leaves no question that Christ is regarded as sinless. He is declared to be the perfect Son of God in every respect.
sin offering: Major ritual expressions of religious life with accompanying rites, such as libations, effusions, and sacred meals. The ideology expressed in Israel’s ritual complex made its religion unique in the ancient Near East.
sin unto death: Sin mentioned in 1 John 5:16; in this verse John discourages prayer for those who sin in this way. Most likely, John was speaking of those who decisively turn their backs upon the truth, as well as those false teachers who deceive the church.
sion: 1. KJV designation for Mt Hermon in Deuteronomy 4:48.
siphmoth: Town in southern Judah to which David gave part of the spoils of his victory over the Amalekites because its residents had aided him in his flight from Saul.
sippai: Alternate form of Saph, a descendant of the giants, in 1 Chronicles 20:4 (NLT mg).
sirah: Well or cistern where Joab’s messengers intercepted Abner as he returned from pledging allegiance to David in Hebron. Its site is probably the same as the present ‘Ain Sarah, located about one and a half miles (2.4 kilometers) northwest of Hebron.
sisera: 1. Commander of the army of Jabin, king of Canaan.
sismai: Eleasah’s son and the father of Shallum; a Judahite from the house of Hezron and Jerahmeel’s line.
sister: In Bible times, the family comprised members of a household, including not only parents and children, along with other relatives and concubines, but also servants, travelers, aliens, and anyone else who happened to be within the house and was therefore under the protection of the head of the family.
sistrum: Ancient percussion instrument consisting of a thin metal frame with numerous metal rods or loops that jingled when shaken, translated as “castanets” (NLT) in 2 Samuel 6:5.
sithri: Kohathite Levite and Uzziel’s third son. Sithri was the cousin of Aaron and Moses.
sitnah: Well dug by Isaac’s servants in the region of Gerar, receiving its name (meaning “enmity”) from a dispute between Isaac’s servants and the herdsmen of the region. Its location was possibly near Rehoboth (Gn 26:21-22; see NLT mg).
sivan: Name of a Hebrew month, perhaps of Babylonian origin (Est 8:9, NLT mg).
six hundred sixty-six: Number of the beast of the earth envisioned in the book of Revelation.
skull hill: Place in Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified. Golgotha is the Greek transliteration of the Aramaic word for “skull.” See Golgotha.
skull, place of the: Place in Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified. Golgotha is the Greek transliteration of the Aramaic word for “skull.” See Golgotha.
slander: The utterance of false charges or accusations that defame another person’s reputation; when directed toward God, such accusations are considered blasphemy.
slave, slavery: Person owned as property by another, and the relationship that bound the owner and the slave. Slavery was widespread in the ancient Near East, although the economy was not dependent upon it.
sleep: Sleep is spoken of in three ways in the Bible: (a) to speak of natural sleep, (b) to refer to moral or spiritual inactivity, and (c) to refer to death.
slime: KJV rendering of “asphalt” or “bitumen” in Genesis 11:3 and Exodus 2:3.
slimepits: KJV rendering of asphalt pits or bitumen pits found in the valley of Siddim.
sling, slinger: Weapon of war used to fire stones or lead pellets, and the thrower.
smith: Worker in metals; a blacksmith. The earliest metalworker mentioned in the Bible is Tubal-cain.
smyrna: Location of one of the seven churches mentioned in the book of Revelation. It is the modern Izmir, located in Turkey.
snail: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
snake: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
snare: Literally, a trap used for entangling birds or others mammals; figuratively, anything that entangles or impedes another person.
so: A king of Egypt, mentioned once in Scripture, with whom Hoshea, king of Israel, sought an alliance. This rebellious move, in part, prompted Shalmaneser V of Assyria to imprison Hoshea.
soap: Cleansing agent extracted from a number of alkali-bearing plants. The alkali was gathered from the ashes of the burned plants and formed into a detergent.
socho: KJV form of Soco, Heber’s descendant, in 1 Chronicles 4:18.
sochoh: KJV form of Socoh, a town in Sharon, in 1 Kings 4:10.
soco (person): Son of Heber, listed in the genealogy of Caleb. Since the Calebites were located in the southern hill country of Judah, Soco may be identified with the city in Joshua 15:48.
soco (place), socoh: 1. One of 14 cities located in the Shephelah, in the territory allotted to Judah’s tribe; it is listed between Adullam and Azekah.
sodi: Father of Gaddiel, one of the 12 spies sent by Moses to search out the land of Canaan.
sodom, sea of: Alternate name for the Dead Sea.
sodom, vine of: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
sodom and gomorrah: Two of the “cities of the plain [valley]” referred to in Genesis 13:12. There were five cities—Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela or Zoar—all situated in the valley of Siddim (i.e., the Salt Sea).
sojourner: Noncitizen or alien, temporary guest, sojourner, or stranger.
soldier: The individual member in every army, whether part of the infantry, cavalry, or group engaged in siege warfare.
solomon (person): Third king over Israel, the second son of David and Bathsheba, who reigned 40 years (970–930 BC). His alternative name was Jedidiah, “beloved of the Lord.”
solomon, pools of: Water-storage pools, whose construction has been attributed to Solomon. Solomon made pools for watering his vineyards, gardens, parks, and orchards, but their location is uncertain.
solomon, song of: Short OT book (eight chapters) containing only poetry. Its beautiful poetic passages describe the many dimensions of human love; there is little in this book that is explicitly religious.
solomon's porch: Part of the outer court of Herod’s temple.
son: In Bible times, the family comprised members of a household, including not only parents and children, along with other relatives and concubines, but also servants, travelers, aliens, and anyone else who happened to be within the house and was therefore under the protection of the head of the family.
song: A natural human expression that probably began with speech-singing and developed into songs, which were then accompanied by instruments.
song of ascents, song of degrees: Song of Ascents, Song of Degrees
Title given to each of the Psalms from 120 to 134. Perhaps these psalms were sung by pilgrims journeying up to Jerusalem for the major feasts.
song of solomon: Short OT book (eight chapters) containing only poetry. Its beautiful poetic passages describe the many dimensions of human love; there is little in this book that is explicitly religious.
song of songs: Short OT book (eight chapters) containing only poetry. Its beautiful poetic passages describe the many dimensions of human love; there is little in this book that is explicitly religious.
song of the three young men: Song of the Three Young Men

Part of the Deuterocanonical works, consists of three supplementary sections to the book of Daniel. This additional material is in the Greek translation of the OT book of Daniel, but not in the ancient Hebrew-Aramaic texts.
son of god: Term used to express the deity of Jesus of Nazareth as the unique divine Son.
son of man: Messianic title used by Jesus to express his heavenly origin, earthly mission, and glorious future coming. It does not refer merely to his human nature or humanity, as some church fathers or contemporary scholars believe.
sons and daughters of god: Expression designating human beings who have been born of God and have become part of his family. When the Bible speaks of God’s sons, it does not intend to exclude females.
sons of the prophets: “Band of prophets” whom Saul met and forerunners of the “schools,” “guilds,” or “sons of the prophets,” which flourished under Israel’s early kings.
sons of thunder: Translation of the word “Boanerges,” the surname given by Jesus to James and John.
soothsayer: One who foretells events; a pagan practice, soothsaying was forbidden in Israel.
sop: KJV term for a thin piece of bread, dipped into a common dish and used as a spoon.
sopater: Man from the church at Berea who, with others, accompanied Paul to Jerusalem to deliver the offering collected by the gentile churches for the Jewish Christians who were suffering from the effects of a famine.
sophereth: Alternate form of Hassophereth, the name of a postexilic Levitical family, in Nehemiah 7:57.
sorcery: Practice whose adherents claim to have supernatural powers and knowledge; the ability to foretell the future and to summon evil spirits through charms and magical spells. Sorcerers were present in the high courts of Egypt, Assyria, and Babylonia.
sore: Any localized abnormality of the skin. It was a well-demarcated skin abnormality with a definite border between the inflamed or abnormal skin and the normal skin.
sorek, valley of: Valley in which Delilah lived. It began in the hill country of Judah, about 13 miles (20.9 kilometers) southwest of Jerusalem, and took a northwesterly course to the Mediterranean Sea.
sorghum: Medium to stout annual grass growing over six feet (1.8 meters) tall; perhaps the “hyssop” to which the sponge of vinegar was attached during Jesus’ crucifixion.
sosipater: Jewish Christian who joined Paul, Timothy, Lucius, and Jason in sending greetings to the church at Rome.
sosthenes: 1. Leader of the synagogue in Corinth who brought legal action against Paul before Gallio, proconsul of Achaia.
sostratus: Governor of the citadel of Jerusalem under Antiochus IV. He attempted to secure from Menelaus, the high priest, the sum of money Menelaus had promised to pay the king for his appointment to the priestly office.
sotai: Head of a family of temple servants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel following the exile.
soul: Term translating the Greek word psuche and the Hebrew nephesh.
sowing: During Bible times agriculture took the same three main forms found in Palestine today. Emphasis on each of these has depended upon the social and technological status of the people.
spain: Name of the most westerly peninsula in southwestern Europe. Biblical references to the peninsula note the role of the Phoenicians, whose far-flung Carthaginian Empire reached into Spain.
sparrow: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
spear, spearman: The location of Palestine at the crossroads of three continents gave it a strategic importance in the ancient world quite out of proportion to its size.
spelt: Hard-grained species of wheat that flourishes in various kinds of soils; hence, it was popular grain among the ancients.
spice, spicery: Fragrant spices and oils or sacrifice that sends up perfumed smoke to God in order to please him.
spider: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
spikenard: Perennial herb with strong, pleasant-smelling roots.
spinner, spinning: Fibers were spun into yarn by women in all periods of Israel’s history, but a class of professional spinners arose alongside them. Women spinners are mentioned in Exodus 35:25-26.
spirit: Designation of that aspect of existence that is noncorporeal and immaterial. Its Latin derivation (as with the Hebrew and Greek words in the Bible—ruach and pneuma) denotes blowing or breathing.
spirit of god: Description of God in action, God in motion. The word “spirit” (Hebrew, ruach; Greek, pneuma) is the word used from ancient times to describe and explain the experience of divine power working in, upon, and around people.
spirit of jesus christ: The Spirit as identified with Jesus Christ.
spirit of man: The innermost being of the human person, corresponding with the nature of God, which is Spirit. Some scholars think the spirit is the same as the soul; others see a distinction.
spirits, discerning of: Phrase regularly used to translate two Greek words, charismata and pneumatika (the plural forms of charisma and pneumatikon). Both words are almost exclusively Pauline within the biblical writings; elsewhere in the NT, they appear only in 1 Peter 2:5 and 4:10.
spirits, unclean: Fallen angel who, under the leadership of Satan, rebelled against God.
spirits in prison: Term used in 1 Peter 3:18-20a. There is little agreement among scholars as to what “spirits in prison” really refers to or why Jesus would have gone to preach to them.
spiritual gifts: Phrase regularly used to translate two Greek words, charismata and pneumatika (the plural forms of charisma and pneumatikon). Both words are almost exclusively Pauline within the biblical writings; elsewhere in the NT, they appear only in 1 Peter 2:5 and 4:10.
spirituality: Term meaning “being made holy, or purified.” It is used broadly of the whole Christian experience, though most theologians prefer to use it in a restricted sense to distinguish it from related terms, such as “regeneration,” “justification,” and “glorification.”
sponge: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
sprinkling of blood: Major ritual expressions of religious life with accompanying rites, such as libations, effusions, and sacred meals. The ideology expressed in Israel’s ritual complex made its religion unique in the ancient Near East.
stachys: Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings, calling him “my beloved”.
stacte: One of the fragrant spices used by Moses to make the incense offering.
stadium: Greek unit of linear measure equivalent to about 200 yards or 182.9 meters.
stag: Large ruminant (cud-chewing) animals. Only the males have antlers (branching horns).
stallion: Przewalski’s horse (Equus przewalskii, an eastern race that roamed about Mongolia until modern firearms destroyed most of them after World War I) and the tarpan (a western race of southern Russia that became extinct in the Ukraine in 1851).
star: Science dealing with the phenomena outside the earth’s atmosphere but especially concerned with the observable arrangements, motions, and characteristics of the heavenly bodies. The word “astronomy” is based on two Greek words meaning “the law of the stars.”
star in the east: Star that guided the magi to the infant Jesus. The magi were residents of some Eastern land (possibly Parthia, Babylon, or Arabia) who came to Herod.
stealing: The science or philosophy of law is called jurisprudence. Although modern jurisprudence bears little resemblance to biblical concepts of law, the Scriptures have played a definite role in its development.
steer: Domestic animals of the bovine species (Bos primigenius). The OT often emphasized the beauty of cattle.
stephanas: Christian believer at Corinth. He and his household were evidently Paul’s first converts in Achaia.
stephen: One of the first deacons and the first martyr of the apostolic church. For Luke, Stephen represents the growing Hellenistic interest of certain members in the early Jerusalem church.
stocks: Common form of punishment and confinement in Bible times.
stoicism, stoics: A widespread Greek philosophy, well represented in the audience at Athens listening to Paul.
stonecutter: A stonemason who removed stone from the quarry and squared it up for use in large buildings like palaces, the temple, administrative buildings, and large houses.
stones, precious: A lengthy list of the precious stones used in OT times occurs in Exodus 28:17-20 and 39:10-13, where four rows of three stones, each engraved with the name of one of the 12 tribes of Israel, were set in the high priest’s breastplate.
stoning: The science or philosophy of law is called jurisprudence. Although modern jurisprudence bears little resemblance to biblical concepts of law, the Scriptures have played a definite role in its development.
stony arabia: A division of Arabia, also called Rocky Arabia.
storax tree: Small, stiff-branched tree from which stacte was extracted for making incense.
stork: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
straight street: Street in Damascus where Paul lodged after his encounter with the risen Jesus and where, in the house of Judas, he was baptized by Ananias and recovered his eyesight. The street is called “Straight” because, unlike many others, this one was straight.
stranger: Noncitizen or alien, temporary guest, sojourner, or stranger.
strangling: One of four practices from which the early gentile Christians were asked to abstain out of respect for their Jewish Christian brothers and sisters.
stringed instrument: Stringed, wind, and percussion instruments used to make music.
strong drink: Any intoxicating liquor. It was forbidden to Levites who were entering the tent of meeting; to those taking the Nazirite vow; to kings and rulers; and to John the Baptist.
stumbling block: Term used both literally and figuratively to refer to anything that might cause one to stumble.
stylus: Instrument used for writing characters on clay tablets.
suah: Zophah’s son, who was a leader in his father’s household and a mighty warrior in Asher’s tribe.
sucathite: Family of scribes living at Jabez of Judah and descendants of the Kenites.
succoth: 1. Town in the Jordan Valley listed along with other towns as belonging to the tribe of Gad.
succoth-benoth: Deity and shrine worshiped by Babylonians settled in Samaria by Assyria after the fall of Israel in 722 BC. Various opinions exist as to the specific understanding of Succoth-benoth.
suchathite: KJV spelling of Sucathite, a family of scribes, in 1 Chronicles 2:55.
suffering: Anything causing pain or distress; calamity. From the biblical viewpoint, affliction began with the entrance of sin into the world.
suffering servant: Title applied to a variety of persons in the Bible. The basic term, “servant,” covers a range of meanings.
suicide: The act of taking one’s own life voluntarily and intentionally. Though the word “suicide” does not appear in most Bible translations (see, however, Jn 8:22, NLT), the OT records suicides by Saul and his armor bearer, Ahitophel, and Zimri.
sukkiim, sukkiims, sukkites: A tribe who joined forces with King Shishak of Egypt and entered Palestine to wage war against King Rehoboam of Judah (930–913 BC). The Sukkites are mentioned with the Libyans and the Ethiopians.
sulfur: Old name for the nonmetallic element sulfur, literally “the stone that burns.” Sulfur ignites at a relatively low temperature and burns to produce acrid fumes of sulfur dioxide. Sulfur occurs naturally in volcanic regions such as the valley of the Dead Sea.
sumer, sumerians: Sumer was a region settled before 3500 BC in the lower part of Mesopotamia, now called Iraq. The Sumerians had a highly civilized society, developing cuneiform (a type of writing), medicine, mathematics, and astronomy.
sun: A luminary created by God to be one of the great lights in the heavens, “to rule over the day”. The new day begins with its setting, and the daily sacrifices were offered in accordance with its position: the first burnt offering with its rising.
sun, city of the: Phrase in Isaiah 19:18; generally taken as a reference to Heliopolis.
sunday: Expression occurring once in the NT, where John says, “On the Lord’s Day I was in the Spirit” (NIV); synonym for “Sunday” in modern usage.
sundial: Instrument used for telling time installed by King Ahaz of Judah (735–715 BC) in the royal palace of Jerusalem. Some suggest that this time indicator was not a sundial but a stairway.
suph: Region mentioned in Deuteronomy 1:1, which was “beyond the Jordan in the wilderness, in the Arabah over against Suph” (RSV; KJV “the Red Sea”). The exact location of Suph is uncertain.
suphah: Place east of the Jordan in the land of Moab; translated as “Red Sea” by the KJV.
supper, lord's: The supper Jesus shared with his disciples a few hours before he was arrested and taken to his trial and death (thus often called “The Last Supper”); the ceremony of partaking of the bread and wine that Christians have come to call the Lord’s Supper, the…
supplication: The addressing and petitioning of God. Prayer to a god or gods is a feature of many, if not all, religions, but here attention will be restricted to the biblical teaching and some of its implications.
sur gate: Gate in Jerusalem linking the king’s palace to the temple. It is mentioned in 2 Kings 11:6 in connection with the enthronement of Jehoash over Judah and the murder of Athaliah.
surgery: The field of knowledge dealing with the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of diseases, as well as the actual substances used to diagnose, treat, or prevent disease.
susa: Capital of the non-Semitic people and district of Elam. Susa (modern Shush) is located in southwest Iran, about 150 miles (241.4 kilometers) north of the Persian Gulf and due east of the well-known city of Babylon.
susanchite: KJV translation for “men of Susa” or “Shushanchites” in Ezra 4:9.
susanna: 1. One of the women who ministered to Jesus out of her own resources.
susanna and the elders: Part of the Deuterocanonical works, consists of three supplementary sections to the book of Daniel. This additional material is in the Greek translation of the OT book of Daniel, but not in the ancient Hebrew-Aramaic texts.
susi: Gaddi’s father from Manasseh’s tribe. Gaddi was one of the 12 spies sent to search out the land of Canaan.
swaddling clothes: KJV translation of the kind of clothes that were wrapped around the baby Jesus. The NLT translation describes this in modern terms: “She [Mary] wrapped him snugly in strips of cloth”.
swallow: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
swan: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
swearing: Solemn vow or promise to fulfill a pledge. There are two terms in Hebrew that mean “oath”: ‘ala and sebu’a.
sweet cane: It is thought that there were two species of sugarcane indigenous to and growing wild in the Holy Land. One of these, Saccharum sara, is known to be only from Lebanon.
sweet storax: Small stiff-branched tree from which stacte was extracted for making incense.
swine: Most properly, newborn swine. “Swine” is technically the better name for the species, but it is rarely used in common speech today.
sword: The location of Palestine at the crossroads of three continents gave it a strategic importance in the ancient world quite out of proportion to its size.
sycamine: Black mulberry tree, valued for its fruit.
sycamore: Large, spreading tree bearing a figlike fruit.
sychar: Town in Samaria, mentioned in the Bible only in John 4:5. The name has been taken as a variant form of the Greek transliteration of the Hebrew name Shechem.
sychem: KJV form of Shechem in Acts 7:16.
syene: Southern Egyptian village (modern Aswan) demarcating Egypt’s border with Ethiopia. The Hebrew form possibly derives from a word for “market” or “trading center,” reflecting the importance of the outpost as a place of commerce.
symeon: Alternate spelling of Simeon, the name of a member of the church in Antioch.
synagogue: Transliteration of the Greek word sunagoge, meaning “a gathering together.” It is used more than 50 times in the NT, mostly for the religious gathering places of Jewish communities in Palestine and throughout the Dispersion.
synoptic gospels: Term (literally meaning “same view”) applied to Matthew, Mark, and Luke because they see the ministry of Jesus from generally the same point of view, which is quite different from John’s Gospel.
synoptic problem: Term (literally meaning “same view”) applied to Matthew, Mark, and Luke because they see the ministry of Jesus from generally the same point of view, which is quite different from John’s Gospel.
syntyche: Woman encouraged by Paul to reconcile her differences with Euodia. Syntyche worked with Paul in proclaiming the gospel and evidently held a position of leadership in the Philippian church.
syracuse: Town on the east coast of Sicily and the island’s most important city. Here Paul’s ship, on which he traveled to Rome as a prisoner, made a three-day stop following his shipwreck and three-month stay in Malta.
syria, syrians: Terms used in the Septuagint and in some English translations to render the names Aram, Arameans.
syrophoenicia: Homeland of the Greek woman who approached Jesus in the region of Tyre and Sidon and pleaded with him to cast a demon out of her daughter. The region of Phoenicia was located in the Roman province of Syria.
syrtis: Two bodies of water off the northern coast of Africa dreaded by ancient mariners. The larger was known as Syrtis Major and the smaller as Syrtis Minor.
taanach: One of the Canaanite fortress cities bordering the plain of Esdraelon and the valley of Jezreel, including Jokneam, Megiddo, Ibleam, and Beth-shan. The modern site, about five miles (8 kilometers) southeast of Megiddo, retains the ancient name, Tell Taanak.
taanath-shiloh: City on the northeast border of the territory allotted to Ephraim’s tribe for an inheritance, positioned between Micmethath and Janoah.
tabaliah: Son of Hosah, a Merarite Levite and a temple gatekeeper who served during the postexilic period.
tabbaoth: Ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile.
tabbath: Town on the outskirts of Abel-meholah on the east side of the Jordan River in the hill country of Gilead, to which Gideon and his small army chased the fleeing Midianites.
tabeal, tabeel: 1. Ruler in Samaria who, with his associates, wrote a letter to King Artaxerxes I of Persia (464–424 BC) protesting Zerubbabel’s rebuilding of the Jerusalem wall.
taberah: Temporary stopping place for Israel in the wilderness of Paran, listed with Massah and Kibroth-hattaavah as places where Israel complained against the Lord. Taberah was named for the fire that God used to judge the grumbling Israelites.
tabernacle: Place of worship during the earliest years of the history of Israel.
tabernacles, feast of: Also known as the Feast of Booths, Shelters, or Ingathering. It was one of the three great festivals of Israel, celebrating the completion of the agricultural year.
tabitha: Aramaic name meaning “gazelle”; the name in Greek is Dorcas.
table: Items of material culture used in homes, palaces, and temples. Because of its close geographical proximity to other nations, Israel had extensive contact with neighboring cultures.
table of showbread: Piece of furniture in the tabernacle and temple upon which the bread of the Presence was placed.
tablet: The process that goes into producing books.
tabor (place): City mentioned in 1 Chronicles 6:77 in a list of the towns of Zebulun. In a similar list in Joshua 19:12 the city is named Kisloth-Tabor; if the same city is meant, the Chronicler may have abbreviated the name here.
tabor, mount: Important hill in lower Galilee located in the northeast area of the Jezreel Valley. About six miles (9.7 kilometers) east of Nazareth, Tabor rises abruptly from the valley floor.
tabor, oak of: Place near Bethel and perhaps in Benjamin’s tribal territory where Saul was to meet three men. This encounter was the second of four signs given to Saul to confirm his appointment as king.
tabret: KJV rendering of tambourine in Genesis 31:27 and 1 Samuel 10:5, and timbrel in 1 Samuel 18:6, Job 17:6, Isaiah 5:12, 24:8, 30:32, and Jeremiah 31:4.
tabrimmon, tabrimon: Hezion’s son and the father of Ben-hadad I, king of Syria.
tachmonite: KJV form of Tahkemonite, designation for one of David’s mighty men, in 2 Samuel 23:8.
tadmor: Ancient city whose name appears in a list of Solomon’s building achievements in 2 Chronicles 8:4. The parallel verse in 1 Kings 9:18 reads “Tamar” in some Hebrew manuscripts and it is uncertain if the same city was intended.
tahan: 1. Ephraim’s son and the father of the Tahanite family.
tahanite: Descendant of Tahan from Ephraim’s tribe.
tahapanes: KJV alternate spelling of Tahpanhes, an Egyptian city, in Jeremiah 2:16.
tahash: Son of Nahor and Reumah his concubine; Abraham’s brother.
tahath (person): 1. Son of Assir and a descendant of Levi through Kohath’s line.
tahath (place): Temporary camping place for the Israelites during their wilderness wanderings, mentioned between Makheloth and Terah.
tahkemonite: Variant reading for Hacmonite in 1 Chronicles 11:11. There was probably an error in copying where the Hebrew letter “h” was confused for a “t.” See Hacmonite.
tahpanhes: Important Egyptian center in the eastern Delta. Listed with Memphis among Israel’s enemies, it is the place to which Jews fled after the murder of Gedaliah in 586 BC when Jeremiah was taken to Egypt (43:7-9; 44:1; 46:14).
tahpenes: Egyptian queen who lived during the reigns of David (1000–961 BC) and Solomon (970–930 BC). Pharaoh gave her sister to Hadad the Edomite in marriage.
