tahrea: A descendant of King Saul, in 1 Chronicles 8:35 and 9:41. An alternate spelling is Tarea.
tahtim-hodshi: One of the towns polled in David’s census of Israel. Tahtim-hodshi is listed between Gilead and Dan-jaan.
talent: Unit of measure used in weighing gold or silver.
talitha cumi: Aramaic words spoken by Jesus and retained by Mark in his Gospel. Jairus, a synagogue official in the Galilean region, called on Jesus to heal his sick daughter; however, she died before Jesus arrived.
talmai: 1. Son of Anak and brother of Ahiman and Sheshai.
talmon: Head of a Levite family who served as temple gatekeepers. His descendants returned from the exile with Zerubbabel and served as gatekeepers in the rebuilt temple.
talmud: Word meaning “to study,” “to learn.” It is a body of literature in Hebrew and Aramaic, covering interpretations of legal portions of the OT, as well as wise sayings from many rabbinical sources; it spans a time period from shortly after Ezra, about 400 BC, until approximately the AD 500s.
tamah: KJV spelling of Temah in Nehemiah 7:55.
tamar (person): 1. Wife of Er, the firstborn son of Judah by a Canaanitess.
tamar (place): City located southwest of the Dead Sea in Judah’s tribe. Tamar is listed in some Hebrew manuscripts of 1 Kings 9:18 as one of the places built up by Solomon in his campaign to increase the might and grandeur of the Jewish empire.
tamarisk: Small, desert tree with small flowers.
tambourine: Percussion instrument consisting of a shallow one-headed drum with small metal discs attached on the side, which jingle when the instrument is tapped or shaken.
tammuz: Chief Sumerian deity whose name derived from the Sumerian dumuzi. He is the god of fertility, of vegetation and agriculture, and of death and resurrection, and he is the patron deity of shepherds.
tanach: KJV spelling of Taanach, a Levitical town, in Joshua 21:25.
tanhumeth: Seraiah’s father from the town of Netophah in Judah. Seraiah was the captain of an army of Netophathite men, who served under Gedaliah during the Babylonian suzerainty.
tannaim: Teachers of the oral law mentioned in the Mishnah during the period beginning with the students of Shammai and Hillel in AD 10 and ending with the pupils of Judah HaNasi I in AD 220.
tanned, tanner, tanning: Worker and process of changing hide into leather. The tanner converted hides and skins into leather by soaking them in lime and the leaves and juices of certain plants.
taphath: Solomon’s daughter and the wife of Ben-abinadab, Solomon’s officer in Naphoth-dor.
tappuah (person): Hebron’s son and a descendant of Caleb from Judah’s tribe.
tappuah (place): 1. One of 14 cities located in the Shephelah assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance, mentioned between En-gannim and Enam.
tarah: KJV spelling of Terah, one of the stopping places during the wilderness journey, in Numbers 33:27-28.
taralah: One of 26 cities in the land assigned to Benjamin’s tribe for an inheritance, listed between Irpeel and Zelah. Taralah was possibly situated to the northwest of Jerusalem.
tarea: A descendant of King Saul, in 1 Chronicles 8:35 and 9:41. An alternate spelling is Tarea.
targum: An Aramaic translation of the OT. While technically this Hebrew word may be used to refer to any translation, targum commonly designates an Aramaic paraphrase or interpretive translation of a portion of the OT.
tarpel, tarpelites: KJV rendering of “officials” in Ezra 4:9. Its precise meaning is uncertain but possibly is a Persian title or an ethnic name.
tarshish (person): 1. One of Javan’s four sons and a descendant of Noah through Japheth’s line.
tarshish (place): Place regarded as being very distant from Israel. Many countries have been proposed as the site for Tarshish, from Sardinia to Great Britain.
tarsus: Birthplace and hometown of Saul (Paul) and the capital and chief city of the Roman province of Cilicia in Asia Minor. The city is mentioned only five times in the Bible, all in the book of Acts.
tartak: Deity worshiped by the Avvites in Samaria. This deity may be a union of the deities Athtar and Anath, and thus a fertility god.
tartan: Title of the highest-ranking Assyrian official, second in command only to the king. The tartan was the commander in chief of the Assyrian army.
taskmaster: An overseer of public workers who enforced their performance. Taskmasters are depicted on Egyptian bas-reliefs with whips in their hands to enforce discipline.
tatian: Apologist and heretic; creator of the Diatessaron.
tattenai: Persian governor of a province west of the Euphrates River who opposed the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple and walls under Zerubbabel during the postexilic period.
tax, taxation: Amount of money or goods that was extracted by the powerful nations from those whom they subjected. It commonly consisted of gold, silver, animals, produce, or forced labor.
tax collector: One who collected taxes for the government. In NT times the Romans collected a variety of taxes.
teacher: Teachers conserved the values and academia of a nation and passed them on to each new generation. In OT times the first teachers were often parents.
teacher of righteousness: A designation of the founder of the Essene community at Qumran. The commentaries on biblical books found at Qumran provide us with some insight into the importance of the Teacher.
teachings of jesus: Because of the wide variety of forms in which the teachings of Jesus have been preserved, it is difficult to bring out the essence of that teaching in a systematic way. Jesus did not present us with a theological system.
tebah (person): Son of Abraham’s brother Nahor. His mother was Reumah, Nahor’s concubine.
tebah (place): City of King Hadadezer from which David received a large quantity of bronze as booty. Hadadezer was the king of Zobah, which is located in the region of Hamath in Syria, so the location of Tebah was likely in that region.
tebaliah: Son of Hosah, a Merarite Levite and a temple gatekeeper who served during the postexilic period.
tebeth: Month in the Hebrew calendar corresponding to about mid-December to mid-January (Est 2:16; see NLT mg).
tehaphnehes: Alternate spelling of Tahpanhes, an Egyptian city, in Ezekiel 30:18.
tehinnah: Forefather of the people of Ir-nahash in Judah’s tribe.
teil: KJV rendering of terebinth in Isaiah 6:13.
tekel: Aramaic word interpreted as “weighed” in Daniel 5:25-27.
tekoa, tekoites: City about six miles (9.7 kilometers) southeast of Bethlehem on the edge of the Judean desert, and its residents. Tekoa may also be the name of a person, the son of Ashur of Judah’s tribe; “father” could mean founder or leader of Tekoa.
tel-abib: Village on the river Kebar where Ezekiel visited the Babylonian exiles. Although the exact location of the site is unknown, it was probably in the delta region of southern Babylonia.
telah: Resheph’s son, father of Tahan, and an ancestor of Joshua the son of Nun from Ephraim’s tribe.
telaim: Place where Saul organized Israel’s army in preparation for war with the Amalekites. Telaim is perhaps identifiable with Telem, a city situated near Edom’s border in the southern extremity of the territory allotted to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance.
tel-assar: Principal city of the people of Eden who were conquered by Sennacherib of Assyria. The conquest is mentioned in Rabshekah’s taunt that the Lord would similarly be unable to protect Jerusalem.
telem (person): One of the gatekeepers who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife.
telem (place): Alternate name of the city Telaim in 1 Samuel 15:4.
tel-harsha: One of the Babylonian villages from which some returning exiles could not establish their genealogy. Its precise location is uncertain, though it is likely near the Persian Gulf in the lowland region of Babylonia.
tell: Arabic word (Hebrew, tel) meaning an artificial mound composed of many layers of occupational debris, representing the ruins of successive cities, roughly like layers of a cake.
tel-melah: One of the Babylonian towns situated in the vicinity of the Kebar River near the city of Nippur from which exiles, who were unable to establish their Israelite descent, returned to Palestine with Zerubbabel following the Babylonian captivity.
tema (person): Ninth son of Ishmael who became chief of a powerful nomadic tribe in the north Arabian wilderness. The descendants of Tema were primarily caravan traders who controlled access to important routes across the desert.
tema (place): Town generally identified with Teima’, an oasis located 200 miles (321.8 kilometers) north of Medina and 40 miles (64.4 kilometers) south of Dumah. Teima’ was located on an ancient caravan route that connected the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Aqaba.
temah: Forefather of a family of temple servants who returned with Zerubbabel to Jerusalem following the exile.
teman (person): One of the chiefs of the Edomites and Eliphaz’s firstborn son. He was likely either the founder or a chief of the Edomite city of Teman.
teman (place): In the prophetic writings, Teman seems to have been considered the principal city of Edom and is often used as a poetic parallel for the entire land of Edom.
temeni: Ashhur’s son by his wife Naarah, and a descendant of Judah.
temple: David’s capture of Jerusalem and his designation of it as the nation’s capital is one of the great masterstrokes of history.
temple assistants, temple servants: Term appearing only in the books written after Israel’s return from exile (1 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah).
tempt, temptation: The process of proving one’s worth. When ascribed to God in his dealings with people, it means that God tests his peoples’ faith and moral character.
tempter: Spirit being who opposes God and seeks to frustrate his plans and lead his people into rebellion.
ten commandments, the: List of commands given by God to Moses.
tentmaker: Artisans who made tents from the cloth of woven goats’ hair. The Greek term for tentmaker may have served to denote a range of activities in cloth and leather.
terah (person): Father of Abram (Abraham), Nahor, and Haran. Though Abram is listed first among his sons, it is likely that Abram was not the oldest.
terah (place): One of the stopping places of the Israelites during their wilderness wanderings, listed between Tahath and Mithcah.
teraphim: Idols associated with pagan magical rites. In the OT, the term is often translated “household gods,” indicative of talismans, which were kept in family shrines.
terebinth: Large deciduous tree, also called the turpentine tree.
teresh: One of two chamberlains who guarded the chambers of King Ahasuerus (Xerxes). When the two planned to kill the king, Mordecai discovered their plot and informed Esther, who in turn told the king.
tertius: Paul’s amanuensis (secretary) for the book of Romans. Since his name is a common Roman name, he was probably Roman and known by the recipients of the letter.
tertullus: Prosecuting attorney chosen by the Sanhedrin to lead in the trial of Paul before Felix, Roman procurator of Judea. It is not clear whether Tertullus was a Roman, Greek, or Jew.
test: The process of proving one’s worth. When ascribed to God in his dealings with people, it means that God tests his peoples’ faith and moral character.
testament: English word translated from the Greek signifying the covenantal administrations of God. Prior to Christ, this covenant is known as the Old Testament; under Christ’s administration, it is called the New Testament.
testimony: One who tells what he or she has seen or personally experienced, often in a court of law. The term may also refer to the testimony the person has given.
tetragrammaton: Term referring to the four consonants of one of the primary Hebrew names, for God (from Greek tetra, “four,” and gramma, “a letter of the alphabet”). These letters are the Hebrew equivalents of English Y (or J), H, W, and H.
tetrarch: Title of a class of Roman provincial officials. Tetrarchs were tributary princes who were not deemed important enough to be designated kings.
textus receptus: Copies of the NT books produced by scribes and editions made from these copies.
thaddaeus, the apostle: One of the 12 original apostles according to the lists in Mark 3:18 and Matthew 10:3 (KJV “Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus”). It is quite likely that this is the same person as Judas son of James (not Iscariot) in Luke 6:16 and Acts 1:13.
thahash: KJV spelling of Tahash, Reumah’s son, in Genesis 22:24.
thamah: KJV spelling of Temah in Ezra 2:53.
thamar: KJV spelling of Tamar, wife of Judah’s firstborn son, in Matthew 1:3.
thank offering: Major ritual expressions of religious life with accompanying rites, such as libations, effusions, and sacred meals. The ideology expressed in Israel’s ritual complex made its religion unique in the ancient Near East.
thanksgiving: Natural expression of thanks in response to blessings, protection, or love. In the Judeo-Christian tradition, gratitude is not a tool used to manipulate the will of God.
thara: KJV form of Terah, Abraham’s father, in Luke 3:34.
tharshish: 1. KJV alternate spelling of Tarshish, a port city, in 1 Kings 10:22 and 22:48.
theater: A flat, semicircular orchestra surrounded by an open-air auditorium, a Greek creation in the sixth century BC. A chorus and actors performed in the orchestra, and the audience sat on the raised hillside before them.
thebes: City appearing in the OT as No or No-Amon. No means “city” and is equivalent to the Egyptian Waset or Greek Thebes.
thebez: City where Abimelech was killed when “a certain woman” dropped a millstone on him. Abimelech had attacked Thebez after burning down the Tower of Shechem but had failed to capture the fortress within the city.
thelasar: KJV alternate form of Tel-assar in 2 Kings 19:12.
theocracy: Form of government that acknowledges God alone as the highest political authority, whether or not he is represented by a human ruler such as a king. Thus, Deuteronomy 17:14-20 argues that a human king rules only as one designated for kingship by the Lord.
theophany: An appearance or manifestation of God; a compound word derived from the Greek noun for “God” (theos) and the Greek verb “to appear” (phano). A theophany is a manifestation of God in temporary forms perceptible to the external senses.
theophilus: 1. Person to whom the books of Luke and Acts are addressed.
thessalonians, first letter to the: Paul’s first epistle to the church at Thessalonica.
thessalonians, second letter to the: Paul’s second epistle to the church at Thessalonica.
thessalonica: Chief city of Macedonia and the seat of Roman administration in the century before Christ. In addition to having a magnificent harbor, Thessalonica had the good fortune of being located on the overland route from Italy to the East.
theudas: Rebel referred to by Gamaliel in his speech before the Sanhedrin as an example of the fact that false messiahs would fall without anyone’s intervention. Theudas evidently led an unsuccessful rebellion against Rome in which he and 400 others were killed.
thistle: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
thomas, the apostle: One of the 12 apostles whose name appears in all four Gospels. The name is a transliteration of an Aramaic word meaning “twin” and appears in the NT as Thomas.
thorn: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
three taverns: Place where the believers came to meet Paul when he arrived in Rome. It was on the Appian Way located at milepost 33 (30.5 English miles or 49.1 kilometers).
thresher, threshing, threshing floor: During Bible times agriculture took the same three main forms found in Palestine today. Emphasis on each of these has depended upon the social and technological status of the people.
throne: Elevated, ceremonial chair, symbolizing the importance and the authority of the person seated on it. With the widespread use of the word “throne,” the term came to symbolize kingship and became equivalent in meaning to the kingdom itself.
thummim: Two untranslated Hebrew words that might mean “lights and perfections.” They refer to some kind of stones or tokens that the ancient high priests of Israel used for discovering the will of God.
thunder, sons of: Translation of the word “Boanerges,” the surname given by Jesus to James and John.
thutmose: Egypt figured significantly as a stage on which the biblical narrative was enacted. Here Abraham lived in time of famine.
thyatira: Location of one of the seven local churches in the book of Revelation. The city was founded by the Lydian kingdom and later captured by Seleucus, Alexander’s general.
thyine: KJV translation for “scented wood” in Revelation 18:12. Thyine was a dark-colored, fragrant, and valuable wood used for making furniture.
tiberias: City midway along the western shores of Lake Galilee, built about AD 20 by Herod Antipas, Herod the Great’s son and the tetrarch of Galilee and Perea (4 BC–AD 39), who named the town in honor of the emperor Tiberius.
tiberias, sea of: Alternate name for the Sea of Galilee in John 6:1 and 21:1.
tiberius: Roman emperor (AD 14–37) during Jesus’ earthly ministry.
tibhath: City of King Hadadezer (1 Chr 18:8, NLT “Tebah”) called Betah in the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 8:8.
tibni: Ginath’s son, who competed with Omri to be king of Israel after Zimri’s suicide. Tibni ruled over half of Israel from 884–880 BC before Omri defeated him in a civil war.
tidal: King of Goiim who fought with Kedorlaomer’s confederation against Sodom.
tiglath-pileser: Name of three Assyrian kings, the most important of whom was Tiglath-pileser III (745–727 BC). The name means “my trust is in the son of the temple Esharra,” and appears in various forms (cf. 2 Kgs 15:29; also called Tilgath-pilneser in 1 Chr 5:6; 2 Chr 28:20).
tigris river: One of the two major rivers that drains the Mesopotamian plain. Unlike the Euphrates, it is seldom mentioned in the Bible.
tikvah: 1. Harhas’s son, father of Shallum, and the father-in-law of Huldah the prophetess; alternately called Tokhath (KJV “Tikvath”) in 2 Chronicles 34:22.
tikvath: KJV spelling of Tokhath, an alternate name for Tikvah, Harhas’s son, in 2 Chronicles 34:22.
tilgath-pilneser: Alternate spelling of the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III’s name in 1 Chronicles 5:6, 26 and 2 Chronicles 28:20.
timaeus: Father of Bartimaeus, the blind beggar whose sight Jesus restored near the gateway leading from Jericho.
time: Systematic arrangements showing the beginning and length of each year and its division into days, weeks, and months. The modern calendar is usually taken for granted.
timeus: Father of Bartimaeus, the blind beggar whose sight Jesus restored near the gateway leading from Jericho.
timna (person): 1. Daughter of Seir, sister of Lotan, and a native Horite inhabitant of Edom.
timnah (place): 1. One of the cities on the northern boundary of Judah’s inheritance, located between Beth-shemesh and Ekron.
timnath: KJV spelling of Timnah, a town in northern Judah, in Genesis 38:12-14 and Judges 14:1-5.
timnath-heres, timnath-serah: The city that Joshua the son of Nun asked for and that was given to him as his inheritance when the land was divided among the tribes of Israel. Joshua rebuilt the city and settled there.
timnite: Inhabitant from the town of Timnah in northern Judah.
timon: One of the seven men of the Jerusalem church of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, appointed to minister to the widows.
timothy (person): Paul’s convert and companion, whose name means “one who honors God.”
timothy, first letter to: The first of Paul’s epistles to his young coworker Timothy.
timothy, second letter to: Many of those who deny the Pauline authorship of the Pastoral Epistles recognize that 2 Timothy contains some true Pauline fragments in the numerous personal references in the letter.
tin: A “mineral” is a naturally occurring substance, normally an ore that must be mined and treated before the metal can be extracted. A “metal” is a chemical element such as iron or copper, which is free from contamination by other materials.
tiphsah: 1. City on the northeastern boundary of Solomon’s empire.
tiras: Japheth’s seventh son listed in the “table of nations”. His descendants have been alternately linked to the Thracians, the Agathyrsi, the tribes of the Taurus mountain region, and the maritime Tyrrheni, but all of these identifications are purely speculative.
tirathites: First of three families listed as scribes living at Jabez; perhaps belonging to the Kenite family.
tirhakah: Ethiopian king who marched north to fight against the Assyrian army, thus diverting Sennacherib’s siege of Jerusalem.
tirhanah: Hezronite and the second of Caleb’s four sons by Maacah, his concubine.
tiria: Jahallelel’s son and a descendant of Judah through Caleb.
tirshatha: KJV translation of a Hebrew word designating a title of authority with the connotation of “governor.” It is appended to Zerubbabel’s name and Nehemiah’s name, both of whom held the office in Jerusalem during the postexilic period.
tirzah (person): One of the daughters of Zelophehad of Manasseh’s tribe. Since her father had no sons, she and her sisters asked for and received their father’s inheritance.
tirzah (place): Early capital city of the divided kingdom of Israel. It was one of the cities captured by Joshua, but it did not gain prominence until Jeroboam established it as his royal residence.
tishbe: Native city of Elijah the prophet and its inhabitants. The Hebrew form of Tishbe in 1 Kings 17:1 prompted the KJV to translate the word as “of the inhabitants [of Gilead].” Most translations follow the Septuagint, however, in considering Tishbe a proper noun.
tishri: Hebrew month corresponding to about mid-September to mid-October.
tithe, tithing: Words deriving from Old English for “tenth” and representing a charge upon produce or labor levied for the maintenance of religious activities.
titius justus: Believer in Corinth with whom Paul stayed.
tittle: Tiny ornamental “horn” on certain Hebrew letters.
titus (person): 1. One of Paul’s converts—“my true child in a common faith” (Ti 1:4, NASB)—who became an intimate and trusted associate of the apostle in his mission of planting Christianity throughout the Mediterranean world.
titus, letter to: Paul’s epistle to his coworker, Titus.
tob: Place where Jephthah fled after his half brothers threw him out for being illegitimate. During the reign of David, the Ammonites hired 12,000 men from Tob as mercenaries to fight against David.
tob-adonijah: One of the Levites under Jehoshaphat who went out into the cities of Judah to teach the law.
tobiah: 1. Forefather of a family of people who returned with Zerubbabel to Jerusalem following the exile.
tobias: The hero of the book of Tobit, who with divine aid marries his kinswoman Sarah, in spite of a jealous evil spirit, and restores his father Tobit’s sight.
tobijah: 1. Levite sent by King Jehoshaphat to teach the law in the cities of Judah.
tobit (person): Primary character of the deuterocanonical book of Tobit.
tobit, book of: One of several deuterocanonical books of the Bible. It was received as canonical by the Council of Trent (1546) and is found in the Roman Catholic Bible, but it was never included in the Hebrew Old Testament and is placed with the Apocrypha by Protestants.
togarmah: Third son of Gomer, a descendant of Japheth. Beth-togarmah (“house of Togarmah”) appears in Ezekiel’s prophecy against the nations that opposed Israel.
toi: King of Hamath at the time David defeated the armies of Hadadezer (2 Sm 8:9-10; alternately called Tou in 1 Chr 18:9-10). He sent his son Joram to congratulate and give gifts to David.
token: One of the villages settled by Simeon’s tribe (1 Chr 4:32, KJV “Tochen”). The name does not appear in the parallel passage in Joshua 19, but in that list it does appear as Thokka in the Septuagint.
tokhath: Alternate form of Tikvah, the father-in-law of Huldah the prophetess, in 2 Chronicles 34:22 (see NLT mg).
tolad: Alternate form of Eltolad, a city in Simeon’s territory, in 1 Chronicles 4:29.
tolaite: Descendant of Tola from Issachar’s tribe.
tomb: The Bible makes frequent reference to burial practices. A society’s burial customs are a reflection of its views about death and the afterlife.
tongues, speaking in: Supernatural manifestation of speech in a language not known to the speaker; the Greek term is glossolalia.
tongues of fire: Phrase occurring only in Acts 2:3, describing the visible manifestation of the Spirit. The tongues of fire seem to be the fulfillment of John the Baptist’s proclamation that the Coming One would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire.
topaz: A lengthy list of the precious stones used in OT times occurs in Exodus 28:17-20 and 39:10-13, where four rows of three stones, each engraved with the name of one of the 12 tribes of Israel, were set in the high priest’s breastplate.
tophel: Place where Israel camped opposite the Jordan, “in the Arabah over against Suph, between Paran and Tophel”. Tophel has been identified with et-Tafileh, east of the Dead Sea.
topheth: Location within the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem where Israel profaned the Lord by offering human sacrifices to Molech. As part of his religious reform, Josiah defiled Topheth and tore down its altars.
torah: Word translated “law” in the OT, derived from the Hebrew verbal root yarah, which means “to throw” or “to shoot.” The idea behind the word is to inform, instruct, direct, or guide.
tortoise: Reptiles of the suborder Lacertilia. Their skin is covered with scales.
tou: Alternate form of Toi, the king of Hamath, in 1 Chronicles 18:9-10 (see NLT mg).
tower: Walls, citadels, and sometimes moats protecting most cities in the ancient world. Fortifications followed the natural contour of the area encircling a city.
tower of babel: Translation of a Hebrew word in Genesis 10:10 and 11:9. Elsewhere it is translated “Babylonia” or “Babylon” (see 2 Kgs 17:24).
tower of shechem: Fortress erected on the acropolis of Shechem, housing the temple of Baal-berith and situated inside the city walls. The city of Shechem was located in the hill country of the tribe of Ephraim near Mt Gerizim.
tower of siloam: Edifice that collapsed, killing 18 people. Jesus compared those killed by the fallen tower to the rest of the people living in Jerusalem.
tower of the furnaces: KJV translation for “Tower of the Ovens,” a tower in Jerusalem, in Nehemiah 3:11.
tower of the hundred: Tower at the northernmost part of the Jerusalem wall (near where the wall crosses over the Tyropeon Valley). It stood west of the Sheep Gate near the Tower of Hananel (Neh 3:1; 12:39; KJV “tower of Meah”).
town clerk: An official in municipal administration whose duties included those of scribe or secretary. He published the decrees of the civic authority but also acted as a liaison officer between the administration of a city and the Roman provincial government.
trachonitis, traconitis: One of the five Roman provinces east of the Jordan River, along with Batanea, Gaulanitis, Auranitis, and Iturea. The region of Traconitis (apparently including Gaulanitis, Batanea, and Auranitis) was part of the tetrarchy of Philip, the brother of Herod.
trade routes: In biblical times travelers found roads bad and often impassable. Sea voyages were made in comparatively small ships, usually by military and commercial personnel, and hardly ever for simple tourist traffic.
tradition: Respect for tradition was particularly strong among Jews during the period at the beginning of the Christian era. Among these traditions, the most important collection was Pirke Aboth (Traditions of the Fathers).
tradition, oral: Oral tradition is both sharply distinguished from written tradition and yet closely connected with it. Many literary traditions are based on oral traditions, making it necessary to investigate how transitions were made from one to the other.
transfiguration: Event in Jesus’ earthly ministry described in four passages in the NT, wherein Jesus was glorified in the presence of three disciples: James, Peter, and John.
transformation: An inward renewal and reshaping of the mind through which a Christian’s inner person is changed into the likeness of Christ. Paul told the Roman believers, “Be transformed by the renewing of your minds”.
transgression: Evildoing that is not only against humanity, society, others, or oneself, but against God. The concept of God, therefore, gives to the idea of sin its many-sided meaning.
transjordan: Territory on the east side of the Jordan River. Although this name does not appear in the Bible, numerous events took place there in biblical history.
travel: In biblical times travelers found roads bad and often impassable. Sea voyages were made in comparatively small ships, usually by military and commercial personnel, and hardly ever for simple tourist traffic.
treasurer: An officer in charge of financial matters. In OT times he had charge of the royal or sacred treasures, which consisted of goods, documents, money, and jewels.
tree: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
tree of knowledge of good and evil: Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil

Forbidden tree in Eden, whose fruit imparted knowledge and subsequent death, i.e., separation from God and ultimate expiration. The tempting serpent promised Eve equality with God if she ate the fruit.
tree of life: Tree placed by God in the midst of the Garden of Eden, a tree whose fruit could give eternal life. God told Adam that he could eat from every tree of the Garden except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (vv 16-17).
trespass: Evildoing that is not only against humanity, society, others, or oneself, but against God. The concept of God, therefore, gives to the idea of sin its many-sided meaning.
trespass offering: Major ritual expressions of religious life with accompanying rites, such as libations, effusions, and sacred meals. The ideology expressed in Israel’s ritual complex made its religion unique in the ancient Near East.
tribes, territories of the: Terms referring to Israel’s winning of the Promised Land and the distinctive way in which it was divided among the Israelite tribes.
tribulation: An experience of suffering, distress, affliction, trouble, or persecution. The Greek word appears in the NT about 45 times.
tribune: Roman military official who served as the commander of a cohort (1,000 men). In NT usage it designated the commander of the Roman garrison in Jerusalem (e.g., Acts 21:31; 22:24; 23:10; 24:22).
tributary, tribute: Amount of money or goods that was extracted by the powerful nations from those whom they subjected. It commonly consisted of gold, silver, animals, produce, or forced labor.
trichotomy: The threefold division of human nature into body, soul, and spirit.
trinity: Term designating the three members of the triune God: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
triumphal entry: A term that denotes Jesus Christ’s entry into Jerusalem, where the multitudes welcomed him and hailed him as Son of David, King of the Jews. Ironically, this event occurred just a few days prior to his betrayal, arrest, trial, and crucifixion.
troas: City in Turkey on the Aegean shore, 10 miles (16.1 kilometers) south of the ancient site of Troy, scene of the Trojan War immortalized by the poet Homer.
trogyllium: Rocky straits between Samos and Miletus. In Acts 20:15, some manuscripts indicate that Paul’s ship stopped at this place on his trip to Jerusalem near the end of his third missionary journey.
trophimus: One of the Asians who accompanied Paul on his final trip to Jerusalem. Because the Jews had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with Paul in Jerusalem, they incorrectly assumed that he had accompanied Paul into the temple (21:29).
trumpet: Stringed, wind, and percussion instruments used to make music.
trumpets, festival of: Day of solemn rest and remembrance of God’s provision for his people through the Sinai covenant.
truth: That which is real and verifiable by experience.
tryphaena, tryphena: Christian woman of Rome. Along with Tryphosa, Paul called her one of the “Lord’s workers”.
tryphosa: Christian woman of Rome. Along with Tryphena, Paul called her one of the “Lord’s workers”.
tubal: Fifth of the listed sons of Japheth in the table of nations. Tubal later gained significance in the prophetic writings of Isaiah and Ezekiel as one of the nations that would be judged for threatening God’s people.
tubal-cain: Son of Lamech by his wife Zillah.
tulip: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
tumbleweed: KJV rendering of “whirling dust” in Psalm 83:13 and Isaiah 17:13.
tumor: Abnormal swelling or growth in any part of the body. The only significant occurrence of this term is in 1 Samuel 5–6.
tunic: Clothing mentioned in the Bible is usually referred to in such general terms as “inner garment,” “outer garment,” or “tunic.” Few descriptions give specific details of costumes or clothing, and it is therefore necessary to rely on paintings, pottery,…
turtledove: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
twelve, the: Designation for the 12 apostles in 1 Corinthians 15:5 and other verses.
twin brothers: Twin sons of Zeus. Paul sailed to Rome on a ship whose figurehead was the Twin Brothers.
tychicus: One of the believers who accompanied Paul in his trip to collect and deliver the offering for the Jerusalem church. Since he is often mentioned with Trophimus of Ephesus, Tychicus was likely also a native of that city.
type: The English word “type” is derived from the Greek tupos, which has the basic meaning of “a visible impression or mark made by a blow or by pressure.” In the Greek NT, the word occurs 16 times, with various meanings.
tyrannus, hall of: Place in Ephesus where Paul taught daily for two years. Paul’s ministry in Ephesus had begun at the synagogue, where he had preached for three months.
tyre: Ancient Phoenician city-state located on the Mediterranean coast 20 miles (32.2 kilometers) south of Sidon and 23 miles (37 kilometers) north of Acre.
ucal: Disciple of Agur, the wise man whose sayings are recorded in the book of Proverbs (Prv 30:1; see NLT mg). The meaning of the passage is obscure.
uel: Bani’s descendant and a priest who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife during the postexilic era.
ugarit: City in northwest Syria during the second millennium BC. Though the city is not mentioned in the Bible, it is a significant archaeological site that illuminates OT language and history.
ulai: River near the Persian capital city of Susa where Daniel received a vision concerning the end times. It is likely the same as the Eulaeus, which is described by both Greek and Roman geographers as a stream that flowed to the west of the citadel of Susa.
ulcer: Any localized abnormality of the skin. It was a well-demarcated skin abnormality with a definite border between the inflamed or abnormal skin and the normal skin.
ummah: One of the villages inherited by Asher’s tribe after the conquest of Canaan. Neither the location of Ummah nor the accompanying villages (Aphek and Rehob) are known.
uncircumcision: Natural condition of the male, that is, with the foreskin covering his penis.
unclean, uncleanness: Aspect of Hebrew religion having physical, ceremonial, moral, and spiritual significance.
unforgivable sin: Attributing to Satan what is actually the work of the Holy Spirit as demonstrated through Jesus Christ. This sin is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.
unicorn: KJV rendering for an animal called a “wild ox” in the NLT and most modern translations. Unicorn is an unfortunate translation (following the Septuagint) because the animal had two horns, not one.
unleavened bread: Bread made without leaven (yeast). In ancient times, bread makers used a piece of dough remaining from a former baking process, a piece that had fermented and developed a certain acid content—the yeast that caused bread to rise.
unleavened bread, festival of: Occasions of public or private rejoicing to commemorate some significant event or personage. The element of celebration has a special meaning in the cycle of religious occasions and the rites and ceremonies associated with these particular days.
unni: 1. One of the musicians appointed by the chief of the Levites to sing and play the harp as part of the temple service during David’s reign.
unno: One of the Levites who participated in the temple service during the postexilic era.
unpardonable sin, the: Attributing to Satan what is actually the work of the Holy Spirit as demonstrated through Jesus Christ. This sin is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.
upharsin: Aramaic word interpreted as “divided” in Daniel 5:25 (KJV).
uphaz: Region well known for its gold. Some contend that Uphaz is a scribal error for Ophir (only one consonant is different), another region famous for its fine gold.
upper gate: One of the gates leading to the temple mount in Jerusalem. It was built by Jotham and served as the principal access between the royal palace and the temple area.
upper room: Second-story room of a Hebrew or a Greek house; often like a tower, built on the flat roof of a Hebrew home for privacy, for comfort during the hot season, or for the entertainment of guests. In some instances it could accommodate large gatherings of people.
ur (person): Father of Eliphal, one of David’s mighty men; probably the same as Ahasbai in the parallel passage.
ur (place): Hometown of Terah, the father of Abraham, and the birthplace of Abraham and Sarah. It is mentioned by name only four times in the Bible, always with the full name “Ur of the Chaldeans.”
urbanus: Believer greeted as one of Paul’s coworkers in Christ.
uri: 1. Father of Bezalel from Judah’s tribe, and a builder of the tabernacle.
uriah: 1. Hittite who joined the people of Israel, became a leader in David’s army, and was listed among the king’s mighty men.
urias: KJV spelling (in Matthew 1:6) of Uriah, Bathsheba’s husband, whom David had killed.
uriel: 1. Levite of the Kohathite branch who is listed as the son of Tahath and the father of Uzziah.
urim and thummim: Two untranslated Hebrew words that might mean “lights and perfections.” They refer to some kind of stones or tokens that the ancient high priests of Israel used for discovering the will of God.
uthai: 1. One who returned to Israel following the exile.
uz (person): 1. Aram’s firstborn son and a descendant of Shem.
uz (place): Homeland of Job. The name appears in parallels with Edom and is associated with the Uz in the family tree of the original Horites in Seir.
uzai: Father of Palal, a repairer of the Jerusalem wall during Nehemiah’s day.
uzal (person): Son of Joktan, a descendant of Eber through Shem’s line.
uzal (place): Place mentioned with Dan and Javan in an obscure passage; it is identifiable with modern Sana (ancient Awzal), the capital of Yemen.
uzza: 1. Owner or initial planter of a garden that served as the burial place for kings Manasseh and Amon of Judah.
uzzah: 1. Son of Abinadab who was killed while accompanying the cart that carried the ark of the covenant when it was returned from the Philistines.
uzzen-sheerah: Town built by Sheerah, who was either the daughter or granddaughter of Ephraim.
uzzi: 1. Descendant of Eliezer who was in the direct ancestral line of high priests, though he apparently never served in that capacity.
uzzia: One of David’s mighty men. He was described as an Ashterathite, which probably means that he was from Ashtaroth, a town on the east side of the Jordan.
uzziah: 1. Judah’s king from around 792 to 740 BC (cf. 2 Kgs 14:21-22; 15:1-7; 2 Chr 26:1-23), the son of King Amaziah and Jecoliah of Jerusalem.
uzziel: 1. Youngest of the sons of Kohath of Levi’s tribe, who became the head of the Uzzielite division of the Kohathites.
vaizatha, vajezatha: One of Haman’s ten sons, who was killed during the Jews’ retaliation when Haman plotted to kill them.
valley gate: Gate from which Nehemiah went out to inspect the walls of Jerusalem and by which he reentered. It was on the west side of the city facing the Tyropeon Valley.
valley of craftsmen: Translation and alternate name for Ge-harashim in Nehemiah 11:35.
valley of decision: Valley near Jerusalem alternately called the valley of Jehoshaphat in Joel 3:2, 12.
valley of hinnom: Valley on the south side of Jerusalem, called Gehenna in the Greek NT.
valley of jehoshaphat: Valley mentioned in prophecy as the place of future judgment, sometimes called the valley of decision (v 14). Its exact location is disputed.
valley of jezreel: Largest and richest valley in the land of Israel. It was named after Jezreel, and it was apparently the only town on the plain where the Israelites had gained a foothold in the early stages of their conquest (cf.
valley of rephaim: Geographical landmark forming part of the common boundary of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin (KJV “the valley of the giants” in Jos 15:8; 18:16); a broad valley in the southwestern outskirts of Jerusalem thought to be frequented by giants like the Anakim and the Nephilim.
valley of shaveh: Valley near Salem, also called the King’s Valley in Genesis 14:17.
valley of siddim: Location of the battle between four kings from Mesopotamia and five allied kings living near the Dead Sea. The precise location of the battle in the vicinity of the Dead Sea has proved impossible to determine; one is left with conjectures.
vaniah: Bani’s son and one of the priests who divorced his foreign wife at Ezra’s command.
vashni: KJV alternate name for Joel, Samuel’s son, in 1 Chronicles 6:28.
vashti: Queen during the reign of Ahasuerus (Xerxes I) who was deposed for refusing to show herself to the guests at a royal banquet.
vegetable: Substances required by the body to sustain life, and the methods of making them edible. Food consumed in Bible times included bread, milk products, fruit, meat, and fish.
veil of the temple: Curtain in the sanctuary separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.
vespasian: Roman general who entered Palestine in AD 66 to quell the rebellious Jews, and later became emperor of Rome (AD 69–79).
vestments: Servants of God in the OT. There were three basic classes of religious personnel in ancient Israel: prophets, wise men, and priests and Levites.
vinedresser: Plants cultivated for the production of grapes, raisins, and wine. The grapevine is mentioned frequently in Scripture both in a literal and a figurative sense.
vinegar: Substances required by the body to sustain life, and the methods of making them edible. Food consumed in Bible times included bread, milk products, fruit, meat, and fish.
vine of sodom: Designation for a plant that produces an enticing but inedible fruit.
vines, vineyard: Plants cultivated for the production of grapes, raisins, and wine. The grapevine is mentioned frequently in Scripture both in a literal and a figurative sense.
viol: KJV rendering of harp in Isaiah 5:12; 14:11; Amos 5:23; and 6:5.
viper: One of the 20 poisonous snakes found in Israel and surrounding countries, also referred to as cockatrice and viper.
virgin: Word used only of women and (metaphorically) of places, nations, and the church. Literally, it describes a woman who has reached physical maturity but has not experienced sexual intercourse.
virgin birth of jesus: Doctrine, drawn from the birth narratives of Matthew 1 and Luke 1–2, which states that Jesus Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary.
vision, visions: Visual experiences of any kind, but in the Bible the word usually refers to supernatural revelations of a prophet. In early OT prophecy there are cases of extraordinary sight, which was regarded as evidence of the visionary endowment of a prophet.
vophsi: Man appointed by Moses from Naphtali’s tribe to spy out the land of Canaan.
vow, vows: Serious promises or pledges made to God. The making of vows to God is a religious practice frequently mentioned in Scripture.
vulgate, the: Latin version of the Bible, commonly identified as the work of Jerome.
vulture: Feathered vertebrates of the class Aves. Over 8,000 species of birds are known.
wadi: Intermittent stream or torrent in the arid and semiarid regions of the Middle East. Although the streambeds were usually dry, they could attain flood stage during spring runoff or after heavy rainfalls.
wages: Payment received by a laborer in return for his work. Usually wages are calculated in terms of a medium of exchange, such as money, but they can be paid in any kind of goods or services.
waheb: Town in the area of Suphah.
walnut: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
wanderings in the wilderness: When the Israelites came out of Egypt, they spent some 40 years wandering in the wildernesses of the Sinai Peninsula and the Negev. Then they moved on to conquer the Promised Land.
war, holy: Warfare as described in the book of Deuteronomy, especially in chapter 20.
warfare: The means by which one nation seeks to impose its will upon another by force. An index to the importance of warfare in antiquity is provided by the amount of technical skill directed to perfecting devices for destruction and defense.
war of the sons of light against the son: War of the Sons of Light against the Sons of Darkness

Scroll found in Cave One at Qumran (1947–48). It casts light on military regulations of the Jewish forces, on the religious life of the sectarians at Qumran, and particularly on their eschatological expectations.
wars of the lord, book of the: Wars of the Lord, Book of the
Document mentioned once in the OT; it is found in a description of Moab’s border at the Arnon. The book was used as a source but is no longer extant.
watch: Time unit for the division of the night in both the OT and NT. During the OT period, the night was divided into three military watches.
watchman: Military or civil security person who had the responsibility to protect ancient towns or military installations from surprise attack or civil disasters. Watchmen also had the responsibility of announcing the dawning of a new day.
watchtower: Platform from which farmers protected their land and livestock and from which soldiers guarded their cities. Watchtowers were built in the vineyards of Palestine.
water: One of the essentials of life, which covers much of the earth’s surface and is the primary component of the human body. Life cannot be sustained more than a few days without it.
water gate: One of the principal gates on the east side of Jerusalem. It was rebuilt during Nehemiah’s day and served as the location for Ezra’s reading of the law.
water hen: Designation for several birds living near water, such as the marsh hen, swan, or even the horned owl.
water lily: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
waters of merom: Site of Joshua’s victory over Jabin, king of Hazor, and his allies, mentioned only twice in the Bible.
wave offering: Major ritual expressions of religious life with accompanying rites, such as libations, effusions, and sacred meals. The ideology expressed in Israel’s ritual complex made its religion unique in the ancient Near East.
way, the: One of the names applied to the early Christian community. It was apparently used by both the Jewish and the secular community and appeared in both positive and negative assessments of the church (19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22).
wealth: Abundance, usually of money or material goods, whose value is ordinarily expressed in terms of some understood unit, such as a national currency. It is virtually synonymous with riches, and both may refer to family, friends, or even moral qualities.
weapons: The location of Palestine at the crossroads of three continents gave it a strategic importance in the ancient world quite out of proportion to its size.
weasel: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
weaving: Since antiquity, cloth has been made from such natural fibers as flax, wool, cotton, silk, and hair. Linen (spun from flax), wool, and sackcloth (woven from goat’s or camel’s hair) are the fabrics most frequently mentioned in Scripture.
wedding: The joining together of male and female in matrimony, as practiced by various cultures.
weeds: Identifying biblical plants has always been a difficult task, partly because people continue to identify the biblical elm, sycamore, lily, rose, and vine with modern plants, and also because they assume that all the plants now growing in the Holy Land were…
week: Systematic arrangements showing the beginning and length of each year and its division into days, weeks, and months. The modern calendar is usually taken for granted.
weeks, feast of: Celebration of the beginning of the wheat harvest, occurring seven weeks after Passover on the sixth day of Sivan (June); also known as the Feast of Pentecost.
weights and measures: Units of measure in the ancient world were largely based on practical standards: the length of an arm, a day’s journey, how much a donkey could carry, and so forth. While this was a convenient system, it also suffered from a lack of standardization.
well: Man-made reservoir fed either by subterranean springs or by rainwater. Because the majority of the biblical world ranges from arid to semiarid, wells were a critical source of water for humans, livestock, and the irrigation of crops.
western text: According to the classification of B. F.
whale: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
wheat: During Bible times agriculture took the same three main forms found in Palestine today. Emphasis on each of these has depended upon the social and technological status of the people.
wheel: Device originating in the region of Mesopotamia, probably dating from about 3500 BC. The earliest known form is the two-wheeled cart of Sumer.
whirlwind: Term descriptive of any strong, potentially destructive wind.
white: The OT and NT have no exact word for “color,” although the word appears several times in our English Bibles. The words translated “color” have quite different meanings in the original languages.
whore: Person guilty of illicit sexual relationships; figuratively, one who worships an idol. The term “prostitute” translates four different words found in the Bible.
wickedness: Evildoing that is not only against humanity, society, others, or oneself, but against God. The concept of God, therefore, gives to the idea of sin its many-sided meaning.
widow: A woman whose husband has died. In the Scriptures, widows are often listed with the fatherless and orphans.
wife: In Bible times, the family comprised members of a household, including not only parents and children, along with other relatives and concubines, but also servants, travelers, aliens, and anyone else who happened to be within the house and was therefore under the protection of the head of the family.
wilderness: Land that is basically wild and sparsely inhabited or unfit for permanent human settlement. It may be desert, mountains, forest, or marsh.
wilderness wanderings: When the Israelites came out of Egypt, they spent some 40 years wandering in the wildernesses of the Sinai Peninsula and the Negev. Then they moved on to conquer the Promised Land.
wild ox: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
wild vine: Any plant with a flexible stem that climbs, twines, or creeps along a surface or support. The common grapevine (Vitis vinifera) is mentioned throughout the Bible.
will of god: Important NT term indicating God’s choice and determination, emanating from desire.
willow: Any of several trees of the genus Populus with leaves attached by flattened leafstalks so that they tremble or “quake” in the wind.
willows, ravine of the: Ravine by which Moab’s abundance would be carried off (Is 15:7, NIV “Ravine of the Poplars”). Isaiah’s language suggests that it marked the southern border of Moab.
wine: Beverage made from fermented grape juice.
winepress: A sunken area into which the grape harvest was thrown and then trodden with bare feet, amid shouts of joy and traditional vintage work songs (Jer 48:33; cf. Is 65:8).
wineskins: Containers made of animal hide for keeping wine. The term is prominent in Jesus’ maxim that new wine cannot be put in old wineskins but must be put in new wineskins because the new wine, when it ferments and expands, will break the old wineskins and spill out.
winnower: One who removes chaff from grain.
wisdom: The ability to direct one’s mind toward a full understanding of human life and toward its moral fulfillment. Wisdom is thus a special capacity, necessary for full human living; it can be acquired through education and the application of the mind.
wisdom literature: Literature in the OT that has wisdom as its central theme. It comprises principally the books of Job, Proverbs, and Ecclesiastes and may also be found in portions of the Psalms and Prophets.
wisdom of jesus ben sirach: Deuterocanonical book that is also known as Ecclesiasticus (to be distinguished from the canonical book Ecclesiastes).
wisdom of solomon: Deuterocanonical work containing a treasury of wisdom. A theological and/or philosophical treatise, the Wisdom of Solomon seeks to blend the piety of orthodox Judaism with the best of Greek philosophy.
wise men: “Wise men” (NLT, KJV) appearing in Matthew 2:1-12 who, following a star, came to Jerusalem and then to Bethlehem in order to pay homage to the newborn “king of the Jews.” Matthew’s account forms a significant introduction to his Gospel by drawing attention to…
witch, witchcraft: Practice whose adherents claim to have supernatural powers and knowledge; the ability to foretell the future and to summon evil spirits through charms and magical spells. Sorcerers were present in the high courts of Egypt, Assyria, and Babylonia.
withered hand: Any obvious physical abnormality. In the OT sacrificial system both the animal to be sacrificed and the priest who performed the sacrifice (ch 21) had to be perfect physical specimens, without defect or blemish.
witness: One who tells what he or she has seen or personally experienced, often in a court of law. The term may also refer to the testimony the person has given.
witness, altar of: Altar built by the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh in the frontier of Israel near the Jordan. The building of the altar incited the remainder of Israel to threaten war for the presumed treachery.
wizard: Attempt to influence or control people or events through supernatural forces. These forces are called upon by means of ceremonies, the recitation of spells, charms, incantations, and other forms of ritual.
woe: An exclamation denoting pain or displeasure. Less frequently, it occurs as a noun denoting a disaster or calamity.
wolf: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
wonders: A divine act by which God reveals himself to people. The classical definition of miracle assumes that it is contrary to natural law, but this is a misnomer for two reasons.
wool: Important commodity of the ancient Near East. King Mesha of Moab, a sheep breeder, annually sent the wool of 100,000 rams as tribute to King Ahab of Israel, and the people of Damascus traded wool with Tyre’s merchants.
word, word of god, words of god: Word, Word of God, Words of God
A “word” is an expression that communicates. On the level of human communication, “words “usually refer to verbal expression.
work: A term referring either to God’s activity or to people’s regular occupation or employment.
world: An important NT term from the Greek word kosmos (meaning that which is ordered or arranged), having five different meanings:
worm: In biblical usage, all members of the animal kingdom. Animals are mentioned throughout the Bible from Genesis to Revelation.
wormwood: Strong, bitter-tasting plant that symbolized bitterness and sorrow.
worship: Expression of reverence and adoration of God.
wrath of god: A term for God’s displeasure with human beings and their sinful actions.
writer: Professional scribe and/or secretary; religious scribe and/or secretary.
writing: The process that goes into producing books.
xanthicus: Name of the month in the Macedonian calendar corresponding to the Hebrew month Nisan (March–April); mentioned in 2 Maccabees 11:27-38.
xerxes: NIV and NLT rendering of Ahasuerus in Ezra 4:6 and the book of Esther.
xestes: Liquid measure equivalent to about one and one-sixth pints (552 milliliters).
yahweh (yhwh): Most holy name for God in the OT, usually translated “LORD.” See God, Names of (Yahweh).
year: Systematic arrangements showing the beginning and length of each year and its division into days, weeks, and months. The modern calendar is usually taken for granted.
yeast: Any substance that produces fermentation when added to dough.
yellow: The OT and NT have no exact word for “color,” although the word appears several times in our English Bibles. The words translated “color” have quite different meanings in the original languages.
yiron: One of the fortified cities of Naphtali’s tribe. Some have identified Yiron with the present village of Jarun, southeast of Bint Jebeil.
yoke: The wooden bar that allowed two (or more) draft animals to be coupled (yoked) so that they might effectively work together. In addition to this literal usage, the Bible frequently uses the term metaphorically to refer to work or bondage.
yom kippur: One of the feast days of Israel involving atonement for the sins of the nation.
zaanaim: KJV spelling of Zaanannim in Judges 4:11.
zaanan: Village mentioned in Micah’s lament over Jerusalem. Zaanan is probably a play on the Hebrew word yatsa’, “to come forth.” The village was in the Shephelah; it is probably the same place as Zenan.
zaanannim: One of the markers of the border of Naphtali listed between Heleph and Adami-nekeb. Judges 4:11 puts it near Kedesh.
zaavan: Second son of Ezer, a Horite clan chief.
zabad: 1. Son of Nathan and a descendant of Ahlai the daughter of Sheshan (vv 30, 34-36).
zabbai: 1. Bebai’s son and one of the priests who divorced his foreign wife at Ezra’s command.
zabbud: KJV form of Zaccur, Bigvai’s descendant, in Ezra 8:14.
zabdiel: 1. Father of Jashobeam, the commander of the first division of David’s army.
zabud: Priest in Solomon’s court and the “king’s friend”. The phrase “king’s friend” may be an official title given to one of the king’s advisers.
zabulon: KJV spelling of Zebulun in Matthew 4:13-15 and Revelation 7:8.
zaccai: Forefather of a family who returned with Zerubbabel to Judah following the exile.
zacchaeus: Jewish tax collector who collected taxes for the Romans at Jericho. He probably secured this position by purchasing the exclusive right to collect revenue in that region or by working as a subcontractor for another affluent official.
zacchur: KJV spelling of Zaccur, Hammuel’s son, in 1 Chronicles 4:26.
zaccur: 1. Reubenite and father of Shammua, one of the 12 spies in the reconnaissance of Canaan.
zachariah: 1. KJV spelling of Zechariah, king of Israel, in 2 Kings 14:29 and 15:8, 11.
zacharias: 1. KJV spelling of Zechariah, Jehoiada’s son, in Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:51.
zacher: KJV form of Zechariah, or Zeker, in 1 Chronicles 8:31.
zaham: One of Rehoboam’s sons by his wife Mahalath.
zair: Place where Joram attacked and defeated the Edomites. In the parallel passage of 2 Chronicles 21:9, the phrase “to Zair” is replaced by the phrase “with his commanders” (the Hebrew words are similar).
zalaph: Hanun’s father. Hanun repaired a section of the Jerusalem wall during Nehemiah’s day.
zalmon (person): One of David’s mighty men; alternately called Ilai the Ahohite in 1 Chronicles 11:29.
zalmon (place): Mountain from which Abimelech took brush to burn down the tower of Shechem.
zalmonah: Place where the Israelites camped after they set out from Mt Hor. The name suggests that it was a gloomy valley leading up to the Edomite plateau.
zalmunna: Two Midianite kings who slaughtered Gideon’s brothers at Tabor. Gideon subsequently killed them in order to avenge his brothers’ deaths.
zamzummim, zamzummites: Ammonite name for the Rephaim, who are described as a “people great and many, and tall as the Anakim”. The Zamzummites were displaced by the Ammonites, just as the Horites were displaced by the Edomites and the Avvim by the Caphtorim.
zanoah (person): Descendant of Caleb from Judah’s tribe. Zanoah was the son of Jekuthiel and, depending on the translation of the Hebrew text, may have been related to Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh.
zanoah (place): 1. One of the cities “in the lowland” that was part of Judah’s inheritance.
zaphenath-paneah: Name given to Joseph by Pharaoh when Joseph assumed his governmental responsibilities in Egypt. The name most likely means “says the god, he will live.” See Joseph #1.
zaphon: Town located east of the Jordan River and included as part of the inheritance of Gad’s tribe (v 24). Egyptian records (13th century BC) refer to a town known as Dapuna, while an Amarna text spells the name Sapuna.
zara, zarah: KJV alternate forms of Zerah, Judah’s son, in Genesis 38:30, 46:12, and Matthew 1:3.
zareah, zareathite: KJV spelling of Zorah and Zorathite in Nehemiah 11:29 and 1 Chronicles 2:53, respectively.
zared: KJV spelling for the valley of Zered in Numbers 21:12.
zarephath: Village where the woman who provided food and lodging for Elijah lived. Obadiah later prophesied that the Israelite exiles of Halah would “possess Phoenicia as far as Zarephath”.
zarethan: City or region near the Jordan River north of Jericho. It is first mentioned in connection with the “cutting off” of the waters of the Jordan that occurred at Adam, “the city that is beside Zarethan”.
zareth-shahar: KJV spelling of Zereth-shahar, a Reubenite city, in Joshua 13:19.
zarhite: 1. KJV spelling of Zerahite, a descendant of Zerah’s family in Simeon’s tribe, in Numbers 26:13.
zartanah, zarthan: KJV alternate forms of Zarethan in 1 Kings 4:12 and 7:46, respectively.
zatthu: KJV rendering of Zattu in Nehemiah 10:14.
zattu: 1. Clan chief with whom 945 people returned with Zerubbabel (Ezr 2:8; Neh 7:13 cites 845 returnees).
zavan: KJV spelling of Zaavan, Ezer’s son, in 1 Chronicles 1:42.
zaza: Jonathan’s son, in the family of Jerahmeel, a member of Judah’s tribe.
zealot: Term used for the second Simon among the Twelve to distinguish him from Simon Peter.
zealot, simon the: Greek form of a Hebrew/Aramaic name meaning “God has heard.” Nine men in the NT had this name:
zebadiah: 1. One of the sons of Beriah from Benjamin’s tribe.
zebah and zalmunna: Two Midianite kings who slaughtered Gideon’s brothers at Tabor. Gideon subsequently killed them in order to avenge his brothers’ deaths.
zebaim: KJV rendering of a place mentioned in Ezra 2:57 and Nehemiah 7:59.
zebedee: Father of the disciples James and John. Zebedee was in the fishing business and may have been wealthy, considering that he had servants and apparent connections with the high priest.
zebidah: Mother of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, Josiah’s wife and the daughter of Pedaiah.
zebina: Nebo’s son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his foreign wife after the exile.
zeboiim: One of the “cities of the plain” that was destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah. Zeboiim is first mentioned, with Sodom, Gomorrah, and Admah, as one of the Canaanite cities in the “table of nations” in Genesis 10:19.
zeboim: 1. KJV spelling of Zeboiim in Genesis 10:19, Deuteronomy 29:23, and Hosea 11:8.
zebudah: KJV spelling of Zebidah, King Josiah’s wife, in 2 Kings 23:36.
zebul: Ruler of Shechem who served as an officer of Abimelech. Zebul apparently obtained his position when Abimelech was crowned king at Shechem.
zebulun (person): One of Jacob’s 12 sons. He was the sixth and last son borne to Jacob by Leah, who named the boy Zebulun, meaning “abode, dwelling,” for she said, “Now my husband will dwell with me, because I have borne him six sons” (Gn 30:20, NASB, emphasis added).
zebulun, tribe of: Tribe descended from Zebulun, the tenth son of Jacob and the sixth borne to him by Leah. His tribe was divided into three clans named after his three sons: the Seredites, the Elonites, and the Jahleelites.
zechariah (person): Extremely popular name in the Bible; it means “the Lord remembers.”
zechariah, book of: Longest book of the Minor Prophets and the most difficult to understand. One reason for this difficulty is the numerous visions that call for an interpreter.
zecher, zeker: Alternate form of Zechariah, Gibeon’s son, in 1 Chronicles 8:31.
zedad: One of the geographical landmarks of Israel’s northern boundary, mentioned between Hamath and Ziphron.
zedekiah: 1. Judah’s last king and a key political figure in the fateful final decade of the southern kingdom.
zeeb: One of two Midianite princes executed by Gideon’s army.
zela, zelah: City of Benjamin’s tribe where the bones of Saul and Jonathan were buried. Zela was probably the native town of Saul’s father, Kish, and may well have been Saul’s home before he was anointed king.
zelek: Ammonite warrior among David’s mighty men.
zelophehad: Hepher’s son from Manasseh’s tribe. He fathered five daughters but no sons.
zelotes: KJV spelling of “Zealot,” the surname of Simon, one of the 12, in Luke 6:15 and Acts 1:13.
zelzah: Place near Rachel’s tomb where Saul met two men in fulfillment of Samuel’s prophecy concerning the events that would confirm Saul’s anointing.
zemaraim: 1. Town near the northern border of the territory of Benjamin.
zemarites: One of the families of the Canaanites in the ethnological lists of Genesis 10 (v 18) and 1 Chronicles 1 (v 16). The Zemarites were a Hamitic tribe mentioned in connection with the Arvadites and the Hamathites.
zemirah: Beker’s firstborn son, from Benjamin’s tribe.
zenan: One of the cities of the Shephelah inherited by Judah.
zenas: Lawyer whom Paul requested Titus to help with his travels in Crete.
zephaniah (person): 1. Priest during the reign of Zedekiah who was executed at Riblah by the king of Babylon.
zephaniah, book of: One of the books of the Minor Prophets in the OT.
zephath: Canaanite city conquered by Judah and Simeon and subsequently renamed Hormah.
zephathah: Valley where Asa defeated Zerah the Ethiopian. The valley of Zephathah is located in the vicinity of Mareshah and thus in southwestern Judah.
zepho: Eliphaz’s son and a descendant of Esau.
zephon: Firstborn son of Gad and the father of the Zephonite family.
zer: One of the fortified cities of Naphtali’s tribe. From the surrounding names in the list, it may be inferred that it was located on the southwest side of the Sea of Galilee.
zerah: 1. One of the chiefs of the Edomites, listed as the son of Reuel, Esau’s son by his wife Basemath, and likely the ancestor of Jobab, who later assumed the position of king of the Edomites.
zerahiah: 1. Uzzi’s son and ancestor of Ezra from the priestly line of Eleazar.
zered: Valley and brook by which the Israelites encamped, listed between Iye-abarim and a stopping place near the Arnon River to the north.
zereda: KJV spelling of Zeredah in 1 Kings 11:26.
zeredah: 1. Birthplace (or hometown) of Jeroboam, Israel’s first king during the period of the divided kingdom.
zeredathah: KJV rendering of Zeredah in 2 Chronicles 4:17.
zererah: City mentioned in connection with Gideon’s defeat of the Midianites; perhaps also identifiable with Zarethan.
zeresh: Wife of Haman the Agagite who advised him to build the gallows for hanging Mordecai.
zereth: Asshur’s son by his wife Helah from Judah’s tribe.
zereth-shahar: One of the cities inherited by Reuben’s tribe, described as being on “the hill of the valley.”
zeri: One of the sons of Jeduthun who prophesied with the lyre in thanksgiving to the Lord. He may be the same person as Izri (v 11).
zeror: Benjaminite, Becorath’s son, the father of Abiel, and an ancestor of King Saul.
zeruah: Mother of Israel’s King Jeroboam I.
zerubbabel: Babylonian-born Jew who returned to Palestine in 538 BC to serve as governor of Jerusalem under Persian rule. The name presumably means “seed [offspring] of Babylon,” referring to someone born in Babylon.
zeruiah: Nahash’s daughter and the sister of Abigail. Zeruiah eventually bore three sons: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel, all of whom were David’s friends during his reign.
zetham: One of Ladan’s descendants, a Gershonite, in charge of the temple treasuries.
zethar: One of King Ahasuerus’s seven chamberlains, who was commanded to bring Queen Vashti before the king for public display of her beauty.
zeus: Chief god of the Greek pantheon (Roman Jupiter). Zeus was initially worshiped as part of an animistic cult, as the sky god with thunder as his principal manifestation.
zia: One of the clan leaders of Gad’s tribe dwelling in Bashan.
ziba: Former servant of Saul whom David commissioned to find survivors of the house of Saul so that he might “show them kindness”. In the period following Saul’s death, Ziba apparently had not only gained his freedom but had also become a successful landowner.
zibeon: Ancestor of Oholibamah, the Canaanite wife of Esau. He is listed as a Hivite in Genesis 36:2 but is probably the same as Zibeon the son of Seir the Horite.
zibia: One of the seven sons borne to Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh.
zibiah: Mother of King Jehoash of Judah, from the town of Beersheba.
zichri, zicri: 1. Kohathite Levite and a descendant of Izhar.
ziddim: Fortified city in the land assigned to Naphtali’s tribe.
zidkijah: KJV form of Zedekiah, a priest in Nehemiah 10:1.
zidon, zidonian: KJV forms of Sidon and Sidonian, a city and its inhabitants in Asher’s territory.
zif: KJV form of Ziv, the name of the Hebrew month, corresponding to about mid-April to mid-May.
ziggurat: Term meaning “temple tower”; a ziggurat was similar in profile to the step pyramid of Egypt and was used for worship. They were frequent in the major cities of Mesopotamia.
ziha: 1. Ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile.
ziklag: Philistine city ruled by David for 16 months before he moved to Hebron to become the king of Judah. Ziklag was deeded to David by Achish of Gath, presumably to ensure David’s continued neutrality.
zillah: Second wife of Lamech and mother of Tubal-cain and Naamah.
zillethai: 1. One of Shimei’s sons from Benjamin’s tribe.
zilpah: Mother of Jacob’s sons Gad and Asher. Laban had given her to his daughter Leah as a handmaid.
zilthai: KJV spelling of Zillethai in 1 Chronicles 8:20 and 12:20.
zimmah: Gershonite Levite and ancestor of Joah; possibly the same Joah who assisted Hezekiah.
zimran: One of the sons of Abraham by Keturah. Unlike the other sons of Abraham by Keturah, there is little evidence that Zimran is associated with a later tribal group.
zimri (person): 1. Clan chief of Simeon’s tribe who was killed by Phinehas for consorting with a Midianite woman at Peor.
zimri (place): Place and peoples of the East, listed along with Elam and Media, against whom God’s wrath would fall. Zimri’s location and history are unknown; some identify its progenitor with Zimran, Abraham and Keturah’s son.
zin, wilderness of: Area lying in the northern portion of the Sinai Peninsula, while the wilderness of Sin lies in the southern portion.
zina: Alternate form of Ziza, Shimei’s son, in 1 Chronicles 23:10.
zinc: A “mineral” is a naturally occurring substance, normally an ore that must be mined and treated before the metal can be extracted. A “metal” is a chemical element such as iron or copper, which is free from contamination by other materials.
zion: The Jebusite fortress in Jerusalem conquered by David. Thereafter, Zion was used by biblical writers to identify other areas of Jerusalem and was used as a designation of the entire city.
zion, daughter of: Term used primarily in prophetic literature to designate the inhabitants of Jerusalem (Zion) and its surrounding regions. The term was further applied to those in Babylon who had been exiled from Jerusalem and the Judean countryside.
zior: One of the cities of the hill country allotted to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance. Since it is associated with Hebron in the text, Zior is likely identified with modern Sa’ir, the traditional location for Esau’s tomb.
ziph (person): 1. Descendant of Caleb from Judah’s tribe.
ziph (place): 1. One of the cities in the extreme south assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance.
ziphah: Jehallelel’s second son (or possibly daughter, since the form is feminine), listed in 1 Chronicles 4:16.
ziphims: KJV rendering of Ziphites, the inhabitants of Ziph, in the title of Psalm 54.
ziphite: Inhabitant of Ziph (1 Sm 23:19; 26:1; Ps 54 title).
ziphron: Geographical landmark defining the northern boundary of the Canaanite land to be possessed by Israel.
zippor: Father of the Moabite king Balak. Balak called on Balaam to curse Israel.
zipporah: Wife of Moses and mother of his sons Gershom and Eliezer. Though she is listed as the daughter of Reuel (v 18), Reuel was probably the father of Hobab (Nm 10:29; also called Jethro, Ex 3:1; 4:18), who in turn was the father of Zipporah.
zither: Stringed, wind, and percussion instruments used to make music.
zithri: KJV spelling of Sithri, Uzziel’s son, in Exodus 6:22.
ziv: Name of the Hebrew month corresponding to about mid-April to mid-May.
ziz, ascent of: Mountain pass going up from the Dead Sea to the Judean highlands. This ascent was the route used by the Ammonites and the Moabites prior to their defeat by Jehoshaphat as prophesied by Jehaziel.
ziza: 1. Chief of Simeon’s tribe descending from Shemaiah.
zoan: One of the principal cities in the delta region of ancient Egypt.
zoar: One of the “cities of the plain” confederate with Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim.
zobah: Aramean nation suffering military defeat from Israel during the early kingdom period. King Saul defeated the kings of Zobah.
zobebah: One of the sons of Koz (or possibly a daughter, since the noun is feminine) from Judah’s tribe. The genealogy is obscure.
zodiac: Pseudoscience dealing with the supposed influence of the heavenly bodies on human character and destiny.
zoheleth, stone of: Alternate rendering for “Serpent’s Stone” in 1 Kings 1:9.
zophai: Alternate form of Zuph, one of Samuel’s ancestors, in 1 Chronicles 6:26.
zophar: One of the “counselors” of Job who is listed as a Naamathite. He offers the most direct accusations against Job but later offers sacrifice for Job as commanded by the Lord (42:9).
zophim: Place from which Balaam pronounced his second blessing upon Israel. Zophim must have been on or near Mt Pisgah.
zorah, zorathite: A city of the Shephelah and its people, attributed to both the tribe of Dan and of Judah. It was part of Judah’s original allocation but was settled by Danites until they established their own territory near Laish.
zorites: Descendants of Salma from Judah’s tribe. They possibly represent half of the Manahathite clan.
zorobabel: KJV form of Zerubbabel, Jerusalem’s governor after the exile, in Matthew 1:12-13 and Luke 3:27.
zuar: Father of Nethanel, the leader of Issachar’s tribe at the start of Israel’s wilderness wanderings.
zuph (person): Ancestor of Elkanah, the father of the prophet Samuel. Zuph was a member of the Kohathite branch of Levites and is listed as the son of Elkanah (different than above) and the father of Toah.
zuph (place): Place where Saul looked for his father’s donkeys prior to his meeting with Samuel. It was near the tomb of Rachel, which is traditionally placed near the northern border of Benjamin.
zur: 1. Midianite prince who was the father of Cozbi, the Midianite woman who was killed by Phinehas for consorting with Zimri after the incident at Baal-peor.
zuriel: Son of Abihail and the head of the Merari family of Levites during the wilderness wanderings.
zurishaddai: Father of Shelumiel, the leader of Simeon’s tribe at the start of Israel’s wilderness wanderings.
zuzim, zuzites: One of the kingdoms attacked and defeated by Kedorlaomer’s confederation, mentioned as residents of Ham. They were likely located somewhere north of the Arnon River, since the general path of Kedorlaomer was from north to south along the King’s Highway.
abdon: 1. Hillel’s son who judged Israel for eight years.
abel: Second male child of Adam and Eve. The name is probably related to Sumerian and Akkadian words meaning “son” and was thus used as a generic term for the human race.
abel-beth-maacah: Alternate name for Abel, a fortified city in upper Galilee in 1 Kings 15:20 and 2 Kings 15:29. It was also called Abel of Beth-Maacah (Maachah) in 2 Sm 20:14-15.
adam: First man and father of the human race. Adam’s role in biblical history is important not only in OT considerations but also in understanding the meaning of salvation and the person and work of Jesus Christ.
adar: Babylonian name for a Hebrew month.
addar: Alternate name for Ard, one of Benjamin’s descendants, in 1 Chronicles 8:3.
alexander jannaeus: Jewish ruler of the Hasmonean dynasty.
amon: 1. Governor of the city of Samaria during the reign of Ahab in Israel.
amos: Hebrew prophet of the eighth century BC. Nothing is known about Amos apart from the book that bears his name.
ananiah: Azariah’s grandfather. Azariah was one of three men who repaired the Jerusalem wall near their homes after the exile.
aner: Amorite ally of Abram and brother of Mamre and Eshcol. With his brothers, Aner helped Abram defeat a confederation of four kings who had plundered Sodom and Gomorrah and had captured Abram’s nephew Lot.
aram-maacah: Alternate name for Maacah in 1 Chronicles 19:6.
argob: Individual supposedly killed with King Pekahiah of Israel in Pekah’s revolt. The early church father Jerome thought the name Argob (along with Arieh) referred to a place.
ariel: 1. Person or thing overcome in a heroic deed by Benaiah, chief of David’s bodyguard.
asher: Jacob’s son born to Leah’s maid Zilpah. The name Asher, probably meaning “happy,” was given to the child by Leah in her delight at his birth.
avvim: 1. Ancient people who lived in villages near Gaza before they were largely destroyed by a Philistine invasion.
azmaveth: 1. Warrior among David’s mighty men who were known as “the thirty.” Bahurim was his hometown.
baal: Name of the most prominent Canaanite deity. As the god of fertility in the Canaanite pantheon (roster of gods), Baal’s sphere of influence included agriculture, animal husbandry, and human sexuality.
